Getting there: End of the Akrotiri road, about 30 min from Fira. Parking is scarce, so park 1–2 min before and walk. Strong winds; wear good shoes.
Hours: Open access

name: Tomato Industrial Museum, D. Nomikos
description: Restored 1945 tomato-paste factory telling the story of Santorini's pre-tourism economy, with an audio guide, tastings and a souvenir can you seal yourself.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ticket at the door (about €12)
Getting there: Vlychada beach, south coast, about 25 min from Fira; free parking nearby.
Hours: Tue–Sun 10:00–18:00; closed Mon

name: Vlychada Beach
description: Long, quiet black-sand beach backed by wind-carved, honeycomb-like pumice cliffs, next to the marina. Parking is easy and there is a beach café.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: South coast near Vlychada marina, about 25 min from Fira.
Hours: Open access

name: Kamari Beach
description: Lively black-pebble beach under the cliff of Mesa Vouno, lined with a promenade of tavernas and bars, with planes landing nearby. Water shoes help on the hot pebbles.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in; loungers usually rented or tied to a food minimum
Getting there: East coast, about 15 min by bus or taxi from Fira. Water taxis link it to Perissa.
Hours: Open access

name: Perissa Beach
description: Long black-sand beach under the Mesa Vouno headland, joined to Perivolos and Agios Georgios by about 3 km of shoreline, with beach bars, watersports and free spots.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: Southeast coast, about 20 min from Fira.
Hours: Open access

name: Perivolos
description: Continuation of Perissa with dark volcanic sand, comfortable beach-club loungers (often free with food or drinks) and clear water.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: South of Perissa, about 20–25 min from Fira.
Hours: Open access

name: Ancient Thera
description: Ruins of the Hellenistic and Roman city strung along the Mesa Vouno ridge 360 m above Kamari and Perissa, with temples, theatre and agora and stunning views both ways. There is little shade or signage and no restrooms.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ticket on site
Getting there: Narrow hairpin road from Kamari (experienced drivers only; tour shuttles available), or a roughly 45 min hike up from Perissa in proper shoes. A half-day commitment.
Hours: Thu–Tue 8:30–15:00; closed Wed

name: Diocletian's Palace
description: The vast retirement palace of Roman Emperor Diocletian (c. AD 305), today a living UNESCO-listed old town where some 3,000 people live among Roman walls, medieval lanes, cafés, and shops. It is the heart of any Split visit, especially early morning or at dusk.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free); individual monuments ticketed
Getting there: Directly behind the Riva; about a 5–10 minute walk from the cruise and ferry port. Enter by the Bronze Gate from the Riva.
Hours: Open 24 hours (public streets)

name: Saint Domnius' Cathedral
description: Originally Diocletian's own mausoleum, now one of the oldest cathedrals in continuous use in the world, with a domed interior, carved wooden doors, and a treasury. Combo tickets also cover the bell tower, crypt, and baptistery.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Tickets at the office opposite the bell tower (several combo options)
Getting there: On the Peristyle, center of the palace.
Hours: Mon–Sat 8:00–20:00; closed Sunday to tourists (seasonal)

name: Saint Domnius Bell Tower
description: The 57 m Romanesque-Gothic campanile that defines Split's skyline, with a 360° view over palace roofs, the harbor, Marjan, and the islands. The climb is narrow and steep, with see-through metal stairs at the top.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ticket at the cathedral ticket office (included in some combos)
Getting there: On the Peristyle beside the cathedral.
Hours: Mon–Sat 8:15–15:30; Sun 13:00–17:30 (seasonal)

name: Vestibul
description: The circular, open-domed entrance hall to Diocletian's private quarters, famous for acoustics where klapa a cappella singers often perform. Look up through the oculus to the sky.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: Just south of the Peristyle. For an aerial view, use the small paid stairway to the left of the museum ahead (about €2).
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Diocletian's Cellars
description: The remarkably intact Roman substructures beneath the palace, mirroring the vanished imperial apartments above and used as a Game of Thrones filming location. The central hall is a free souvenir passage, while the side halls are ticketed.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ticket at the entrance for the side halls
Getting there: Enter from the Riva through the Bronze Gate.
Hours: Daily 8:30–20:00 (seasonal)

name: Split Golden Gate
description: The palace's grand north gate, the emperor's ceremonial entrance, flanked by arcaded niches. It is beautiful in evening light.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: North side of the palace on Dioklecijanova, beside the Gregory of Nin statue.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Eastern (Silver) Gate
description: The palace's east gate, linking the main Roman street to the Green Market, restored after WWII bombing.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: East wall of the palace, beside the Green Market.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Iron Gate
description: The best-preserved palace gate and the only one in continuous use for 17 centuries, beneath a medieval clock tower with a 24-hour dial. It opens onto People's Square.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: West side of the palace, leading to Pjaca.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Gregory of Nin Statue
description: Ivan Meštrović's towering bronze of the 10th-century bishop who championed Croatian-language liturgy. Rubbing his gleaming big toe is said to bring luck; it is lit at night.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: Outside the Golden Gate.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: People's Square (Pjaca)
description: Split's medieval civic square just outside the Iron Gate, lined with the Gothic Old Town Hall, Venetian palaces, and cafés. It is lively day and night.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: West of the palace through the Iron Gate.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Radić Brothers Square (Fruit Square)
description: A charming square with Meštrović's statue of poet Marko Marulić, a Venetian tower, and the Baroque Milesi Palace. A pleasant café stop one minute from the Riva, sometimes with free concerts.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: Just west of the palace, off the Riva.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Republic Square (Prokurative)
description: A grand 19th-century neo-Renaissance square framed on three sides by arcades and open to the harbor, home to cafés and summer concerts.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: West end of the Riva.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Split City Museum
description: A museum in the Gothic Papalić Palace tracing Split from Roman times, with archaeology, medieval sculpture, Diocletian coins, and multimedia on the cathedral doors. Compact, at about 30–60 minutes.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ticket at the door
Getting there: Papalićeva 1, inside the palace near the Golden Gate.
Hours: Tue–Sun 9:00–20:00; closed Monday (seasonal)

name: Split Ethnographic Museum
description: Traditional Dalmatian costumes, jewelry, and weapons displayed in palace-era rooms, with access to the remains of St. Andrew's church. Climb to the top terrace for a bird's-eye view of the Peristyle.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ticket at the door
Getting there: Iza Vestibula 4, by the Vestibule.
Hours: Mon–Fri 9:00–17:00; Sat 10:00–14:00; closed Sunday

name: Split Synagogue
description: One of Europe's oldest functioning synagogues (16th century), tucked into the palace's west wall on Židovski prolaz (Jewish Lane).
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (donation)
Getting there: Židovski prolaz 1, off People's Square.
Hours: Mon–Fri 10:00–14:00; closed Saturday–Sunday

name: Green Market
description: Split's open-air 'Pazar' outside the Silver Gate, with figs, cherries, olive oil, lavender, honey, and souvenirs from local growers. Go in the morning.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: Stari pazar, outside the palace's east wall; about a 5-minute walk from the port.
Hours: Daily 6:00–14:00

name: Fishmarket (Peskarija)
description: The bustling 19th-century fish market under an iron canopy, famously fly-free thanks to nearby sulfur springs. Fishermen sell the morning Adriatic catch; watch the scales when buying.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: Obrov 5, two blocks west of People's Square.
Hours: Mon–Fri, Sun 6:00–13:00; Sat 7:00–13:00

name: Croatian National Theater in Split
description: An elegant 1893 theatre staging affordable opera, ballet, and drama, and the hub of the Split Summer Festival. Smart-casual dress is advised.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Box office or hnk-split.hr
Getting there: Trg Gaje Bulata 1, about 5 minutes north of the palace.
Hours: Box office Mon–Fri 9:00–21:00

name: Archaeological Museum in Split
description: Croatia's oldest museum (1820), with Roman and early Christian finds from Salona and a large garden lapidarium of sarcophagi and inscriptions. A combo ticket with Salona is good value; some labels are Croatian only.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ticket at the door (combo with Salona available)
Getting there: Zrinsko-Frankopanska 25, about a 15-minute walk north of the palace.
Hours: Mon–Fri 9:00–14:00 and 15:00–20:00; Sat 9:00–14:00; closed Sunday

name: Marjan Hill Stairs
description: The main stepped trailhead into Marjan Forest Park, climbing from the Varoš quarter past viewpoints, friendly cats, and the Vidilica café. It is the gateway to all Marjan walks.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: Start at the top of Marasovića St in Varoš, about 10 minutes from the Riva. Bring water and a hat.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Marjan viewpoint (Vidilica)
description: The classic first Marjan lookout, about 250 steps up, with a postcard view over the palace roofs, the harbor, and the islands beyond. There is a café-restaurant next to the old Jewish cemetery.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: About a 15–20 minute climb from Varoš via the Marjan stairs.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Old Jewish cemetery
description: A shaded 16th-century Jewish cemetery on Marjan's slope, one of Europe's oldest, with weathered headstones and a poignant history.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: Next to the Vidilica café; entrance just right of the restaurant.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Church of St. Nicholas
description: A tiny 13th-century Romanesque church (1219) in the pines just above Vidilica, with a cold-water fountain beside it. It is usually closed but is a lovely rest stop.
mapQuery: Church of St Nicholas Marjan Split
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: A few minutes uphill from the Vidilica viewpoint.

name: Telegrin Peak
description: Marjan's 178 m summit, crowned by a stone cross, with 360° views over Split, the mountains, and the islands. A rewarding 30–50 minute climb, or ride the seasonal tourist train.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: Follow the stairs and paths past Vidilica and St. Nicholas. Wear proper shoes.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Vidikovac (Marjan Observation Tower)
description: A new glass-and-steel observation tower in western Marjan with free lift or stairs, free telescopes, and toilets. Sweeping views over Kaštela Bay, the airport approaches, and the islands.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free; limited numbers at the top)
Getting there: Marangunićevo šetalište, western Marjan; walk or cycle the park road.
Hours: Daily 9:00–20:00

name: Meštrović Gallery
description: Sculptor Ivan Meštrović's grand seaside villa, filled with his powerful marble and bronze works and set in sculpture gardens with sea views. The ticket includes the nearby Kaštilac chapel.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ticket at the door
Getting there: Šetalište Ivana Meštrovića 46, about 25 minutes on foot west of the Riva along the coast, or a short taxi ride.
Hours: Tue–Sun 8:00–18:00; closed Monday (seasonal)

name: Meštrovićeve Crikvine - Kaštilac
description: A 16th-century fortified summer house whose chapel holds Meštrović's 28 carved wooden panels of the life of Christ, set in an olive grove with a sea-view terrace.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Included in the Meštrović Gallery ticket
Getting there: Šetalište Ivana Meštrovića 39, a 200 m walk west of the gallery.
Hours: Tue–Sun 8:00–18:00; closed Monday

name: Sustipan
description: A peaceful clifftop park on a former monastery and cemetery site, with a gazebo, pines, and lovely views back over the harbor and the Riva. A tourist-free sunset spot.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: Sustipanski put, a 15-minute walk southwest of the Riva past the ACI marina.
Hours: Daily 6:00–23:00

name: Kasjuni Beach
description: A scenic pebble cove on Marjan's south side, with clear water and limestone cliffs, beloved by locals. There are no facilities, so bring water, food, and something to lie on.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: Bus 12 from the Riva area to the end of the line, or a taxi. Parking is very limited.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Bene Beach
description: A pine-shaded pebble beach on Marjan's north tip, with crystal water, showers, changing rooms, and a bar. Reached only on foot or by bike through the forest park.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free; sunbeds for hire)
Getting there: The park road is closed to cars: park at the Marjan entrance or take bus 12, then walk about 20–25 minutes. Water shoes help.

name: Poljud Stadium
description: The clamshell-roofed 1979 home of Hajduk Split, famed for its fervent Torcida fans. Match days are electric, and stadium museum tours run on other days.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Match tickets via hajduk.hr; tours by appointment
Getting there: 8 Mediteranskih igara 2, north side of Marjan; about 25 minutes on foot or a short taxi from the old town.

name: Bačvice City Beach
description: Split's famous sandy city beach, home of picigin (the local ball game), with shallow water ideal for kids and a lively bar scene. Busy and urban; sand quality draws mixed reviews.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free; sunbeds for hire)
Getting there: About a 10-minute walk east of the port and bus station.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Ovčice Beach
description: A quieter cove just east of Bačvice, with a small sandy-pebble beach, a diving board, and concrete sunbathing areas. Watch for sea urchins, so wear water shoes.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: Šetalište Petra Preradovića, a 5-minute walk east of Bačvice.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Firule Beach
description: A small, shallow sandy beach popular with locals for picigin, with a jumping pier, close to the center.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: About a 15-minute walk east of the port via the Bačvice promenade.

name: Žnjan City Beach
description: Split's long, newly renovated beach with solar-roof shade pavilions, a diving platform, volleyball courts, a cycle path, and cafés. It is uncrowded even in summer.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: About 4 km east of the center by bus or taxi. Garage parking behind the beach (about €1/hour).
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Salona Archaeological Site
description: The sprawling ruins of Roman Salona, capital of Dalmatia and Diocletian's birthplace, with an amphitheatre, basilicas, sarcophagi, and city walls in a quiet rural setting. QR codes show 3D reconstructions.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ticket at the main entrance (combo with Split's Archaeological Museum)
Getting there: Solin, about 6 km north of Split; bus 1 to the main entrance (20–30 minutes). Allow 2 hours plus travel, a half-day outing. There is little shade, so bring water.
Hours: Daily 9:00–18:00 (seasonal)

name: Izvor Jadra (Jadro Spring)
description: The crystal-clear source of the Jadro river that fed Diocletian's aqueduct, now a landscaped nature park with picnic and barbecue areas, a café, and a playground.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: Mravince, above Solin; about 20 minutes by car from Split. A half-day outing combined with Salona or Klis.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Klis Fortress
description: A dramatic clifftop fortress guarding the pass above Split, with 2,000 years of history from Illyrian stronghold to Ottoman bastion, and Meereen in Game of Thrones. Superb views over Split and the islands.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ticket at the gate
Getting there: Klis, about 12 km northeast of Split; about 25 minutes by car or bus 22/34/35/36. The small car park fills, so use the overflow lot below the village and walk the steep cobbled lane. A half-day outing.
Hours: Daily 9:00–19:00 (seasonal)

name: Kaštilac (Kaštel Gomilica)
description: A picturesque 16th-century sea castle built by Benedictine nuns on an islet linked by a bridge, used as Braavos in Game of Thrones. Free to wander, with a few residents still living inside.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: Kaštel Gomilica, about 20 minutes by car or bus west of Split. Paid marina parking is about 10 minutes away. A half-day outing with the other Kaštela castles.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Kaštela City Museum (Vitturi Castle)
description: A 16th-century seaside castle in Kaštel Lukšić housing the Kaštela museum, with a virtual-reality tour and the tale of Miljenko and Dobrila, Kaštela's Romeo and Juliet.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ticket at the door
Getting there: Brce 1, Kaštel Lukšić, about 25 minutes west of Split. A half-day outing.
Hours: Mon–Fri 9:00–20:00; Sat 9:00–13:00; closed Sunday

name: Kaštel Rušinac (Miljenko's Castle)
description: The small castle of Miljenko from Kaštela's tragic love story, with a medieval garden that hosts summer tastings and concerts. Reached along the seafront promenade linking the seven castles.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in; events via the Mastrinka society
Getting there: Šetalište Miljenka i Dobrile, Kaštel Lukšić; a short walk from Vitturi Castle. A half-day outing.

name: Trogir Old Town
description: A UNESCO-listed medieval island town of Romanesque and Renaissance lanes, palaces, and a palm-lined riva. It is often called 'Little Venice' and is calmer than Split.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: About 27 km west of Split; 30–50 minutes by bus 37 or the summer boat from the Riva. Go early, before tour groups. A half-day outing.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: North Old Town Gate (Land Gate)
description: Trogir's 17th-century Baroque Land Gate, topped by a statue of patron saint John of Trogir and leading straight into the old town.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: Trogir, at the bridge from the mainland. A half-day outing from Split.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: St. Lawrence's Cathedral
description: Trogir's masterpiece cathedral (begun 1213), famed for Master Radovan's carved Romanesque portal and the Renaissance chapel of St. John. The bell-tower climb gives grand views.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ticket required (cathedral and tower); shoulders must be covered
Getting there: Trg Ivana Pavla II, Trogir. Buy tickets at the office across the square. A half-day outing from Split.
Hours: Daily 8:00–16:00 (seasonal)

name: City Loggia Trogir
description: The 15th-century Venetian loggia on Trogir's main square, once its courthouse, with a Meštrović relief inside.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: Trg Ivana Pavla II, opposite the cathedral. A half-day outing from Split.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: South Gate (Sea Gate)
description: Trogir's iron-studded Renaissance Sea Gate (1537) on the waterfront promenade, set in a stretch of 13th-century walls.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: Obala bana Berislavića, Trogir. A half-day outing from Split.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Kamerlengo Castle
description: A 15th-century Venetian fortress on Trogir's western tip, with ramparts and a tower overlooking the marina and Čiovo. The courtyard hosts summer concerts and film nights.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ticket at the gate
Getting there: Obala bana Berislavića, Trogir. A half-day outing from Split.
Hours: Daily 9:00–22:00 (seasonal)

name: Španjola Fortress (Hvar Fortica)
description: A 16th-century hilltop fortress above Hvar Town, reached by a shaded garden path, with dungeons and a café. The views over the harbor and Pakleni Islands are stunning at sunset.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ticket at the gate
Getting there: Hvar Town, about a 15–20 minute walk up from the square. Hvar is about 1 hour by catamaran from Split; plan a full day and check return sailings against all-aboard time.
Hours: Daily 9:00–20:00 (seasonal)

name: St. Stephen's Square (Pjaca)
description: Dalmatia's largest square, stretching from Hvar's harbor to the Renaissance cathedral and lined with cafés and Venetian façades.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: Hvar Town center, about 1 hour by catamaran from Split. A full-day trip.
Hours: Open 24 hours

name: Saint Stephen's Cathedral
description: Hvar's Renaissance cathedral with a graceful bell tower and polychrome marble altars inside. Photography is not allowed and a small entry fee applies.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Small entry fee
Getting there: Head of St. Stephen's Square, Hvar Town. A full-day trip from Split.
Hours: Daily 9:00–12:30 and 16:30–19:30

name: Pakleni Islands
description: An archipelago of pine-covered islets off Hvar with turquoise coves for swimming and snorkeling, best by boat tour or water taxi.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Book boat tours or taxis in advance in summer
Getting there: Water taxis from Hvar Town harbor (10–20 minutes), or full-day speedboat tours from Split (50–60 minutes each way).

name: Golden Horn Beach (Zlatni Rat)
description: Croatia's iconic shape-shifting pebble spit on Brač, set against pine woods, with clear water and windsurfing afternoons. It is very crowded after 10:00 in summer.
mapQuery: Zlatni Rat Golden Horn Beach Bol
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free; paid showers and sunbeds)
Getting there: A 20-minute walk west of Bol town on Brač; Bol is reached by catamaran from Split (about 1 hour). Paid parking is about 5 minutes away. A full-day trip.

name: Vidova gora
description: The highest peak of the Adriatic islands (778 m), looking straight down on Zlatni Rat with Hvar and Vis beyond. Drive up through pine forest, or take the strenuous 3–4 hour hiking trail from Bol.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: Road access from the island interior, with a small free car park and a 5–10 minute walk. Hiking trail from Gornje Podbarje in Bol. A full-day trip from Split.

name: Blaca Hermitage
description: A 16th-century monastery built into a cliff on Brač, preserved as a museum with an observatory and library, seen on guided tours.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Guided tour at the site (cash reported)
Getting there: About a 2 km rocky hike (30–45 minutes) down from the road-end car park, or up from Blaca bay by boat. Bring water. A full-day trip from Split.
Hours: Tue–Sun 9:00–15:00; closed Monday

name: Line 1 metro is the pickpocket hotspot
description: The green Line 1 between Piraeus and Monastiraki/Omonia is where most visitors lose wallets and phones. Thieves work the crowded doors as the train boards. Keep bags zipped and in front, phones out of back pockets, and step back if someone crowds you at the doors.
mapQuery: Line 1 metro is the pickpocket hotspot Athens (Piraeus)

name: The Acropolis marble is slippery
description: Centuries of footsteps have polished the rock and marble paths on the Acropolis to a glassy finish, and falls are common, especially going down. Wear shoes with real grip rather than flat sandals, and take extra care on the steps near the Propylaea.
mapQuery: The Acropolis marble is slippery Athens (Piraeus)

name: Summer heat can close the Acropolis
description: In July and August, midday temperatures can reach the high 30s °C or more, and during official heatwaves the Acropolis has closed in the early afternoon. Go at opening time, carry water, and check for heatwave closures the day before; there is very little shade on the hill.
mapQuery: Summer heat can close the Acropolis Athens (Piraeus)

name: Piraeus port is bigger than it looks
description: Cruise terminals, ferry gates and the metro station can be a long walk apart in a busy port with heavy traffic, and ferry gates are numbered differently from cruise terminals. Use the port shuttle or a taxi to the metro, and allow plenty of time to get back for all-aboard.
mapQuery: Piraeus port is bigger than it looks Athens (Piraeus)

name: Taxi meters and fixed fares
description: Licensed Athens taxis are yellow and should use the meter, while airport transfers to the center run on set fares. Confirm the price or meter before setting off, and be wary of unofficial drivers soliciting at the port exits.
mapQuery: Taxi meters and fixed fares Athens (Piraeus)

name: Crossing streets and scooters
description: Drivers in Athens often don't stop at zebra crossings, and scooters weave through traffic and sometimes ride on pavements. Cross with the lights and look both ways even on one-way streets.

name: Strikes and demonstrations
description: Transport strikes are frequent in Greece and can halt the metro, trams or ferries for a day, usually with a day or two's notice. Demonstrations often gather at Syntagma Square; they are usually peaceful but best avoided. Check the news the day before you rely on public transport.

name: Wildfire season on the coast and hills
description: On high fire-risk days in summer, Greek authorities can close forests and trails, and fires have hit Attica's hills and coast in recent years. If you plan a hike or a drive to Sounion, check local fire-risk warnings and follow any evacuation messages sent to phones.
mapQuery: Wildfire season on the coast and hills Athens (Piraeus)

name: Cretan drivers use the hard shoulder
description: On the main national road (VOAK), slower drivers pull onto the shoulder to let traffic overtake, often down the middle. That means cars come straight at you in your lane on hills and bends. Drive defensively, expect overtakers, and watch for vehicles drifting onto the shoulder ahead.
mapQuery: Cretan drivers use the hard shoulder Chania

name: Rental insurance and the Balos road
description: Many rental agreements exclude damage to tires, undercarriage and cars driven on dirt roads. The long, rough track to Balos is a classic place to scrape a car. Read your policy before you go, or take a boat tour from Kissamos instead.
mapQuery: Rental insurance and the Balos road Chania

name: Samaria Gorge is a one-way commitment
description: Once you start the 13–16 km descent from Omalos, there is no road out except the ferry from Agia Roumeli, and the gorge closes in strong winds, heat or heavy rain because of rockfall risk. It cannot be done on a standard port day. Wear proper boots, carry water, and know the last ferry time before you set off.
mapQuery: Samaria Gorge is a one-way commitment Chania

name: Red flags and rough water on windy days
description: North-coast beaches like Platanias and Agia Marina, and exposed spots like Falasarna and Elafonissi, can get strong waves and currents when the wind is up. Obey red flags, which are common in midsummer, and choose sheltered coves on blustery days.
mapQuery: Red flags and rough water on windy days Chania

name: Steep scrambles to the famous coves
description: Seitan Limania and the Katholiko gorge path both involve steep, rocky descents with loose stones and a hard climb back in full sun. Sandals and flip-flops cause sprained ankles here; wear trainers and go early or late.
mapQuery: Steep scrambles to the famous coves Chania

name: Sea urchins on rocky beaches
description: Rocky entries at places like Seitan Limania, Marathi's edges and many small coves are carpeted with sea urchins, and their spines are painful and hard to remove. A cheap pair of water shoes solves the problem.
mapQuery: Sea urchins on rocky beaches Chania

name: Theft from cars at beaches and trailheads
description: Rental cars left at popular beaches and gorge car parks are occasional targets. Thieves know visitors leave bags in the boot. Take valuables with you or leave them at the hotel, and don't leave anything visible inside.
mapQuery: Theft from cars at beaches and trailheads Chania

name: Goats, rockfall and mountain roads
description: Mountain roads to Theriso, Omalos and the south coast are narrow and winding, with goats on the tarmac and occasional fallen rocks after rain. Drive slowly on blind bends, use your horn on tight hairpins, and allow more time than the map suggests.
mapQuery: Goats, rockfall and mountain roads Chania

name: Narrow roads and tour bus traffic
description: Corfu's roads are narrow, twisting and busy with tour buses, and scooter and quad accidents among visitors are common. If you rent, wear a helmet, avoid riding at night or after drinks, and take the hairpins to Paleokastritsa and Pelekas slowly.
mapQuery: Narrow roads and tour bus traffic Corfu

name: West-coast beaches have real waves
description: Glyfada, Agios Gordios and Myrtiotissa face open sea and can get surf and strong currents when the wind is up, unlike the calmer east coast. Swim near lifeguards where they exist and stay out on red-flag days.
mapQuery: West-coast beaches have real waves Corfu

name: Cliff jumping at Canal d'Amour
description: The sandstone cliffs at Sidari's Canal d'Amour attract jumpers, and injuries happen when people misjudge depth or hidden rocks. If you jump, check the landing zone first and never jump after drinking.
mapQuery: Cliff jumping at Canal d'Amour Corfu

name: Drink bottled water
description: Tap water in many parts of Corfu is brackish or not recommended for drinking, though it varies by area. Bottled water is cheap and widely available, so locals and most hotels advise using it.

name: Old Town crowds and pickpockets
description: Corfu Town's narrow lanes and the Liston promenade get very crowded when several ships are in, and pickpocketing can happen in the crush. Keep bags closed and in front, especially in the lanes around the main shopping streets.
mapQuery: Old Town crowds and pickpockets Corfu

name: Sun, sea urchins and wasps
description: Rocky coves on the north and east coasts have sea urchins, so water shoes are worthwhile. In late summer, wasps can bother outdoor diners, so cover sweet drinks.
mapQuery: Sun, sea urchins and wasps Corfu

name: The city walls in heat
description: The 2 km walk around the city walls is steep, one-way and almost entirely in full sun. Afternoon heat is brutal in summer. Go at opening time or late afternoon, carry water, and allow about two hours.
mapQuery: The city walls in heat Dubrovnik

name: Polished limestone is slippery
description: Stradun and the old town lanes are paved with limestone polished smooth by centuries of feet. When wet, even with light rain or cleaning, they become like ice. Wear shoes with grip and take the stepped side streets slowly.

name: Cliff jumping off the walls
description: At the cliff bars outside the walls, people jump into the sea from the rocks. Injuries happen when jumpers misjudge depth or swell. If you jump, check the water first and avoid it in rough sea or after drinking.
mapQuery: Cliff jumping off the walls Dubrovnik

name: Cable car and boats in high winds
description: The Mount Srđ cable car closes during strong bura winds, and Lokrum ferries and kayak tours can be cancelled. Have a backup plan for these, and note the last ferry back from Lokrum, as overnight stays on the island are not allowed.
mapQuery: Cable car and boats in high winds Dubrovnik

name: Ship-day crowds and pickpockets
description: When several cruise ships are in, the old town is shoulder-to-shoulder and pickpocketing increases around the Pile Gate and Stradun. Keep bags closed and in front, and consider visiting the walls before the crowds arrive.

name: Border queues to Montenegro
description: Day trips to Kotor cross the Croatia–Montenegro border, where summer queues can take one to several hours each way. Allow plenty of buffer before all-aboard, and carry your passport.

name: Heat at an exposed archaeological site
description: Ancient Olympia is spread across open ground, and summer afternoons regularly reach the high 30s °C. Shade under the pines is patchy and you will walk several kilometres. Go in the morning, carry water, and wear a hat and sunscreen.
mapQuery: Heat at an exposed archaeological site Katakolon

name: Know your way back to the ship
description: Katakolon is tiny, but Olympia is about 40 minutes away, and the train service between them has been irregular in some seasons. If you go independently, confirm the return schedule or a taxi pickup time, and leave a generous buffer before all-aboard.
mapQuery: Know your way back to the ship Katakolon

name: Agree taxi fares before you go
description: Taxis wait at the port for Olympia runs and many work on a set round-trip price with waiting time. Agree the fare, the waiting time and the return time clearly before leaving, so there are no surprises later.
mapQuery: Agree taxi fares before you go Katakolon

name: Rocky beaches and water shoes
description: Agios Andreas and nearby coves have rocky entries and pebbly bottoms, and the water can have waves when the wind blows from the west. Water shoes help, and children should be watched on the uneven rocks.
mapQuery: Rocky beaches and water shoes Katakolon

name: Mosquitoes around lakes and wetlands
description: Kaiafa Lake, the coastal pine forests and wetlands to the south and north have lots of mosquitoes, especially at dusk. Bring repellent if you go nature walking.
mapQuery: Mosquitoes around lakes and wetlands Katakolon

name: Wildfire risk in summer
description: The Ilia region has suffered major wildfires, including near Olympia in 2007 and 2021. On high-risk days, check local warnings, avoid forest walks, and never discard cigarettes or use open flames outdoors.

name: Fortress climb: no shade, no toilets
description: The climb to San Giovanni fortress is about 1,350 uneven stone steps in full sun, with loose sections and no toilets. Start early or late, carry water (vendors take cash only), and wear grippy shoes; heat exhaustion is common in summer.
mapQuery: Fortress climb: no shade, no toilets Kotor

name: The serpentine road to Lovćen
description: The P1 road up to Njeguši and Lovćen has 25 hairpin bends, single-lane stretches and tour buses that take the full width. Only confident drivers should attempt it. Go slowly, use your horn on blind bends, and pull into passing places.
mapQuery: The serpentine road to Lovćen Kotor

name: Aggressive local driving
description: Montenegrin drivers can overtake on blind bends and tailgate, and the bay road is narrow with few safe places to stop. Drive defensively and avoid the coast road at peak cruise times.

name: Thunderstorms in the mountains
description: Summer afternoons can bring sudden thunderstorms over Lovćen and the mountains above the bay, making steep paths slick. Check the forecast before hiking and get off exposed ridges if storms build.

name: Taxi pricing
description: Some taxis near the port and old town quote high flat fares to visitors. Agree the price before getting in, or use a taxi company with a meter.

name: Border crossings eat your day
description: Trips to Dubrovnik cross the Montenegro–Croatia border, where summer queues can take hours. Carry your passport and plan a generous buffer before all-aboard.
mapQuery: Border crossings eat your day Kotor

name: Stray cats are part of town
description: Kotor's famous street cats are generally friendly, but avoid handling them roughly, as scratches can get infected. Wash your hands after petting.
mapQuery: Stray cats are part of town Kotor

name: Scooter bag-snatching
description: Naples' best-known petty crime is the scippo, a bag or phone snatched from a moving scooter. Keep bags on the side away from traffic, don't hold your phone loosely at the curb, and keep a firm grip in crowded streets.

name: Circumvesuviana: pickpockets and delays
description: The Circumvesuviana train to Pompeii, Herculaneum and Sorrento is notorious for pickpockets in the crush and for delays and cancellations. Keep valuables secure, and leave a large buffer before all-aboard, or use a tour or private transfer on a port day.

name: Pompeii is big, hot and uneven
description: Pompeii covers a huge area of rutted Roman paving with little shade, and visitors routinely underestimate how long and tiring it is. Allow at least three hours, wear sturdy shoes, carry water, and use the site's fountains to refill.
mapQuery: Pompeii is big, hot and uneven Naples

name: Vesuvius trail and closures
description: The Gran Cono trail is short but steep, dusty and exposed, and it can close in high wind, fire risk or bad weather. Entry is timed and must be booked in advance; check status the day before and bring layers, as it can be cool and windy at the top.

name: Campi Flegrei ground movement
description: The Campi Flegrei area west of Naples is experiencing bradyseism, a slow uplift with swarms of small earthquakes, and some sites like the Solfatara crater have been closed. Follow civil-protection advice and check site status before visiting Pozzuoli.

name: Traffic, crossings and ZTL fines
description: Naples traffic is chaotic: scooters run lights and ride on pavements, so cross decisively but carefully. Driving into the historic center's limited-traffic zones (ZTL) triggers automatic camera fines, often charged to rental cars months later.
mapQuery: Traffic, crossings and ZTL fines Naples

name: Amalfi Coast road and parking
description: The SS163 Amalfi road is narrow, with tour buses meeting on blind bends and very little parking in Positano and Amalfi. Many visitors are happier on ferries or buses than driving; if you drive, go early and expect delays.
mapQuery: Amalfi Coast road and parking Naples

name: Use official taxis with fixed fares
description: Use licensed white taxis from official ranks, and ask for the set fare (tariffa predeterminata) for common routes such as the port to the station or airport. Avoid drivers who approach you inside the station.
mapQuery: Use official taxis with fixed fares Naples

name: The train from Civitavecchia sets the clock
description: Rome is roughly an hour or more by train from Civitavecchia, and Italian rail strikes or delays do happen. Check for strike notices (sciopero) before your port day, and plan to be on a train back with at least an hour to spare before all-aboard.
mapQuery: The train from Civitavecchia sets the clock Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: Pickpockets on Metro A and bus 64
description: Metro Line A between Termini and the Spanish Steps and the 64 bus to the Vatican are famous for pickpockets, who work in teams around the doors. Keep valuables in a front pocket or zipped cross-body bag, and be alert when crowds surge in.
mapQuery: Pickpockets on Metro A and bus 64 Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: Street scams near landmarks
description: Around the Colosseum, Trevi Fountain and Vatican, people may tie 'free' bracelets on your wrist, ask you to sign petitions, or offer photos in costume, then demand money. A firm 'no, grazie' and walking on is the best response.

name: Rules at the Spanish Steps and Trevi
description: Sitting on the Spanish Steps is banned, and wading into the Trevi Fountain or other fountains brings fines. Municipal police enforce these at busy times.
mapQuery: Rules at the Spanish Steps and Trevi Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: Vatican dress code and bag rules
description: St Peter's and the Vatican Museums require covered shoulders and knees and turn away visitors who don't comply. Large bags are restricted at security. Carry a light scarf, and arrive early or book timed entry to avoid long lines in the sun.
mapQuery: Vatican dress code and bag rules Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: Heat, cobblestones and free drinking water
description: Summer days in Rome often reach the mid-30s °C, and the sampietrini cobbles are uneven and slippery when wet. Wear supportive shoes, and refill bottles at the city's free nasoni fountains, which provide safe drinking water.
mapQuery: Heat, cobblestones and free drinking water Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: ZTL camera fines and official taxis
description: Driving into Rome's limited-traffic zones triggers automatic fines, so don't drive into the center. Use official white taxis from ranks, which have set fares on some routes such as the airports.
mapQuery: ZTL camera fines and official taxis Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: Quads and scooters cause the worst injuries
description: Rented ATVs and scooters are behind a large share of visitor injuries on Santorini. Roads are narrow, winding, busy with tour buses, and often lack shoulders, and many renters have little experience. If you rent one, wear a helmet, skip it after drinking, and give buses a wide berth on the cliff roads.
mapQuery: Quads and scooters cause the worst injuries Santorini

name: Cable car queues and tender timing
description: Cruise passengers land by tender at the old port below Fira, and the only ways back up and down are the cable car, the long stepped path or donkeys. Cable car lines can stretch for an hour or more on busy days. Head back down well before your last tender, as missing the ship here is a real risk.
mapQuery: Cable car queues and tender timing Santorini

name: The Fira steps and donkey traffic
description: The 500-plus zigzag steps between the old port and Fira are steep, uneven and slick with donkey dung, and you share them with animals that do not give way. Walk on the wall side, step aside when a train of donkeys passes, and wear proper shoes.
mapQuery: The Fira steps and donkey traffic Santorini

name: Caldera cliff edges have few railings
description: Many viewpoints and rooftop terraces along the caldera rim in Fira, Imerovigli and Oia have low walls or none at all, and people have fallen while stepping back for photos. Keep an eye on children and don't climb onto walls or domes for the shot.
mapQuery: Caldera cliff edges have few railings Santorini

name: Fira–Oia hike: no shade, no water
description: The caldera path from Fira to Oia is about 10 km of exposed ridge with stretches of loose volcanic gravel and almost no shade or water after Imerovigli. Start early, carry at least 1.5 litres per person, and wear a hat; in midday summer heat it is genuinely draining.
mapQuery: Fira–Oia hike: no shade, no water Santorini

name: Black sand burns and rockfall at Red Beach
description: Dark volcanic sand at Perissa, Kamari and Vlychada gets hot enough to burn bare feet by midday, so wear sandals right to the water. At Red Beach, authorities have warned of rockfall from the cliffs; respect any closure signs and don't sit under the cliff face.
mapQuery: Black sand burns and rockfall at Red Beach Santorini

name: Meltemi winds and boat cancellations
description: In July and August the meltemi wind can blow hard for days, making the sea rough and causing catamaran cruises and sometimes tenders to be cancelled or cut short. Build flexibility into boat plans, and take seasickness precautions on windy days.
mapQuery: Meltemi winds and boat cancellations Santorini

name: Drink bottled water and know earthquake basics
description: Tap water on Santorini is mostly desalinated and generally not recommended for drinking, so buy bottled. The island also sits on an active volcanic system and had a strong earthquake swarm in early 2025; follow any civil-protection alerts and avoid cliff paths if authorities advise.
mapQuery: Drink bottled water and know earthquake basics Santorini

name: Sunset crowds in Oia attract pickpockets
description: Thousands squeeze into Oia's lanes and castle viewpoint for sunset, and bag theft happens in the crush. Keep valuables in a front pocket or cross-body bag, and plan your bus or taxi back early, because demand at dusk is huge.
mapQuery: Sunset crowds in Oia attract pickpockets Santorini

name: Bura and jugo winds disrupt boats
description: The bura, a sudden, gusty northeasterly, can whip up the channels within an hour and cancel catamarans, speedboat tours and the Blue Cave trip. The southerly jugo brings rough seas too. Have a backup plan if island hopping, and be careful getting back for your ship if a boat is cancelled.
mapQuery: Bura and jugo winds disrupt boats Split

name: Public conduct fines in the old town
description: Split has introduced fines for public drunkenness, walking around the center in swimwear or shirtless, and drinking in some public areas, aimed at rowdy tourism. Cover up away from the beach and keep drinking to bars and terraces.
mapQuery: Public conduct fines in the old town Split

name: Crowds and pickpockets on the Riva
description: Diocletian's Palace and the Riva promenade are extremely crowded on ship days, and pickpockets work the narrow passages and squares. Keep bags zipped and phones secure, especially in the Peristyle.
mapQuery: Crowds and pickpockets on the Riva Split

name: Sea urchins and slippery rocks
description: Many swimming spots around Marjan and the rocky coves have sea urchins and slick algae-covered stone, so water shoes are worth buying. Bačvice's sandy shallows are easier for children.
mapQuery: Sea urchins and slippery rocks Split

name: Heat on Marjan's stairs
description: The steps up Marjan Hill from Varoš are steep and exposed in the afternoon sun. Carry water and go early or late if you want the view without heat exhaustion.

name: Swimming bans at Krka
description: Swimming at the famous Skradinski Buk falls in Krka National Park has been banned since 2021, despite older photos online. Tours still go there, so plan to admire the falls from the boardwalks, and allow a full day.

name: Piraeus has been Athens' port for 2,500 years
description: Your ship docks where the Athenian navy did. In the 5th century BC, Themistocles fortified Piraeus, and the Long Walls ran about 7 km inland to protect the road between the port and the city. Athens' power came from these harbors, which is why the Acropolis treasury could pay for the Parthenon.
mapQuery: Piraeus has been Athens' port for 2,500 years Athens (Piraeus)

name: Why the Parthenon is always under scaffolding
description: The Parthenon was built between 447 and 432 BC. It survived mostly intact as a temple, a church and then a mosque until 1687, when a Venetian shell hit the gunpowder the Ottoman garrison had stored inside. The cranes you see belong to a restoration that began in 1975, and experts are still fitting original marble back into place. It is a long-term reconstruction, not neglect.
mapQuery: Why the Parthenon is always under scaffolding Athens (Piraeus)

name: The gaps in the Acropolis Museum are deliberate
description: On the top floor of the Acropolis Museum, the Parthenon frieze is laid out at the temple's exact dimensions. Original marbles sit beside pale plaster casts, and each cast stands in for a piece Lord Elgin removed in the early 1800s that is now in the British Museum. The blanks are a quiet, permanent argument for reunification, and most Greeks feel strongly about it.
mapQuery: The gaps in the Acropolis Museum are deliberate Athens (Piraeus)

name: Modern Athens is surprisingly young
description: When Athens became capital of the new Greek state in 1834, it was a small town of a few thousand people beneath the ruins. Most of the grand neoclassical buildings, including the University, Academy and Library trio on Panepistimiou, went up afterward under Greece's Bavarian-born King Otto. The whitewashed lanes of Anafiotika below the Acropolis were built by stonemasons from the island of Anafi who came to work on those buildings.
mapQuery: Modern Athens is surprisingly young Athens (Piraeus)

name: Little churches below the pavement
description: Byzantine chapels such as Kapnikarea sit in the middle of Ermou Street and below street level. The city's ground level rose around them over centuries, so they appear to be sinking. Greece is overwhelmingly Greek Orthodox, and these are working churches. Step in quietly, cover shoulders and knees, and don't photograph people praying.
mapQuery: Little churches below the pavement Athens (Piraeus)

name: Reading the Evzones' uniform
description: The Presidential Guard wears a uniform descended from the dress of the mountain fighters of the 1821 War of Independence. Tradition says the fustanella kilt has 400 pleats, one for each year of Ottoman rule. The red tsarouchia shoes are nail-studded and famously heavy. Those slow, high-kicking steps are a ceremonial drill held hourly at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, and the full-company ceremony happens on Sundays at 11:00.

name: 28 October is a national holiday
description: 'Ohi Day' (No Day) commemorates Greece's refusal of Mussolini's ultimatum on 28 October 1940. Schools, the military and civic groups march in parades, flags hang everywhere, and many shops and some sites run reduced hours. If your call falls on or near that date, check opening times and expect closed streets. 25 March, Independence Day, works the same way.
mapQuery: 28 October is a national holiday Athens (Piraeus)

name: Rebetiko was born in Piraeus
description: After the 1922–23 population exchange with Turkey, more than a million Greek refugees from Asia Minor arrived, and many settled around Piraeus. Their music mixed with the port's underworld songs to create rebetiko, often called the Greek blues, played on bouzouki and baglamas. An evening in a music taverna where the room sings along is one of the most authentic things you can do here.
mapQuery: Rebetiko was born in Piraeus Athens (Piraeus)

name: Dinner is late, and meals are shared
description: Athenians rarely dine before 21:00, and tavernas fill around 22:00, so an early table means eating mostly among other visitors. Meze dishes go in the middle for everyone. Lingering for hours is normal, and you will usually have to ask for the bill.
mapQuery: Dinner is late, and meals are shared Athens (Piraeus)

name: A few gestures that mean something else
description: 'Ne' means yes, and a quick upward nod with raised eyebrows means no. Never push an open palm with fingers spread toward someone. That is the moutza, an old and serious insult, so wave with a cupped hand or a closed fist when signalling a taxi.
mapQuery: A few gestures that mean something else Athens (Piraeus)

name: You actually dock at Souda, not Chania
description: Cruise ships berth at Souda Bay, about 7 km from Chania's old town. Souda is also a Greek and NATO naval base, so photography restrictions apply around the military areas. Shuttle buses and taxis do the 15–20 minute run into town. The Commonwealth War Cemetery at Souda holds Allied soldiers from the 1941 Battle of Crete.
mapQuery: You actually dock at Souda, not Chania Chania

name: A harbour built by Venice and finished by Egypt
description: The Venetians ruled Chania from the 13th century until 1645 and built the arsenals, walls and harbour. The slender lighthouse at the harbour mouth, with its minaret-like profile, was rebuilt in the 1830s during the brief period when Crete was governed by Egypt. Read the waterfront as layers of Venetian, Ottoman and Egyptian work.
mapQuery: A harbour built by Venice and finished by Egypt Chania

name: Crete's first mosque
description: The domed Mosque of the Janissaries on the harbour was built after the Ottomans took Chania in 1645 and is considered the oldest Ottoman building on Crete. It is now an exhibition space. Minarets elsewhere in the old town, including in Splantzia, are reminders of 250 years of Ottoman rule that ended only in 1898.

name: Crete joined Greece late
description: After a string of uprisings, Crete became an autonomous state under Ottoman suzerainty in 1898 and joined Greece only in 1913. Chania was the island's capital until 1971. That fierce independence is central to Cretan identity, and locals often say they are Cretan first and Greek second.

name: The quiet story of the Jewish quarter
description: Chania had a Jewish community for over 2,000 years, centered on the Evraiki quarter and the Etz Hayyim synagogue. In 1944 the Germans deported them, and the ship Tanais, carrying almost the entire community, was sunk in the Aegean. The restored synagogue is a moving place to stop. Visitors are welcome, and it is respectful to check its opening times first.
mapQuery: The quiet story of the Jewish quarter Chania

name: Venizelos, Crete's statesman
description: Eleftherios Venizelos, the Cretan-born statesman who doubled Greece's territory in the early 20th century and was prime minister several times, is buried on the Akrotiri hill above town. The site has one of the best views over Chania. His name is on squares and streets everywhere.

name: Raki after dinner is hospitality, not a sales pitch
description: At the end of a meal, most Cretan tavernas bring a small carafe of tsikoudia (raki) and a sweet or fruit, free of charge. It is a gesture of hospitality, and accepting a sip and toasting 'yamas' is polite even if you don't finish it. Cretans also improvise rhyming couplets called mantinades to lyra music, which you may hear at a village feast.
mapQuery: Raki after dinner is hospitality, not a sales pitch Chania

name: Knives with poems
description: On the old 'Machairadika' knife street, a few craftsmen still make the traditional Cretan knife, often engraved with a mantinada verse on the blade. Leather Street (Skridlof) is the other surviving artisan lane. If you buy a blade, check your airline's rules before packing it.

name: The Greek island the Ottomans never took
description: Corfu resisted major Ottoman sieges in 1537 and 1716 and was never ruled by the Ottomans. Instead it was Venetian for about four centuries, then briefly French, then a British protectorate until it joined Greece in 1864. That is why the old town looks more Italian than Greek, and why its UNESCO listing praises its Venetian fortifications.
mapQuery: The Greek island the Ottomans never took Corfu

name: Cricket and ginger beer, courtesy of the British
description: The British left a cricket pitch in the middle of the Spianada, the town's great square, and matches are still played there. Locals also drink tsitsibira, a ginger beer made from a British-era recipe, and the island's kumquat liqueur came from a British-introduced fruit.
mapQuery: Cricket and ginger beer, courtesy of the British Corfu

name: The Liston was designed by the French
description: The arcaded Liston promenade facing the Spianada was built under Napoleonic French rule and modeled on Paris's Rue de Rivoli. Its name is said to come from the 'list' of noble families once allowed to stroll there. Today it is Corfu's living room for an evening coffee or aperitivo.
mapQuery: The Liston was designed by the French Corfu

name: Saint Spyridon is carried through the streets
description: The island's patron saint lies in a silver casket in the church with the red-domed bell tower in the old town, and Corfiots credit him with saving the island from plague and siege. Four times a year (Palm Sunday, Holy Saturday, 11 August and the first Sunday of November), his relics are paraded through town with brass bands. It is the most important day of the year for many locals.
mapQuery: Saint Spyridon is carried through the streets Corfu

name: Easter pots fly from balconies
description: On Holy Saturday morning, Corfiots hurl large clay pots filled with water from their balconies into the old town's streets, smashing them to celebrate the Resurrection and drive out bad luck. Corfu's Easter is famous throughout Greece. Expect huge crowds and brass bands playing through the town.
mapQuery: Easter pots fly from balconies Corfu

name: A town of brass bands
description: Under the Venetians and British, Corfu developed a strong musical tradition, and it still has more philharmonic bands than most of Greece. The oldest, the Philharmonic Society, dates to 1840. If you hear a band rehearsing in an old-town hall in the evening, it is a living tradition, not a tourist show.
mapQuery: A town of brass bands Corfu

name: Sissi's palace and a royal birthplace
description: The Achilleion was built for Empress Elisabeth ('Sissi') of Austria as a retreat after her son's death and was later owned by Kaiser Wilhelm II. Mon Repos villa in Corfu town is where Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, was born in 1921. Royal Europe passed through Corfu often.
mapQuery: Sissi's palace and a royal birthplace Corfu

name: The Durrells' Corfu
description: Gerald Durrell's memoir 'My Family and Other Animals' made 1930s Corfu famous, and his brother Lawrence wrote 'Prospero's Cell' about the island. The White House at Kalami on the north-east coast, Lawrence's home, is now a taverna, a pilgrimage spot for fans.

name: Venetian flavors on the table
description: Corfiot cooking differs from the rest of Greece. Try sofrito (veal in garlic-and-vinegar sauce), pastitsada (spiced beef or rooster with pasta) and bourdeto (fiery fish stew), all dishes with Venetian roots and Italian-sounding names. You will find them in old-town tavernas rather than on generic Greek menus.
mapQuery: Venetian flavors on the table Corfu

name: Dubrovnik was a country, not a town
description: For roughly four and a half centuries, until Napoleon ended it in 1808, Dubrovnik was the Republic of Ragusa, a merchant sea power rivaling Venice. It survived by diplomacy and by paying tribute to the Ottomans. Its motto, 'Libertas', is still on the city flag and carved over Fort Lovrijenac: 'Freedom is not sold for all the gold in the world.'
mapQuery: Dubrovnik was a country, not a town Dubrovnik

name: A ruler who served one month
description: To prevent any one man from seizing power, the Republic's rector served only a single month. During his term he could not leave the Rector's Palace without the council's permission. The palace is now the City Museum, and it is worth seeing with that story in mind.
mapQuery: A ruler who served one month Dubrovnik

name: Ahead of its time
description: Ragusa introduced one of the world's first systematic quarantines in 1377, and the Lazareti buildings east of Ploče Gate housed arriving traders. It abolished the slave trade in 1416. The pharmacy inside the Franciscan monastery has operated since 1317, among the oldest still working in Europe.

name: The roofs tell the story of 1991
description: During the 1991–92 siege by the Yugoslav People's Army, the Old Town was heavily shelled. A map near Pile Gate marks each hit. From the walls, the bright orange new tiles show where roofs were destroyed, and the faded older tiles are the survivors. Many residents remember the siege personally, so treat the subject with care.
mapQuery: The roofs tell the story of 1991 Dubrovnik

name: Why the Stradun looks so uniform
description: A catastrophic earthquake in 1667 killed thousands and destroyed much of the city. The main street, the Stradun, was rebuilt with matching Baroque house fronts and ground-floor shop doors, giving it that orderly, polished-limestone look.
mapQuery: Why the Stradun looks so uniform Dubrovnik

name: Orlando's arm was the official ruler
description: The knight Orlando's column in front of St. Blaise's Church is where public decrees were read and the Libertas flag still flies. The length of his forearm served as the Republic's standard unit of measure, the Ragusan ell, about 51 cm, so merchants measured cloth against it.
mapQuery: Orlando's arm was the official ruler Dubrovnik

name: St. Blaise holds the city in his hands
description: Look for small statues of Sveti Vlaho, the city's patron, on the gates and walls, holding a model of Dubrovnik. His feast on 3 February has been celebrated for over a thousand years, with processions, relics and flags, and it is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
mapQuery: St. Blaise holds the city in his hands Dubrovnik

name: Rules for a crowded UNESCO town
description: To manage overtourism, the city works with cruise lines to limit how many ships are in port at once. The Old Town also has rules against walking around in swimwear or shirtless, and offenders can be fined. Dressing as you would in a city, not on a beach, is both respectful and practical.
mapQuery: Rules for a crowded UNESCO town Dubrovnik

name: Game of Thrones, in perspective
description: Dubrovnik was the main filming location for King's Landing, and the Jesuit Stairs ('walk of shame') draw constant crowds. Many residents have mixed feelings about the series. The real story of the Ragusan Republic is richer, and a good local guide will gladly give you both.
mapQuery: Game of Thrones, in perspective Dubrovnik

name: Katakolon is the doorway to Olympia
description: Katakolon is a small fishing village whose role is to land visitors for Ancient Olympia, about 35 km and 40 minutes inland. This is where the Olympic Games were held from 776 BC until the late 4th century AD, when the Christian emperor Theodosius suppressed pagan festivals. Plan around the transfer: buses, taxis and tours run, but the local train has had long service interruptions, so check whether it is running before relying on it.
mapQuery: Katakolon is the doorway to Olympia Katakolon

name: The modern Olympic flame is lit here
description: Months before every Olympic Games, actresses dressed as priestesses light the torch at the ruined Temple of Hera in Olympia, using a parabolic mirror to focus the sun. When you stand by those Doric columns, you are at the starting point of every modern torch relay since 1936.
mapQuery: The modern Olympic flame is lit here Katakolon

name: A Wonder of the World once stood here
description: The great Temple of Zeus at Olympia housed Phidias' gold-and-ivory statue of the seated Zeus, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. Earthquakes toppled the temple, and its huge column drums still lie where they fell. Phidias' workshop was identified by a little cup inscribed 'I belong to Phidias', now in the site museum.
mapQuery: A Wonder of the World once stood here Katakolon

name: Walk the tunnel the athletes used
description: Athletes entered the stadium through a vaulted stone tunnel, and you can walk through it onto the original track, about 192 m long. There were no stone seats; up to 40,000 spectators sat on grassy embankments. Most visitors can't resist a sprint on the track itself.
mapQuery: Walk the tunnel the athletes used Katakolon

name: Cheaters paid for statues of Zeus
description: Along the approach to the stadium, a row of stone bases once held the Zanes, bronze statues of Zeus paid for by fines on athletes caught cheating or bribing. Their names were inscribed for all to see. Winners received no medal, only a wreath cut from the sacred olive tree, though they were showered with honors back home.
mapQuery: Cheaters paid for statues of Zeus Katakolon

name: Don't skip the Olympia museum
description: The Archaeological Museum at Olympia holds the Hermes of Praxiteles, the soaring Nike of Paionios and the pediment sculptures of the Temple of Zeus. It explains the ruins far better than the bare site. The valley gets very hot in summer, so see the shaded ruins first and the air-conditioned museum second.
mapQuery: Don't skip the Olympia museum Katakolon

name: Scars from the 2007 fires
description: In August 2007, devastating wildfires swept the region and burned the slopes of Kronos Hill right up to the edge of the sanctuary before firefighters saved the ruins. The regrown pines around the site are part of that story, and wildfire risk is a serious summer concern across this part of the Peloponnese.

name: Katakolon's own small surprises
description: Back in the village, the Museum of Ancient Greek Technology shows working reconstructions of ancient inventions such as automata, an early robot servant and the Antikythera mechanism. The Ilia region is also wine country, and estates near Katakolon pour local varieties such as Refosco and Mavrodaphne. It is a good use of the time if you choose not to go to Olympia.

name: Not quite a fjord
description: The Bay of Kotor is often called Europe's southernmost fjord, but geologically it is a ria, a river canyon drowned by the sea, not a glacier-carved fjord. Either way, the limestone mountains plunge straight into the water, and sailing in at dawn is the arrival.

name: Venice's walls on a mountain
description: Kotor was Venetian from 1420 to 1797. The walls zigzagging about 4.5 km up the mountain to St. John's fortress were built to hold off the Ottomans. The town is UNESCO-listed and was badly damaged in a 1979 earthquake, so much of what you see was carefully restored afterward.
mapQuery: Venice's walls on a mountain Kotor

name: A maze on purpose
description: The Old Town's tangled lanes and lack of a straight route are often explained as a defensive design to disorient invaders. They certainly disorient visitors. Locals navigate by squares, such as Arms, Flour and Milk squares, rather than street names, so use those as landmarks.

name: Catholic and Orthodox side by side
description: Kotor's Romanesque Cathedral of St. Tryphon, consecrated in 1166, is Catholic. A short walk away, the Serbian Orthodox Church of St. Nicholas serves the other main community. That coexistence is typical of the Bay, which has been a meeting point of faiths and empires for centuries, so visit both and dress modestly.
mapQuery: Catholic and Orthodox side by side Kotor

name: The cats of Kotor
description: Cats are everywhere in the Old Town and are its unofficial symbol. Sailors' ships carried them to control rats, and locals have fed them ever since. There is even a small Cats Museum, and shopkeepers take their care seriously.

name: A seafaring brotherhood older than nations
description: The Bokelj Navy (Bokeška mornarica), a maritime fraternity, traces its roots to the year 809, when it is said to have received the relics of St. Tryphon. Its members still parade in traditional costume and dance their kolo at the saint's festivities each February. The Maritime Museum in the Old Town tells the story.
mapQuery: A seafaring brotherhood older than nations Kotor

name: An island built by hand
description: Off the village of Perast, the islet of Our Lady of the Rocks was built artificially. According to tradition, sailors dropped stones on a reef after finding an icon there in the 15th century. Every 22 July, locals row out at sunset to throw more stones in the Fašinada procession, continuing the work.
mapQuery: An island built by hand Kotor

name: Euros, but not the EU
description: Montenegro uses the euro even though it is not in the European Union; it adopted the currency unilaterally. It is also outside Schengen, so travelers coming from Dubrovnik cross a real border with passport checks, and the queues can be long in summer.
mapQuery: Euros, but not the EU Kotor

name: The road to the old royal capital
description: The old caravan path behind the town, the Ladder of Kotor, and the serpentine road above it lead to Njeguši, home of famous smoked prosciutto and cheese. From there the route continues to Cetinje, Montenegro's royal capital until 1918. Atop Mount Lovćen is the mausoleum of Petar II Petrović-Njegoš, the 19th-century prince-bishop and the nation's greatest poet.
mapQuery: The road to the old royal capital Kotor

name: Still walking a Greek street plan
description: Naples was founded by Greeks as Neapolis, 'new city'. Its historic center still follows the ancient grid of three long decumani crossed by narrow lanes. Spaccanapoli, the street that 'splits Naples', is one of them, and the whole center is a UNESCO site.
mapQuery: Still walking a Greek street plan Naples

name: A second city underground
description: Beneath the streets lies a network of tunnels and cisterns carved from soft yellow tuff stone. The ancient Greeks quarried it, Romans built aqueducts through it, and Neapolitans sheltered in it during WWII air raids. Guided underground tours show how much of Naples is hollow beneath your feet.

name: Living with Vesuvius
description: Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum in AD 79 and last erupted in 1944. Hundreds of thousands of people still live in the official red zone around it, under a long-standing evacuation plan. Neapolitans treat the volcano with fatalistic affection, and you will see it on everything from pizza boxes to football scarves.

name: The miracle of San Gennaro
description: Three times a year (the Saturday before the first Sunday of May, 19 September and 16 December), the dried blood of the patron saint, San Gennaro, is displayed in the Duomo, and the faithful wait for it to liquefy. A quick liquefaction is a good omen; failure is taken seriously, as a warning of disaster.
mapQuery: The miracle of San Gennaro Naples

name: Pizza is UNESCO heritage here
description: The art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list. A true Neapolitan pizza is soft, with a puffy, slightly charred rim, and is often eaten with a knife and fork. For a cheap snack, try a pizza a portafoglio, folded in quarters and eaten while walking.
mapQuery: Pizza is UNESCO heritage here Naples

name: Nativity scenes all year round
description: Via San Gregorio Armeno is the street of presepe makers, artisans who craft elaborate nativity scenes and figurines year-round. Alongside shepherds and the Holy Family, they make figures of footballers, politicians and celebrities, a cheeky Neapolitan tradition of putting the present into the manger.
mapQuery: Nativity scenes all year round Naples

name: Caffè sospeso and coffee at the bar
description: Neapolitans drink espresso standing at the bar, quickly and often with a glass of water first to cleanse the palate. The caffè sospeso, a 'suspended coffee', is the custom of paying for an extra one so a stranger in need can claim it later. Some bars still honor it.
mapQuery: Caffè sospeso and coffee at the bar Naples

name: Once the largest city in Italy
description: Under the Bourbons, Naples was capital of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and one of Europe's great cities. The Royal Palace and the Teatro di San Carlo from that era remain; opened in 1737, San Carlo is the oldest continuously active opera house in Europe. Many Neapolitans still feel that Italian unification in 1861 worked against the South.
mapQuery: Once the largest city in Italy Naples

name: Maradona is a saint here
description: Diego Maradona led SSC Napoli to its first league titles in 1987 and 1990, and murals and shrines to him fill the Quartieri Spagnoli. Napoli's recent league wins have only deepened the devotion. Football is not a casual subject in this city.
mapQuery: Maradona is a saint here Naples

name: The cult of the forgotten dead
description: In the Fontanelle Cemetery, a former tuff quarry filled with the bones of plague and cholera victims, Neapolitans once 'adopted' anonymous skulls. They cleaned them, prayed for their souls and asked them for favors in return. The Church banned the practice in 1969, but the cemetery shows how intimately this city lives with death.
mapQuery: The cult of the forgotten dead Naples

name: Civitavecchia is Trajan's port
description: Emperor Trajan founded the harbor here in the early 2nd century AD as Centumcellae to serve Rome. Rome itself is about 80 km away, roughly 1 to 1.5 hours each way by train from Civitavecchia station, so a 'day in Rome' is really a long day trip. Michelangelo is credited with work on the massive Forte Michelangelo that guards the port.

name: A Japanese story in an Italian port
description: In 1615, the samurai envoy Hasekura Tsunenaga landed at Civitavecchia on a diplomatic mission to the Pope. Civitavecchia's church of the Japanese Martyrs, decorated by a Japanese artist, recalls that link, and the city is twinned with Ishinomaki in Japan. Few visitors expect it.
mapQuery: A Japanese story in an Italian port Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: Etruscan tombs just up the coast
description: Before Rome there were the Etruscans. About 20 km north, the UNESCO-listed necropolis of Tarquinia has painted underground tombs showing banquets, dancers and games. It is a rewarding alternative for anyone who has already seen Rome or wants to avoid the crowds.
mapQuery: Etruscan tombs just up the coast Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: You are walking on top of ancient Rome
description: The ancient city lies meters below today's streets, built up by centuries of flooding and rebuilding. That is why the Forum and Largo di Torre Argentina sit in pits below the sidewalks. The Pantheon, rebuilt under Hadrian around AD 125, still has the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome.
mapQuery: You are walking on top of ancient Rome Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: The Vatican is another country
description: Vatican City is an independent state, the world's smallest. Its dress code for St. Peter's and the Vatican Museums (covered shoulders and knees) is enforced at the door. Photography is not allowed in the Sistine Chapel, and guards will remind you to keep quiet.
mapQuery: The Vatican is another country Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: Free water from the 'big noses'
description: Rome's cast-iron street fountains, the nasoni or 'big noses', run constantly with cold, drinkable water from the city's aqueduct system. Cover the spout's end with a finger, and water jets up from a hole on top for drinking. Locals refill bottles at them all day.
mapQuery: Free water from the 'big noses' Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: SPQR is still official
description: 'Senatus Populusque Romanus', the Senate and People of Rome, appears on manhole covers, buses and public buildings because it is still the city government's emblem. It is a small, constant reminder that Romans see their city as one continuous story.

name: The rules of Roman pasta
description: Rome's four classic pastas are cacio e pepe, gricia, carbonara and amatriciana. All are built on guanciale (cured pork cheek), Pecorino Romano and black pepper in different combinations, and carbonara has no cream. Romans also skip cappuccino after a meal; it is custom, not a rule, but you will be noticed.
mapQuery: The rules of Roman pasta Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: Some monuments have behavior rules
description: Rome fines people for sitting on the Spanish Steps and for wading in or climbing on fountains such as the Trevi. The tradition there is to toss a coin over your left shoulder to ensure your return, and the coins are collected for charity. Respect the barriers and wardens, who do enforce them.
mapQuery: Some monuments have behavior rules Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: You are standing on the rim of a drowned volcano
description: The crescent you sail into is what remains of a volcanic island that blew apart in the Late Bronze Age, around 1600 BC, in one of the largest eruptions in human history. The sea flooded the collapsed center to form the caldera. Nea Kameni in the middle is the still-active vent; it last erupted in 1950 and is monitored around the clock.
mapQuery: You are standing on the rim of a drowned volcano Santorini

name: Akrotiri: a Bronze Age town with no bodies
description: Under the ash at Akrotiri lies a sophisticated Bronze Age town with multi-storey houses, drains and vivid frescoes. Unlike Pompeii, no victims have been found, which suggests the inhabitants had warning and fled. Many of the best frescoes are in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. Fira's Museum of Prehistoric Thera holds others and the famous small gold ibex.
mapQuery: Akrotiri: a Bronze Age town with no bodies Santorini

name: Cave houses were for the poor
description: Today's luxury cave suites began as yposkafa, homes dug into the soft volcanic rock by farmers and sailors who could not afford timber or stone. The rock kept them cool in summer and warm in winter. In Oia, wealthy 19th-century sea captains built proper mansions on the ridge, while their crews lived in the caves below.
mapQuery: Cave houses were for the poor Santorini

name: Why everything is white
description: Whitewash is lime, and islanders used it because it reflected the brutal sun and worked as a cheap disinfectant. A 1938 law encouraged whitewashing during a cholera concern. The classic blue domes are mostly church tradition and later tourism aesthetics. The story that the colors were mandated to mirror the Greek flag is largely romantic myth.

name: The 1956 earthquake reshaped the island
description: In 1956 a powerful earthquake destroyed much of Oia and Fira. Many families emigrated to Athens or abroad, and Oia sat half-ruined for years. The picture-perfect village you see is largely a careful rebuilding from the 1970s onward, when the Greek tourism body began restoring traditional houses.
mapQuery: The 1956 earthquake reshaped the island Santorini

name: Vines grown in baskets
description: Santorini's Assyrtiko vines are woven into low, basket-shaped coils called kouloura that hug the ground, so the grapes shelter from fierce winds and drink the night-time sea mist in a place with almost no rain. The volcanic soil kept out the phylloxera plague, so some rootstocks are believed to be centuries old. Try Vinsanto, the island's sweet wine made from sun-dried grapes.

name: An island without fresh water
description: Santorini has no rivers or springs to speak of, and today it runs largely on desalination plants. Its famous foods grew from that scarcity. Small, intensely sweet cherry tomatoes and the PDO-protected fava, a yellow split pea purée, are dry-farmed, so try them as the island's real flavor.
mapQuery: An island without fresh water Santorini

name: The donkeys and the Fira steps
description: Mules and donkeys still work the roughly 588-step path from the Old Port to Fira. Animal-welfare complaints led Greece in 2018 to bar them from carrying riders over 100 kg. Many visitors now take the cable car or walk instead, and that choice is respected here.
mapQuery: The donkeys and the Fira steps Santorini

name: A Catholic quarter in an Orthodox island
description: Santorini was ruled for centuries by Venetian-era lords of the Duchy of Naxos, and its Catholic community has survived to this day. Fira has a Catholic cathedral and quarter, and the much-photographed 'Three Bells of Fira' church is Catholic, not Orthodox.
mapQuery: A Catholic quarter in an Orthodox island Santorini

name: A city living inside a Roman palace
description: Emperor Diocletian built his retirement palace here around AD 295–305, and he is the only Roman emperor who voluntarily gave up the throne. In the 7th century, refugees from nearby Salona fled invaders by moving inside the walls. Their descendants never left, which is why people still live, shop and hang laundry inside an emperor's palace today.
mapQuery: A city living inside a Roman palace Split

name: The persecutor's tomb became a saint's cathedral
