Getting there: Right beside the cable car top station. Cruise tenders land at Fira Old Port; go up by cable car (long queues when several ships are in) or by the roughly 588-step mule path (steep, slippery, and fouled by donkeys). Head north along the rim for Firostefani, Imerovigli, and Oia.
Hours: Open access

name: Sunset of Santorini
description: This public caldera viewpoint is on Mitropoleos Street at the southern end of Fira's rim walkway. Here the sun sets straight ahead over the caldera rather than to the side as in Oia. Narrow lanes wind between cliff hotels and cocktail bars, so a short evening stroll can end with a drink and an unobstructed sunset.
mapQuery: Sunset of Santorini Mitropoleos Street Fira
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: A 5–10 min walk south from the cable car along the rim, paved with steps. Combine with the Fira–Firostefani stretch for a 1–2 km evening loop.
Hours: Open access

name: Santorini Walking Tours
description: This Firostefani-based outfit runs small-group and private guided hikes, notably the Imerovigli–Oia caldera trek and multi-village walks. Guides add the island's geology, history, and wild herbs along the way. Sunrise departures (around 05:00 pickups in summer) beat the heat, and some walks end with a traditional meal in Oia. It is the safest way to do the rim for less-confident hikers.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Book in advance by phone (+30 2286 036496) or through their website; private and group options
Getting there: Based in Firostefani with hotel pickups. The Imerovigli–Oia route is about 8 km (5 mi), 3–4 hrs, with about 300 m of cumulative gain. CRUISE: confirm the start time against your tender time and the cable car queue; this is a half-day commitment.
Hours: Office 09:00–21:00 Mon–Sat, 10:00–19:00 Sun

name: Oia to Fira Hike (Start)
description: This is the Oia trailhead of the caldera hike, at the east end of the village near the bus station, for walkers doing the route southbound. Starting here front-loads the steepest ridges while your legs are fresh and puts the sun at your back on the morning leg. You finish in Fira near the cable car, which suits cruise passengers who need to return to the port.
mapQuery: Oia to Fira Hike Start Santorini
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: About 10 km (6.2 mi) one-way to Fira, with roughly 300–350 m of cumulative gain. Allow 3–5 hrs. Reach Oia by KTEL bus from Fira (about 25 min) or by boat from Old Port. Terrain is rocky gravel with steep loose descents. There is one basic makeshift toilet and a few seasonal snack stands en route. CRUISE: a half-day commitment; check your last tender time before starting.
Hours: Open trail; start early to avoid the heat

name: Church of Agios Georgios
description: This sand-colored church with a blue dome sits on an open square at the eastern end of Oia's main lane, close to where the caldera trail to Fira begins. It is quieter than the churches in the center of Oia, with benches and open caldera views. It works as the first or last waypoint of the long hike.
mapQuery: Church of Agios Georgios Oia Santorini
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: At the east end of Oia's marble main street, about 5 min from the bus station; the Fira trail continues south-east from here. Paved.
Hours: Exterior always accessible; interior often closed

name: Sunset Spot
description: This little-known high point is on the trail east of Oia, toward Finikia and the start of the Fira path. It offers the same sunset without the crush of people at Oia Castle. Visitors often have it almost to themselves, and it is free.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: About 30 min on foot from the Oia bus station, with a short uphill on dirt path at the end. Take a headlamp for the return after dark.
Hours: Open access

name: Views of Santorini & Caldera
description: This is the lookout at the western tip of Oia, where the stepped path down to Ammoudi Bay begins. It frames the caldera, Thirasia, and the red cliffs dropping to the harbor below. It is the trailhead for the Ammoudi steps and a prime sunset position, so expect a crowd from about an hour before sunset in season.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: At the far west end of Oia near the castle, about 15 min on foot from the bus station along the main lane. The Ammoudi steps descend from here.
Hours: Open access

name: Castle of Oia
description: The ruined Venetian Agios Nikolaos castle at Oia's western point is just a few walls now, but it has close to 270° views over the caldera and sea. It is the island's most famous sunset spot. A side stair through a small gate leads to a chapel and an old building that few visitors find.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free, no gate or ticket)
Getting there: West end of Oia, a short paved walk from the main lane with steps. For sunset in summer, claim a wall spot about 90 min ahead. Cruise visitors usually arrive from 09:30, so before 08:00 is quiet.
Hours: Open access

name: Windmills of Oia
description: This row of restored windmills, several now holiday rentals, stands on the quieter western ridge of Oia. They give a different angle back over the town and caldera. A short stroll gets you away from the main-lane crowds, and the castle offers the shot with all three mills together.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: About 8 min on foot from the Oia sunset car park; paved lanes with steps.
Hours: Open access

name: Ammoudi Bay
description: This tiny fishing harbor sits at the foot of Oia's red cliffs, reached by a long zigzag stairway that is the classic Oia mini-hike. At the bottom are waterfront fish tavernas and boats to Thirasia, and the climb back up is a real workout. Walkers share the steps with working donkeys; many visitors choose not to ride them.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in; book waterfront tavernas for sunset
Getting there: About 300 steps, roughly 100 m (330 ft) of elevation, from the top near Oia Castle. Allow 20 min down and 25–35 min up. Wear grippy shoes because the cobbles are slick and fouled; step to the wall when donkeys pass. A road also reaches the bay, with a car park at the top and a golf-cart shuttle down.
Hours: Open access

name: Ammoudi (Αμμούδι)
description: Past the Ammoudi tavernas, a short rough path over black lava rock leads to the swim ledges facing the islet of Agios Nikolaos. Here people swim in very clear, deep water and jump from the rocks. It is not a beach, just rock ledges, but it is one of the few places to swim near Oia and a fine reward after the stairs.
tags: verify: path access (gate reported closed at times)
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: From the bottom of the Ammoudi steps, turn left past the tavernas, then follow about 5–10 min of uneven lava path. Water shoes help. There is no lifeguard, no shade, and the water is deep straight away.
Hours: Open access; best before 10:00

name: Volcano Hiking Tour
description: Guided boat-and-hike trips cross the caldera to Nea Kameni, the black lava island that last erupted in 1950. The trail climbs to steaming fumaroles at the crater rim with views back to the cliff villages. Many trips add a swim at the Palea Kameni sulfur springs. Good guides explain the Minoan eruption that shaped the island.
mapQuery: Volcano Hiking Tour Nea Kameni Santorini
tags: verify: current entry fee and departure times
details:
Reservations / tickets: Book ahead through Old Port operators or online; the volcano park entry fee is charged separately at the dock
Getting there: Boats leave Fira Old Port (where cruise tenders land), about 20 min each way. The trail is about 1.5 km each way with about 130 m (430 ft) of gain on black cinder, with no shade and no toilets on the trail. Allow 30–45 min up. CRUISE: a half-day commitment of 3–4 hrs total; choose the earliest departure.

name: Nea Kameni
description: This young volcanic island in the center of the caldera is a protected geological park of jagged lava fields and cinder slopes. A maintained trail climbs to the main craters, where you can smell sulfur and feel warm ground. The panorama of the caldera wall from the top is the island's most dramatic view from the water side.
tags: verify: park hours and entry fee
details:
Reservations / tickets: Boat ticket plus park entry fee at the dock
Getting there: Reached only by boat from Fira Old Port, Athinios, or Ammoudi, about 20 min. The marked trail runs about 1.5 km each way with about 130 m of gain on loose cinder. Allow 1–1.5 hrs on the island. Wear closed shoes (not flip-flops) and bring a hat and water. CRUISE: a half-day commitment.

name: Therasia
description: Thirasia is the quiet western fragment of the original island, with a few hundred residents and a timeless feel that is hard to find on Santorini now. From Korfos harbor, a long stepped path climbs the caldera wall to Manolas village, which looks back at Oia across the water. Rough tracks run on to Potamos and Agrilia for more walking. Simple fish tavernas line the harbor.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ferry or caldera-cruise ticket; check return times
Getting there: Small ferries run from Ammoudi Bay (Oia) and Athinios, and many caldera cruises stop here, about 10–25 min crossing. Korfos to Manolas is a steep stepped path of about 140 m (460 ft), 20–30 min up. Allow 2–3 hrs on the island. CRUISE: a half-day commitment that depends on the boat schedule.

name: Προφήτης Ηλίας (Profitis Ilias Peak)
description: At 567 m, Profitis Ilias is Santorini's highest point, a limestone summit older than the volcano, with views over the whole island and on clear days to Ios and Anafi. The summit holds an 18th-century monastery and military antennas. It is a popular sunrise and sunset goal from the hill village of Pyrgos below.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: From Pyrgos (KTEL bus stop), follow the old path and road up, about 3 km one-way with about 220 m (720 ft) of gain. Allow 2–2.5 hrs round trip. It is exposed and windy. A paved road also reaches the top, with free parking. CRUISE: a half-day commitment by taxi or bus to Pyrgos (about 15 min from Fira).
Hours: Summit open access

name: Monastery of Prophet Elias of Thira
description: This fortified 1711 monastery crowns the island's highest peak and is the trailhead for the best ridge walk on Santorini. The red-dot path drops along the limestone spine to the Sellada saddle and Ancient Thera, with Kamari and Perissa beaches on either side below. Only the small church and a shop selling monastery liqueurs are usually open to visitors.
mapQuery: Monastery of Prophet Elias of Thira Santorini
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free); modest dress for the church
Getting there: Ridge trail to Ancient Thera: about 3–3.5 km one-way, mostly downhill to Sellada and then up about 90 m to the site. Allow 1.5–2 hrs one-way, then descend to Perissa or Kamari. It is rocky, narrow, and unshaded, with red-dot waymarks. Free parking at the top. CRUISE: a half-day commitment; taxi to the monastery, hike, then taxi back from Kamari or Perissa.
Hours: 09:00–17:00 Mon–Sat; closed Sun

name: Castle of Pyrgos Kallistis
description: Pyrgos is the island's best-preserved medieval hill village. Its Venetian kasteli is reached by climbing a maze of vaulted lanes and steps to ruined walls with 360° views over vineyards to both coasts. It is free and far less crowded than the caldera towns, with tavernas near the top.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: From the Pyrgos bus stop or car park, 10–15 min uphill on stepped lanes, about 60 m of gain. Google Maps misroutes here; follow signs toward the cafés at the top. Not suitable for limited mobility.
Hours: 07:00–20:00 daily

name: Heart of Santorini
description: This wind-carved hole in the caldera cliff below Megalochori once had a heart shape, now softened by erosion. It frames the caldera and is a quiet alternative sunset spot. A steep sandy path continues past a small bell chapel down to a rocky shore with clear water.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: About 10 min on foot from the Gavalas Winery area at Megalochori to the viewpoint. Going down to the shore adds about 150 m of steep, slippery descent and re-climb (about 1 hr round trip). Use grippy shoes; it is windy. CRUISE: taxi from Fira, about 15 min.
Hours: Open access

name: Venetian Castle of Emporio
description: Emporio, the island's largest village, hides a 15th-century kasteli. It is a tight, fortified warren of houses whose blank outer walls once kept out pirates. Wandering its tunnels and alleys, with bougainvillea and tiny chapels, is a short, atmospheric urban walk that few visitors make.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: Park by the main square and walk up into the kasteli, about 30–45 min of wandering on uneven steps. It is a maze, so expect to get lost. Combine it with the Gavrilos windmill ridge just above the village.
Hours: 09:00–21:00 daily

name: Akrotiri Lighthouse
description: Built in 1892, this lighthouse stands at the island's south-western tip, looking back up the whole caldera and out to the Christiana islets. The building is closed, but a short footpath scrambles out over the rocks to the point. It is the calmest sunset spot on Santorini, far from the Oia crowds.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: About 16 km from Fira (25–30 min drive). Roadside parking is tiny, so park 1–2 min before the end and walk. The point is a 10–15 min round trip over uneven rock with strong wind. CRUISE: a half-day commitment by car, ATV, or taxi; the bus reaches only Akrotiri village and Red Beach.
Hours: Open access; lighthouse interior closed

name: Ancient Thera
description: This hilltop city on Mesa Vouno, 360 m up, was founded by Dorian settlers and later used by Ptolemaic, Roman, and Byzantine occupants. It has an agora, theater, temples, and houses spread along a ridge between Kamari and Perissa. The climb up is part of the experience, with both black-sand beaches far below.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ticket at the gate (around €10)
Getting there: From Perissa: a stony footpath of about 2 km with about 330 m (1,080 ft) of gain, 45–60 min up. Steep, loose, and unshaded. From Kamari: a cobbled serpentine road (cars and seasonal shuttle) to the Sellada car park, then a 10 min climb. There are no toilets or shade at the site. CRUISE: a half-day commitment; the site closes mid-afternoon.
Hours: 08:30–15:00; closed Wed

name: Μέσα Βουνό (Mesa Vouno)
description: Mesa Vouno is the limestone mountain separating Kamari from Perissa, with Ancient Thera on its ridge. It is a superb sunrise hike, with wildflowers and herbs carpeting the slopes in April–May. The views run over both beaches, the airport plain, and across the Aegean to Anafi.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: Kamari side: a paved switchback road, about 3 km with about 330 m of gain, roughly 1 hr up, with benches. Perissa side: a poorly marked stony path, 45–60 min. Carry an offline map. Very windy on top. CRUISE: a half-day commitment by bus or taxi to Kamari or Perissa (about 20 min from Fira).
Hours: Open access

name: Zoodochos Pigi cave
description: This small cave chapel is built into the cliff on the old footpath between Kamari and Ancient Thera, beside a natural spring, the only one on this side of the mountain. It is a peaceful halfway stop with views down to Kamari beach, and few hikers find it.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: On the Kamari-side approach to Ancient Thera, partway up Mesa Vouno. Allow about 30–40 min up from Kamari on rough path. The spring is often dry by late spring, so bring your own water.
Hours: Open access

name: Παραλία Βλυχάδα (Vlychada Beach)
description: Vlychada is a long black-sand beach on the south coast, backed by pale pumice cliffs that the wind has carved into honeycomb shapes. Walking its length is an easy shoreline hike that feels like another planet. It sits next to a small marina with fish tavernas.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in (free)
Getting there: About 1.5–2 km of flat sand end to end (30–45 min round trip). Ample parking by the marina, and a café rents loungers. About 25 min by car from Fira; buses run via Emporio. CRUISE: a half-day commitment.
Hours: Open access

name: Greet by the clock
description: Greeks greet according to the time of day: 'kalimera' (good morning) until roughly early afternoon, then 'kalispera' (good evening). 'Yia sas' is a polite hello or goodbye to anyone you don't know, and 'yia sou' is the friendly version for one person. Saying one of these as you walk into a small shop or kiosk, before you ask for anything, makes a real difference to how you are received.

name: Nodding 'no' and saying 'ne' for yes
description: 'Ne' means yes, which catches many English speakers out. 'No' is 'ochi', and it is often given without words, as a small upward tilt of the head with raised eyebrows, sometimes with a click of the tongue. If a waiter tips his head back when you ask for something, he is telling you they are out of it, not agreeing.
mapQuery: Nodding 'no' and saying 'ne' for yes Athens (Piraeus)

name: Never show the open palm
description: Pushing an open hand, fingers spread, towards someone is the moutza, an old and genuinely offensive gesture in Greece. Visitors do it by accident when waving goodbye, signalling five, or stopping a taxi. Wave with your palm facing you, or simply raise a hand slightly with the fingers together.
mapQuery: Never show the open palm Athens (Piraeus)

name: Churches are working places of worship
description: Athens' small Byzantine churches, like Kapnikarea on Ermou Street, are in daily use. Cover your shoulders and knees, speak quietly, don't photograph people lighting candles or praying, and never walk behind the iconostasis, the icon screen at the front, which only clergy enter. It is customary to drop a coin in the box if you take a candle.
mapQuery: Churches are working places of worship Athens (Piraeus)

name: Hands off the marble at the Acropolis
description: Guards on the Acropolis will blow a whistle if you touch, lean on or climb the ancient stones, and taking even a pebble from any archaeological site is illegal in Greece. Flying a drone over archaeological sites requires official permission, and tripods or professional photo shoots also need a permit. Personal photos are fine; posing for them on the monuments themselves is not.
mapQuery: Hands off the marble at the Acropolis Athens (Piraeus)

name: The guards at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier are on duty
description: The Evzones in front of the Parliament on Syntagma Square are serving soldiers on ceremonial guard, not performers. Photograph them freely, but don't touch them, stand in their path or step onto the monument platform; they will warn you, sometimes with a tap of the rifle on the ground. The full Sunday ceremony at 11:00 draws big crowds, so arrive early and stay behind the line.
mapQuery: The guards at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier are on duty Athens (Piraeus)

name: Ordering, sharing and asking for the bill
description: Greeks order plates for the middle of the table and share everything, so asking for your own separate dish of meze can seem odd. The bill will not arrive until you ask for it, usually with 'to logariasmo, parakalo'; lingering is normal and polite. Service is not usually added; rounding up or leaving around 5–10% for good service is appreciated rather than required.
mapQuery: Ordering, sharing and asking for the bill Athens (Piraeus)

name: Paper goes in the bin
description: In much of Greece, the plumbing in older buildings has narrow pipes, so used toilet paper goes in the small lidded bin beside the toilet rather than down the bowl. It feels strange, but where you see a bin and a sign asking you to do so, please follow it; a blocked toilet is a real problem for small tavernas and guesthouses. Modern hotels often have no such rule.
mapQuery: Paper goes in the bin Athens (Piraeus)

name: 'Efharisto' goes a long way
description: 'Efharisto' (thank you) and 'parakalo' (please, and also you're welcome) are the two words that open doors. Athenians are generally warm and direct; conversation can sound loud and animated, which is enthusiasm rather than anger. People stand closer and touch arms more than many North Americans are used to.

name: Rooftops and blue domes are not public
description: Many of Santorini's famous photo spots, including terraces, rooftops and church domes, belong to private homes, hotels or working churches. Climbing onto them for photographs, or walking onto hotel terraces uninvited, is a real problem for residents, and many places now post signs asking people to stay off. Take your pictures from the public paths.
mapQuery: Rooftops and blue domes are not public Santorini

name: Weddings and services happen in those churches
description: The little blue-domed churches of Oia and Fira host baptisms, weddings and services, and couples often book them for ceremonies. If you come across one, keep a respectful distance, don't walk into the photos and don't enter while a service is under way. Cover shoulders and knees when you go inside any church, Orthodox or Catholic.
mapQuery: Weddings and services happen in those churches Santorini

name: Sharing the path with the mules
description: On the steps between the Old Port and Fira, the mules and donkeys have right of way. Step to the inside of the path, away from the edge, and let them pass; don't touch or feed them. Greek rules prohibit riders over 100 kg, and many visitors choose to walk or take the cable car instead.
mapQuery: Sharing the path with the mules Santorini

name: Swimwear stays on the beach
description: Walking through Fira, Oia or the village lanes in swimwear or bare-chested is considered disrespectful, even in high summer. Throw on a shirt or cover-up when you leave the beach or pool. In churches, monasteries and museums, covered shoulders are expected.
mapQuery: Swimwear stays on the beach Santorini

name: Sunset in Oia is shared
description: At sunset in Oia, crowds gather on the castle walls and terraces, and it is common for people to applaud as the sun goes down. Space is tight, so avoid standing on walls in front of others or holding up phones and tablets over their heads. Arrive early, keep to your spot and be patient when everyone leaves at once.
mapQuery: Sunset in Oia is shared Santorini

name: Water is precious here
description: Santorini has almost no natural fresh water, and much of its supply comes from desalination. Hotels and guesthouses may ask you to take short showers and not to leave taps running, and they mean it. Most visitors drink bottled water rather than tap water.

name: Greek courtesies still matter in a busy place
description: Even in crowded Fira, people respond warmly to 'kalimera' (good morning), 'kalispera' (good evening) and 'efharisto' (thank you). Many people working on the island in summer come from elsewhere in Greece and work very long hours; a little patience and a greeting are noticed and appreciated.
mapQuery: Greek courtesies still matter in a busy place Santorini

name: Accept the raki
description: At the end of a meal, most Cretan tavernas bring a small carafe of raki, also called tsikoudia, and a sweet, without charge. It is a gesture of hospitality; accepting a small sip, raising your glass and saying 'yamas' (cheers) while making eye contact is the courteous response. You don't have to finish it, but refusing outright can seem cold.

name: Cretan hospitality runs deep
description: Cretans take enormous pride in welcoming strangers, and you may be offered fruit, a coffee or a taste of something in a shop or village. Accepting a little, even if you don't want much, is polite; a firm refusal can come across as rejecting the person. A warm 'efharisto poli' (thank you very much) is always welcome.

name: No photos at Souda's naval base
description: Cruise ships dock at Souda Bay, which is also a Greek and NATO naval base. Photographing military installations, ships and personnel is not permitted, and signs make this clear. Point your camera at the mountains and the bay rather than the warships.
mapQuery: No photos at Souda's naval base Chania

name: Visiting Etz Hayyim synagogue
description: Chania's restored Etz Hayyim synagogue in the old Jewish quarter is an active place of prayer and remembrance for a community almost entirely lost in 1944. Visitors are welcome, but dress modestly, keep your voice low, and check opening times; men may be offered a head covering. The memorial to the deported is a place for quiet reflection, not photo posing.

name: Monasteries ask for modest dress
description: Monasteries such as Agia Triada on the Akrotiri peninsula are working religious communities. Shoulders and knees should be covered, and some monasteries lend wraps at the entrance. Keep voices low, don't photograph monks without asking, and respect areas marked closed to visitors.
mapQuery: Monasteries ask for modest dress Chania

name: Quiet at the war cemetery
description: The Commonwealth War Cemetery at Souda Bay holds Allied soldiers who died in the 1941 Battle of Crete. It is a place of remembrance, and visitors are asked to behave accordingly: speak quietly, keep to the paths and don't use it as a picnic spot. Many Cretans have deep family memories of the battle and the occupation that followed.
mapQuery: Quiet at the war cemetery Chania

name: Paper in the bin
description: As in much of Greece, older buildings in Chania have narrow drains, so toilet paper usually goes in the bin beside the toilet. Look for a small sign and follow it; tavernas will be grateful.

name: Buying a Cretan knife
description: The knife-makers' lane in the old town sells traditional Cretan knives, sometimes engraved with a verse. They make lovely souvenirs, but you will need to pack them in checked luggage, and cruise lines generally require blades to be handed in on boarding and returned at the end of the voyage. Ask the ship before you buy.

name: Ruins are for looking, not climbing
description: At Ancient Olympia, guards will whistle if you sit on fallen columns, climb walls or step over ropes. The temple remains are fragile, and some have stood for more than two thousand years. Taking a stone, even a small one, from any Greek archaeological site is illegal.
mapQuery: Ruins are for looking, not climbing Katakolon

name: The flame-lighting spot is roped off
description: At the Temple of Hera, the altar area where the Olympic flame is lit for each modern Games is cordoned off. Visitors often want to stand on the exact spot; please respect the barrier. You can still take a fine photograph from beside it.
mapQuery: The flame-lighting spot is roped off Katakolon

name: Running on the ancient track is allowed
description: Almost everyone runs a few metres on the stadium track at Olympia, and it is perfectly acceptable. What is not appreciated is blocking the tunnel entrance for photos or turning the track into a stage for long, noisy group shoots. Be quick, and let others have their turn.
mapQuery: Running on the ancient track is allowed Katakolon

name: Tripods and drones need permission
description: Personal photography is welcome at Olympia, but tripods and professional equipment at Greek archaeological sites usually require a permit, and drones need official permission. Smoking is not allowed on the site; in a region with a real wildfire risk, this is taken very seriously.
mapQuery: Tripods and drones need permission Katakolon

name: Greet the shopkeepers
description: Katakolon is a tiny village that welcomes many visitors at once. A 'kalimera' (good morning) or 'yia sas' (hello) as you enter a shop or taverna, and 'efharisto' (thank you) as you leave, is noticed and appreciated. Many shops are family run, and the owners are often happy to chat.

name: Agree on taxi fares before you go
description: Taxis at Katakolon often offer fixed return fares to Olympia with waiting time. It is normal and polite to agree the price, the waiting time and the return time clearly before you set off, so there is no misunderstanding later. Pay at the end of the trip, not before.
mapQuery: Agree on taxi fares before you go Katakolon

name: Dress for churches, not for the site
description: Ancient Olympia is an archaeological site rather than a place of worship, so ordinary summer clothing is fine there. The village churches in Katakolon and nearby are a different matter: cover shoulders and knees if you step inside.
mapQuery: Dress for churches, not for the site Katakolon

name: Venerating Saint Spyridon
description: The relics of Saint Spyridon, Corfu's beloved patron, rest in a silver casket in his church in the old town. Many visitors queue alongside locals to pass the casket; dress modestly, wait your turn, keep silent and follow what people in front of you do. Photography inside is often not permitted, so check the signs and respect them.

name: Give way to the processions
description: Four times a year, on Palm Sunday, Holy Saturday, 11 August and the first Sunday of November, the saint's relics are carried through the town with brass bands and clergy. Watch from the side of the route, don't push forward with cameras, and keep children close. For many Corfiots this is the most important day of the year.
mapQuery: Give way to the processions Corfu

name: Stand clear on Holy Saturday
description: On the morning of Holy Saturday, Corfiots throw large clay pots filled with water from their balconies onto the streets of the old town. It is a joyful tradition, but the pots are heavy. Watch from a safe spot, away from the balconies, and follow local guidance.
mapQuery: Stand clear on Holy Saturday Corfu

name: Don't cross the cricket pitch
description: The Spianada has a cricket pitch in the middle, a legacy of British rule, and matches are played there. If a game is on, walk around the edge rather than across the field. Locals take it seriously.
mapQuery: Don't cross the cricket pitch Corfu

name: Monasteries lend wraps
description: At the Monastery of Paleokastritsa and other religious sites, shoulders and knees must be covered. Some monasteries provide wraps or skirts at the entrance, but bringing your own scarf saves trouble. Keep voices low in the church and courtyard.

name: Swimwear only on the beach
description: Walking around Corfu Town in swimwear or without a shirt is considered disrespectful. Cover up when you leave the beach. In the old town's narrow lanes, keep your voice down in the evening; people live in those tall Venetian houses.
mapQuery: Swimwear only on the beach Corfu

name: Greek greetings with an Italian flavour
description: Corfiots speak Greek, and the usual greetings, 'kalimera', 'kalispera' and 'efharisto', apply. Older Corfiots may know some Italian, a reminder of the island's Venetian centuries. A friendly greeting before asking for something is always appreciated.
mapQuery: Greek greetings with an Italian flavour Corfu

name: Croatian greetings that matter
description: 'Dobar dan' (good day) is the polite greeting in shops and restaurants; 'bok' is a casual hi or bye among friends. 'Hvala' means thank you, and 'molim' means both please and you're welcome. A greeting on entering a shop is expected, and staff will often greet you first.

name: Shirts on in the old town
description: Split has rules against walking around the old town in swimwear or bare-chested, and fines are possible. Keep a shirt or cover-up for the walk back from Bačvice or the sea. Inside the cathedral and other churches, cover shoulders and knees.
mapQuery: Shirts on in the old town Split

name: The cathedral is a working church
description: The Cathedral of Saint Domnius, in Diocletian's mausoleum, is an active place of worship. Check whether a service is under way before entering, keep voices low, and avoid flash. On Sundays it may be closed to sightseers during Mass.
mapQuery: The cathedral is a working church Split

name: Listening to klapa
description: When klapa singers perform in the Vestibule, the domed hall of the palace, the acoustics are part of the experience. Stop talking while they sing, keep phones from blocking others' views, and if you enjoyed it, buy a CD or leave a contribution. Filming is generally fine, but chatting through the music is the one thing people get wrong.

name: Football colours matter
description: Split is fiercely loyal to Hajduk Split. Wearing the shirt of their great rivals, Dinamo Zagreb, around town is likely to draw unfriendly looks or comments. The red-and-white checkerboard of the Croatian national team is always welcome.

name: Handle the recent past with care
description: Croatia declared independence from Yugoslavia in 1991, and the war that followed is within living memory. Avoid calling Croatians 'Yugoslavs' or treating the region's countries as interchangeable, and listen rather than offer opinions if the subject comes up.
mapQuery: Handle the recent past with care Split

name: Coffee is not a quick stop
description: On the Riva, a single coffee can last an hour, and nobody will rush you or bring the bill unasked. When you're ready, ask for 'račun, molim' (the bill, please). Service is not usually included; rounding up or leaving around 10% for good service is appreciated, and tips are often easier to leave in cash.
mapQuery: Coffee is not a quick stop Split

name: Swimwear and bare chests are not allowed in the Old Town
description: Dubrovnik prohibits walking around the Old Town in swimwear or without a shirt, and offenders can be fined. If you've been swimming at Banje or off the rocks, put a shirt on before you walk back through the gates.
mapQuery: Swimwear and bare chests are not allowed in the Old Town Dubrovnik

name: Monuments are not seats
description: Climbing on Onofrio's Fountain, Orlando's Column or other monuments is not permitted, and sitting or picnicking on historic steps and fountains is discouraged. The Old Town is a living UNESCO site with residents, and its stone is protected.

name: People live up those stairs
description: The steep side streets off the Stradun, including the Jesuit Stairs famous from Game of Thrones, are lined with homes. Keep your voice down, don't sit in doorways, and don't recreate the series' 'walk of shame' loudly outside people's windows. After dark, noise travels a long way in the stone lanes.
mapQuery: People live up those stairs Dubrovnik

name: The siege is still remembered
description: The city was shelled during the siege of 1991 and 1992, and many residents lived through it. Treat the subject with respect; the Pile Gate map of shell damage and the memorials are not backdrops for jokes. It is also important not to refer to Croatia as part of Yugoslavia or to confuse its people with their neighbours.
mapQuery: The siege is still remembered Dubrovnik

name: Dress for the churches and monasteries
description: The Franciscan and Dominican monasteries, the cathedral and the church of Saint Blaise are all places of worship. Covered shoulders and knees are expected, and some ask visitors to stay quiet and avoid flash. Services take priority over sightseeing.
mapQuery: Dress for the churches and monasteries Dubrovnik

name: Greet, then ask
description: As elsewhere in Croatia, 'dobar dan' (good day) on entering a shop or restaurant, 'hvala' (thank you) and 'molim' (please) are the essentials. Many people speak excellent English, but beginning in Croatian is warmly received.

name: Saint Blaise is the city's own
description: Sveti Vlaho, Saint Blaise, is Dubrovnik's patron, and his feast on 3 February is the most important day in the city's calendar, with processions, relics and flags. If you see his image or his relics carried through the streets, give the procession space and take your photographs quietly.
mapQuery: Saint Blaise is the city's own Dubrovnik

name: Montenegrin greetings
description: Montenegrin is close to Croatian and Serbian, and both the Latin and Cyrillic alphabets are used. 'Dobar dan' (good day), 'zdravo' (hello), 'hvala' (thank you) and 'molim' (please) will see you through. A greeting on entering a shop is expected.

name: Catholic and Orthodox side by side
description: Kotor's Cathedral of Saint Tryphon is Catholic, while the nearby Church of Saint Nicholas is Serbian Orthodox. In both, cover shoulders and knees and keep voices low. In Orthodox churches, worshippers stand rather than sit, and services can be long; slip in and out quietly at the back.
mapQuery: Catholic and Orthodox side by side Kotor

name: Identity is a sensitive subject
description: Montenegro became independent from its union with Serbia in 2006, and questions of national identity, language and church affiliation remain sensitive. Avoid assuming that Montenegrins are Serbs, or vice versa, and steer clear of politics unless your host raises it.
mapQuery: Identity is a sensitive subject Kotor

name: Look after the cats
description: Kotor's cats are a symbol of the town and are cared for by residents. Admire and photograph them, but avoid picking them up, chasing them or feeding them unsuitable food. Locals take their welfare seriously.

name: Our Lady of the Rocks is a church
description: The little island church off Perast is a place of pilgrimage and devotion, not just a photo stop. Dress modestly, keep your voice down inside, and respect any areas that are roped off. The votive offerings and silver plaques left by sailors over centuries are treasured.
mapQuery: Our Lady of the Rocks is a church Kotor

name: Hospitality comes with rakija
description: In homes and family-run places, you may be offered a glass of rakija, a fruit brandy, as a welcome. Accepting a sip and toasting 'živjeli' (cheers) is the polite response; you don't have to drink much. Refusing all hospitality can seem cold.

name: Ask before photographing people
description: Kotor's residents are used to visitors, but people at markets, in cafés or at their windows are not part of the scenery. Ask before photographing anyone up close, and respect a refusal.

name: Greetings change after lunch
description: 'Buongiorno' (good morning, good day) is used until early afternoon, after which Neapolitans switch to 'buonasera'. 'Permesso' is what you say when squeezing past someone, and 'scusi' is the polite excuse me. 'Grazie' and 'per favore' are the essentials.

name: Pay first, then order your coffee
description: In many Neapolitan bars, especially busy ones, you pay at the till first and take your receipt, the scontrino, to the counter to order. Coffee is drunk quickly standing at the bar; sitting down at a table usually costs more. Asking for a 'latte' gets you a glass of milk; ask for a 'caffè latte' if that's what you want.
mapQuery: Pay first, then order your coffee Naples

name: The shrines in the walls are sacred
description: All over the historic centre and the Quartieri Spagnoli you will see small street shrines, edicole votive, with saints, candles, flowers and photographs of the dead. They are tended by local families and are genuinely sacred. Don't touch the offerings, lean on them or use them as props for selfies.
mapQuery: The shrines in the walls are sacred Naples

name: Churches enforce their dress codes
description: The Duomo, Gesù Nuovo, Santa Chiara and other churches expect covered shoulders and knees, and some will turn visitors away. Avoid visiting during Mass if you are sightseeing, keep your voice low, and avoid flash. In the Sansevero Chapel, home of the Veiled Christ, photography is not allowed.
mapQuery: Churches enforce their dress codes Naples

name: Respect the homes of the Quartieri
description: In the Quartieri Spagnoli, many families live in the bassi, single ground-floor rooms whose doors open directly onto the street. Their doorways are their living rooms. Don't photograph into people's homes or of residents without asking, and keep your voice down.
mapQuery: Respect the homes of the Quartieri Naples

name: Maradona is not a joke
description: Diego Maradona is revered in Naples as a near-saint, and his mural and shrine in the Quartieri Spagnoli are places of genuine devotion. Visitors are welcome, but treat the shrine respectfully. Criticising Napoli or Maradona in a bar is a quick way to lose friends.
mapQuery: Maradona is not a joke Naples

name: Pizza has its own customs
description: In Naples, each person usually orders their own whole pizza rather than sharing slices, and it is often eaten with a knife and fork or folded in quarters. Asking for pineapple, or for the pizza to be cut into slices, may raise an eyebrow. A 'coperto', a cover charge, on the bill is legitimate and normal.
mapQuery: Pizza has its own customs Naples

name: The Fontanelle Cemetery deserves silence
description: The Fontanelle Cemetery holds the bones of many thousands of plague and cholera victims, and for generations Neapolitans tended individual skulls and prayed for their souls. It is a place of popular devotion as well as history. Speak quietly and don't touch the remains or the offerings left by locals.
mapQuery: The Fontanelle Cemetery deserves silence Naples

name: Vatican dress codes are enforced at the door
description: St Peter's Basilica and the Vatican Museums require covered shoulders and knees, and staff turn visitors away if they don't comply, even on hot days. Carry a scarf or light layer. Inside St Peter's, chapels set aside for prayer, such as the Blessed Sacrament chapel, are for worshippers only.
mapQuery: Vatican dress codes are enforced at the door Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: Silence in the Sistine Chapel
description: Photography and filming are not allowed in the Sistine Chapel, and guards regularly ask the crowd for silence. It is worth respecting both; the room is a working chapel where papal conclaves are held.
mapQuery: Silence in the Sistine Chapel Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: Seeing the Pope
description: When the Pope is in Rome, he usually holds a general audience on Wednesday mornings and appears for the Angelus prayer at noon on Sundays in St Peter's Square. Tickets for the audience are free and issued by the Vatican, never sold. Dress modestly, and remember that for many people around you this is a deeply religious occasion.

name: Steps and fountains are not for sitting or wading
description: Rome prohibits sitting on the Spanish Steps and wading in or climbing on fountains such as the Trevi, and fines are issued. Eating and drinking on the steps of monuments is also discouraged by city rules. Toss your coin into the Trevi from the edge and move on to make room for others.
mapQuery: Steps and fountains are not for sitting or wading Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: Coffee customs
description: Italians drink cappuccino mainly in the morning; ordering one after a big meal is not forbidden, but it marks you as a visitor. A coffee drunk standing at the bar costs less than one served at a table. A 'coperto', a per-person cover charge on restaurant bills, is legitimate and normal.

name: Greet before you ask
description: 'Buongiorno' in the morning and early afternoon, 'buonasera' later, and 'grazie' and 'per favore' always. Starting with a greeting before asking for something in a shop, café or ticket office is basic Roman courtesy, and people notice when it is missing.

name: Drink from the nasoni without touching the spout
description: Rome's cast-iron drinking fountains, the nasoni, run with free, safe water. Locals block the spout with a finger so that a jet of water shoots up from a small hole on top, and they drink from that. Putting your mouth on the spout itself is frowned upon.
mapQuery: Drink from the nasoni without touching the spout Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: Civitavecchia's churches have their own stories
description: In Civitavecchia, the Church of the Japanese Martyrs honours Japanese Christians martyred in the sixteenth century, and the town has deep links with Japan. Like all churches in Italy, it expects modest dress and quiet behaviour, especially during services.
mapQuery: Civitavecchia's churches have their own stories Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: Cards work almost everywhere, but carry coins
description: Greek businesses are generally required to accept card payments, and tapping a card or phone works in most shops, tavernas and on the metro gates. Still carry small euro notes and coins for kiosks (periptera), street snacks like koulouri bread rings, church candles and public toilets, where cards may not be practical.
mapQuery: Cards work almost everywhere, but carry coins Athens (Piraeus)

name: Tipping is a thank-you, not a rule
description: Service is not usually added to bills in Greece, and tipping is appreciated rather than expected. Rounding up or leaving around 5–10% in cash on the table for good service is the norm; a card machine often has no tip option, so keep a few coins handy.
mapQuery: Tipping is a thank-you, not a rule Athens (Piraeus)

name: The Acropolis ticket costs more than people expect
description: The standard Acropolis ticket rose to €30 in 2025, and it covers only the Acropolis and its slopes. If you plan to see several sites, the combined ticket can be better value; check current prices on the official Hellenic Heritage site before you go, as fees change seasonally.
mapQuery: The Acropolis ticket costs more than people expect Athens (Piraeus)

name: Metro is cheap; the airport line is not
description: A standard metro ticket from Piraeus into central Athens is a small fixed fare, one of the best bargains of the day. Journeys to or from the airport on Line 3 cost considerably more, which catches travellers out if they are heading straight to a flight.
mapQuery: Metro is cheap; the airport line is not Athens (Piraeus)

name: Agree on taxi fares from the port
description: Yellow taxis should run on the meter, with surcharges for things like late-night hours and luggage. At the cruise terminal some drivers quote flat fares for sightseeing loops; agreeing the price and the itinerary before you get in avoids arguments at the end.
mapQuery: Agree on taxi fares from the port Athens (Piraeus)

name: Watch out for dynamic currency conversion
description: Many independent ATMs, especially the brightly branded ones near tourist areas, charge high withdrawal fees and offer to convert your withdrawal into your home currency at a poor rate. Use a bank ATM when you can and always choose to be charged in euros.
mapQuery: Watch out for dynamic currency conversion Athens (Piraeus)

name: VAT is already in the price
description: Greek prices on menus and price tags include VAT, which is 24% on most goods, so what you see is what you pay. Non-EU visitors buying goods above a minimum spend in shops displaying tax-free signs can claim VAT refunds; ask for the paperwork at the till.
mapQuery: VAT is already in the price Athens (Piraeus)

name: The cable car is pay-as-you-go
description: The cable car between Fira's old port and the town costs about €10 per person each way, with no return tickets, and payment is at the bottom or top station. Donkey rides cost about the same, while the long staircase is free, if steep.
mapQuery: The cable car is pay-as-you-go Santorini

name: Oia prices reflect the view
description: Coffee, cocktails and dinner on the caldera rim in Oia, Fira and Imerovigli cost noticeably more than in the inland villages, and sunset tables often come with minimum spends. Pyrgos, Megalochori and the beach strips at Kamari and Perissa offer much gentler prices for similar food.
mapQuery: Oia prices reflect the view Santorini

name: Cruise passenger levy
description: Greece introduced a per-passenger cruise levy in 2025, highest on Santorini and Mykonos during the peak months. It is normally collected by the cruise line rather than charged ashore, so check your booking terms rather than expecting a bill on the island.

name: Bring cash for buses and small purchases
description: The KTEL public buses from Fira are inexpensive and tickets are bought on board or from conductors, where cash is the safe bet. Small tavernas in the villages and beach kiosks may also prefer cash, though most larger businesses accept cards.
mapQuery: Bring cash for buses and small purchases Santorini

name: Sunbeds and boat trips add up
description: On organised beaches, a pair of loungers and an umbrella is typically charged per day, or in exchange for a minimum food and drink spend, and prices are highest at the trendiest beach clubs. Volcano and caldera cruises vary widely in price; the island entry fee for Nea Kameni is usually paid on top.
mapQuery: Sunbeds and boat trips add up Santorini

name: Tipping guides and boat crews
description: Tips for tour guides, drivers and catamaran crews are appreciated but not obligatory. Around 10% or a few euros per person for a good half-day tour is a common and gracious gesture, ideally in cash.
mapQuery: Tipping guides and boat crews Santorini

name: Wine tastings are priced like experiences
description: Winery visits usually involve a paid tasting flight rather than free sips, and the price rises with the number of wines and food pairings. It is still among the best-value experiences on the island, and buying a bottle is never expected.
mapQuery: Wine tastings are priced like experiences Santorini

name: Cash still matters away from town
description: Cards are widely accepted in Chania's old town, but village tavernas, mountain kafeneia and beach canteens along the south coast may prefer or require cash. ATMs thin out quickly once you leave the main towns, so withdraw before heading into the hills.
mapQuery: Cash still matters away from town Chania

name: Gorge and reserve fees
description: Popular hikes carry small entrance fees: Samaria Gorge was about €10 and Imbros about €5 in recent seasons, paid at the kiosks. Parking at busy spots like Elafonisi and Balos usually costs a few euros, and Balos access has its own reserve fee.

name: The Cretan treat at the end of the meal
description: Many tavernas bring a complimentary raki and a small dessert at the end of a meal, so do not be surprised if you did not order it. Tipping around 5–10% for good service, left in cash on the table, is appreciated but not required.
mapQuery: The Cretan treat at the end of the meal Chania

name: Harbourfront tables cost more
description: Restaurants directly on the Venetian harbour charge for the view and some use touts to pull in diners. A few lanes back, in the old town and Splantzia, you will often eat better for less.

name: South coast boats and buses
description: Ferries along the south coast between Chora Sfakion, Loutro, Agia Roumeli and Sougia, and the KTEL buses over the mountains, are inexpensive but sold as separate tickets. Buy them in advance in peak season, and carry cash for small boat operators.
mapQuery: South coast boats and buses Chania

name: Taxis from Souda
description: Taxis between Souda port and Chania are metered or quoted at fixed fares; confirm the price before departing. The public bus is a cheaper option for the same journey.

name: Olympia is the real cost of the day
description: Katakolon itself is free to wander, but most visitors spend their money getting to Ancient Olympia and on its entrance ticket, which covers the site and museum. Prices change seasonally, so check the official rate before you go.
mapQuery: Olympia is the real cost of the day Katakolon

name: Taxis to Olympia are negotiated
description: Drivers at the pier offer return trips to Olympia, typically priced per car with waiting time included. Agree the price, the time at the site and the return time clearly before leaving, and consider sharing with fellow passengers to split the cost.
mapQuery: Taxis to Olympia are negotiated Katakolon

name: Village prices are gentle
description: Away from the tourist shops, coffee, pastries and simple taverna meals in Katakolon and Pyrgos are among the most reasonably priced on the itinerary. Cards are usually fine, but carry small notes for kiosks.

name: Wine tastings nearby
description: Several wineries in the hills around the Elis plain offer tastings, often paid by the flight. These are usually part of organised excursions, so budget for transport as well as tasting fees.

name: Tipping is low-key
description: As elsewhere in Greece, tipping is appreciated rather than expected: round up or leave around 5–10% in cash for good service. A few euros for a helpful driver or guide is a kind gesture.

name: The Liston comes at a premium
description: Sitting under the arcades of the Liston facing the Spianada is one of Corfu's great pleasures, and it is priced accordingly. A drink there costs noticeably more than in the back lanes of the old town; treat it as paying for the setting.
mapQuery: The Liston comes at a premium Corfu

name: Cards are common, but buses want cash
description: Most shops and restaurants in Corfu Town accept cards, but the green KTEL and blue city buses, small village tavernas and some beach kiosks are simplest with cash. Keep small notes and coins on hand.
mapQuery: Cards are common, but buses want cash Corfu

name: Taxis often quote fixed fares
description: Taxis from the port to the old town or to sights like the Achilleion and Paleokastritsa often operate on posted fixed fares or agreed prices. Confirm the price before you set off, especially for longer island loops with waiting time.
mapQuery: Taxis often quote fixed fares Corfu

name: Beach costs on the west coast
description: At popular beaches such as Paleokastritsa, loungers and umbrellas are usually rented by the day, and boat trips to the coves are sold separately. Parking near the most famous beaches can be limited and occasionally paid.
mapQuery: Beach costs on the west coast Corfu

name: Tips in Corfu
description: Tipping is not obligatory but appreciated: rounding up or around 5–10% for good service at a taverna, left in cash. Guides and drivers welcome a few euros per person for a good tour.

name: Sight entry fees
description: Corfu's Old Fortress, the Achilleion and several museums charge separate entry fees, which vary by season. If you are planning several in one day, budget for each rather than expecting a combined pass.

name: Croatia uses the euro
description: Croatia adopted the euro in 2023, so older guidebooks quoting kuna are out of date. Cards are widely accepted, but small cafés, market stalls and some island boats still prefer cash.

name: Tipping is modest
description: Service is rarely included, and tipping around 10% for good restaurant service is common but not mandatory. Card machines often do not allow tips, so leave cash if you want to.

name: The palace is free; some parts are not
description: Walking through Diocletian's Palace and the Peristyle costs nothing, but the cathedral, bell tower, cellars and other individual sites each charge separate entry fees. Combined tickets for the cathedral complex can save a little.
mapQuery: The palace is free; some parts are not Split

name: Island day trips cost more than the ferry
description: Jadrolinija ferries and catamarans to Brač and Hvar are reasonably priced, but Hvar Town in particular is one of the most expensive places on the Croatian coast for food and drink. Buy return tickets early in summer, when boats sell out.
mapQuery: Island day trips cost more than the ferry Split

name: Riva prices versus back streets
description: Cafés along the Riva charge a premium for their palm-lined view. Varoš and the streets just outside the palace walls offer the same coffee and grilled fish for noticeably less.
mapQuery: Riva prices versus back streets Split

name: Avoid expensive ATMs
description: Independent cash machines near the waterfront often charge high fees and push dynamic currency conversion. Use a bank ATM and always choose to be charged in euros.

name: VAT is high but included
description: Croatian VAT is 25% on most goods and is included in displayed prices. Non-EU visitors can claim refunds on qualifying purchases from shops participating in tax-free shopping.
mapQuery: VAT is high but included Split

name: The city walls ticket is steep
description: Walking the city walls costs around €40 per person, among the most expensive single attractions on this voyage. The Dubrovnik Pass, at a similar price, adds Fort Lovrijenac, the Rector's Palace and several museums plus public transport, so it is usually the better buy.
mapQuery: The city walls ticket is steep Dubrovnik

name: Lokrum and the cable car add up
description: The boat to Lokrum, including the island entry fee, costs around €27–30, and the cable car up Mount Srđ is about €30 return. Buy cable car tickets at the official station rather than from resellers who add fees.
mapQuery: Lokrum and the cable car add up Dubrovnik

name: Old town prices are high
description: Food and drink inside the walls, especially on the Stradun, are among the priciest in Croatia. Restaurants in Gruž, Lapad and Cavtat offer better value for comparable quality.
mapQuery: Old town prices are high Dubrovnik

name: Buses need tickets in advance or exact change
description: Libertas city buses from Gruž to the Pile Gate are inexpensive; tickets bought from kiosks are slightly cheaper than paying the driver. The Dubrovnik Pass includes bus travel.
mapQuery: Buses need tickets in advance or exact change Dubrovnik

name: Tipping in Dubrovnik
description: Around 10% for good restaurant service is appreciated but not required. Guides and boat crews welcome a cash tip for a memorable trip.

name: Cash for small boats and markets
description: Most businesses accept cards, but kayak rentals, small boat operators and market stalls at Gundulić Square may prefer cash. Avoid the high-fee independent ATMs near Pile Gate.
mapQuery: Cash for small boats and markets Dubrovnik

name: Montenegro uses the euro, but is not in the EU
description: Montenegro uses the euro even though it is not an EU member, so you will not need to change money. Because it is outside the EU, some EU mobile roaming plans do not cover it, and data charges can be high; check your plan before arriving.
mapQuery: Montenegro uses the euro, but is not in the EU Kotor

name: Cash is more important here
description: Cards are accepted in many restaurants and shops in Kotor's old town, but cash is still common for taxis, small boats, market stalls and some cafés. Public toilets in the old town typically charge a small fee.
mapQuery: Cash is more important here Kotor

name: The fortress climb has a fee
description: The climb to the San Giovanni fortress along the city walls costs €15 per person, paid at the booth or ticket machine. Cash is the most reliable option.
mapQuery: The fortress climb has a fee Kotor

name: Boats to Our Lady of the Rocks
description: Small boats from Perast to the island church usually cost around €10 per person return, with a separate small fee to enter the church and museum. Boat touts may offer packages with parking; compare before you commit.
mapQuery: Boats to Our Lady of the Rocks Kotor

name: Lovćen has two fees
description: Lovćen National Park charges a small entry fee per person, and the Njegoš Mausoleum at the summit charges a separate ticket. Both are usually paid on site.

name: Tipping is around 10%
description: Tipping roughly 10% for good restaurant service is customary but not obligatory. Drivers and guides appreciate a cash tip for a good day out.

name: Taxis should be agreed in advance
description: Taxis are inexpensive compared with western Europe, but meters are not always used. Agree the price before you go, especially for trips along the bay or up the Serpentine road.
mapQuery: Taxis should be agreed in advance Kotor

name: Expect a cover charge
description: Many restaurants add a coperto, a per-person cover charge for bread and table setting, typically a couple of euros. It is legal and normal; check the menu, where it should be listed.

name: Pizza is a bargain
description: Naples is one of the best-value food cities in Italy: a classic margherita at a traditional pizzeria often costs less than a coffee and pastry in some other ports. Sfogliatelle and espresso at a bar counter are similarly cheap.

name: Coffee is cheaper at the bar
description: Drinking espresso standing at the counter costs far less than sitting at a table with service, a distinction strictly observed in Italian cafés. In busy squares, sitting down can double or triple the price.
mapQuery: Coffee is cheaper at the bar Naples

name: Use official taxis with fixed fares
description: Official white taxis offer fixed fares for common routes, including the port to the centre; ask for the 'tariffa predeterminata' before departing. Avoid unofficial drivers who approach you at the cruise terminal.
mapQuery: Use official taxis with fixed fares Naples

name: Tipping is light
description: Tipping is not expected in Italy, especially when a coperto has been charged. Rounding up or leaving a few euros for excellent service is appreciated; guides and drivers welcome a small cash tip.

name: Watch your wallet
description: Pickpocketing is a real concern on the Circumvesuviana, the metro and in crowded streets like Spaccanapoli. Carry only what you need and keep bags zipped and in front of you.

name: Capri and the islands cost more
description: Ferry and hydrofoil tickets to Capri are not cheap, and the island's prices for food, drink and sunbeds are among the highest on the coast. Small landing taxes for Capri are typically included in boat tickets.
mapQuery: Capri and the islands cost more Naples

name: The train is the cheapest way into Rome
description: A regional train ticket from Civitavecchia to Rome costs a fraction of a private transfer or taxi, which can be many times more expensive. Tickets can be bought at the station or on the Trenitalia app; paper tickets must be validated before boarding to avoid fines.
mapQuery: The train is the cheapest way into Rome Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: Cover charges and service
description: Like elsewhere in Italy, many restaurants add a per-person coperto, and some in tourist areas add a service charge as well. Check the bill before tipping; if service is included, no extra tip is needed.

name: Timed tickets drive the budget
description: Major sights like the Colosseum, Vatican Museums and the Pantheon require paid tickets, often timed. Booking on the official sites in advance avoids reseller markups and long queues.
mapQuery: Timed tickets drive the budget Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: Free water everywhere
description: Rome's public drinking fountains, the nasoni, provide cold, safe water for free all over the city. Carrying a refillable bottle saves money and helps on hot days.

name: Coffee prices depend on where you stand
description: An espresso at the bar is cheap; the same coffee at a table in a famous piazza can cost several times more. In historic cafés near the Spanish Steps or Pantheon, sitting down is part of the price.
mapQuery: Coffee prices depend on where you stand Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: Beware street hustles
description: Costumed 'gladiators' near the Colosseum charge for photos, and bracelet or rose sellers may push items into your hands then demand payment. Politely decline and keep walking; pickpocketing is also common on crowded buses and the metro.

name: Use bank ATMs
description: Bank-affiliated ATMs (Bancomat) usually offer better rates than independent machines. Always choose to be charged in euros to avoid poor conversion rates.

name: Civitavecchia itself is good value
description: If you stay in port, cafés, the covered market and seafood trattorie in Civitavecchia are noticeably cheaper than central Rome. A few spots near the cruise gate overcharge visitors, so check prices before ordering.
mapQuery: Civitavecchia itself is good value Rome (Civitavecchia)

name: Plaka and Anafiotika: The Village Under the Rock
description: Athens' oldest lived-in quarter wears its tourist trade on the surface. Climb a few lanes higher and you reach a whitewashed island village that has no business being in a capital city.
details:
Everyone ends up in Plaka. It is the neighbourhood folded around the north and east slopes of the Acropolis, the one that appears on postcards with bougainvillea over a doorway and a cat asleep on a step, and on any warm afternoon it carries more visitors than residents. That is the first thing to know about it, and also the least interesting. Plaka has been continuously lived in for longer than almost anywhere else in the city, and if you give it a little time it shows you that history in layers, from the street up.

The lower streets, Adrianou and Kydathineon especially, are the ones you will walk first. In the morning they are almost gentle. Shopkeepers hose down the marble, waiters wipe tables under the plane trees, and the air smells of coffee and wet stone. By midday the same streets are a slow-moving river of tour groups, sandal shops and menus in six languages. It is easy to decide Plaka is a souvenir arcade and leave. Don't. The trick is to keep walking uphill.

Above Plaka, pressed against the very foot of the Acropolis rock, is Anafiotika, and it is one of the most surprising corners of any European capital. In the nineteenth century, when Athens was being rebuilt as the capital of the new Greek state, builders and stonemasons came from the small Cycladic island of Anafi to work on the grand neoclassical buildings below. They needed somewhere to live, and the story goes that they simply built their own little island village overnight on the steep ground nobody else wanted, in the style they knew from home. Whether it really happened overnight is local legend; that they came from Anafi and built it themselves is the accepted history.

The result is a handful of whitewashed cube houses, blue shutters and potted geraniums, joined by passages so narrow you sometimes have to turn sideways. There are no shops worth the name. Signs ask you, politely, to keep your voice down, because people really do live here, some of them descendants of those first families. You will not find it by looking for it on a map so much as by following the lanes that seem to lead nowhere. Above you, close enough to feel, is the rock face of the Acropolis.

Plaka's other gift is its churches. Tucked between houses are small Byzantine chapels, some older than anything else around them, lit by oil lamps and smelling of beeswax. The tiny church of Agios Nikolaos Rangavas, at the edge of Anafiotika, is one of them; its bell is said to have been the first to ring out after Athens was freed from Ottoman control. Step inside any open church quietly, cover your shoulders, and you will often find an old woman tidying the candle stand who will nod you in.

There are museums here that the crowds walk straight past. The Museum of Greek Folk Musical Instruments, near the Roman Agora, lets you put on headphones and hear the lyra, the bagpipe and the bouzouki that you will hear later in the tavernas. The house museum of the folklorist Angeliki Hatzimichali shows how ordinary Greeks lived and dressed a century ago. Neither takes more than an hour, and both make the rest of the walk richer.

In the evening Plaka changes character again. The day-trippers drain away, the lanes cool, and the restaurants with rooftop terraces turn their tables to face the floodlit Parthenon. Some of these places trade on the view more than the cooking, and it is fair to be choosy. But there is nothing quite like eating grilled octopus and drinking a glass of house white while the temple glows gold above the rooftops. Later still, the stepped streets around Mnisikleous fill with families and couples, and someone will usually be playing a bouzouki.

What is Plaka good for? Wandering without a plan, a slow lunch in the shade, the best close-up views of the Acropolis from below, and that particular pleasure of turning a corner into silence. What is it not good for? Serious shopping, cheap eating on the main drag, or a sense of everyday modern Athens; for that you have to cross Ermou and go north into Psyrri or the market streets. And it is not a place to rush. The lanes double back on themselves, the signs are inconsistent, and the steps are polished smooth by two centuries of feet.

Go early if you can, before ten, when the light is soft and Anafiotika belongs to the cats and the people who live there. Go back at dusk if you have the time, when the rock above turns from white to honey to rose. In between, let yourself get a little lost. Plaka has been absorbing visitors for a very long time, and the best of it still rewards the ones who wander slowly.

name: Psyrri and Monastiraki: Where Athens Shops, Eats and Stays Up Late
description: A flea market at breakfast, a meat market at lunch, street art all afternoon and live music past midnight. This is the Athens Athenians actually use.
details:
If Plaka is Athens dressed for company, Monastiraki and Psyrri are Athens in its work clothes. The two neighbourhoods run into each other just north-west of the Acropolis, divided roughly by Ermou Street, and between them they hold the city's flea market, its central food market and some of its best late-night eating. They are loud, a little scruffy and wonderfully alive.

Start at Monastiraki Square, where the metro brings you up into the noise. There is a small Byzantine church in the middle of it and a former Ottoman mosque on one side, and above them all, framed perfectly, is the Acropolis. On the square itself you will smell koulouri, the sesame bread rings sold from carts, and roasting corn. Westward runs Ifestou, the street of the flea market, which in the mornings is a jumble of copper pots, old records, military surplus, icons, leather sandals and tat. The real antiques come out on Sunday mornings in Avissynias Square, where dealers spread furniture and old photographs on the cobbles and locals come to haggle seriously.

Walk north up Athinas Street and you reach the Varvakios Central Market, built in the nineteenth century under iron and glass. It is not a showpiece. Butchers call out prices over hanging lamb, the fish hall gleams wet under bare bulbs, and men in rubber boots push carts through the crowd. The surrounding streets are lined with spice merchants, olive sellers and shops selling cured meats and cheeses from every corner of Greece. Come in the morning, wear shoes you do not mind getting splashed, and you will see how a city of millions feeds itself.

Psyrri lies just west of the market. Thirty years ago it was a neighbourhood of small workshops, tanneries and warehouses, a little down-at-heel and a little rough. Then the bars and tavernas moved in, and it became one of the places Athenians go out at night. The workshops have not entirely gone; you can still find a cobbler, a basket-maker or a coppersmith tapping away in a doorway. But the walls are now covered in murals and street art, some of it striking, and the squares are filled with tables.

By day Psyrri can feel half-asleep. Shutters are down, a few cafés serve freddo espresso to people reading on their phones, and the street art is easy to see without crowds. This is the time to walk it, to look at the walls, and to find the small family places serving lunch. By night it is another neighbourhood entirely. From about ten o'clock the tables fill, music spills from doorways, and on weekends the noise carries on well past midnight. Some tavernas here have live rebetiko or laiko, the Greek popular music of the bouzouki, and on a good night the whole room sings along.

There is a gentler side, too. On Theatrou Square, at the market's edge, there are old tavernas where you can eat slow-cooked lamb under vines while musicians play. Wine bars and tasting rooms have opened in restored buildings, where you can be talked through Assyrtiko and Agiorgitiko by someone who knows. And there are now cooking schools, some of which begin with a walk through the market to buy ingredients, which is one of the best ways to spend a morning here.

Is it for everyone? Not quite. Parts of Psyrri and the streets towards Omonia can look neglected, and late at night some blocks are best avoided if you are unsure of your way; stick to the busy streets and squares. Pickpockets work the Monastiraki metro and the crowds around the flea market, as they do in any busy city centre. None of this is a reason to stay away. It is just the reality of a working neighbourhood rather than a museum.

What Psyrri and Monastiraki give you is the sense that Athens is a living city and not a backdrop to its ruins. You can buy a kilo of olives, an old brass coffee pot and a pair of hand-stitched sandals in a single morning, have lunch where the market traders eat, and come back at night to dance to bouzouki music under the same Acropolis you climbed that morning. Few places put ancient and everyday side by side so carelessly, or so well.

name: Koukaki: The Neighbourhood Behind the Museum
description: Five minutes from the Acropolis Museum, Koukaki is where Athenians drink coffee for two hours and visitors discover they would quite like to live.
details:
Koukaki does not have a single famous monument. That is part of its charm. It is a residential grid of apartment blocks, orange trees and small squares that sits just south of the Acropolis, between the new Acropolis Museum and the pine-covered slopes of Filopappou Hill. For years it was simply where ordinary Athenians lived. Over the last decade it has become one of the city's favourite places to stay, and somehow it has kept its neighbourly feel.

Begin on Dionysiou Areopagitou, the wide pedestrian avenue that curves around the southern foot of the Acropolis. It is one of the most beautiful walks in Athens: marble paving, olive trees, buskers, joggers in the morning and families strolling in the evening. On one side is the rock and the ancient theatre of Dionysus; on the other is the glass and concrete of the Acropolis Museum, opened in 2009, with excavated ruins visible beneath its glass floor. Makrygianni is the small, smart quarter around the museum. Koukaki starts just behind it.

The heart of the neighbourhood is Georgiou Olympiou and the pedestrian streets off it, especially Drakou. In the morning this is where Koukaki takes its coffee. Athenians do not do coffee quickly. A freddo espresso or a Greek coffee in a small cup can easily last an hour, and the tables fill with retirees reading newspapers, young parents, students with laptops and people who seem to have nowhere particular to be. Bakeries sell spanakopita and koulouri, and the corner kiosk, the periptero, sells everything from cigarettes to phone cards to cold water.

What Koukaki does best is the unhurried meal. There are neighbourhood tavernas here where the menu is written on a board, the wine comes in metal jugs and the owner may well be the one cooking. There are newer places too, run by young chefs doing lighter, modern versions of Greek dishes, and good bakeries and ice-cream shops. None of it is grand. All of it is a reminder that you are in a place where people live.

There is craft here, too. On the edge of the neighbourhood is the workshop of the Melissinos family, who have made leather sandals by hand in Athens for generations and became famous as the 'poet sandal maker'. A short walk in the other direction, a mother-and-daughter team runs cooking classes in their own home. Koukaki is full of these small, personal businesses, and they are part of why it feels like a neighbourhood rather than a district.

To the west, Filopappou Hill offers one of the best escapes in central Athens. Paths climb through pine and wild herbs past the little church of Agios Dimitrios Loumbardiaris, past the cave known locally as the 'prison of Socrates' (a tradition, not a documented fact), to the monument of Philopappos at the top. The view back across to the Parthenon is wide and quiet, and at sunset you will find Athenians up there with a bottle of wine, watching the light change. On summer evenings the open-air Dora Stratou theatre on the hill stages traditional Greek dances.

At night Koukaki is calm compared with Psyrri or Gazi. It has bars, but they are neighbourhood bars, the sort where you can hear yourself speak. That is exactly why many visitors choose to stay here. You can be at the Acropolis gate in ten minutes, wander back along Dionysiou Areopagitou under the floodlit rock, eat a late dinner without a reservation, and sleep without music from the street.

What is it not good for? Big sights, shopping beyond the everyday, or the energy of a nightlife quarter. And because it has become fashionable, some streets now hold more short-term rentals than permanent residents, which locals feel keenly. Treat it as the neighbourhood it still is.

If you have only a few hours in Athens, Koukaki is a natural place to finish: the museum in the morning, a long lunch on Drakou, a climb up Filopappou to watch the sun go down. If you have a few days, it is one of the best places in the city to come home to.

name: Piraeus Beyond the Ferry Gates: Kastella and Mikrolimano
description: Most cruise passengers see Piraeus only through a coach window. Walk twenty minutes from the terminal and you find a hilltop of sea captains' houses and a horseshoe harbour full of fishing boats.
details:
For most visitors Piraeus is a place you pass through. The ship ties up beside an enormous ferry port, the coaches are waiting, and within half an hour you are on the motorway to Athens. It is easy to come away thinking of it as a working port and nothing more. But Piraeus is a city in its own right, with a history as long as Athens' and a character quite separate from it, and two of its neighbourhoods reward anyone with a spare afternoon or evening.

The port has been the gateway to Athens since the fifth century BC, when the general Themistocles fortified it and the Long Walls linked it to the city. In the twentieth century it became something else as well: the landing place for many of the refugees from Asia Minor after 1922, and the birthplace of rebetiko, the music that grew out of their hardship in the port's tavernas and hashish dens. That rough, proud, seafaring identity is still here, even in the smartest corners.

Kastella is the hill that rises above the eastern side of Piraeus. Its streets climb in steep steps past neoclassical houses built by ship-owners and sea captains, with balconies that look out over the whole Saronic Gulf. At the top is the church of Profitis Ilias and, beside it, the open-air Veakio theatre, which hosts concerts on summer evenings. The view from up here takes in the commercial port, the islands of Salamina and Aegina, and on a clear day the mountains of the Peloponnese. In the morning Kastella is quiet and residential, with old men playing tavli in cafés and children walking to school down the steps.

Below Kastella, tucked into a little bay, is Mikrolimano, the 'small harbour'. It is a perfect horseshoe of water filled with fishing boats and sailing yachts, ringed by a promenade of seafood restaurants whose tables reach almost to the water's edge. This is where Athenians come for a long Sunday lunch of grilled fish, fried calamari and salads, or for an ouzo at sunset. In antiquity it was one of the three harbours of Piraeus; today it feels more like an island waterfront than part of a city of half a million.
