The rhythm of the harbour is very Greek. Lunch begins late and lasts for hours. In the late afternoon the light turns gold on the water and the yacht crews hose down their decks. In the evening the restaurants fill with families and couples, the waiters move between tables with platters held high, and the conversation grows louder as the night goes on. Prices on the waterfront can be high, especially for fish sold by weight, so it is fair to ask what a dish will cost before you order it.

Further round the coast is Zea, also called Pasalimani, a bigger marina where superyachts tie up beside the Hellenic Maritime Museum. And back in the centre of Piraeus, near the metro station, the neoclassical Municipal Theatre and the busy central market are reminders that this is a working city, not a resort. The old church of Agios Nikolaos, the patron saint of sailors, stands near the cruise terminal, and seamen still light candles there before sailing.

Piraeus is not where you go for ancient monuments; the best of those are in Athens. It is not a shopping destination either, and some streets around the port are busy and unlovely. But if your ship stays late, or you arrive a day early, an evening here gives you something Athens cannot: dinner by the water, with the sea breeze and the fishing boats close enough to touch.

There is also music. In a few tavernas near the centre, small bands still play the old songs on weekend nights, and the room joins in. It is the same music that was born here a century ago, sung by people whose grandparents may have arrived on those refugee ships.

Piraeus asks only that you get off the coach. Walk up the steps of Kastella in the late afternoon, come down to Mikrolimano as the lights come on, and you will understand why so many Athenians would rather spend their Sunday here than anywhere else.

name: Fira: The Capital on the Cliff Edge
description: Fira is where most of Santorini arrives, and on a busy day it can feel like the whole Aegean has come with you. Then the ships leave, the light softens, and the town remembers it is a town.
details:
Fira sits on the very lip of the caldera, more than two hundred metres above the sea, and for cruise passengers it is the first thing on the island. You come ashore at the Old Port far below, look up at a cliff of red and black volcanic rock striped with a zigzag path, and realise that the white town at the top is where you are going. You can ride the cable car, walk the hundreds of steps, or take one of the mules that still work the path. However you go, you arrive breathless in the middle of everything.

And for much of the day, everything is a lot. Fira is the island's capital and its commercial heart, and when several ships are anchored in the caldera its narrow lanes fill shoulder to shoulder. The main shopping street, Ypapantis, which locals call Gold Street for its jewellers, becomes a slow procession. Souvenir shops spill onto the paving, restaurants hold out menus, and the views are photographed from every possible angle. If this is all you see, Fira can seem like a beautiful place that has been overwhelmed.

But Fira has another rhythm, and it is worth catching. Early in the morning, before the first tender lands, the town belongs to the people who keep it running: delivery men pushing trolleys up the lanes, waiters sweeping terraces, the smell of bread from bakeries tucked behind the main streets. The caldera is still and blue, the cliffs are lit pink, and you can walk the edge in near silence. In the evening, once the last ship has left, a similar calm returns. Diners move to the cliff-edge terraces, and the sun drops behind Thirasia across the water.

Fira also has things that the caldera views tend to hide. The Museum of Prehistoric Thera holds finds from Akrotiri, the Bronze Age town buried by the great eruption, including delicate frescoes and a small gold ibex. The Orthodox cathedral, rebuilt after the 1956 earthquake, is large and bright. In the upper town there is a Catholic quarter, a legacy of the centuries when the island was ruled by Venetian lords, with its own cathedral and a convent. The famous blue-domed church often called the 'Three Bells of Fira', a short walk north, is Catholic too.

From Fira, the caldera path runs north along the cliff through Firostefani to Imerovigli, and eventually all the way to Oia. Even if you walk only the first stretch, twenty minutes to Firostefani, you leave most of the crowds behind and gain some of the island's best views. The path is paved and gentle here, with chapels and cave houses dug into the rock below you, and it is the easiest way to see the island's architecture up close.

At night Fira is the island's liveliest town, with bars that stay open late and clubs that cater to a young crowd in summer. If you want a quiet dinner, choose one of the caldera-view restaurants away from the main lanes, or walk up to Firostefani, which is calmer. If you want music and noise, it is here.

What is Fira good for? Practical things: banks, pharmacies, the bus station for getting around the island, and the main museums. Views of the caldera from right above the cruise anchorage. Sunsets with a dinner table rather than a crowd. What is it not good for? Peace in the middle of a busy cruise day, value for money on the main streets, or the sense of a traditional village; for that, you need to go inland.

A practical word about the steps. The path from the Old Port has roughly six hundred steps, and it is shared with the mules, which are not always gentle about it. The cable car is quicker, but on a busy day the queue to go back down can take a long time, so allow far more time than you think you need before your last tender. That single piece of planning makes the difference between a relaxed afternoon in Fira and a frantic one.

Fira is the island's front door, and front doors are always busy. Arrive early, leave late, and walk a little way along the cliff, and you will see why people have been building on this impossible edge for centuries.

name: Oia: Beauty, Crowds and the Hour Before Dawn
description: Oia is the Santorini of every photograph, and at sunset it can feel like everyone on earth has come to watch. Go when no one else does, and the village shows you why it was worth rebuilding.
details:
There is no point pretending Oia is undiscovered. It is, by some distance, the most photographed village in Greece: a cascade of white houses, blue domes and windmills down the northern tip of the caldera, facing west into the sunset. On summer evenings thousands of people gather along its walls and in the ruins of its little castle to watch the sun go down, and applaud when it does. Some visitors find this magical. Others find it too much. Both are right.

The village itself has a story that the crowds rarely hear. In the nineteenth century Oia was a prosperous port, home to sea captains whose ships traded across the Mediterranean. The captains built handsome mansions on the ridge, and the sailors and their families lived in cave houses dug into the soft volcanic rock below. In 1956 a powerful earthquake destroyed much of the village, and many families left for Athens or abroad. For years Oia was half empty. Its careful restoration from the 1970s onward is what turned it into the place you see today.

The best time to see it is the one almost nobody chooses: early morning. At seven o'clock the marble lanes are empty, the shopkeepers are only just opening their shutters, and the light comes from behind you, washing the white walls gold and turning the caldera a deep, clear blue. You can stand at the castle wall alone, walk down to the windmills without stepping round anyone, and hear the swifts. By ten, the first coaches have arrived. By late afternoon the lanes are full.

Oia has more to offer than the view. Below the village, a long stairway zigzags down the cliff to Ammoudi Bay, a tiny harbour of fishing boats and fish tavernas built right on the rocks. It is a stiff climb back up, but the reward is lunch at the water's edge and, for strong swimmers, the clear deep water off the rocks beyond. Another path leads down to Armeni, where small boats once moored. On the ridge itself there is a maritime museum in an old captain's house that tells the story of the families who made Oia rich.

Oia's main lane is lined with galleries and jewellers, some of them genuinely good, and with bookshops, including a much-loved independent one built into a cave. Among the cave houses you will find small hotels where the terraces drop one below the other down the cliff, each with its own plunge pool. Many visitors stay here for exactly that reason. In the evening, when the sunset crowds have gone, the village returns to them, and it becomes peaceful and intimate.

The sunset itself deserves honesty. It is beautiful, and the atmosphere can be joyful. But in high season the castle and the walls fill up an hour or more before the sun sets, and leaving afterwards means joining a slow crowd and a long queue for buses and taxis. Some people prefer to watch from a restaurant terrace, booked well ahead. Others walk a little way out along the caldera path towards Fira, where the view is almost as good and there is room to breathe.

What is Oia good for? The classic Santorini views, a romantic stay, Ammoudi's fish tavernas, and the extraordinary architecture of cave houses and captains' mansions. What is it not good for? Solitude at sunset, budget eating, or a quick visit on a tight cruise schedule; it is about twenty-five minutes by road from Fira, and getting back can take longer than you expect.

If you can, give Oia the quiet hours. Arrive early, walk down to the water, eat fish by the boats, and leave before the evening rush, or stay overnight and have it to yourself at dawn. The village is a survivor, rebuilt from rubble by people who loved it. It deserves to be seen when it can be heard as well as looked at.

name: Pyrgos: The Village That Looks Inland
description: On an island that faces the caldera, Pyrgos turns its back on it. That is exactly why you should go.
details:
Pyrgos sits on a hill in the middle of Santorini, about fifteen minutes by road south of Fira, and it is the village most people would choose if they were told they had to live here. It does not hang over the caldera. It rises in a cone of whitewashed houses and stepped lanes around the ruins of a Venetian castle, with views in every direction: over vineyards to the east coast, across to the caldera in the west, and up to the monastery on Profitis Ilias, the island's highest peak.

Its history is the history of Santorini's inland villages. For centuries, the threat of pirates meant that islanders built away from the coast, on high ground, behind walls. Pyrgos was one of the island's fortified settlements, a kasteli, with houses built tight against each other so that their outer walls formed a defence. Inside, the lanes twist and climb and double back. Today those lanes are some of the most beautiful on the island, and much quieter than Oia's.

Walk up from the small square where the buses stop. The paths are steep, paved with stone and whitewashed at the edges, and they lead past tiny churches, flowering courtyards and blue doors. Some of the old houses are restored, others still crumbling. Near the top, the castle is little more than walls and a viewpoint, but the view is extraordinary: the whole island laid out around you, with the caldera on one side and the dark sand of the east coast on the other. At the very top is a small church, and on summer evenings a café or two for a glass of wine.

In the morning Pyrgos is almost silent. You will meet more cats than people, and the occasional donkey carrying rubbish down from the upper lanes, which is how it still has to be done. At sunset some visitors drive up for the view, which looks west over the whole length of the caldera, and the terraces fill gently. But it never has the crush of Oia, and once the light has gone, the village quietens quickly.

Pyrgos is surrounded by vineyards, and this is the best part of the island for understanding Santorini wine. The vines are trained in low, basket-shaped coils called kouloura, lying flat on the volcanic soil to protect the grapes from wind. Several wineries sit within a few minutes of the village, and some offer tastings of Assyrtiko, the island's crisp, mineral white grape, and of Vinsanto, a sweet wine made from grapes dried in the sun. A tasting here, looking over the vines that made the wine, explains Santorini better than any guidebook.

From Pyrgos, an old path climbs to the monastery of Profitis Ilias, founded in the early eighteenth century, at the island's summit. It takes an hour or so on foot, though you can also drive. From the top, on a clear day, the view takes in the whole island and neighbouring ones far across the sea. The monastery itself is often closed to visitors, but the views are worth the walk.

What is Pyrgos good for? A slow, quiet walk through a traditional village; sunset without the crowds; wine; good tavernas with honest food; and a sense of the island's life away from the cliff edge. What is it not good for? Beaches, nightlife or the classic blue-domed photograph. And if you have mobility problems, the steep lanes are hard going; there are no cars in the upper village.

It is easy to visit Santorini and see only its western face, the face it shows to the cruise ships. Pyrgos is a reminder that the island has another side, with farms and churches and families who have lived here for generations. Go for an hour if that is all you have. It will be the hour you remember.

name: Kamari and Perissa: Santorini's Black-Sand Coast
description: On the far side of the island from the caldera, the cliffs give way to long black beaches, beach bars and a mountain with a lost ancient city on top. This is where Santorini goes to swim.
details:
The caldera side of Santorini is all drama: cliffs, sunsets, white houses on the edge of nothing. The east coast is a different island. Here the land slopes gently down to the sea and ends in long beaches of black volcanic sand and pebbles, warm underfoot and dark under clear water. Two resort villages, Kamari and Perissa, sit at either end of a great limestone mountain called Mesa Vouno, and between them they offer the island's best swimming.

Kamari is the more grown-up of the two. A long, paved promenade runs the length of the beach, lined with tavernas, cafés and small hotels, and in the evening it becomes a place to stroll. Families walk with ice creams, couples eat grilled fish with their feet almost in the sand, and older Greek visitors take their evening coffee watching the sea go dark. There is an open-air cinema in summer, one of the oldest on the island, where you watch films under the stars with a drink in your hand.

Perissa, on the other side of the mountain, is more relaxed and a little younger. Its beach runs south for kilometres, merging into Perivolos and Agios Georgios, and it is lined with sunbeds, umbrellas and beach bars that play music from late morning onward. It is cheaper and more casual than the caldera villages, and in high summer it draws a young crowd. Out of season it can be almost deserted, with just a few tavernas open and the wind blowing across the sand.

Between them stands Mesa Vouno, and on its ridge, more than three hundred metres up, are the ruins of Ancient Thera. This was the main city of the island from around the ninth century BC, after the great Bronze Age eruption, and it was occupied through Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine times. You can reach it by road from Kamari, up a cobbled, steep series of switchbacks, or by a stony path from Perissa. The site, with its agora, theatre, temples and houses spread along a windy ridge, is one of the most atmospheric on the island, and the views down to both beaches are dizzying.

The beaches themselves come with a few things worth knowing. The black sand gets extremely hot in the afternoon sun, so bring shoes. The water deepens quickly in places. In summer, sunbeds in front of bars usually come with an expectation that you will order something, and prices vary. And the meltemi, the strong north wind of the Aegean summer, can make some days choppy and blustery on this side.

Mornings are the best time for a swim, when the water is calm and the beaches are still being raked. Late afternoon is lovely, too, as the light softens and the crowds thin. Evenings on the promenades are relaxed and sociable, very different in mood from the sunset vigil on the caldera. Kamari in particular has a lived-in feel; many of its residents work in the island's tourism and live here year-round.

What are Kamari and Perissa good for? Swimming, lazy beach days, family holidays, cheaper eating, and the ancient city on the mountain. They are also convenient for the airport and the island's wineries. What are they not good for? Caldera views or the traditional village atmosphere of Pyrgos and Oia. Neither village is especially beautiful in itself; their beauty is the sea and the mountain.

If you have time to swim on Santorini, this is where to do it. Combine an early climb to Ancient Thera with a long, lazy lunch on the beach below, and you will see a side of the island that most cruise passengers never reach.

name: The Venetian Harbour: Chania's Front Room
description: A crescent of Venetian façades, an Ottoman mosque and an Egyptian-built lighthouse, all reflected in the same water. By day it is a stage; at night it becomes Chania's living room.
details:
There are few harbours in the Mediterranean as beautiful as Chania's, and almost none that tell so much history in one glance. Stand on the quay at the corner by the old mosque and look around. The curve of tall, faded houses in ochre and rose and peeling blue are Venetian, built when the Republic of Venice ruled Crete from the thirteenth century until 1645. The domed building beside you is the Mosque of the Janissaries, raised by the Ottomans after they took the city, and the oldest Ottoman building on the island. At the end of the long breakwater stands the lighthouse, slender and pale, rebuilt in the 1830s during the brief years when Crete was governed from Egypt. Its slightly minaret-like shape is a clue to who finished it.

Cruise ships do not dock here; they berth at Souda Bay, a few kilometres away, and passengers come in by shuttle or taxi. That short journey is worth it. The moment you walk through the lanes onto the harbour front, the whole sweep opens up, and it is one of those places that makes people stop and simply look.

In the morning the harbour is at its most honest. Fishermen sort nets on the quay, cafés put out their chairs, and the light comes low across the water, turning the Venetian façades gold. Locals sit with a coffee and a bougatsa, the creamy filo pastry Chania is known for, and the waiters have time to talk. It is the best hour for walking out along the breakwater to the lighthouse, past the old fortress walls, and looking back at the whole town with the White Mountains rising behind it.

By midday the harbour belongs to visitors. Restaurants along the waterfront set out long rows of tables and send people out with menus to bring you in. Horse-drawn carriages wait for fares, and boats offer trips along the coast. Some of the waterfront restaurants cook well; many trade on the view. It is fair to look at the menu carefully and to know that the better and cheaper food is often one street back.

Behind the harbour, on the eastern side, are the great stone arches of the Venetian arsenals, where galleys were built and repaired. Some have been restored as exhibition spaces; one holds a reconstruction of a Minoan ship. On the western side is the Firkas fortress, now home to the Maritime Museum of Crete, and the spot where the Greek flag was raised over Crete in 1913, when the island finally joined Greece. That date matters here. Crete spent the late nineteenth century in revolt against Ottoman rule, became an autonomous state in 1898, and united with Greece only fifteen years later. Chania was its capital until 1971, and the town still carries a proud, slightly separate air.

Evening is when the harbour comes into its own. As the sun goes down, the whole town seems to drift towards the water. Families walk the quay with ice cream, young people gather on the steps by the mosque, and the restaurants fill. Lights come on in the windows of the old houses and reflect in the water, and from somewhere there is often the sound of a lyra, the Cretan three-stringed fiddle. It is not quiet, but it is joyful in a way that feels genuinely local.

The harbour is good for a first look at Chania, for coffee in the morning and a drink at sunset, and for walking. It is not the place to find the city's best food, nor its quietest corners; for those you need to slip into the lanes behind it. And in high summer the waterfront can be very crowded in the middle of the day.

The best way to use it is as your starting point and your ending point. Come down in the morning to see it waking, disappear into the old town for the day, and come back at dusk when everyone else in Chania does. The harbour has been the centre of this city for eight hundred years. It still knows how to gather people in.

name: Splantzia: The Quiet Square Behind the Crowds
description: Five minutes from the busy harbour, a plane tree shades a square where church and minaret stand side by side, and Chania goes about its day.
details:
Splantzia is the old quarter that sits just behind the eastern end of the harbour, and it is where many visitors first realise how much of Chania is hidden. You turn off the busy waterfront, walk up a lane or two, and arrive in a small square shaded by an enormous plane tree. Around it are cafés with mismatched chairs, a few small shops, and a church with an unusual feature: a minaret.

That church, Agios Nikolaos, explains a great deal about Splantzia. It began as a Venetian Dominican monastery church, was turned into a mosque by the Ottomans, and became an Orthodox church after the Ottoman period ended. Today it has both a bell tower and a minaret, which makes it, by local reckoning, one of very few churches anywhere with both. Nearby are the ruins of other churches and the old Ottoman baths. In Splantzia, layers of Chania's past sit next to each other without fuss.

This was the heart of the Turkish quarter in Ottoman times, and later a working-class neighbourhood of artisans and small traders. For a long time it was a little forgotten, and some houses were left to fall down. Over the last couple of decades it has been gently revived. Old houses have become small guesthouses, the square has become a meeting place, and there are craft workshops, a few galleries and some of the best small restaurants in the old town.

The morning in Splantzia is lovely. The square is in shade, people sit under the plane tree with coffee, and you can hear the bells of Agios Nikolaos. The light falls through the leaves onto the cobbles. It is a good time to wander the surrounding lanes, where houses still show Venetian doorways and Ottoman wooden balconies, and where the cats outnumber the tourists.

At lunchtime and in the evening, the tavernas around the square and in the lanes nearby fill with a mix of locals and visitors who have found their way here. This is a good part of town to try Cretan cooking, which is quite distinct from the rest of Greece: dakos, a barley rusk topped with tomato and soft cheese; boureki, a baked dish of courgette, potato and cheese; snails cooked with rosemary; wild greens; and slow-cooked lamb. Many places will finish the meal by bringing raki and a sweet to the table without charging for it. Accepting is a courtesy.

Just to the west of Splantzia, a few lanes away, are two streets that have kept their old crafts. Skridlof is lined with leather shops, and the knife-makers' street still has craftsmen making the traditional Cretan knife, sometimes engraved with a verse. These are the last traces of an artisan town, and they are worth a slow look.

Splantzia is good for slowing down. For coffee under the plane tree, for an unhurried lunch, for a sense of how people actually live in the old town. It is not good for big sights or for the dramatic harbour views; you need to walk back down to the water for those. And because it has become popular, the square can get busy on summer evenings, though never with the same crush as the waterfront.

If the harbour is Chania's front room, Splantzia is its kitchen table. It is where the town sits down, catches up and eats properly. Find it once, and you will probably keep coming back.

name: Evraiki and Topanas: Lanes of Memory
description: West of the harbour, the old Jewish quarter and the Venetian aristocrats' streets hold the prettiest lanes in Chania and one of its most moving stories.
details:
The western half of Chania's old town is a tangle of narrow lanes, stone archways and tall houses with balconies wrapped in bougainvillea. It is the part of the city that most closely resembles an old Venetian town, and it divides into two quarters that blur into one another: Topanas, the old aristocratic neighbourhood, and Evraiki, the Jewish quarter. Walking here is the great pleasure of a day in Chania.

Topanas takes its name from the Ottoman word for the artillery that was once stored here, near the Firkas fortress. In the Venetian period, wealthy families built grand houses on these streets, with carved stone doorways and coats of arms, many of which survive. Theotokopoulou Street, running along the inside of the old sea wall, is one of the most photographed lanes in the city, its old houses now holding small hotels, workshops and galleries. Climb onto the Venetian walls nearby, and you look straight out to sea.

Evraiki sits just inland. A Jewish community lived in Chania for over two thousand years, and this was their quarter. Its centre was the synagogue of Etz Hayyim, a former Venetian church converted to a synagogue in the Ottoman period. In 1944, the occupying German forces arrested Chania's Jewish community and put them aboard a ship called the Tanais, which was sunk in the Aegean; almost the entire community died. For decades afterwards, the synagogue stood derelict.

In the 1990s, it was restored, and today it is again a place of prayer, study and remembrance, open to visitors of every faith. A small garden holds the graves of rabbis; a memorial lists the names of those who were lost. It is a quiet, beautiful place, and many visitors find it the most affecting thing they see in Chania. It is courteous to check its opening times and to visit respectfully.

The atmosphere of these lanes changes through the day. In the morning they are still and cool, shaded by tall walls, with the sound of someone sweeping a doorstep or a radio from an open window. This is the best time to walk them and to notice the details: Venetian lintels, Ottoman wooden balconies, carved fountains, the odd half-ruined house with a fig tree growing out of it.

In the evening, the lanes become the most romantic part of the city. Small restaurants put out tables in the alleys and on tiny squares, strings of lights hang overhead, and diners eat in the warm air under the balconies. Some of Chania's best restaurants are here, and some of its most touristy, too. A good rule is to choose places where you can hear Greek being spoken at the next table.

The western old town is good for wandering, photography, small boutique hotels, and memorable dinners. It is not good for anyone in a hurry; the lanes are a maze, signage is poor, and the cobbles are uneven and slippery when polished by feet. In high summer the most famous lanes can be crowded with people taking the same photograph. Turn a corner or two, and you will usually find yourself alone.

This is the part of Chania that rewards the patient. Walk slowly, look up, and remember that these were homes for communities that are no longer here. The beauty of the place is real. So is its memory.

name: Halepa and Koum Kapi: Chania by the Sea, Away from the Walls
description: East along the shore, the consuls' mansions of Halepa and the seafront cafés of Koum Kapi show you a Chania of neoclassical villas, sea breezes and local life.
details:
Most visitors never leave the old town, and it is easy to see why. But follow the sea wall east from the harbour, past the arsenals and the old walls, and the city opens out into a different landscape: a long seafront promenade and, above it, a hillside of grand nineteenth-century houses. This is Koum Kapi and, beyond it, Halepa, and together they show a Chania that is more relaxed, more residential and very much lived in.

Koum Kapi is the seafront just outside the old town walls. Its name comes from Turkish and refers to the sand gate in the old fortifications. The neighbourhood has a mixed history; at one time it was home to a community from North Africa who came during the Ottoman period. Today it is mostly known for its long line of cafés and bars along the water, where Chaniots come to sit facing the sea. In the morning it is quiet, with joggers and dog walkers on the promenade. On summer evenings it fills with people of all ages taking a drink or an ice cream in the cooler air.

Climb inland and uphill, and you reach Halepa. In the late nineteenth century, when Crete was moving towards independence from the Ottomans and then became an autonomous state, this was the smart part of town. Foreign consuls built residences here, and wealthy Cretan families built neoclassical villas with gardens and high windows looking out to sea. Prince George of Greece, who was High Commissioner of the autonomous Cretan State, lived here too. Some of the old mansions are beautifully kept; others are faded and overgrown, which has its own charm.

Halepa is also closely associated with Eleftherios Venizelos, the Cretan statesman who went on to become one of Greece's most important prime ministers. His family home here is now a museum telling his story and the story of Crete's struggle for union with Greece. Venizelos is buried on the Akrotiri hill above the city, at a site with one of the best views over Chania, which you can reach by taxi in a few minutes.

The atmosphere of these neighbourhoods is the main reason to come. They are quieter, greener and airier than the old town. Old men play tavli in cafés, grandmothers sit on doorsteps, and there are neighbourhood tavernas and fish restaurants where most of the customers are local. It is a good place to see how Chaniots spend an ordinary evening by the sea.

There are small city beaches too, rocky bays where locals swim, and a gentle sea walk that you can follow for a long way. In the early evening, with the light turning gold on the water and the White Mountains rising behind the town, it is one of the loveliest walks in Chania.

What are Halepa and Koum Kapi good for? A seafront stroll, a quiet drink by the water, local tavernas, history away from the crowds, and a sense of the modern city. What are they not good for? The postcard harbour views or the dense medieval lanes of the old town. They are also a walk of twenty minutes or more from the centre, so allow time if you are on a cruise schedule.

Chania is not only its harbour and its old town. Walk east along the sea at sunset, past the cafés of Koum Kapi and up into the villas of Halepa, and you will see the city as it sees itself: proud, sociable and in no hurry at all.

name: Katakolon: A Fishing Village That Hosts the World
description: Most passengers rush through it on the way to Olympia. Linger, and Katakolon turns out to be a sleepy, sea-salted village with one street, one harbour and a lot of patience.
details:
Katakolon is not a town so much as a waterfront. A single street runs along the harbour, lined on one side by low houses, cafés and shops and on the other by the sea, and behind it a green hill rises steeply. On a day when no ship is in, it has a few hundred residents, a handful of fishing boats and a pace of life that makes it hard to believe it is a cruise port at all. On a day when a big ship ties up, several thousand people walk off the gangway onto that single street. The village absorbs them with remarkable good humour.

Its role is simple. Katakolon is the nearest port to Ancient Olympia, about forty minutes inland, and most passengers spend only a few minutes here before boarding coaches. That is a shame, because the village has a gentle charm of its own. In the morning, before the shops open, fishermen sort their nets on the quay, old men take their first coffee of the day outside the kafeneio, and the water in the harbour is flat and clear enough to see the fish. Swallows dart over the rooftops. It is very quiet.

Later, the main street wakes up to meet the visitors. Shops sell olive oil, honey, local wine, leather goods and souvenirs; tavernas set out tables by the water; and the prices, while geared towards visitors, are usually gentler than in the big island ports. The tavernas here serve simple, honest food: grilled sardines and octopus, Greek salads with tomatoes that taste of something, fried courgettes, local feta and village bread. On a hot day, sitting with your feet almost in the harbour and a cold glass of retsina in front of you is hard to beat.

There is more to see than you might expect. In the village, the Museum of Ancient Greek Technology displays working reconstructions of ancient inventions, from water clocks and automata to models of the Antikythera mechanism, the ancient Greek astronomical calculator. It is a small place but a fascinating one, and a good complement to Olympia, especially for families. A walk out along the headland brings you to the lighthouse, with a sweeping view of the Ionian coast, and on the high ground towards neighbouring Agios Andreas are the scant remains of a medieval fortress known locally as Pontikokastro, the 'mouse castle'.

Katakolon also has a small station, the end of a branch railway that once carried visitors and freight between the port, the town of Pyrgos and Olympia. Service on the line has been interrupted for long periods, so whether a train is running when you visit is something to check on the day rather than assume. When it does run, the slow journey through olive groves and farmland is a lovely way to travel.

The surrounding countryside is the region of Ilia, one of the agricultural heartlands of the Peloponnese. Olive groves stretch to the horizon, along with vineyards and fields of watermelons and tomatoes. A few wine estates are within a short drive, and some welcome visitors for tastings. If you have already seen Olympia, or simply do not want to spend the day on a coach, a visit to one of them, followed by lunch back at the harbour, makes a very pleasant alternative.

In the evening, if your ship sails late, the village returns almost instantly to itself. The cafés fill with locals, children play by the water, and the light over the Ionian turns orange and then violet. There is no nightlife to speak of, which is part of the appeal.

What is Katakolon good for? A relaxed hour or two by the sea, simple seafood, local products, the technology museum, and a gentle walk up to the lighthouse. What is it not good for? Big-city sights, serious shopping or anything lively after dark. It is also very hot in summer, with little shade along the waterfront at midday.

Most people remember Katakolon as the place where the coach left from. Those who stay a little longer remember the quiet harbour, the friendly waiters and the feeling of a Greek village that has learned to welcome the world without losing itself.

name: Ancient Olympia: The Village Beside the Sanctuary
description: Everyone comes for the ruins. Fewer notice the small modern village next door, which lives quietly in the shade of the most famous sports ground on earth.
details:
There are two Olympias. The first is the sanctuary of Zeus, where the ancient Olympic Games were held for more than a thousand years: a wooded valley at the meeting of two rivers, full of fallen columns, temple foundations and the famous stadium, entered through a vaulted stone tunnel. The second is the modern village of Archaia Olympia, a short walk away, which grew up in the last two centuries to serve the archaeologists and then the visitors who followed them. Most people see only the first. The second is worth a little of your time.

The setting explains why the ancient Greeks chose it. The sanctuary lies in a green, sheltered valley below the pine-covered hill of Kronos, between the Alfeios and Kladeos rivers. Even in summer, the old plane trees and pines give shade, and the place has a stillness that is very different from the crowded sites of Athens. This is where athletes from across the Greek world gathered every four years, where the great Temple of Zeus once held Phidias' gold-and-ivory statue, and where, today, the flame for every modern Olympic Games is lit at the ruined Temple of Hera.

The best time to visit the sanctuary is first thing in the morning, before the coaches from the cruise port and from Athens arrive, or in the late afternoon. Midday is hot and busy, and the site, though shaded in parts, can be draining. The Archaeological Museum, across the road, is one of the finest in Greece: the sculptures from the Temple of Zeus, the Hermes attributed to Praxiteles and the winged Nike of Paionios are worth the visit alone. If the heat becomes too much, it is a cool place to retreat.

The modern village stretches along one main street lined with cafés, tavernas, souvenir shops and small hotels. It is not old or especially beautiful, but it is friendly and practical. In the morning it is quiet; shopkeepers set out displays of olive wood, honey, olive oil and replica statues, and locals take coffee before the buses arrive. By midday it is busy with tour groups eating lunch before heading back to the coaches. In the evening, when the last of them have gone, the village becomes peaceful, and the few visitors who stay overnight have the place, and often the tavernas, almost to themselves.

There are smaller museums in the village that most visitors skip. The Museum of the History of the Olympic Games in Antiquity tells the story of the ancient competitions through objects and inscriptions. There is also a museum dedicated to the modern Olympic revival. Above the village, on the hillside, the International Olympic Academy keeps alive the idea of the Games as education rather than only sport, and the monument to Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the modern Olympics, stands nearby; his heart is buried there, in keeping with his wishes.

The surrounding hills carry the marks of the devastating wildfires of 2007, which burned up to the edge of the sanctuary before they were stopped. Much has regrown, but the memory is still raw here, and in summer the risk of fire is taken seriously across the region.

What is Olympia good for? Ancient history at its most evocative, an outstanding museum, and a quiet overnight stay if you have the time. What is it not good for? Nightlife, beaches or a quick visit at midday in August, when the heat and crowds can take the pleasure out of it. Allow at least three hours for the site and museum together.

Walking out of the stadium tunnel onto the ancient track, it is hard not to break into a run. Almost everyone does. It is the one place in Greece where a ruin invites you not only to look but to take part, and the small village beside it seems to understand that its job is simply to look after the people who come to try.

name: Pyrgos: The Market Town Nobody Visits
description: Twenty minutes from the ship, the capital of Ilia is a real Greek provincial town, with neoclassical squares, a grand old market hall and not a souvenir in sight.
details:
Between Katakolon and Olympia lies Pyrgos, the capital of the Ilia region, and almost every cruise coach drives through it without stopping. That is understandable; it has no famous monuments and no beach. But if you are curious about how ordinary Greeks live, away from the islands and the ruins, Pyrgos offers something the tourist sites cannot: a working provincial town with its own rhythm, and no interest at all in performing for visitors.

Pyrgos grew up as a market town for the farms of the surrounding plain, which is some of the most fertile land in the Peloponnese. Its wealth came from agriculture, especially currants, and in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries that wealth paid for handsome neoclassical buildings, many of which still line its central streets and squares. The finest of them is the old municipal market hall, a grand building attributed to Ernst Ziller, the German-born architect behind much of neoclassical Athens. Restored in recent years, it is now used as a cultural space.

The centre of town is built around a series of squares, with cafés spreading under trees and pedestrian streets running between them. In the morning these squares fill with people doing their errands, drinking coffee and catching up on gossip. There are bakeries, butchers, fruit sellers and shops selling everything from agricultural tools to wedding dresses. On market days, stalls of fresh produce from the local farms show what this region grows: tomatoes, watermelons, peaches, olives and greens.

Pyrgos is not beautiful in the way that Chania or Corfu is. Parts of the town are modern and plain, and the traffic can be busy. But it has a lived-in warmth, and its cafés and tavernas are where local families and farmers eat, at local prices. In the evening, especially on weekends, the central squares fill with families, young people and older couples taking their volta, the slow evening stroll that is one of the great Greek pleasures. If you sit with a drink and watch, you will see a side of Greece that has nothing to do with tourism.

For visitors with a little time, Pyrgos works best as a stop on the way to or from Olympia, perhaps for a coffee and a walk around the centre, or for lunch in a taverna where the menu is in Greek and the owner will happily point you towards what is good today. It is also a practical place: there are banks, pharmacies, larger shops and transport links, which can be useful if you have extended your stay in the region.

What is it not good for? Sightseeing in the usual sense, beaches, or a romantic island atmosphere. If your time ashore is short, Olympia is the obvious priority. But if you are spending a few days in the region, or are simply the kind of traveller who likes to see how a country lives on a Tuesday, Pyrgos is a quietly rewarding place.

Greece is more than its islands and its ruins. It is also the plain, the market and the square, the farmer in town for supplies, the café where the same men have met every morning for thirty years. Pyrgos is that Greece, and it is just twenty minutes from your ship.

name: Agios Andreas and the Ilia Coast: Sea, Sand and a Sunken City
description: Just south of Katakolon, a small bay hides the remains of an ancient harbour under its clear water, and the long beaches of the Ionian stretch away beyond it.
details:
If your idea of a perfect port day involves sea rather than stone, the coast around Katakolon has more to offer than most passengers realise. The western Peloponnese faces the Ionian Sea, and its shoreline here is a long run of sandy beaches backed by dunes, pines and farmland. A few minutes from the port, tucked behind the headland, is the small bay of Agios Andreas, and it is one of the quiet treasures of the region.

Agios Andreas is a simple place: a little beach, a few tavernas and cafés, a scattering of houses, and a small church above the water. In the morning the sea is usually calm and clear, and you will share it with a handful of local swimmers. What makes it special lies just offshore. Under the shallow water are the remains of the ancient town of Pheia, which archaeologists believe served as a harbour for the region in antiquity and was later submerged, probably as a result of earthquakes and changes in the land. With a mask and snorkel, swimmers can see stone foundations and walls on the seabed. It is not a museum, there are no signs underwater and you should never touch or remove anything, but the experience of swimming over a lost town is unforgettable.

Above the bay, on the headland, are the remains of the medieval fortress known as Pontikokastro, built on the site of the ancient acropolis. Not much stands today, but the walk up gives wide views over the bay and along the coast.

South and north of Katakolon, the beaches grow longer and wilder. Long stretches of sand run for kilometres, with relatively few buildings, and in summer some have beach bars and sunbeds while others are almost empty. The sea here is open to the west, so it can be calm one day and wavy the next. These beaches are where local families come on summer weekends, and they have an unpretentious feel very different from the island resorts.

In the evening, the Ionian coast does sunsets as well as any Greek island. The sun drops straight into the sea, and the tavernas along the shore fill with families eating grilled fish and drinking local wine. If your ship sails late or you are staying in the area, it is a lovely way to end the day.

There are practical things to know. Public transport to the beaches is limited, so you will generally need a taxi or a hire car. In high summer the sand gets very hot and there is little natural shade, and some beaches have no facilities at all. Lifeguards are not guaranteed. And as everywhere on this coast, take care with currents on windy days.

What is this coast good for? Swimming, snorkelling over ancient ruins, long empty beaches, simple seaside lunches, and sunsets. What is it not good for? Sightseeing or shopping. If you have already seen Olympia, or simply need a day of sea and sun after a busy cruise, it is ideal.

It is a curious thing to float in warm, clear water above the stones of a town that sank long ago, and then to sit on a beach and watch the sun set over the same sea. The Ilia coast offers exactly that, and almost no one else from your ship will be there.

name: Campiello: Lost in the Venetian Maze
description: Behind the old fortress lies a knot of tall, peeling houses, laundry lines and stone stairways that feels more like Venice than Greece. Leave the map in your pocket.
details:
Corfu Town is unlike anywhere else in Greece, and Campiello is the reason why. This is the oldest part of the old town, a dense quarter wedged between the Old Fortress and the harbour, and it was shaped almost entirely by four centuries of Venetian rule. Corfu was never taken by the Ottomans, so instead of minarets and bazaars you find tall, narrow houses in faded ochre, pink and cream, iron balconies, arched doorways, and lanes so tight that neighbours could almost shake hands across them.

The houses are tall for a reason. The old town was hemmed in by fortifications, and as the population grew there was nowhere to go but up. Some buildings rise five or six storeys, which is unusual for a Greek town, and the lanes between them, called kantounia, stay in shade for most of the day. Washing hangs between windows, pots of geraniums sit on sills, and stone stairways lead to tiny squares, each with its well-head or its church.

The best way to see Campiello is to get lost in it, and you will, whether you mean to or not. Morning is the loveliest time. The lanes are cool, shutters open one by one, and the sounds are domestic: a radio, a broom on stone, a conversation from one balcony to another. You will pass small churches with Venetian bell towers, some Orthodox and some Catholic, a reminder of the island's mixed heritage. In the little squares, you may be the only stranger.

At the southern edge of the old town is the former Jewish quarter, the Evraiki. Corfu once had a large and long-established Jewish community, and in 1944 almost all of its members were deported by the occupying Germans; very few returned. The old synagogue still stands, and a memorial nearby remembers those who were lost. It is a sobering stop on a walk through such a beautiful place.

As the morning goes on, the edges of Campiello fill with visitors heading from the cruise port to the Liston, and the main shopping streets, Nikiforou Theotoki and Evgeniou Voulgareos, become busy with souvenir shops, kumquat liqueur, olive-wood bowls and leather. A few steps off these streets, however, the crowds disappear again. That is the trick of Campiello: it is never more than two turns away from silence.

At lunch and in the evening, small tavernas set tables in the lanes and squares. This is the place to try Corfiot dishes that you will not find elsewhere in Greece, many with Venetian roots and Italian-sounding names: sofrito, veal cooked slowly with garlic and vinegar; pastitsada, spiced beef or rooster with pasta; and bourdeto, a fiery fish stew. The cooking here is different because the history is different.

At night the lanes are atmospheric and, in summer, lively in places, with music drifting from bars near the main streets. In the depths of Campiello, though, the nights are quiet and the old street lamps throw long shadows on the walls.

What is Campiello good for? Wandering, photography, small tavernas, a sense of what life inside a Venetian fortified town was like, and the discovery of tiny churches and squares. What is it not good for? Anyone who hates getting lost, or anyone with limited mobility; the lanes are uneven and full of steps. Signposting is minimal, and street names are often hard to find.

Corfu's old town is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and Campiello is its beating heart. It is also simply a neighbourhood where people hang out their washing and argue about football. Walk it slowly, and it will remind you that a place can be both.

name: The Spianada and the Liston: A Square Fit for Empires
description: French arcades, a British palace, a Venetian fortress and a cricket match. Corfu's great square is a lesson in European history you can take with a coffee.
details:
Every town in Greece has a central square. Corfu has the Spianada, and it is one of the largest and most unusual in the Mediterranean. Originally it was an open space cleared by the Venetians in front of the Old Fortress so that defenders would have a clear line of fire. Today it is a wide expanse of lawns, trees and paths at the edge of the old town, and around it stand buildings that tell the story of every power that ruled the island.

On the western side is the Liston, a long row of arcaded buildings built during the brief period of French rule in the early nineteenth century and modelled on the Rue de Rivoli in Paris. Its name is often said to come from the list of noble families once permitted to stroll there, though that is more tradition than documented fact. Under the arches today are cafés, their tables spilling out under the trees, and this is where Corfu comes to see and be seen.

In the morning the Liston is relaxed. Waiters set out chairs, older Corfiots read newspapers over coffee, and the light falls through the trees onto the lawns. Have a coffee here and try tsitsibira, the island's ginger beer, made from a recipe left behind by the British, who ruled Corfu as a protectorate from 1815 until the island joined Greece in 1864. At midday the cafés fill with visitors from the cruise ships, and the prices reflect the setting.

Then there is the cricket pitch. In the middle of the Spianada is a patch of green where, in summer, Corfiots play cricket, a legacy of the British that most Greeks find baffling. If a match is on, it is a wonderfully unexpected sight: white-clad players, the thwack of the ball, and the Venetian fortress walls in the background.

At the northern end of the square stands the Palace of St Michael and St George, built by the British in the early nineteenth century as the residence of their High Commissioner. Its colonnaded façade is very English Regency in style, and inside is a surprising Museum of Asian Art. Close by, in the gardens, is a small round temple, the Maitland Rotunda, built in memory of the first British governor. Facing the square to the east, across a moat, is the Old Fortress itself, Venetian in its present form, with a church built like a Greek temple and views over the town and sea from the top.

In the evenings the Spianada becomes the island's living room. Families stroll the paths, children play on the grass, and the cafés of the Liston fill with Corfiots dressed for the evening. On special days, especially during the processions of Saint Spyridon, the island's patron saint, and at Easter, the square is packed with people, brass bands and clergy. Corfu has a long musical tradition, and its philharmonic bands are a central part of these celebrations.

What is the Spianada good for? A coffee with a view, people-watching, the evening stroll, history laid out around a single square, and a gentle introduction to Corfu for anyone with only a short time ashore. What is it not good for? Cheap eating, or a quiet moment at midday in high season. It is also very exposed to the sun in the middle of the day, so the shade of the arcades is welcome.

There are few places where you can sit under French arches, look at a British palace and a Venetian fortress, and watch a game of cricket, all while drinking Greek coffee. That mix is what Corfu is. The Spianada simply puts it all in one view.

name: Garitsa, Mon Repos and Kanoni: Corfu's Gentle Southern Shore
description: South of the old town, a curving bay leads to a royal villa in a wooded park, ancient ruins and the most famous view on the island.
details:
Walk south from the Spianada along the sea, and the old town gives way to Garitsa, a curving bay lined with a broad promenade and elegant nineteenth-century houses. It is a residential neighbourhood, and it feels it. In the morning there are joggers, swimmers and people walking dogs along the seafront; in the evening there are families strolling and couples sitting on the sea wall. Behind the promenade, quiet streets hold villas, gardens and neighbourhood cafés where you will hear more Greek than any other language.

At the far end of the bay is the entrance to Mon Repos, a large wooded estate with a neoclassical villa at its centre. It was built in the early nineteenth century for the British High Commissioner and later became a summer residence of the Greek royal family. Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, was born here in 1921. Today the villa houses a small museum about the history of the estate and the archaeology of the area, and the park around it is open to the public.

The park is one of the most peaceful places in Corfu. Paths wind through woods of pine, eucalyptus and old olive trees, and among them are the ruins of Paleopolis, the ancient city of Corcyra, including the remains of temples. It is a place to walk slowly in the shade, to hear the cicadas and to stumble across a fallen column in the undergrowth. In the late afternoon, the light through the trees is lovely.

Further south, the road climbs onto the Kanoni peninsula, named after a cannon that the French once mounted here. From the viewpoint at the end of the peninsula is the most photographed scene on the island: the white monastery of Vlacherna, reached by a narrow causeway, and just beyond it the small wooded islet of Pontikonisi, Mouse Island. Local legend says that Pontikonisi is the ship of Odysseus, turned to stone; it is a story, not a fact, but it suits the view perfectly. Planes from Corfu airport land and take off over the lagoon right beside it, which adds an unexpected thrill.

Kanoni is busy in the middle of the day with tour coaches and visitors photographing the view. Early in the morning, or in the evening, it is calmer. You can walk down the steps and across the causeway to Vlacherna, and in summer take a small boat to Pontikonisi, where there is a little chapel.

These neighbourhoods are good for a slower, greener Corfu: a seafront walk, a picnic in the park, an archaeological wander and the island's most famous view. They are not good for nightlife or for the dense atmosphere of the old town. Garitsa and Mon Repos are a pleasant walk from the centre; Kanoni is further, and it is easiest to take a bus or taxi up and walk back down.

Corfu Town is often seen as a place of narrow lanes and grand squares, and it is. But just to the south, the town relaxes into gardens, sea views and history half-buried in the woods. It is worth an afternoon of anyone's time.

name: Paleokastritsa: Coves, Monks and a Castle in the Clouds
description: On Corfu's wild west coast, emerald coves cut into cliffs, a monastery sits on its headland, and a ruined Byzantine castle hangs over the sea.
details:
Many people consider Paleokastritsa the most beautiful place on Corfu, and when you arrive you understand why. It is on the west coast, about forty minutes by road from Corfu Town, where the island turns its face to the open Ionian. Here the mountains drop steeply into the sea, and the coastline breaks into a series of small coves with water of an almost unreal green and blue, backed by olive groves and cypress trees.

The village itself is spread out along the coast, more a collection of bays, hotels and tavernas than a traditional town. In the morning it is still and sparkling. The water in the coves is calm and clear, small boats wait at the jetties, and the first swimmers are in the sea. By late morning, tour coaches arrive, and the main beaches become busy. Boats leave to explore the sea caves along the cliffs, where the water inside glows blue.

At the end of the headland, above the bays, stands the Monastery of Paleokastritsa. Its foundation is traditionally dated to the thirteenth century, though the buildings you see today are later. It is a working monastery, white and peaceful, with a courtyard full of flowers, a small museum of icons, and views down to the coves on either side. Visitors are welcome, but modest dress is expected; shoulders and knees should be covered.

High above the coast, a short drive away, are the ruins of Angelokastro, a Byzantine castle perched on a crag. It played a role in defending the island over several centuries, and the climb up rewards you with one of the most spectacular views on Corfu: the whole west coast laid out below, and on a clear day a long way out to sea.

There is a tradition, popular with guides, that Paleokastritsa is where Odysseus was washed ashore and met the princess Nausicaa in Homer's Odyssey. Corfu is often identified with the land of the Phaeacians, but there is no way to pin the story to one bay, and several places claim it. It is a good story to keep in mind while you swim.

In the evening, Paleokastritsa becomes quieter as the coaches leave. The tavernas along the bays serve seafood with the sound of the water close by, and the sunset over the open sea is magnificent. If you stay overnight, you will have the coves almost to yourself in the morning.

What is Paleokastritsa good for? Swimming in clear water, boat trips into sea caves, the monastery, the castle, and a long seafood lunch. What is it not good for? Nightlife or a quick visit on a tight cruise schedule; the road from town is winding, and traffic can be slow in summer. The water here can also be colder than on the east coast, as it comes from the open sea.

Corfu is a green island, gentler and lusher than most of the Greek islands. Paleokastritsa shows that beauty at its most dramatic. If you have a full day, it is a wonderful one to spend here.

name: Inside Diocletian's Palace: Living in an Emperor's House
description: Seventeen centuries ago a Roman emperor built a palace to retire in. Today people hang their washing from its windows, and you can have breakfast in its courtyard.
details:
There is nowhere quite like it. Split's old town is not built near a Roman palace, or on top of one. It is built inside one. Emperor Diocletian, who ruled Rome at the end of the third century, built himself a vast fortified residence on this stretch of the Dalmatian coast for his retirement, and in 305 he did something no other Roman emperor did: he gave up the throne voluntarily and came here to grow cabbages, as the story goes. His palace was half villa, half military camp, with high walls, four gates and a grid of streets.

After the empire fell, the palace did not. In the seventh century, people from nearby Salona, fleeing invaders, took refuge inside its walls and began to build homes in the emperor's halls and corridors. Their descendants never left. Over the following centuries, medieval houses, Venetian palaces, churches and shops filled in the spaces, so that today a couple of thousand people still live within the ancient walls. You will see Roman columns built into kitchen walls and a Gothic window set into an imperial façade.

The palace is at its most magical early in the morning. At seven, the marble paving of the lanes shines, polished by centuries of feet, and the only sounds are delivery carts, church bells and swallows. Café owners set out chairs on the Peristyle, the palace's grand central courtyard, where columns of granite and marble frame the steps to what were the emperor's apartments. Sit with a coffee and you are sitting in Diocletian's ceremonial hall. One of the sphinxes he brought from Egypt still crouches on the side, headless and patient.

The irony of the place is never far away. Diocletian launched the last great persecution of Christians, and among the victims was Domnius, the bishop of Salona. Centuries later, the emperor's octagonal mausoleum was converted into a cathedral dedicated to Saint Domnius, and Diocletian's tomb disappeared. Many Splićani enjoy that story. Climb the cathedral bell tower and the whole palace is laid out below you.

By mid-morning, the palace changes completely. Tour groups follow umbrellas through the gates, and the narrow lanes become crowded, especially when several cruise ships are in. It is still beautiful, but it is busy. This is the time to slip into the quieter corners, the tiny lanes in the north and east of the palace, or to go underground into the cellars, the vast vaulted substructures that mirror the layout of the lost imperial rooms above. Part of the central passage is a lively market of crafts and souvenirs; the side halls, ticketed, are cool and atmospheric.

Outside the southern wall runs the Riva, Split's seafront promenade, a long line of palm trees and café tables facing the harbour. It is where the whole city comes to sit, talk and watch the ferries. Dalmatians have a word, fjaka, for a pleasant state of sun-drugged idleness, and the Riva is where you see it practised. A single coffee here can last two hours, and no one will hurry you.

In the evening the palace becomes an intimate, glowing place. Restaurants fill the lanes, and in the domed Vestibule, groups of klapa singers sometimes perform, their unaccompanied harmonies rising towards the open roof. Klapa is recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage, and hearing it inside these ancient walls is unforgettable. In summer, the Peristyle becomes an open-air stage for opera during the Split Summer Festival.

What is the palace good for? History you can touch, morning coffee in an imperial courtyard, wandering, eating, and the evening atmosphere. What is it not good for? Peace at midday in high season, cheap eating on the main lanes, or anyone who wants a polished, museum-like experience. It is a living town, with noise, washing lines and scooters.

Diocletian chose this place to spend his final years, and it is easy to see why. The light, the sea and the mountains behind are the same. What he could not have imagined is that, seventeen centuries later, his house would still be full of people living their lives in it.

name: Varoš: The Old Suburb on the Slopes of Marjan
description: Just west of the Riva, the old quarter of fishermen and farmers climbs towards Marjan Hill in a maze of stone houses, steps and courtyards.
details:
When Split was confined within the palace walls and the medieval town beside it, the people who worked the land and the sea lived outside. Their neighbourhood was Varoš, which spreads up the slopes west of the old town towards Marjan Hill. It was home to farmers and fishermen, people who went out to the fields and vineyards on the peninsula and to the fishing grounds beyond, and it has kept much of that character.

Varoš is a tangle of narrow lanes, stone houses, small gardens and stepped streets climbing the hillside. It has no grand monuments. What it has instead is atmosphere: laundry flapping in the breeze, cats asleep on warm steps, a grandmother tending tomatoes on a balcony, and glimpses of the sea between the houses. Walk up from the Riva, past the fishermen's harbour of Matejuška, and within minutes the bustle of the old town seems far away.

Matejuška itself is worth a pause. It is the small harbour at the foot of Varoš where wooden fishing boats are still moored and nets dry in the sun. Older fishermen gather here, and in the evening locals sit on the sea wall with a beer to watch the sunset. It feels a world away from the polished Riva, though it is only a few minutes' walk.

In the morning, Varoš is very quiet. The lanes are in shade, and you will mostly meet residents going to the shops or walking to work. It is a lovely time to climb the stepped path that leads from Varoš onto Marjan, the forested peninsula that Splićani call the lungs of their city. The stairs zigzag up past cats and terraces to the Vidilica café, from where you see the whole of Split, the palace, the harbour and the islands spread out below. It is a ritual walk for many locals.

At lunchtime and in the evening, Varoš is known for its konobas, the traditional Dalmatian taverns. Some of them have been here for generations and serve the kind of food that families cook at home: pašticada, beef slowly braised in wine and spices; black risotto made with cuttlefish ink; grilled fish with chard and potatoes; and, in some places, peka, meat or octopus slow-cooked under an iron bell covered with embers. Other places are newer, run by young chefs who give the old dishes a lighter touch. Many of the best are small and fill up quickly.

At night, Varoš is calm. There are a few bars and wine bars at its edges, near the old town, but the upper lanes are residential and quiet. That is why many visitors choose to stay here: close to everything, but away from the noise of the palace and the Riva.

There is a village side to Varoš, too. Its parish church, the Church of the Holy Cross, is the centre of neighbourhood life, and on the way up to Marjan you pass the tiny medieval chapel of Saint Nicholas. Like the rest of Split, Varoš keeps its feast days with processions, and on those days the lanes fill with neighbours rather than visitors.

What is Varoš good for? A quiet walk, traditional konobas, the climb to Marjan, sunset at Matejuška, and a peaceful base. What is it not good for? Anyone who struggles with steps; the lanes are steep and stepped. It also has little in the way of shopping or sights in the usual sense.

Varoš is where Split remembers that it was once a town of fishermen and farmers. Walk its lanes in the evening, when the smell of grilling fish drifts from the doorways and the last light catches the stone, and you will feel that memory very close.

name: Bačvice and Firule: Where Split Goes to Swim
description: Ten minutes from the palace, Split's city beach is the birthplace of a ball game played in ankle-deep water, and the heart of its summer nights.
details:
Split is a city that swims. On hot days, people come down to the sea from offices and apartments at lunchtime, after work and late in the evening, and the most beloved spot of all is Bačvice. It is a shallow, sandy bay just east of the ferry port and the old town, about ten minutes on foot from the palace. Sandy beaches are rare on this rocky coast, which helps explain Bačvice's popularity.

The bay is shallow for a long way out, and that shallowness gave birth to Split's own sport: picigin. Players stand in ankle- or knee-deep water and keep a small ball in the air between them, with dramatic dives and splashes, never letting it touch the water. There are no points and no winners; the aim is simply to keep the ball up and look good doing it. It was invented on Bačvice in the early twentieth century, according to local tradition, and Splićani play it all year, including a famous game in the sea on New Year's Day. Watching a group of locals play picigin is one of the most Split things you can do.

In the morning, Bačvice belongs to older locals who come for an early swim and to chat in the water. By midday in summer, it is crowded with families, students and visitors, and space on the sand can be scarce. The water is shallow and calm, which makes it good for children. In the evening the mood changes again. The beach bars and clubs at the edges of the bay come to life, and on summer nights this is one of the centres of Split's nightlife, busy with young people until late.

Walk east along the coastal path from Bačvice, and you reach a series of smaller bays and beaches: Firule, Zenta and beyond. They are less famous, often less crowded, and favoured by locals. The neighbourhood around them is residential, with apartment blocks, gardens and cafés where you will hear mostly Croatian. There are some good small restaurants and wine bars here, where you can sit on a terrace near the sea in the evening without the crowds of the old town.

It is worth being honest about Bačvice. It is a city beach, not a pristine island cove. On busy days, the sand is crowded and not always spotless, and you will hear music from the bars. If you want crystal-clear water and peace, you will be happier on Marjan's beaches, such as Kašjuni, or on an island. But if you want to see how Split lives in summer, Bačvice is the place.

What is it good for? A quick swim close to the ferry and cruise port, watching picigin, families with small children, and summer nights out. What is it not good for? Quiet, seclusion or the kind of crystal-clear water you see in brochures. In the height of summer, arrive early if you want a place to put your towel.

Split is a city that never quite separates work from pleasure, or the street from the sea. Bačvice is where that shows most clearly: people in business clothes kicking off their shoes for a swim after work, grandparents playing a game invented by their own grandparents, and teenagers dancing on the sand at midnight. Join in, even if it is only to dip your feet.

name: Trogir: A Medieval Island Town Half an Hour Away
description: On a tiny island joined to the mainland by bridges, Trogir packs Romanesque churches, Renaissance palaces and a waterfront promenade into a few hundred metres.
details:
Trogir is about half an hour west of Split by road, and it feels like a smaller, quieter version of the city's old town, with a character all its own. The historic centre sits on a small island between the mainland and the larger island of Čiovo, connected to both by bridges, and almost all of it can be walked in an hour. In that small space are some of the best-preserved Romanesque and Renaissance buildings on the Adriatic, and the whole town is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

Trogir was founded by Greek colonists in antiquity, and its street plan still reflects that ancient grid. Later it was ruled by Byzantium, Hungary-Croatia and, for nearly four centuries, Venice. What survives today is a medieval town of narrow stone streets, small squares and handsome houses, enclosed by remains of walls and guarded at its western tip by the fortress of Kamerlengo.

At the heart of the town is the Cathedral of Saint Lawrence, begun in the thirteenth century. Its western portal, carved by a master named Radovan in 1240, is one of the great works of medieval sculpture in this part of Europe. Adam and Eve stand on either side, above lions, and around them are scenes from the Bible and from everyday life: the months of the year, shown through the work of the season, from slaughtering pigs to harvesting grapes. Look closely, and you will see how ordinary medieval life was carved into the stone. Inside, the Renaissance chapel of the Blessed John of Trogir is equally remarkable.

Morning is the best time for Trogir. The streets are cool, the light is soft, and the cathedral square is quiet. The town is small enough that a wave of cruise or tour visitors can make it feel crowded by late morning, so arriving early pays off. In the late afternoon and evening, the town calms again, and its waterfront, the Riva, fills with locals and visitors strolling along the palm-lined promenade and eating at its restaurants as the yachts come in.

Trogir is a living town as well as a monument. People live in its old houses, children play in its squares, and the market near the bridge sells fruit, vegetables and local produce. It is quieter and less commercial than Split's palace, though summer brings plenty of visitors. Across the bridge on Čiovo, there are beaches and seafood restaurants where you can swim and eat looking back at the town.

What is Trogir good for? A compact, beautiful medieval town, Radovan's portal and the cathedral, a lovely waterfront walk, and an easy half-day trip from Split. What is it not good for? A long stay if you want nightlife or big beaches, or a visit at the busiest midday hours in high season. The stone streets are polished and can be slippery, so wear sensible shoes.

Getting there is easy. Buses run frequently from Split, and in summer, boats also connect the two along the coast. The road can be slow at busy times, so allow extra time if you are on a cruise schedule.

Trogir is sometimes treated as a side trip to Split, but it holds its own. Walk its lanes early, stand in front of Radovan's portal for a while, and finish with a drink on the waterfront. You will leave wondering why it is not better known.

name: The Old Town: A Republic Inside Its Walls
description: Dubrovnik's walled city was once a nation. At midday it can feel like a theme park; at dawn and after dark, it becomes a stone town of astonishing beauty again.
details:
Dubrovnik's Old Town is one of the most famous townscapes in Europe, and for good reason. A complete ring of stone walls, up to twenty-five metres high in places, wraps around a small city of pale limestone streets and terracotta roofs on a rock above the sea. It looks impregnable, and for centuries it effectively was, though its real defence was diplomacy rather than stone.

For around four and a half centuries, until Napoleon's forces ended it in 1808, this was the Republic of Ragusa, an independent maritime state that rivalled Venice in trade. It kept its freedom by negotiating with everyone, paying tribute to the Ottomans, and trusting no single ruler; its rector served for just one month at a time and could not leave the palace without permission. The word on its flag was Libertas. The city still carries itself like a capital, because it once was one.

The main street, the Stradun, runs straight from the Pile Gate in the west to the old port in the east, paved in limestone polished so smooth by feet that it shines like water after rain. The houses that line it look strikingly uniform, and there is a reason: a catastrophic earthquake in 1667 destroyed much of the city, and the Stradun was rebuilt in a single, sober style, with shops on the ground floor and their doors and windows combined in one arch.

There are two Dubrovniks, and they depend on the clock. Early in the morning, from about six to eight, the city belongs to its residents. Shopkeepers wash the paving, waiters set out tables, old ladies walk to Mass, and the swifts scream over the rooftops. The light is gold and the Stradun almost empty. This is the time to walk it, to climb the side streets that rise steeply on either side, and to feel how intimate the city really is. From mid-morning, when cruise passengers and tour groups arrive, the Old Town becomes intensely crowded, especially at the Pile Gate and along the Stradun. It is still beautiful, but it is hard to love in a crush.

In the late afternoon, the crowds thin as the day visitors leave, and in the evening the Old Town turns soft and golden again. Restaurants set tables on the stepped side streets and on the little squares, people sit on the stone steps with ice creams, and music drifts from cafés. Bars are perched on the rocks outside the sea walls, reached through small openings, where you can sit with a drink at the edge of the sea and watch swimmers dive off the rocks into the sunset.

The walls themselves are the city's great walk. The full circuit is about two kilometres, with many steps, and it takes between one and two hours. The views over the roofs and out to sea are unforgettable. Look closely at the roof tiles from up there: the brighter orange ones are new, replacing tiles destroyed during the siege of 1991 and 1992, when the city was shelled. A map near the Pile Gate marks where the shells fell. Many residents lived through it, so the subject deserves care.

Inside the walls, there is a great deal to see: the Rector's Palace, the Franciscan monastery with one of the oldest working pharmacies in Europe, the Dominican monastery, the cathedral treasury and the church of Saint Blaise, the city's patron. But part of the joy is simply in the small things: laundry strung across an alley, a cat on a step, the sound of a piano from an open window.

What is the Old Town good for? History, architecture, the walls, evening atmosphere and dining in extraordinary settings. What is it not good for? Peace at midday in the busy season, budget eating, or anyone who struggles with steps; the side streets are very steep. The city has rules intended to protect it, including against walking around in swimwear, and fines are possible.

Dubrovnik was built to be seen from the sea, and to be lived in by the people inside it. Visit at the edges of the day, when the stone is warm and the streets are quiet, and you will understand both.

name: Ploče: The View Back Through the East Gate
description: Step out of the eastern gate and Dubrovnik shows you its best face: the walled city, the old harbour and the island of Lokrum, all at once.
details:
Most visitors enter Dubrovnik's Old Town through the Pile Gate in the west and leave the same way. But walk the length of the Stradun and out through the eastern Ploče Gate, and you find a different neighbourhood and some of the finest views of the city. Ploče stretches along the coast east of the walls, rising up the hillside towards the road and the slopes of Mount Srđ above.

Right outside the gate is the old Lazareti, a long row of stone buildings on the waterfront. This was the city's quarantine station, where merchants and travellers from abroad were held before entering the city, part of a public health system that the Republic of Ragusa developed from the late fourteenth century. Today the buildings host cultural events, concerts and a craft space. It is a reminder that this small republic was often ahead of its time.

Beyond the Lazareti is Banje Beach, the closest proper beach to the Old Town. It has a famous view: the walls, the old port and the island of Lokrum all framed together.
