It is popular and in summer often crowded, with a beach club on part of it, but swimming here with the walled city behind you is one of the classic Dubrovnik experiences.

Ploče is essentially residential and upmarket. Along the coast road and on the hillside are villas, small hotels and some of the city's most famous luxury hotels, many with terraces looking straight back at the Old Town. The streets are steep, with stairways linking the levels. In the morning, the neighbourhood is quiet and full of light, and walkers climb the stepped paths for the view.

Ploče also gives access to the old path up Mount Srđ, which zigzags up the bare hillside to the fort at the top. Alternatively, the cable car station sits just above the Old Town, on the edge of the neighbourhood. From the top, the whole of Dubrovnik, the islands and the coast lie below you, and at sunset the view is spectacular.

In the evening, Ploče's restaurants and hotel terraces fill with diners looking across at the lit walls of the Old Town. This is one of the most romantic places in Dubrovnik for dinner. The walk back through the Ploče Gate into the quietening Old Town at night is magical.

What is Ploče good for? The best views of the Old Town, a swim at Banje, luxurious hotels, romantic dinners, and access to Mount Srđ. What is it not good for? Budget travel, or anyone who finds steps difficult. It is quieter than the Old Town, and it has none of the dense historic streets that make the walled city special.

The Old Town is best appreciated from a little distance, and Ploče is where that distance is perfect. Walk out through the eastern gate in the late afternoon, swim at Banje, and stay for dinner with the walls glowing across the water. It is the view that Dubrovnik was built to give.

name: Gruž: Where the Ships Come In and Dubrovnik Shops for Dinner
description: Gruž is where your ship docks and most visitors leave in a hurry. Stay for the morning market and the fishermen, and you will meet the Dubrovnik that lives here.
details:
Gruž is Dubrovnik's working harbour, about three kilometres west of the Old Town, and if you arrive by cruise ship or ferry, this is where you will step ashore. Most people head straight for the buses and taxis to the walled city. That is natural enough. But Gruž has a life of its own, and a short walk along its waterfront shows you the everyday Dubrovnik that the Old Town rarely reveals.

In the days of the Republic, wealthy Ragusan families built summer villas along the shores of Gruž bay, with gardens running down to the water. A few of these Renaissance summer residences survive among the modern buildings, though most are hidden behind walls. The harbour itself has long been the city's main port, and today it handles cruise ships, ferries to the islands and a fleet of fishing boats and excursion vessels.

The best time to see Gruž is early in the morning. Along the waterfront, the Gruž market sets up its stalls, with farmers from the surrounding villages selling fruit, vegetables, herbs, honey, olive oil and cheese. Nearby, fishermen bring in their catch, and the small fish market fills with locals buying for lunch. It is noisy, fresh and very local, and it gives you an idea of how Dubrovnik actually eats.

As the day goes on, Gruž becomes a transit zone, with buses and taxis queuing, ferry passengers waiting for boats, and cafés serving coffee to people in a hurry. It is busy and practical rather than beautiful, and the traffic around the harbour can be heavy. But behind the waterfront, the neighbourhood is residential, with apartment blocks and local cafés, and it has some good small restaurants and bars at local prices.

In the evenings, Gruž has become a modest nightlife hub, with a handful of bars, wine bars and restaurants where young people from Dubrovnik go, rather than visitors. The atmosphere is relaxed and unpretentious.

From Gruž, boats leave for the Elafiti Islands, Koločep, Lopud and Šipan, quiet, car-free or nearly car-free islands with villages, beaches and walking paths. If you have a day to spare, one of these trips is a lovely escape from the crowds of the Old Town.

Gruž is also where you feel most clearly how Dubrovnik balances its two lives. The same harbour that welcomes thousands of visitors a day is where local families catch the ferry to visit grandparents on the islands, where fishermen still land the night's catch, and where the city's supplies arrive. Sit at a café on the waterfront for half an hour and you will watch both worlds pass in front of you, rarely touching.

What is Gruž good for? The morning market, fresh fish, local life, convenient ferries to the islands, and an honest, unpolished glimpse of the city. What is it not good for? Sightseeing in the usual sense, beaches or the historic atmosphere of the Old Town. It is also not especially attractive in parts.

If you have a little time when you dock, walk along the harbour to the market before you take the bus into town. Buy some figs or a bag of dried lavender, drink a coffee where the fishermen do, and watch the city begin its day. When you reach the Old Town afterwards, you will see it with fresh eyes.

name: Lapad and Babin Kuk: Dubrovnik's Green Peninsula
description: West of the port, a pine-covered peninsula of beaches, promenades and family hotels is where Dubrovnik goes to relax, and where many visitors end up wishing they had stayed.
details:
Lapad is the peninsula that stretches west from the port of Gruž, wooded with pines and edged with bays and beaches. It is a mainly residential area mixed with hotels, and its outer tip, Babin Kuk, is home to several large resorts. For visitors who want to see the Old Town but sleep somewhere quieter and closer to the sea, it is the natural choice, and for locals it is simply where many people live and swim.

The heart of Lapad is its long pedestrian promenade, which runs from the bay of Lapad, Uvala Lapad, along the coast towards the tip of the peninsula. It is shaded by trees and lined with cafés, restaurants, ice-cream shops and hotels, and it leads to small beaches and rocky platforms where people swim. In the morning, it is calm and fresh, with locals walking dogs and swimming. In the late afternoon and evening, it fills with families and couples out for a stroll.

Lapad's main beach, at the head of the bay, is shallow and good for families, though in summer it gets busy. Further along, rocky coves offer clearer water and more space. On the Babin Kuk side, Copacabana beach is one of the larger beaches in the area, with facilities and water sports. None of these is a wild, empty cove; they are city beaches, sociable and well used.

Above the promenade is Petka Hill, covered in pine forest and crossed by paths and a car-free road that climbs to the top. It is a quiet escape, with views over the islands and the bay, and locals use it for walks and runs. A cliff path on the western side gives wide views of the sea.

Lapad's atmosphere is relaxed and residential. There are supermarkets, local cafés, bakeries and family restaurants, and prices are generally lower than in the Old Town. At night it is calm, with a few bars along the promenade but nothing like the nightlife of the city centre. For many visitors, that calm is the point.

Getting to the Old Town is easy: frequent city buses run from Lapad and Babin Kuk to the Pile Gate in about fifteen or twenty minutes, depending on traffic. This makes Lapad a practical base for anyone extending their stay before or after a cruise.

What is Lapad good for? Beaches, a family holiday, a calm base, sunset walks along the promenade, and Petka Hill. What is it not good for? Historic atmosphere, as it is a largely modern area, or easy walking to the Old Town; it is a few kilometres away, and most people take the bus. The big resorts of Babin Kuk can also feel somewhat removed from the city.

Dubrovnik is a small city with a very famous centre, and it is easy to think of it only as the walled town. Lapad is a reminder that people live, swim and grow old here, and that the best end to a hot day in the Old Town may be a swim off the rocks at sunset, a few kilometres away.

name: Kotor Old Town: A Maze Beneath the Mountain
description: A triangle of stone lanes, squares and churches wedged between the sea and a sheer mountain wall, with fortifications zigzagging to the sky. It is a place built to confuse its visitors, and it still does.
details:
Sailing into the Bay of Kotor is one of the great arrivals in the Mediterranean. For an hour or more, the ship threads through narrow straits between steep mountains, past villages and little island churches, until at the innermost corner of the bay, it reaches Kotor. The town sits on a flat triangle of land at the foot of a sheer limestone mountain, and from the deck you can see its walls climbing up the slope behind it in a dramatic zigzag to a fortress high above.

Kotor's Old Town is small, compact and almost entirely enclosed by walls. It was ruled by Venice from 1420 to 1797, and much of what you see dates from those centuries, though the town is older and has been rebuilt after earthquakes, including a severe one in 1979. Today it is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and its stone streets, squares and churches are remarkably intact.

Its layout is famously confusing. The lanes twist and turn, branch and rejoin, and there is no obvious straight route through. It is often said that the maze was designed to confuse invaders, though that is more popular explanation than proven fact. Whatever the reason, it confuses visitors very effectively. Locals navigate by the squares: the Square of Arms by the main Sea Gate, the Flour Square, the Milk Square and others. Learn a few names and you will find your way.

The town is full of churches, and they tell its history. The Cathedral of Saint Tryphon, consecrated in 1166, is Catholic, its twin towers rebuilt after earthquakes. A short walk away is the Serbian Orthodox Church of Saint Nicholas, built in the early twentieth century, and several smaller Orthodox and Catholic churches. Kotor has long been a place where these communities live side by side.

Then there are the cats. Kotor is famous for them; they sleep on steps, perch on walls and wander in and out of shops, and the town has adopted them as its unofficial symbol. A small Cats Museum and countless cat-themed souvenirs celebrate them. Locals feed them and care for them, and visitors are asked to be gentle.

Kotor has two very different moods. In the early morning, before the ships disembark, it is quiet and beautiful. The stone is cool, cafés set out tables in the squares, and the mountain casts its shadow over the town. From mid-morning, when one or more large cruise ships are in port, the lanes become crowded, and the main squares fill with tour groups. In the evening, after the ships leave, the town becomes calm and atmospheric again, with restaurants in the squares and lanes, and the floodlit walls glowing on the mountainside.

Those walls are Kotor's great challenge. A path of many hundreds of steps climbs from the Old Town to the Fortress of Saint John, about 260 metres above, passing the Church of Our Lady of Remedy on the way. The views of the town and bay get better with every step, but there is little shade, so the climb is best done early in the morning or late in the afternoon. There is an entrance fee.

What is Kotor good for? Wandering, history, churches, the climb to the fortress, dramatic scenery and evening dining in the squares. What is it not good for? Peace when several ships are in port, beaches, or anyone with mobility problems if they want to climb. The polished stone can be slippery.

Kotor is a small town with a huge setting. Step through the Sea Gate early in the day, let yourself get lost, then climb the walls and look back down. The maze makes sense from above, and the bay, stretching away between the mountains, explains why people have fought over this place for centuries.

name: Dobrota: The Captains' Shore
description: Just north of the Old Town, a long line of stone mansions built by seafaring families looks across the bay. It is where Kotor swims, strolls and eats by the water.
details:
Leave Kotor's Old Town by the north gate and follow the shore, and you soon find yourself in Dobrota, a long, narrow settlement stretched along the edge of the bay. There is not much depth to it; the mountains rise almost straight behind. But along the waterfront stands a remarkable series of stone palaces and mansions, built in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries by the families of sea captains and merchants who made their fortunes on the water.

The Bay of Kotor, the Boka, has a long seafaring tradition. Its men sailed under the flag of Venice and later of Austria, and their wealth went into houses, chapels and churches along the shore. In Dobrota you will see their family palaces, with their coats of arms, small private harbours and walled gardens. Some are restored as hotels or homes; others are crumbling quietly. Together they make Dobrota one of the most atmospheric stretches of the bay.

Dobrota is mainly residential and relaxed. A long waterfront path follows the shore, and it is one of the nicest walks in the Kotor area. In the morning you will find locals swimming from the concrete platforms and small jetties, fishermen preparing their boats, and people walking dogs. There are no sandy beaches here; people swim from rocks and platforms, and the water is deep and clear.

The views are the great luxury of Dobrota. Across the water, the Old Town sits under its mountain, with the walls climbing above, and at night the walls are lit, a line of light zigzagging up the slope. Several restaurants along the shore have terraces right on the water, and eating fresh fish or black risotto here as the sun goes down over the mountains is one of the best experiences in the bay.

There are churches, too. The large church of Saint Eustace, in the middle of Dobrota, is one of the most important Catholic churches in the area. Lace-making has a long tradition among the women of Dobrota, and you may still find examples of it.

The rhythm of the day here follows the water. Early, the bay is often perfectly still, a mirror for the mountains, and the only movement is a rowing boat or a swimmer heading out from a jetty. By afternoon a breeze may ruffle the surface and yachts come and go. In the evening, families come out to sit on the low walls by the sea, children jump from the platforms for one last swim, and the smell of grilled fish drifts from the terraces. It is an unhurried, neighbourly kind of place, and it rewards anyone who simply sits and watches.

What is Dobrota good for? A peaceful walk, swimming from the rocks, waterfront dinners, staying in a converted captain's house, and the view of the Old Town. What is it not good for? Historic street life or shopping; it is a long, thin settlement along a road. The road can be busy with traffic, and the narrow walkway beside it is not always comfortable.

Dobrota is a good place to escape the crowds of the Old Town on a busy cruise day. Walk north for twenty minutes, find a waterfront café, and watch the bay. The captains who built these houses spent their lives at sea. Their homes still look out over it.

name: Perast: A Baroque Village and Its Island Churches
description: A single street of baroque palaces and bell towers faces two tiny islands, one natural and one built, stone by stone, by sailors. It is the most beautiful village in the bay.
details:
Perast lies about twenty minutes by road from Kotor, at a point where the bay narrows, and it is often called the loveliest village in the Boka. It is small, little more than a single long waterfront street and a hillside of houses behind, but it is packed with baroque palaces, churches and bell towers, built at the height of its prosperity in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, when it was a wealthy seafaring town under Venice.

Perast's sailors and shipbuilders were famous. It is often said that its maritime school trained navigators for the Russian navy, a story the village is proud of. Its families built grand stone houses along the water, many with their own small chapels, and a tall bell tower rises above the church of Saint Nicholas. Some of the old palaces are now museums and hotels; others are empty and slowly decaying, which gives the village a melancholy beauty.

The heart of Perast, though, lies offshore. In front of the village are two small islands. One, Saint George, is natural and holds a Benedictine monastery among cypress trees; it is not usually open to visitors. The other, Our Lady of the Rocks, is artificial. According to tradition, in the fifteenth century local sailors found an icon of the Virgin on a rock in the bay, and from then on every sailor returning from a voyage dropped a stone there. Over time, with sunken ships added, the rock became an island, and a church was built on it. Each year on 22 July, in a ceremony called the Fašinada, local people row out in decorated boats to throw stones into the sea around the island, continuing the tradition.

Small boats take visitors from Perast's waterfront to Our Lady of the Rocks, a short trip. The church inside is richly decorated with paintings, and there is a small museum. Among its treasures is an embroidered icon said to have been made over many years by a local woman waiting for her husband to return from sea, using her own hair as thread as it turned grey. It is a story that has been told for generations, and it is very moving to see.

Perast is at its best early in the morning and in the evening. During the day, especially when cruise passengers and tour groups arrive, the narrow waterfront can become crowded, and the boats to the island are busy. In the early morning, it is silent, with the islands floating in still water and the mountains reflected around them. In the evening, the waterfront restaurants serve seafood as the light fades, and the village becomes peaceful again.

What is Perast good for? Beauty, history, the island churches, a waterfront lunch, and photography. What is it not good for? Beaches, nightlife or parking; cars are restricted in the village, and parking spaces fill up early. It is also very small, so a half-day is usually enough.

Perast is a village built by people who lived from the sea and made promises to it. Stand on the waterfront looking at the island their stones created, and you will feel that devotion still.

name: Prčanj and the Quiet Shore: The Other Side of the Bay
description: Across the water from Kotor, a sleepy shore of fishing hamlets, sea captains' homes and a church far too large for its village shows you the bay before the ships arrived.
details:
If Dobrota is the captains' shore north of Kotor, then Prčanj and the villages around it are their counterpart on the opposite side of the bay. Leave the Old Town and follow the road west along the water, past the small fishing village of Muo, and you come to Prčanj, stretched out along the shore beneath steep, green slopes. It is quiet, beautiful and much less visited than Perast or Kotor itself.

Muo, the first village, is tiny: a few houses, a little harbour with fishing boats, and a handful of restaurants on the water. It is a lovely place for lunch, looking back across the bay at Kotor and its walls, and many locals come here to eat fish. In the morning, it is very peaceful, with fishermen preparing their boats and swimmers diving off the rocks.

Prčanj is larger and was once one of the richest maritime villages in the bay. Its sailors and captains travelled the world, and the village produced many famous seafarers. Their wealth built stone houses and palaces along the shore, and it also built the huge church of the Nativity of the Virgin Mary, which rises above the village on a terrace reached by a long flight of steps. It is surprisingly large for such a small place, a statement of faith and prosperity, and from its terrace the view across the bay is wonderful.

The atmosphere of this shore is gentle and residential. There are small family-run guesthouses and a few restaurants, but very little in the way of shops or nightlife. People swim from the stone platforms along the water, sit outside in the evening, and greet each other along the road. Life moves slowly, as it has for a long time.

The great pleasure of this shore is looking back. From Prčanj you see Kotor as sailors once did: a small walled town at the foot of an enormous grey mountain, with its fortifications scratched up the slope above it. In the evening, as the light goes, the walls are floodlit and that zigzag of lights seems to hang in the dark, reflected in the still water between you.

Many of the old houses here have been in the same families for generations, and some stand empty for much of the year while their owners live abroad, a reminder that the people of the Boka have always gone to sea and to distant ports to make a living. In summer, those families return, the shutters open, and the waterfront fills with relatives catching up in the evening air. It gives the village a gently bittersweet character, half lived-in and half waiting.

What is Prčanj good for? A quiet base, swimming, peaceful seafood lunches, beautiful views, and a sense of the bay's traditional life. What is it not good for? Nightlife, shopping or convenience; you will need a car, taxi or bus to get around, and the road along the shore is narrow.

If you have only a few hours in Kotor, the Old Town and the walls will rightly take them. But if you have a day, or more, drive or take a taxi around to this quiet side of the bay. Have lunch at Muo, climb the steps to the church at Prčanj, and swim off the rocks. You will see the Boka as its own people see it: not a cruise destination, but home.

name: Spaccanapoli and the Centro Storico: The Greek Grid That Never Slept
description: Naples' historic centre still follows streets laid out by Greek settlers, and it has been noisy, crowded, devout and hungry ever since. It is exhausting, and it is wonderful.
details:
The historic centre of Naples is not a museum. It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited city centres in Europe, and it feels like it: dense, loud, layered and alive in a way that few historic quarters still are. Its streets follow the plan of Neapolis, the 'new city' founded by Greek settlers, with three long parallel streets, the decumani, crossed by narrow lanes. The middle of them is the street everyone calls Spaccanapoli, because from the hills above it seems to split Naples in two.

Walk Spaccanapoli in the morning and you are walking through a working neighbourhood. Shutters roll up, scooters weave between pedestrians, women lower baskets on ropes from balconies to collect shopping, and the smell of coffee and frying dough drifts from doorways. Shrines to saints and to the dead are built into the walls, decorated with flowers and candles. Washing hangs across the lanes. Every few metres there is a church, often with a plain front that opens onto an explosion of marble, gold and paintings inside.

Some of those churches are among the great treasures of Italy. The Gesù Nuovo has a severe, diamond-pointed stone façade and a riot of baroque inside. The cloister of Santa Chiara is covered in tiles painted with scenes of fruit, vines and country life. In the small Sansevero Chapel, the Veiled Christ, carved in the eighteenth century, shows a figure under a marble shroud so fine it seems transparent; it is one of the most astonishing sculptures you will ever see, and you need a ticket booked ahead. Nearby, the Duomo holds the blood of San Gennaro, the city's patron, which the faithful wait to see liquefy three times a year.

Just north of Spaccanapoli is Via San Gregorio Armeno, the street of the nativity makers. All year round, its workshops sell hand-made figures for presepi, the elaborate nativity scenes Neapolitans build at Christmas. Alongside shepherds and angels, you will find figures of footballers, politicians and celebrities, which tells you a lot about the city's sense of humour. In December, the street becomes almost impassable.

Underneath it all is another Naples. Beneath the historic centre lies a network of tunnels, cisterns and quarries cut into the soft yellow tuff stone, used by Greeks, Romans and, during the Second World War, by Neapolitans sheltering from bombing raids. Guided tours take you down into it, and it gives you a sense of just how deep the city's history goes.

Eating here is a serious business. This is the home of pizza, and some of the most famous pizzerias in the world are on or near Via dei Tribunali, the northern decumanus. Expect queues, put your name on the list, and wait; a true Neapolitan pizza is soft, slightly charred and gone in minutes. The streets also sell fried pizza, sfogliatelle, those crisp shell-shaped pastries, and cuoppo, paper cones of fried seafood or vegetables.

The centre is at its most intense at lunchtime and in the early evening. At night, some streets are lively with students and diners, others quiet and dark. The neighbourhood is perfectly visitable after dark if you stick to the busier streets, but it is sensible to keep a close eye on bags and phones, as in any crowded city centre.

What is the Centro Storico good for? Churches, art, street food, pizza, and the feeling of a city that has never stopped living in its oldest streets. What is it not good for? Calm, cleanliness or quiet strolls; the lanes are narrow, scooters rarely slow down, and the noise rarely stops. Wear flat shoes and give yourself plenty of time.

Naples rewards curiosity and punishes impatience. Walk Spaccanapoli slowly, look into every church you pass, eat whatever smells best, and do not try to see everything. The centre has been here for two and a half thousand years. It will still be here next time.

name: Quartieri Spagnoli: Laundry, Murals and Maradona
description: A grid of steep, narrow lanes just off Via Toledo, once notorious, now one of the most vivid neighbourhoods in Europe, with a footballer as its patron saint.
details:
The Quartieri Spagnoli, the Spanish Quarters, climb up the hillside just west of Via Toledo, Naples' great shopping street. They were laid out in the sixteenth century to house Spanish soldiers when Naples was ruled from Spain, and their plan is a tight grid of very narrow, steep lanes lined with tall buildings. Many families live in bassi, single-room homes at street level with doors opening directly onto the lane, and so daily life spills outdoors: people cook, chat, watch television and play cards on the street.

For a long time, the Quartieri had a reputation for poverty and petty crime, and many visitors stayed away. That reputation has softened, and the area has become one of the most visited and photographed in Naples. But it remains a working-class residential neighbourhood, and that is its character: crowded, intimate, noisy and warm.

The Quartieri's most famous resident is not alive. Diego Maradona, the Argentine footballer who led SSC Napoli to its first league titles in 1987 and 1990, is worshipped here as a kind of secular saint. A large mural of him dominates a small square, now known as Largo Maradona, which has become a shrine, covered with scarves, flags, photographs and messages, especially since his death in 2020. Napoli's more recent championships have only deepened the devotion. On match days, the whole neighbourhood is draped in blue.

In the morning, the lanes are busy with ordinary life: shopkeepers opening up, scooters squeezing through, children going to school, and the clatter of crockery from open doors. Small grocers, bakers and butchers serve the residents. This is a good time to wander, look at the street art and shrines, and get a coffee at a tiny bar where the regulars drink standing up.

As the day goes on, the area around Largo Maradona fills with visitors, and street vendors sell souvenirs. Some lanes are lined with new cafés, bars and small restaurants. In the evening, the Quartieri becomes a lively place to eat and drink, with trattorias serving Neapolitan home cooking at fair prices: pasta e patate with provola, ragù, fried anchovies and frittatas of pasta. Some places are very simple, with plastic chairs and paper tablecloths, and the food is excellent.

There is a practical point to remember. The Quartieri are steep, and the lanes are narrow and often shared with fast scooters. Keep to the side, keep your bag close, and be respectful of residents, whose doorways are their living rooms. Do not photograph people in their homes without asking.

What is it good for? Street life, local food, the Maradona shrine, street art, and the energy of a neighbourhood that lives outdoors. What is it not good for? Quiet or polished sightseeing; there are no great museums here, and the streets can feel chaotic. Some lanes at night are quieter and darker, and it is better to stick to the livelier ones.

Naples is a city of extremes, and the Quartieri Spagnoli show its warmth most clearly. Wander up from Via Toledo, get a little lost, and you will be greeted by laundry, music, saints, footballers and the smell of someone's lunch. It is impossible to forget.

name: Chiaia and the Seafront: Elegant Naples by the Bay
description: Along the bay, Naples dresses up: designer shops, palm-lined gardens, a seafront promenade with Vesuvius on the horizon, and a castle on a little island.
details:
If the historic centre is Naples at its rawest, Chiaia is the city at its most elegant. The neighbourhood stretches west along the bay from Piazza del Plebiscito, with handsome nineteenth-century buildings, smart shops, art galleries, cafés and bars, and in front of it all the long seafront promenade, the lungomare. This is where well-off Neapolitans live, shop and stroll, and it has a polished, relaxed atmosphere very different from the crowded lanes of the centre.

The lungomare, along Via Partenope and Via Caracciolo, is closed to traffic for much of its length and is one of the great urban seafronts of Italy. The view sweeps across the bay to Vesuvius, the Sorrento peninsula and the island of Capri. In the early morning, it is full of joggers, cyclists and dog walkers; at weekends, families stroll with ice creams, and young people sit on the rocks of the sea wall. Some brave locals swim from the rocks in summer.

At the eastern end of the seafront, on a tiny island linked by a causeway, stands the Castel dell'Ovo, the 'egg castle'. According to a medieval legend, the poet Virgil hid a magic egg in its foundations, and if the egg ever broke, disaster would strike Naples. The castle, one of the oldest in the city, is free to visit, and from its terraces you get superb views. Around its base, the little harbour of Borgo Marinari is lined with seafood restaurants, romantic in the evening, though often pricey.

Behind the seafront is the Villa Comunale, a long public park laid out in the eighteenth century, with palm trees, fountains, statues and the aquarium of the Stazione Zoologica, founded in the nineteenth century and one of the oldest in Europe. It is a place for a shady walk, a bench and some people-watching.

Chiaia's inner streets, especially around Piazza dei Martiri and Via dei Mille, are lined with designer shops and elegant boutiques. Further in, the smaller streets around Via Bisignano and Vico Belledonne fill in the evening with the city's young crowd, who gather in bars that spill onto the pavement. The aperitivo hour here is one of the liveliest in Naples, and it carries on late into the night at weekends.

In the morning, Chiaia is calm and elegant. Cafés serve espresso and pastries to people in suits on their way to work, and shopkeepers polish their windows. In the evening, the seafront glows at sunset, the restaurants of Borgo Marinari fill, and the bars of the inner streets become crowded.

What is Chiaia good for? A seafront walk, the view of Vesuvius, Castel dell'Ovo, shopping, aperitivo and nightlife among locals. What is it not good for? The historic churches and street food of the centre, or budget eating along the waterfront. It is also a long walk from the cruise terminal; allow time or take a taxi.

Naples is often described as chaotic, and parts of it are. But walk the seafront at sunset, with Vesuvius turning purple across the water and the whole city out for its evening stroll, and you will see a city that is also graceful, proud and very much at ease with itself.

name: Vomero: Naples on the Hill
description: Ride a funicular out of the noise, and you arrive in a calm, leafy, middle-class neighbourhood with a castle, a monastery and the best view over the whole bay.
details:
Vomero sits on the hill above the centre of Naples, and getting there is half the fun. From the city below, three funicular railways climb steeply up the slope, and within a few minutes of leaving the noise of Via Toledo or Chiaia, you step out into a different world: wide, tree-lined streets, elegant apartment buildings from the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, smart shops and an air of middle-class calm.

Until the late nineteenth century, Vomero was largely countryside, with villas and farms and a few religious houses on the hilltop. As the city grew, it was developed as a residential area, and today it is one of the most comfortable places to live in Naples. Its main streets, Via Scarlatti and Via Luca Giordano, are busy with shoppers and cafés, and the pace is noticeably gentler than below.

At the very top of the hill are two of the city's great sights. The Castel Sant'Elmo, a star-shaped fortress built in the sixteenth century, sits on the summit, and from its ramparts you get one of the most spectacular views in Italy: the whole of Naples spread out below, the curve of the bay, Vesuvius, the islands and the coast stretching away. Next to it is the Certosa di San Martino, a former Carthusian monastery, now a museum, with a beautiful cloister, gardens and a church richly decorated with marble and paintings. It also holds one of the finest collections of Neapolitan nativity scenes.

In the morning, Vomero is a neighbourhood going about its business: people shopping, children going to school, older residents meeting in cafés. There is a lively market in the side streets, and plenty of good bakeries and delis. In the evening, the cafés and bars of Piazza Vanvitelli fill with young people, and the area has a pleasant, sociable buzz without the intensity of the centre.

Vomero is also a good place to see the city at sunset. Several viewpoints along the edge of the hill, including the terrace of Sant'Elmo and some public belvederes, look west and south over the bay, and as the light fades, the city below turns gold and then sparkles.

The funiculars themselves are a little piece of Neapolitan life. They are used mainly by residents rather than visitors, and riding one at rush hour, squeezed among commuters, students and grandmothers with shopping bags, as the car climbs through tunnels and past gardens, is a small, local adventure. Going down again in the evening, you descend from calm back into the noise and glitter of the city below, and the contrast is part of the pleasure.

What is Vomero good for? Views, the castle and monastery, calm shopping, a sense of everyday middle-class Naples, and an easy escape from the noise below. What is it not good for? Street food, historic lanes or the intense atmosphere of the centre. It can feel quite ordinary compared with the drama of old Naples; its charm is its calm.

Many visitors to Naples never leave the historic centre and the seafront. Take the funicular up to Vomero for an afternoon, walk up to Sant'Elmo, and look down. You will see the whole city at once, chaotic, beautiful and overflowing, held between the volcano and the sea.

name: Civitavecchia: The Port Town Most Passengers Never See
description: Thousands of people a day pass through on their way to Rome. A few stay, and find a seaside town with a Michelangelo fortress, Roman baths and an unexpected bond with Japan.
details:
Civitavecchia is one of the busiest cruise ports in the Mediterranean, and almost everyone who arrives here leaves immediately. Rome is about eighty kilometres away, roughly an hour or an hour and a half by train, and that is where the day is spent. Civitavecchia itself becomes a blur seen from a shuttle bus. That is understandable, but it is also a pity, because the town has a long history and a pleasant seaside character, and it can make a very good base or a relaxed alternative to a frantic day in the capital.

The port was founded by the emperor Trajan in the early second century AD, under the name Centumcellae, to give Rome a deep, safe harbour on this coast. Over the following centuries it was attacked, abandoned and rebuilt, and in the Renaissance it became the main port of the Papal States. The massive fortress that still guards the harbour, the Forte Michelangelo, was built in the sixteenth century, and Michelangelo is credited with contributing to its design, notably its upper keep.

The old town lies just behind the port, and a short walk from the cruise terminal takes you into it. It is not grand. Civitavecchia was heavily bombed in the Second World War, and much of it was rebuilt afterwards, so it is a mix of old and modern. But there are corners of real charm: small piazzas with cafés, a covered market where local farmers and fishermen sell their produce, and narrow streets near the sea where families eat lunch at long tables.

The seafront promenade, the Passeggiata Marina, runs along the water south of the port and is the town's living room. In the morning there are joggers and people walking dogs; in the evening, families stroll, children ride bicycles, and young people sit on the sea wall. The sunsets over the Tyrrhenian Sea can be lovely, and the seafood restaurants along the front serve fresh fish at prices far gentler than in Rome.

Civitavecchia has a surprising international story. In 1615, a Japanese diplomatic mission led by the samurai Hasekura Tsunenaga landed here on its way to meet the Pope. That link is remembered in the Church of the Japanese Martyrs, decorated with paintings by a Japanese artist, and the town is twinned with Ishinomaki in Japan. It is a small, quietly remarkable place to visit.

Just north of the town are the Terme Taurine, the remains of a large Roman bath complex associated with the hot springs of the area, and further north still is Tarquinia, with its UNESCO-listed Etruscan painted tombs. Both make rewarding half-day trips for anyone who has seen Rome before.

What is Civitavecchia good for? A relaxed walk, fresh seafood, a seafront promenade, history from Trajan to the Renaissance, and convenient access to Etruscan Tarquinia. What is it not good for? Grand monuments or a sense of Rome's splendour; it is a working port town, and parts of it are plain. Traffic around the port can be heavy on busy ship days.

If you have been to Rome before, or simply do not want to spend three hours of your day on a train, Civitavecchia is worth more than a glance from a bus window. Walk up from the port, have coffee in a piazza, eat fish by the sea, and you will see a side of Italy that most cruise passengers miss.

name: Trastevere: Rome Across the River
description: Ivy-covered lanes, a glowing golden church and the smell of cacio e pepe: Trastevere is the Rome of the movies, and at night it is the city's most joyful dining room.
details:
Trastevere means 'across the Tiber', and for most of its history this neighbourhood on the west bank of the river was a world apart from the city of popes and emperors on the other side. It was home to working people, sailors, artisans and immigrants, and its residents considered themselves the truest Romans of all. Today it is one of the most loved neighbourhoods in Rome, a maze of cobbled lanes, ochre and terracotta houses draped in ivy, small piazzas and hidden courtyards.

Its heart is the Piazza di Santa Maria in Trastevere, with its fountain and its great basilica, one of the oldest churches in Rome. The façade glitters with medieval mosaics, and inside the apse is covered in golden mosaics from the twelfth century that seem to glow from within. Sitting on the steps of the fountain, looking at the church, is one of Rome's simple pleasures.

In the morning, Trastevere is still and residential. Shopkeepers open their shutters, old men read newspapers in the bars, and the local market in Piazza di San Cosimato sells fruit, vegetables and flowers to residents. This is the best time to wander the lanes, which can be very crowded later, and to find the quieter corners: the church of Santa Cecilia, with its marble statue of the martyred saint, and the small lanes towards the river.

By evening, Trastevere becomes one of the busiest dining and drinking areas in Rome. Tables spill into the lanes, candles flicker, and the air fills with conversation and the smell of Roman cooking. This is the place to try the classic dishes of the city: cacio e pepe, carbonara, amatriciana and gricia; carciofi alla giudia, fried artichokes, in season; supplì, fried rice balls with melted mozzarella inside; and saltimbocca. Some restaurants are tourist traps with menus in many languages and photos of the food; others are excellent family trattorias. A good guide is to follow the locals and avoid anyone touting outside.

Later in the evening, Trastevere's bars fill with students and young Romans, and the piazzas become crowded and noisy, especially at weekends. It is lively and fun but not a place for a quiet night.

Above Trastevere, a road and paths climb up the Janiculum Hill, the Gianicolo, which offers one of the best views over the city's domes and rooftops. At noon each day, a cannon is fired from the hill, a tradition that dates back to the nineteenth century. It is a lovely walk at sunset.

What is Trastevere good for? Wandering, Roman food, evening atmosphere, beautiful churches and the views from the Gianicolo. What is it not good for? Peace and quiet at night, or a central base for the big ancient sights; it is across the river, though walking to the centre is easy. Its popularity also means that some streets feel very touristy.

Trastevere is where Rome stops performing and sits down to eat. Arrive in the late afternoon, wander until the lights come on, and choose a table in a lane where the voices around you are Roman. It is the best way to end a day in the city.

name: Monti: The Ancient Slum That Became Rome's Most Charming Village
description: In the shadow of the Colosseum, ancient Rome's rough quarter is now a village of vintage shops, wine bars and ivy-covered piazzas where Romans actually live.
details:
Monti sits on the slopes between the Colosseum, the Roman Forum and the station of Termini, and it is one of the oldest inhabited districts of Rome. In antiquity, it was the Subura, a crowded, noisy and disreputable neighbourhood of tenements, taverns and brothels, right next to the monuments of imperial power. Julius Caesar grew up here, according to ancient writers. Today, it is a lively, bohemian village in the heart of the city.

Its centre is the Piazza della Madonna dei Monti, a small square with a fountain where locals gather at all hours. In the morning, people sit on its steps with coffee and a cornetto; in the evening, it fills with young Romans with beers and wine from the shops around it. The surrounding streets, Via Urbana, Via del Boschetto and Via dei Serpenti, are lined with independent boutiques, vintage clothing shops, artisans, bookshops and small restaurants.

Monti's great advantage is its location. A five-minute walk from the piazza takes you to the Imperial Forums and the Colosseum, and yet the neighbourhood itself feels relaxed and residential. Ivy climbs the walls of old palazzi, washing hangs from windows, and there are corners where you can sit and hear nothing but birds and church bells.

There are fine churches, too. Santa Maria Maggiore, one of Rome's four major basilicas, stands at the edge of the district, its interior glowing with mosaics from the fifth century. San Pietro in Vincoli, closer to the Colosseum, holds the chains said to have bound Saint Peter and, more remarkably, Michelangelo's powerful statue of Moses, made for the tomb of Pope Julius II.

In the evening, Monti becomes one of the best places in central Rome to eat and drink. Wine bars serve Italian wines by the glass with plates of cheese and cured meats; trattorias offer Roman classics; and newer restaurants experiment with lighter, modern cooking. It is busy but rarely rowdy, and it is popular with Romans as well as visitors.

Monti also has a strong sense of itself as a community. Its residents, the monticiani, have long had a reputation in Rome for their independent spirit, and you can still feel it in the way neighbours greet each other across the piazza, in the small craft workshops that survive among the boutiques, and in the local festivals that bring the streets together. It is a neighbourhood that has welcomed visitors without quite surrendering to them.

What is Monti good for? A base close to the ancient sites, independent shopping, wine bars, local life and evenings in the piazza. What is it not good for? Grand views or wide open spaces; its streets are narrow and steep in places. Some streets near Termini station are less attractive, so it is worth staying in the heart of the district around the piazza.

After a morning among the ruins of the Forum and the Colosseum, crowded and baking in the sun, Monti is the perfect place to recover. Walk up the hill, find a table in the shade, order a glass of wine and something to eat, and watch the neighbourhood go by. It has been doing exactly that for two thousand years.

name: Testaccio: Where Rome Really Eats
description: Built around a hill of ancient broken pots and an old slaughterhouse, working-class Testaccio is the soul of Roman cooking, and almost no tourists find it.
details:
Testaccio lies in the south of central Rome, beside the Tiber, and it is unlike any other neighbourhood in the city. Its name comes from Monte Testaccio, a hill around thirty-five metres high that is made entirely of broken pottery. In ancient Rome, this was the river port, where ships unloaded olive oil and other goods. The oil came in large clay amphorae, which could not be reused, so they were smashed and stacked in an orderly way, layer upon layer, for centuries. The result is a man-made hill of ancient rubbish, now covered in grass, and it is one of Rome's strangest sights.

In the late nineteenth century, Testaccio was built as a planned working-class district, with large apartment blocks around courtyards, to house the workers of the new municipal slaughterhouse, the Mattatoio. For decades, the slaughterhouse shaped the neighbourhood's life and its cooking. Workers were sometimes paid partly in offal, the 'fifth quarter' of the animal, and Testaccio's cooks turned these cuts into some of the most famous dishes of Roman cuisine: coda alla vaccinara, oxtail stewed with tomato and celery; trippa alla romana, tripe with tomato and mint; and rigatoni con la pajata, made with veal intestines.

The slaughterhouse closed in the 1970s, and its buildings now house a museum of contemporary art, university faculties, a cultural centre and spaces for events. The neighbourhood remains strongly local, with long-time residents, families and students, and it has a fierce loyalty to its football club, AS Roma.

Testaccio's market, in a modern covered building, is one of the best in Rome. In the morning, stalls sell fruit, vegetables, meat, fish, cheese and bread, and a number of food stands serve sandwiches, pasta and street food at fair prices to locals on their lunch break. It is a good place to eat well and cheaply, and to see how Romans shop.

Nearby, the Pyramid of Cestius, a real Roman tomb built in the first century BC in the shape of an Egyptian pyramid, stands beside the city walls. Next to it is the Non-Catholic Cemetery, a peaceful, green place where the English poets Keats and Shelley are buried, among many others. It is one of the most beautiful and moving corners of Rome.

In the evening, Testaccio's trattorias fill with Romans, and around Monte Testaccio, in the old warehouses and cellars dug into the hillside, there are clubs and bars that stay open late. It is a lively but very local nightlife.

What is Testaccio good for? Authentic Roman food, the market, the Pyramid and the Non-Catholic Cemetery, a genuinely local atmosphere, and an escape from the tourist crowds. What is it not good for? Big monuments or postcard views; it is a working neighbourhood rather than a picturesque one. It is also a short metro or tram ride, or a longer walk, from the historic centre.

Rome's grand sights belong to the world. Testaccio belongs to the Romans. Come here hungry, eat oxtail at a trattoria where the menu has not changed in decades, and walk past a hill made of two-thousand-year-old pots on your way home. It is a uniquely Roman evening.

name: Acropolis at opening time, then the Museum
description: The single best way to see the Parthenon is to be at the gate when it opens, before the tour buses and the heat arrive. Follow it with the Acropolis Museum, whose top-floor Parthenon Gallery lines up the original frieze with views of the temple itself. Book a timed Acropolis ticket online in advance, as entry slots sell out on busy cruise days.

name: Walk the Archaeological Promenade
description: The pedestrian Dionysiou Areopagitou street loops around the Acropolis past the Theatre of Dionysus and the Odeon of Herodes Atticus toward Thissio and the Ancient Agora. It is free, shaded in parts, and links most of the ancient sites without a single taxi. It is lovely again at dusk, when the Acropolis lights up.

name: The Ancient Agora is often skipped, and shouldn't be
description: Most cruise visitors stop at the Acropolis, but the Ancient Agora below it has the best-preserved classical temple in Greece (the Temple of Hephaestus) and the rebuilt Stoa of Attalos museum. It is quieter, greener, and gives a real sense of where Athenians actually lived and argued.

name: A rooftop at sunset with the Parthenon lit up
description: If you are overnighting or have a late departure, an Acropolis-view rooftop bar around Monastiraki or Plaka at sunset is one of the great Athens moments. Popular rooftops book out for golden hour, so reserve ahead and expect a minimum spend at some.

name: Sounion for the sunset, not the midday
description: The Temple of Poseidon at Cape Sounion is about 70 km along the coast and makes sense for an evening trip, when the sun sets over the Aegean behind the columns. It is a half-day commitment and overrated in the midday heat, when the light is flat and the site is exposed.

name: Changing of the guard at Syntagma
description: The Evzone guards change at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in front of Parliament every hour, with a larger ceremony on Sunday mornings. It is free and takes ten minutes, and it is easy to fit in between Plaka and the National Garden.

name: Plaka and Anafiotika's hidden lanes
description: Beyond Plaka's souvenir streets, climb into Anafiotika, a tiny Cycladic-style hamlet of whitewashed houses tucked under the Acropolis rock. It feels like an island village in the middle of the city and takes 20 minutes to wander.

name: Watch the caldera sunset somewhere other than Oia
description: Oia's sunset is famous, but its castle viewpoint is packed shoulder-to-shoulder well before sunset, and getting back afterward is a scramble. Imerovigli and Firostefani have equally dramatic caldera views with a fraction of the crowd. On a tight port day, a caldera terrace in Fira is easier still.

name: The Fira–Oia caldera walk
description: The clifftop path from Fira through Imerovigli to Oia is the island's best experience for active visitors: about 10 km of caldera views, blue domes and Skaros Rock. Go early in the morning and take a taxi or bus back. It is a half-day commitment.

name: Akrotiri, the Bronze Age Pompeii
description: Under a protective roof, the excavated Minoan-era town of Akrotiri preserves multi-storey houses buried by the great eruption about 3,600 years ago. It is one of the most remarkable archaeological sites in the Aegean and is overlooked by many beach-focused visitors. Pair it with the Museum of Prehistoric Thera in Fira, where its frescoes are displayed.

name: A caldera boat to the volcano and hot springs
description: Boat trips from the old port visit the volcanic islet of Nea Kameni and the warm, iron-red springs off Palea Kameni. A catamaran sunset cruise is the classic splurge. Book sunset sailings ahead in summer, and note that meltemi winds can cause cancellations.

name: Wine tasting in volcanic vineyards
description: Santorini's Assyrtiko grows in basket-shaped vines low to the volcanic soil, and its wineries are among Greece's best. A tasting at an estate overlooking the caldera is a memorable alternative to crowded viewpoints; book ahead for sunset slots.

name: Plan your tender and cable car time
description: Cruise passengers reach Fira by tender and then the cable car, steps or donkeys, and queues for the cable car can take over an hour. Build your day around this: do Oia or the hike first, then come back with plenty of time, since missing the last tender is a real risk here.

name: Wander the Venetian Harbour and the Old Town lanes
description: Chania's Venetian harbour, with its lighthouse, domed mosque and pastel houses, is the most beautiful old port on Crete. The real charm lies in the lanes behind it in Topanas, Splantzia and the old Jewish quarter. Walk out to the lighthouse early, before the heat and crowds.

name: Balos lagoon by boat
description: Balos, with its white sand and pale turquoise lagoon, is Crete's most photographed beach, usually reached by boat from Kissamos with a stop at Gramvousa island's fortress. It is a full-day trip that suits overnighters and extended stays, and the boats should be booked ahead.

name: Elafonissi's pink-tinged lagoon
description: Elafonissi's shallow, warm lagoon is perfect for families, with patches of pink sand from crushed shells. The drive takes about two hours each way through mountain villages. It is very crowded by midday in summer, so arrive early.

name: Samaria Gorge for serious walkers
description: Europe's most famous gorge hike runs 13–16 km downhill from the Omalos plateau to the Libyan Sea, ending with a ferry and bus back. It is unforgettable but a full, tiring day, open only seasonally, and not feasible on a normal cruise call.

name: The Akrotiri monasteries and Seitan Limania
description: Close to Souda port, the Akrotiri peninsula combines the handsome Agia Triada monastery, the hike down to the ruined Katholiko monastery, and the dramatic swimming cove of Seitan Limania. It is an ideal port-day loop if you have a car.

name: Cretan food, wine and raki
description: Crete has one of Greece's great food cultures, and Chania is the best place to sample dakos, kalitsounia, snails, lamb and local wines, ending with complimentary raki. A cooking class, an olive oil or winery visit, or the Saturday farmers' market adds a lot to a stay.

name: The Battle of Crete cemeteries
description: For those interested in history, the immaculate Souda Bay Commonwealth War Cemetery, just minutes from the cruise port, and the German cemetery at Maleme tell the story of the 1941 airborne invasion. They make a quiet, moving contrast to the beaches.

name: Ancient Olympia is the reason to come
description: The sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia, birthplace of the Olympic Games, is about 40 minutes inland, and almost every visitor heads there. Walk through the vaulted tunnel into the original stadium and run the track, see the fallen columns of the Temple of Zeus, and allow time for the excellent museum. Go early, before the heat and tour crowds.

name: Don't skip the Olympia museum
description: The Archaeological Museum of Olympia holds the Hermes of Praxiteles, the Nike of Paionios and the pediment sculptures from the Temple of Zeus. Many cruise visitors rush past it, but it brings the ruins to life.

name: Getting to Olympia independently
description: Independent options from the port include taxis on a fixed round-trip price and, in some seasons, a train. The train has had periods of suspension, so check that it is running before relying on it. A shore excursion or a pre-agreed taxi is the simplest way to be sure of returning on time.

name: A lazy harbour lunch in Katakolon
description: If you return early, Katakolon's little waterfront makes for a relaxed fish lunch and a stroll among the cafés and shops. Agios Andreas beach, a short ride or walk north, is a pleasant swim stop with views of ancient Pheia's submerged ruins.

name: Wineries and olive oil near Olympia
description: The Ilia countryside around Olympia has family wineries and olive producers offering tastings. These pair well with the site for those wanting more than ruins; book ahead, as many need appointments.

name: Overrated for the effort: going far afield
description: Trips to places like Pylos, the Neda waterfalls or Strofylia look tempting on a map but take most of a nine-hour port day in driving. On a single call, Olympia plus a harbour lunch is the better use of your time.

name: Corfu Old Town, a UNESCO site
description: Corfu Town's Venetian-era old town is a maze of shaded lanes, arcaded streets and Italianate squares. Highlights include the elegant Liston arcade, the Spianada, and the Church of St Spyridon, whose silver-adorned relics are the island's spiritual heart.

name: The two fortresses
description: The Old Fortress on its promontory and the New Fortress above the port give the best views of the old town and harbour. The Old Fortress is the more rewarding climb, with a lighthouse at the top. Check opening hours, as they vary by season.

name: Paleokastritsa's coves and monastery
description: Paleokastritsa on the west coast has clear coves, boat trips to sea caves, and a hilltop monastery with sweeping views. It is about 40 minutes from town on winding roads, making it a half-day trip from the port.

name: The Achilleion Palace
description: Built for Empress Elisabeth of Austria (Sisi), the Achilleion is a neoclassical palace with terraced gardens and statues of Achilles overlooking the sea. It is about 20 minutes from town and one of Corfu's most visited sights.

name: Kanoni and Mouse Island
description: The view from Kanoni over the white Vlacherna Monastery and Pontikonisi (Mouse Island) is Corfu's postcard image, close to the airport runway where planes fly in low. It is quick to reach from town and worth a short stop.

name: Corfiot food with a Venetian accent
description: Corfu's cuisine shows Venetian influence in dishes like pastitsada, sofrito and bourdeto. A taverna meal is worth seeking out, as are local kumquat liqueur and ginger beer, a British-era legacy.

name: Diocletian's Palace is a living town
description: Split's old town is a Roman emperor's palace that people still live in: cafés in the Peristyle, homes built into the walls, and the cellars below. Explore the substructures and the Cathedral of St Domnius bell tower for the best view over the rooftops.

name: Marjan Hill for views and a swim
description: Climb the steps from Varoš up Marjan Hill for panoramic views over the city and islands. Continue through pine forest to quiet coves for a swim. It is the easiest escape from the old town crowds.

name: Island day trips: Hvar, Brač and the Blue Cave
description: Catamarans connect Split to Hvar and Brač, and speedboat tours go to the Blue Cave on Biševo. These are memorable but weather-dependent full days; book ahead in summer and confirm return times against your ship's departure.

name: Krka National Park and Trogir
description: Krka's waterfalls and boardwalks are about an hour away, and swimming at the main falls is now banned. On the way, the UNESCO-listed medieval town of Trogir is a lovely, compact stop. Both together make a half-day or longer trip.

name: Evening on the Riva
description: The palm-lined Riva promenade fills up in the evening with locals strolling and terraces buzzing. It is the best people-watching in Split, with the palace walls lit behind you.

name: Walk the city walls early
description: The 2 km circuit of the city walls is Dubrovnik's defining experience, with views over the terracotta roofs and the sea. It is one-way, steep in places and fully exposed, so go at opening time before the cruise crowds and heat. It is the single thing visitors most regret skipping.

name: Cable car up Mount Srđ
description: The cable car rises to Mount Srđ for a sweeping view down over the walled city, the islands and the coast, especially beautiful at sunset. It can close in strong winds.

name: Lokrum Island escape
description: A short ferry from the old port takes you to Lokrum, a car-free island with a botanical garden, a monastery, peacocks and rocky swimming spots. It is a calm contrast to the crowded old town; check the last boat back.

name: Kayak around the walls
description: Sea kayak tours paddle beneath the city walls and around Lokrum, often with a stop at a cave beach. It is one of the most memorable ways to see Dubrovnik from the water.

name: Avoid the midday crowd crush
description: When several ships are in, Stradun and the main gates become very crowded from mid-morning. Plan the walls and old town early or late, and spend the middle of the day on Lokrum, the cable car or a boat trip.

name: Climb to the fortress early
description: The climb up the walls to San Giovanni fortress gives the famous view of Kotor's bay. It is about 1,350 steps in full sun, so go at opening time; the free Ladder of Kotor trail offers similar views without the fortress itself.

name: Perast and Our Lady of the Rocks
description: Twenty-five minutes along the bay, baroque Perast is one of the prettiest towns on the Adriatic. A short boat ride takes you to the man-made island church of Our Lady of the Rocks. It is the bay's most rewarding half-day.

name: Get lost in Kotor Old Town
description: Kotor's walled medieval town is compact but full of squares, Romanesque churches and its famous street cats. Early morning and evening, once cruise passengers have left, are the most atmospheric times.

name: Lovćen, Njeguši and the serpentine road
description: The 25-hairpin road above Kotor climbs to Njeguši, famous for smoked ham and cheese, and on to the Njegoš Mausoleum on Mount Lovćen, with one of the Balkans' great views. It is a half-day or more, and best with a driver.

name: A boat trip around the bay
description: Boat tours explore the bay's villages and islands, and speedboats head out to the Blue Cave near the bay's mouth. They are memorable but weather-dependent, so book with a reputable operator and confirm timings.

name: Pompeii or Herculaneum, or both
description: Pompeii is vast and iconic, while Herculaneum is smaller, better preserved and far less crowded, and easier to do well on a port day. Choose based on your time; doing both in one day is tiring.

name: Naples' National Archaeological Museum
description: This museum holds the treasures removed from Pompeii and Herculaneum, including mosaics, frescoes and the famous Farnese sculptures. Many visitors to the ruins never see it, and it is one of the world's great museums of the ancient world.

name: Naples pizza where it was born
description: Pizza is a pilgrimage here, with long lines at the famous old pizzerias in the historic center. Arriving early or going for a mid-afternoon slice helps avoid the queues.

name: Spaccanapoli and Naples Underground
description: Walk Spaccanapoli, the long straight street through the historic center, past churches, nativity workshops on Via San Gregorio Armeno, and street food. Below ground, guided Napoli Sotterranea tours explore Greek and Roman tunnels.

name: The Veiled Christ
description: In the Sansevero Chapel, Giuseppe Sanmartino's marble Veiled Christ seems carved from translucent cloth. Entry is timed and sells out, so book ahead.

name: Capri and the Amalfi Coast
description: Capri and the Amalfi Coast are reachable by ferry and road but are full-day undertakings with weather-dependent boats and heavy traffic. On a single port day, choose one and leave buffer for the return.

name: Vesuvius crater walk
description: The short, steep walk to the rim of Vesuvius gives views over the Bay of Naples and down into the crater. Entry is timed and must be booked in advance, and the trail can close in bad weather; combine it with Pompeii or Herculaneum.

name: Plan around the train from Civitavecchia
description: Rome is roughly an hour or more by train from Civitavecchia, so a port day gives you only a few hours in the city. Prioritize one or two areas, and plan your return train with a generous buffer.

name: Colosseum, Forum and Palatine
description: The Colosseum, Roman Forum and Palatine Hill together are the heart of ancient Rome, and timed tickets sell out. Book in advance, especially for arena-floor or underground access.

name: The City That Kept Rebuilding Itself
description: Athens has been the centre of the world, a forgotten provincial town and a capital built almost from scratch. Everything you see on arrival is a layer of that story.
details:
Stand anywhere in central Athens and look up, and the Acropolis is there. It has been the fixed point of this city for well over three thousand years, a flat-topped limestone rock rising from the Attic plain, close enough to the sea to watch it and high enough to defend. Mycenaean kings built a fortress on it in the Bronze Age. Later Athenians dedicated it to their goddess, Athena, and in the fifth century BC, flush with the wealth and confidence that followed their victories over the Persians, they crowned it with the Parthenon.

That fifth century is the Athens most visitors come looking for, and it is worth understanding how short and how extraordinary it was. In a few generations, this one city developed a form of democracy, built the temples on the Acropolis, staged the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides in the theatre of Dionysus below the rock, and argued philosophy in the Agora, where Socrates questioned anyone who would stop. Its power rested on the sea. Themistocles fortified the harbour of Piraeus, the Long Walls linked it to the city, and the Athenian fleet made the city rich. When your ship docks in Piraeus, you are arriving where that power began.

Then the story turns quieter, and much longer. Athens was defeated by Sparta, absorbed into the Macedonian world and then into the Roman Empire, which admired it as a university town; emperors such as Hadrian adorned it with libraries, arches and the vast Temple of Olympian Zeus. Under the Byzantines, the Parthenon became a church, and small domed chapels rose among the houses; several survive today, sunk below the modern pavement. Under the Franks and then the Ottomans, who held Athens for nearly four centuries, the Parthenon became a mosque, and the Acropolis a fortress with houses crowded onto it.

The temple's ruin came late and suddenly. In 1687, during a Venetian siege, a shell struck the gunpowder the Ottoman garrison had stored inside the Parthenon, and the explosion tore the building apart. In the early nineteenth century, Lord Elgin removed much of its surviving sculpture to Britain, where it remains in the British Museum, a source of lasting grievance in Greece.

By the time Greece won its independence in the 1820s, Athens was a modest town of a few thousand people clustered beneath the rock. That it became the capital at all was partly a romantic choice by the new kingdom and its Bavarian-born king, Otto. Architects laid out a new city of straight avenues and neoclassical buildings, many of which still line Panepistimiou Street. The Acropolis was cleared of its later buildings and turned into the archaeological monument we see now. Stonemasons from the island of Anafi, who came to work on the new buildings, built their own little Cycladic village on the slope beneath the rock; it is still there, and it is called Anafiotika.

The twentieth century changed Athens again, and dramatically. After the Greek defeat in Asia Minor in 1922, more than a million refugees arrived in Greece in the population exchange with Turkey, and many settled in and around Athens and Piraeus, transforming the city's size, its neighbourhoods and its music; rebetiko, the Greek blues, grew out of their experience. After the Second World War and the civil war that followed, people poured in from the countryside, and the city was rebuilt in concrete apartment blocks, the polykatoikies, that now stretch to the mountains.

So what are you looking at when you arrive? An ancient sacred rock with a temple that has been a church, a mosque and a powder magazine. A Roman and Byzantine town folded into its streets. A nineteenth-century capital designed to evoke the past. And a vast, energetic, modern city that grew around all of it in a few decades, noisy and imperfect and full of life.

Athens is often described as a city of ruins, but it is better understood as a city of survivals. Every layer has been damaged, buried, rebuilt or reused, and none has entirely disappeared. Walk from the Agora to the Acropolis, past a Byzantine chapel and a neoclassical mansion to a café in a concrete block, and you are walking through all of them at once.

name: The Island That Blew Itself Apart
description: Santorini's shape, its soil, its wine and even its architecture were made by a volcano. To understand the island, you have to start with the explosion.
details:
Seen from a ship sailing into the caldera, Santorini looks almost impossible: a ring of cliffs, striped red, black and white, rising sheer from deep blue water, with white villages balanced on the rim like snow. What you are looking at is the inside of a volcano. Or rather, what remains of one.

Once, this was a single, roughly round island. Geologists believe it had been shaped by repeated eruptions over hundreds of thousands of years. Then, in the Late Bronze Age, around 1600 BC, came one of the largest volcanic eruptions in human history. The island blew out vast amounts of pumice and ash, the centre collapsed, and the sea poured in to fill the hole. The cliffs you see from the ship are the walls of that collapse, and the islands of Santorini, Thirasia and the tiny islets around them are fragments of the old rim.

Before the eruption, a thriving Bronze Age town stood near the southern tip of the island, at the place now called Akrotiri. Its people built multi-storey houses with drains and painted their walls with vivid frescoes of ships, flowers, swallows and boys carrying fish. They traded across the Aegean and had close links with Minoan Crete. When the eruption came, the town was buried under metres of ash, which preserved it in remarkable detail. Unlike Pompeii, no bodies have been found, which suggests that the inhabitants had warning and left. Where they went, nobody knows.

The eruption has been linked, inevitably, to the legend of Atlantis, the island civilisation Plato said was swallowed by the sea. It is an attractive idea, and you will hear it often on Santorini, but it remains a theory, not a fact, and Plato's story contains much that does not fit. It is fair to enjoy it as one of the island's good stories.

The volcano is not finished. In the middle of the caldera, the dark, barren islands of Nea and Palea Kameni were built by later eruptions, and Nea Kameni last erupted in 1950. It is monitored constantly, and you can walk over its black lava and smell sulphur at its craters.

After the Bronze Age, people returned. Greek settlers built a city, Ancient Thera, on a mountain ridge on the eastern side, and it was occupied through Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine times. In the Middle Ages, Venetian lords ruled the island as part of the Duchy of Naxos, and it is from their time that the name Santorini comes, after Saint Irene. A Catholic community has survived here ever since. Islanders built fortified villages inland, such as Pyrgos and Emporio, against pirates.

Everything else that makes Santorini distinctive flows from the volcano. The soil is volcanic ash and pumice, with almost no water, so islanders learned to farm without irrigation, growing small, intensely flavoured tomatoes and fava, a yellow split pea, and training their Assyrtiko vines into low baskets on the ground to protect them from the wind. The vines are so well adapted that the phylloxera plague, which devastated Europe's vineyards in the nineteenth century, never took hold here. The soft volcanic rock could be dug easily, so poorer islanders carved cave houses into the cliffs, cool in summer and warm in winter. The wealthy sea captains of Oia built mansions above them.

In 1956, a powerful earthquake destroyed much of Oia and Fira, and many families left. For a time, the island was poor and half empty. Its revival, from the 1970s onward, came with tourism, and today Santorini is one of the most visited islands in the world.

So when you stand on the rim at Fira and look down at the caldera, remember what you are seeing: the inside of a volcano, the scar of an explosion that buried a Bronze Age town, and an island that its people rebuilt again and again on the edge of the crater. It is beautiful because it is dangerous, and it has always been.

name: Layers of Empire on a Cretan Harbour
description: Minoans, Venetians, Ottomans, Egyptians and Cretan rebels all left their mark on one small harbour town. Read it right and Chania tells the whole story of Crete.
details:
Chania sits on the north coast of western Crete, between the sea and the White Mountains, whose peaks hold snow well into spring. Its harbour is small and perfectly sheltered, which is why people have lived here for thousands of years, and why so many powers have wanted it.

Beneath the old town lies Kydonia, a Bronze Age settlement of the Minoans, the civilisation that built the palaces of Knossos and Phaistos further east. Excavations near the harbour, on the hill of Kastelli, have revealed parts of it. After the Minoans, Kydonia remained an important city through classical, Roman and Byzantine times.

The town you see today, though, was largely shaped by Venice. After the Fourth Crusade, the Venetians took control of Crete in the early thirteenth century and held it for more than four hundred years. They called the town La Canea, built its harbour walls and its lighthouse, its arsenals for building and repairing galleys, and the fortifications that still ring the old town. Venetian nobles built tall stone houses with carved doorways, and Venice turned Crete into a key stronghold on its trade routes to the East. The culture of this period, a blend of Venetian and Cretan, produced painters, poets and a rich literature in the Cretan dialect.

In 1645, after a siege, the Ottomans took Chania. It was the beginning of more than two centuries of Ottoman rule. They converted churches into mosques, added minarets and baths, and built the domed mosque on the harbour that still dominates the waterfront. The Splantzia quarter became the heart of the Turkish town. Wooden balconies were added to Venetian houses. A Jewish community, which had lived in Chania for many centuries, continued in its own quarter.

Crete never settled quietly under the Ottomans. Throughout the nineteenth century, the island rose in revolt again and again. One of the most famous episodes, the destruction of the monastery of Arkadi in 1866, when defenders blew up the powder store rather than surrender, became a symbol of Cretan resistance across Europe. In 1898, after further uprisings and intervention by the European powers, Crete became an autonomous state under Ottoman suzerainty, with Prince George of Greece as High Commissioner and Chania as its capital. Union with Greece finally came in 1913, when the Greek flag was raised over the Firkas fortress at the harbour.

One of the leaders of that struggle was Eleftherios Venizelos, born near Chania, who went on to become one of the most important statesmen of modern Greece. He is buried on the Akrotiri hill above the city.

The twentieth century brought more upheaval. In 1923, the population exchange between Greece and Turkey led the island's remaining Muslim population to leave. In May 1941, Crete was invaded by German paratroopers in the Battle of Crete, and Chania was heavily bombed. The occupation that followed was harsh, and Cretans fought a long resistance in the mountains. In 1944, the Jewish community of Chania was deported, and almost all of them died when the ship carrying them was sunk. Their synagogue, Etz Hayyim, was restored in the 1990s and is today a place of remembrance and prayer.

Chania remained the capital of Crete until 1971, when Heraklion took that role. Since then, it has become one of the most beloved towns in Greece for visitors, but it has never lost its strong local identity.

So when you stand on the harbour, look around. The lighthouse was rebuilt by the Egyptians in the 1830s, during the brief period when they ruled Crete. The mosque is Ottoman. The arsenals and walls are Venetian. The flag on the Firkas commemorates union with Greece. The people around you are Cretans, fiercely proud of a history that has made them who they are. Few harbours anywhere hold so much in a single view.

name: Where the Games Began
description: Inland from a quiet fishing port lies the sanctuary where Greeks gathered to compete for more than a thousand years. Here is what you are really walking into at Olympia.
details:
Katakolon is a small port, and it has always been one: a sheltered landing on the coast of Elis, the region of the western Peloponnese whose fertile plains and rivers made it rich in grain, olives and vines. Its importance today comes entirely from its neighbour, forty minutes inland, at the meeting of the Alfeios and Kladeos rivers. There, in a green, sheltered valley below a pine-covered hill named after Kronos, lies Olympia.

Olympia was never a city. It was a sanctuary, a sacred place dedicated above all to Zeus, the king of the gods. People worshipped here long before the Games; the earliest offerings go back to the Bronze Age. Over time, it became one of the most important religious centres in the Greek world, filled with temples, altars, treasuries and statues dedicated by cities and individuals from across the Mediterranean.

The Games themselves, by tradition, began in 776 BC, the date from which the ancient Greeks later counted their history. Whether that date is precise is debated by historians, but it is the traditional starting point. The festival was held every four years in honour of Zeus, and during it, a sacred truce allowed athletes and spectators to travel safely to Olympia, even from cities at war. At first there was only a single race, the stade, roughly the length of the stadium. Over time, other events were added: longer races, wrestling, boxing, the pankration, a brutal form of all-in fighting, the pentathlon, chariot racing and horse racing.

The athletes competed naked, and only free Greek men could take part.
