Married women were barred from watching, on pain of severe punishment, according to ancient writers, though unmarried girls could attend, and there was a separate festival in honour of Hera in which young women raced. The winners received no gold, only a wreath cut from the sacred wild olive tree. Back home, though, they were treated as heroes, with statues, poems and, sometimes, free meals for life.

At its height, Olympia was crowded with grand buildings. The Temple of Zeus, completed in the fifth century BC, housed an enormous seated statue of the god made of gold and ivory by the sculptor Phidias. It was counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. The workshop where Phidias made it has been identified at the site, partly thanks to a small cup inscribed with his name. Today, the temple's huge column drums lie where earthquakes toppled them. The Temple of Hera, older and smaller, still has some standing columns, and it is here that the flame for every modern Olympic Games is lit, using the sun's rays focused by a mirror.

Along the approach to the stadium, a row of stone bases once held the Zanes, bronze statues of Zeus paid for with fines imposed on athletes who cheated or bribed. Their names were inscribed for everyone to see, a public warning that has lasted two and a half thousand years.

The ancient Games continued under Roman rule, and even emperors competed; Nero famously took part, and was declared victor in a chariot race despite falling from his chariot. They came to an end in the late fourth century AD, when the Christian emperor Theodosius suppressed pagan festivals. Over the following centuries, earthquakes and floods buried the site under metres of earth, and it was largely forgotten until excavations began in the nineteenth century.

In 1896, inspired in part by the rediscovery of Olympia, the French educator Pierre de Coubertin revived the Olympic Games in Athens. His heart is buried at Olympia, beside the International Olympic Academy.

So when you walk out of the vaulted tunnel onto the ancient track, you are stepping onto the ground where Greek athletes ran for more than a thousand years. It is a simple stretch of earth, but it has given the world one of its greatest traditions.

name: The Island Venice Kept and Britain Borrowed
description: Corfu was never conquered by the Ottomans, which is why it looks so unlike the rest of Greece. Its story is one of fortresses, empires and a stubborn local saint.
details:
Corfu lies at the northern entrance to the Adriatic, close to the coast of Albania and the Greek mainland. Its position has always been its fortune and its danger. Whoever held Corfu controlled the sea route between the Adriatic and the eastern Mediterranean, and so for most of its history, the island has been fought over by larger powers.

In antiquity, it was known as Corcyra, a colony founded by Corinth in the eighth century BC, which soon became a powerful naval city in its own right. Its quarrels with Corinth were one of the sparks that led to the Peloponnesian War. Many Greeks identify the island with Scheria, the land of the Phaeacians in Homer's Odyssey, where the shipwrecked Odysseus was found by the princess Nausicaa. That identification is ancient but unprovable, which makes it a perfect island story.

After Roman and Byzantine rule, and periods of Norman, Angevin and other control, Corfu came under the Republic of Venice in 1386. The Venetians stayed for more than four hundred years, and their rule shaped almost everything you see in Corfu Town. They strengthened the Old Fortress on its rocky promontory, built the New Fortress, and enclosed the town in walls. With space limited, houses rose to five or six storeys, crowded along narrow lanes. Venetian became the language of the elite, Catholicism the faith of the rulers, and Italian culture deeply influenced the island's architecture, cooking and music.

Most importantly, Corfu was never taken by the Ottomans, who conquered almost all of mainland Greece. The island withstood major sieges, most famously in 1537 and again in 1716. The 1716 siege was lifted, and Corfiots credit their patron saint, Saint Spyridon, with the victory. A fourth-century bishop from Cyprus, his relics had been brought to Corfu in the fifteenth century, and his feasts and processions remain the heart of the island's religious life.

When Venice fell to Napoleon in 1797, Corfu passed to the French, then briefly to a Russian and Ottoman alliance, then back to the French. During the French period, the Liston arcade was built along the edge of the Spianada, modelled on the Rue de Rivoli in Paris.

In 1815, after Napoleon's defeat, the Ionian Islands became a British protectorate, with Corfu as their capital. The British built the Palace of St Michael and St George, introduced cricket, which is still played on the Spianada, and left ginger beer and a taste for kumquats. They also built roads and water supplies across the island. In 1864, Britain ceded the Ionian Islands to Greece, and Corfu at last became Greek in government as well as in language and faith.

The late nineteenth century brought royal glamour. Empress Elisabeth of Austria built the Achilleion palace, later bought by Kaiser Wilhelm II. The Greek royal family used the villa of Mon Repos, where Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, was born in 1921. In the twentieth century, the Durrell family made the island famous in English literature.

The Second World War was hard for Corfu. The town was bombed, and in 1944 its Jewish community, which had lived on the island for centuries, was deported; very few survived. After the war, tourism slowly transformed the island's economy.

So when you walk from the cruise port into Corfu Town, you are walking into a Venetian fortress town, with French arcades, a British palace and Greek Orthodox churches where an ancient saint is still carried through the streets. Corfu is Greek in its soul, but its face was shaped by centuries of other people's empires. That is why it feels like nowhere else in Greece.

name: An Emperor's Retirement Home That Became a City
description: Split was not founded so much as moved into. The story of how a Roman palace became a living town explains everything about the city you are about to walk into.
details:
Split has a founding story unlike almost any other city. It did not grow up around a market, a harbour or a castle. It grew up inside the retirement home of a Roman emperor.

Diocletian was born in this part of Dalmatia, probably near the Roman city of Salona, a few kilometres inland. He rose through the army to become emperor in 284, and during his reign he reorganised the empire, dividing power among four rulers. He is also remembered for launching the last and most severe persecution of Christians. Then, in 305, he did something no Roman emperor had done before: he voluntarily gave up the throne. He returned to Dalmatia to a vast palace he had built on the coast, part luxurious villa, part fortified military camp, with high walls, four gates and a grid of streets. According to a much-repeated story, when he was later urged to return to power, he replied that if they could see the cabbages he had grown, they would not ask. Whether he really said it, the story captures something of the man who chose a garden by the sea over an empire.

After his death, the palace remained imperial property for a time. Then, in the seventh century, Salona was sacked by Avars and Slavs, and its refugees fled to the coast and took shelter within the palace walls. They built homes inside the emperor's halls, turned his corridors into streets and his courtyard into a square. Their town grew, and it never left.

Over the centuries, the palace became the medieval city of Split. Diocletian's mausoleum was turned into a cathedral and dedicated to Saint Domnius, a bishop of Salona martyred in the emperor's own persecution; it remains one of the oldest cathedral buildings in the world still in use. A Romanesque bell tower was added. A temple became a baptistery. Houses were built against and into the Roman walls, and when the town outgrew them, it spread west into a new medieval quarter around the square that locals call Pjaca.

Split's history after that is the history of Dalmatia. The town was ruled at various times by Byzantium, by Croatian and Hungarian kings, and, from 1420 until 1797, by Venice. The Venetians added Gothic and Renaissance palaces, and much of Split's medieval character dates from those centuries. After the fall of Venice came a short period of French rule under Napoleon and then more than a century of Austrian rule, during which Split grew into a modern port and the neoclassical arcades of the Prokurative were built on the waterfront.

In the twentieth century, Split became part of Yugoslavia, and after the Second World War it grew rapidly into a major port and industrial city, the second-largest city in Croatia today. In 1991, Croatia declared independence, and the wars that followed brought hardship to the region. Since then, tourism has transformed the city once again.

Diocletian's Palace is now a UNESCO World Heritage site, but it is not a museum. A couple of thousand people still live inside its walls. They hang their laundry from Roman windows, drink coffee on the Peristyle, the emperor's ceremonial courtyard, and walk to work through gates built seventeen centuries ago. Beneath the palace, the vast vaulted cellars that once supported the imperial apartments were filled with rubbish for centuries and have since been excavated; they show the original layout of the rooms above.

Split's culture grew from its streets and its sea. Its people are known for klapa, a style of unaccompanied harmony singing recognised by UNESCO, for their passion for the football club Hajduk Split, and for picigin, a ball game played in the shallow water of Bačvice beach. Above all, they are known for their love of an easy, unhurried life, which they call fjaka.

So when you walk through the Bronze Gate from the Riva into the cellars, and up onto the Peristyle, you are walking into a Roman emperor's house that became a city. It is still being lived in, argued in and sung in, and it will probably go on being lived in for a very long time.

name: The Republic That Chose Freedom over Gold
description: For centuries, this small walled city was an independent nation that survived by wits rather than armies. Its walls are famous; the story behind them is better.
details:
Dubrovnik began, according to tradition, as a refuge. In the seventh century, as the Roman city of Epidaurum, today's Cavtat, was overrun, its inhabitants fled to a rocky islet just off the coast, called Laus or Ragusium. Across a narrow channel, on the mainland, Slavic settlers founded a village among the oak woods, and the word for oak, dubrava, is often given as the origin of the name Dubrovnik. Over time, the channel was filled in, the two settlements merged, and the line of that old channel became the city's great main street, the Stradun. That is the traditional account, and it explains the shape of the city remarkably well.

Through the Middle Ages, the city, known in Latin and Italian as Ragusa, grew as a trading port under the protection of Byzantium and then Venice. In 1358, it freed itself from Venetian control and became, in effect, an independent republic under the nominal protection of the Hungarian-Croatian crown, and later of the Ottoman sultan, to whom it paid tribute. For the next four and a half centuries, the Republic of Ragusa was one of the most remarkable small states in Europe.

It had no great army. It survived through diplomacy, trade and caution. Its merchant ships sailed throughout the Mediterranean, and its consuls were posted in ports across the region. It balanced carefully between the great powers, paying tribute to the Ottomans while trading with Christian Europe. Its government was an aristocratic republic designed to prevent any one person from taking power: the rector, the head of state, served for just one month and could not leave the Rector's Palace during his term without permission. Above the gate of Fort Lovrijenac, a Latin inscription still reads, in translation, 'Freedom is not sold for all the gold in the world.' Libertas was the word on the Republic's flag.

Ragusa was also strikingly progressive for its time. It set up one of the earliest systematic quarantine systems in the world in 1377, isolating arriving travellers and goods to protect against plague. It abolished the slave trade in 1416. The pharmacy in the Franciscan monastery has been operating since the fourteenth century. And the city's walls, built and strengthened over centuries, and especially after the fall of Constantinople in 1453, made it one of the best-fortified cities in the Mediterranean.

In 1667, disaster struck. A catastrophic earthquake destroyed much of the city and killed thousands of people, including the rector. The city was rebuilt, largely in a restrained Baroque style, and the Stradun was lined with matching stone houses, which gives it its uniform appearance today. But the Republic never fully regained its former wealth.

Its end came in the Napoleonic wars. French forces entered the city in 1806, and in 1808 the Republic was formally abolished. After Napoleon's defeat, Dubrovnik passed to Austria and remained part of the Austrian empire until 1918, when it became part of the new Yugoslav state.

In 1991, as Croatia declared independence, Dubrovnik was besieged by the Yugoslav People's Army and shelled, despite its status as a UNESCO World Heritage site. Residents endured months of siege, and many buildings were damaged. After the war, the city was carefully restored, and from the walls today you can still see the difference between the brighter new roof tiles and the older, faded ones that survived.

Since then, Dubrovnik has become one of the most visited places in Europe, helped by its role as King's Landing in Game of Thrones. The city now works hard to balance its popularity with the needs of the people who live within its walls.

So when you walk through the Pile Gate, under the statue of Saint Blaise, the city's patron, holding a model of the town, remember what you are entering. Not just a beautiful walled city, but the capital of a small, proud republic that kept its freedom for centuries by being cleverer than its enemies.

name: A Town at the End of a Drowned Canyon
description: Kotor sits at the innermost corner of a bay carved by rivers, defended by walls climbing a mountain and shaped by sailors who carried its name across the world.
details:
The first thing that strikes anyone arriving in Kotor is the setting. The town sits at the very end of a long, winding bay, surrounded by mountains that rise almost straight out of the water, and above the town, a line of fortifications zigzags up a sheer limestone slope to a fortress more than two hundred metres above the sea.

The Bay of Kotor, the Boka Kotorska, is often called a fjord, but it was not carved by glaciers. It is a ria, a system of river canyons that was drowned by the sea as sea levels rose. Its narrow straits and deep inner basins make it one of the most sheltered natural harbours in the Mediterranean, and that is why people have lived and traded here since ancient times. In the Roman period, a settlement called Acruvium is believed to have stood here.

Through the Middle Ages, Kotor grew into an important trading town, part of the Byzantine world and later of the medieval Serbian state, which valued it as a port. It had its own statutes and a large measure of self-government. In 1166, the Cathedral of Saint Tryphon was consecrated, dedicated to a martyr whose relics, according to tradition, were brought to the town in the ninth century. The local maritime brotherhood, the Bokelj Navy, traces its origins to that event, and still performs its traditional dances at the saint's festivities.

In 1420, Kotor placed itself under the protection of Venice, and it remained Venetian until 1797. It was in these centuries that the town's walls reached their present form. The fortifications run for several kilometres, enclosing the town and climbing the mountainside to the Fortress of Saint John, and they were built to resist the Ottomans, whose territory lay just beyond the mountains. Kotor withstood Ottoman sieges, but its hinterland changed hands many times.

The Boka's wealth came from the sea. Its sailors and captains served on Venetian ships and later on ships of many nations, and their families built grand stone houses and churches in Kotor, Perast, Dobrota and Prčanj. Perast was so renowned for its seamen that it is said to have trained naval officers for Peter the Great of Russia; it is a story the village tells with pride. Off Perast, the island church of Our Lady of the Rocks stands on an artificial island that, according to tradition, sailors built by dropping stones on a reef after finding an icon of the Virgin there.

After the fall of Venice, the Bay passed through French, Russian and Austrian hands, and from 1814 it was part of the Austrian empire for more than a century. The Austrians built roads, including the dramatic serpentine road that climbs from Kotor up the mountain towards Cetinje, the old capital of Montenegro. After the First World War, the Boka became part of the new Yugoslav state.

In 1979, a powerful earthquake caused great damage in Kotor and along the coast. The old town was carefully restored, and in the same year it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site.

Montenegro became independent in 2006, after the dissolution of its union with Serbia. Kotor is now one of the country's great treasures, and one of the Adriatic's most popular cruise ports.

The town itself is a reflection of all these layers. Its lanes form a deliberate maze, with small squares named after the goods once traded there. Catholic and Orthodox churches stand a few steps apart. Venetian lions are carved over the gates. And everywhere, there are cats, which have become the town's beloved symbol.

So when you walk through the Sea Gate, look up at the walls climbing into the sky and remember what you are seeing: a fortified trading town at the end of a drowned canyon, defended for centuries against empires, and home to sailors who carried the name of this small bay to ports all over the world.

name: The New City That Is Nearly Three Thousand Years Old
description: Founded by Greeks, ruled by Romans, Normans, Spaniards and Bourbons, and overshadowed always by a volcano, Naples is a city that has learned to live on the edge.
details:
Naples is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Europe, and it has never stopped being lived in. Greek colonists settled on this curving bay long before Rome was a power. First came a settlement called Parthenope, named after a siren who, according to legend, washed ashore here after failing to lure Odysseus with her song. Later, in the fifth century BC, a new city was founded nearby, and it was called Neapolis, the 'new city'. That name became Napoli.

The Greeks gave Naples its street plan. The historic centre still follows their grid of three long, parallel streets, the decumani, crossed by narrow lanes. The middle one, known as Spaccanapoli, slices straight through the old city. Under Roman rule, Naples remained proudly Greek in language and culture, a favourite retreat for wealthy Romans who built villas along the bay. The emperor Tiberius ruled from nearby Capri, and the poet Virgil is said to be buried in the city.

Naples has always lived beside a volcano. In AD 79, Vesuvius erupted and buried the towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum, preserving them in ash and volcanic material until their rediscovery in the eighteenth century. Vesuvius has erupted many times since, most recently in 1944, during the Second World War. Today, hundreds of thousands of people live in the official danger zone around it. Naples has a fatalistic, affectionate relationship with its volcano, which appears on everything from pizza boxes to paintings.

After the fall of Rome, Naples passed through the hands of Byzantines, Normans, Swabians, French Angevins and Aragonese. Each left monuments: the Angevins built Castel Nuovo, the great fortress by the port, and many of the city's Gothic churches. In the sixteenth century, Naples came under Spanish rule. The Spanish viceroys built Via Toledo and the grid of narrow streets beside it, the Quartieri Spagnoli, to house their soldiers. Under Spain, Naples became one of the largest cities in Europe.

In the eighteenth century, the Bourbons made Naples the capital of their kingdom, later known as the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. It was a glittering period. They built the Royal Palace, the vast palace of Caserta outside the city, and the Teatro di San Carlo, opened in 1737 and the oldest continuously active opera house in Europe. Naples was a great capital of music, art and learning, and a must-see on the Grand Tour.

That changed with Italian unification in 1861. Naples lost its status as a capital, and many Neapolitans still feel that the South paid a heavy price for unification. In the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries, poverty drove millions of southern Italians to emigrate, many of them through the port of Naples, to the Americas and beyond. Cholera epidemics and war brought further hardship.

Through it all, Naples kept its extraordinary popular culture. Its faith is intense and personal, centred on San Gennaro, the patron saint whose dried blood, kept in the cathedral, is expected to liquefy three times a year. Its music, from traditional songs such as 'O Sole Mio' to modern pop, is loved across Italy. Its food, especially its pizza, has conquered the world; the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo is now recognised by UNESCO. And its people are famous for their wit, warmth and resilience.

So what are you looking at when you arrive? A Greek grid of streets crowded with Baroque churches, a Spanish soldiers' quarter, a Bourbon royal capital and a modern city of more than a million people, all squeezed between a volcano and the sea. Naples has survived eruptions, plagues, invasions and neglect, and it is still noisy, devout, funny and alive. That, perhaps, is its greatest monument.

name: All Roads Lead from the Harbour
description: Your ship docks in a port that an emperor built to feed Rome. From there, the story runs to the city that ruled the known world, and then to the church that outlasted it.
details:
Rome is about eighty kilometres from where your ship docks, and the distance is part of the story. Ancient Rome was not built on the sea. It grew on the hills beside the Tiber, some way inland, and for its food, its goods and its armies, it depended on ports along the coast. Civitavecchia is one of them.

In the early second century AD, the emperor Trajan ordered a new harbour built here, called Centumcellae. It was a deep, sheltered port, which Rome needed, and it grew into an important town. After the fall of the empire, it suffered raids and abandonment; in the ninth century, according to tradition, its people fled inland from Saracen raiders and later returned to the 'old city', the civitas vetus, which gave Civitavecchia its name. In the Renaissance, it became the main port of the Papal States, and the massive fortress that still guards the harbour, the Forte Michelangelo, was built in the sixteenth century, with Michelangelo credited with contributing to its design.

Rome itself began, according to its own legend, in 753 BC, when Romulus founded the city after killing his twin brother Remus; the two had been suckled by a she-wolf. Archaeology shows that the hills by the Tiber were indeed inhabited by around that time, but the story of the twins is myth. What is historical is that Rome grew from a small settlement into a kingdom, then a republic, and finally, under Augustus, an empire that ruled the entire Mediterranean world.

The monuments you will see in Rome come from different stages of that story. The Forum was the heart of the republic, where Romans voted, argued and worshipped. The Colosseum, completed in AD 80 under the Flavian emperors, held tens of thousands of spectators for gladiatorial games. The Pantheon, rebuilt under the emperor Hadrian in the second century, still has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, with its open oculus letting in the sky.

Then the story changes. In the fourth century, the emperor Constantine legalised Christianity, and Rome slowly became the centre of the Western Church. Over the following centuries, as the empire collapsed in the west, the bishops of Rome, the popes, became the most powerful figures in the city. Ancient buildings were stripped for stone, turned into churches or fortresses, and the city's population shrank dramatically.

In the Renaissance and Baroque periods, the popes rebuilt Rome as a Christian capital. They commissioned Michelangelo to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling and design the dome of St Peter's Basilica, Bernini to create the great colonnade of St Peter's Square and fountains such as the Four Rivers in Piazza Navona, and the Trevi Fountain was completed in the eighteenth century. Much of the beauty of the city as you see it now dates from these centuries.

In 1870, Rome was taken by the forces of the new Italian kingdom and became the capital of a united Italy. The popes withdrew into the Vatican, and in 1929, Vatican City was recognised as an independent state, the smallest in the world. Modern Rome grew around the ancient and papal city, with new avenues, ministries and neighbourhoods.

So when you step ashore at Civitavecchia and take the road or train to Rome, you are following one of the oldest routes in Europe, from a harbour built to feed an empire to the capital that empire ruled. In the city, you will see an ancient Roman ruin beside a medieval church, a Renaissance palace above a Roman street, and a Baroque fountain fed by an ancient aqueduct. Rome has never thrown anything away. That is why, after nearly three thousand years, it is still the Eternal City.

name: Marble, Memory and the Long Walk to the Sea
description: The Parthenon is the most famous ruin on earth, yet almost nothing about it is what it seems. Here is the story that makes sense of the rock above the city, and of the harbour you arrived in.
details:
It helps to begin not on the Acropolis but at the water, in Piraeus, because ancient Athens made the same choice. In the early fifth century BC the statesman Themistocles persuaded his fellow citizens to turn this rocky peninsula into their harbour and to pour their silver into a fleet. That fleet defeated the Persians at Salamis, just across the water you sailed past, in 480 BC. Afterwards the Athenians joined city and port with the Long Walls, a fortified corridor some seven kilometres long, so that Athens could never be starved while it ruled the sea. The modern metro line you may ride into town runs not far from that old line of defence. Athens has always been a city that looks down to its harbour.

Victory and the wealth of a maritime empire paid for what stands on the hill. Under Pericles, in the middle of the fifth century BC, the Athenians rebuilt the temples the Persians had burned. The Parthenon, dedicated to Athena Parthenos, the virgin goddess, was built between about 447 and 432 BC, designed by the architects Iktinos and Kallikrates, with sculpture overseen by Pheidias. Look closely and you will notice that it contains almost no straight lines: the columns swell slightly and lean inward, the platform curves upward at the centre. These refinements were meant to make the building look perfect to the human eye. It was also, originally, painted, and inside stood a towering statue of Athena in gold and ivory that has long since vanished.

What you see today is a survivor of everything that came after. The Parthenon became a church, dedicated to the Virgin Mary, in late antiquity. Under the Ottomans, who ruled Athens for nearly four centuries, it became a mosque, with a minaret. In 1687, during a Venetian siege, the Ottomans were using the building to store gunpowder; a Venetian shell struck it, and the explosion blew out its centre. Much of the damage you see dates from that single afternoon. In the early nineteenth century, agents of Lord Elgin removed a great part of the surviving sculpture to Britain, where it remains in the British Museum, and its return is still one of the most passionately argued questions in Greek cultural life. The modern Acropolis Museum, at the foot of the hill, was built with a top-floor gallery laid out to the Parthenon's exact dimensions, with original pieces and plaster casts side by side, the gaps left deliberately visible.

Below the rock lies the heart of everyday ancient life: the Ancient Agora, the marketplace and civic centre where citizens argued, bought olive oil, served on juries, and listened to Socrates question everyone he met. The beautifully preserved Temple of Hephaestus looks down on it, and the long colonnaded Stoa of Attalos, rebuilt in the twentieth century, gives you a sense of what a public building there felt like. Nearby, the Roman Agora and the elegant octagonal Tower of the Winds belong to the centuries when Athens was a revered university town under Roman rule.

Then there is the Athens of the last two hundred years. When Greece won its independence, the small Ottoman town clustered around the Acropolis was chosen as the new capital in 1834, and planners laid out boulevards and neoclassical buildings meant to echo the city's ancient glory. In the shadow of the rock, the tiny whitewashed lanes of Anafiotika were built by workers from the island of Anafi who came to build the new capital and recreated a piece of their home on the slopes. In Plaka, Byzantine chapels sit beside Ottoman fountains and nineteenth-century mansions.

So when you stand on the Acropolis, you are not looking at a single moment. You are looking at a temple, a church, a mosque, a ruin, a symbol and a national argument, all at once. The marble has been shaped by every power that has passed through this city, and it still has something to say to each of them.

name: The Island That Exploded: Reading Santorini's Layers
description: Every white house on the caldera rim sits on top of a catastrophe, and the story of that ancient eruption explains almost everything about the island you see today.
details:
Stand anywhere on the rim at Fira and look down: the sheer cliffs beneath you are a cross-section of disaster. The bands of red, black and cream rock are layers of lava and ash laid down by eruption after eruption over hundreds of thousands of years. The greatest of them, sometime in the late Bronze Age, around the seventeenth century BC (scholars still debate the exact date), blew apart the centre of what was then a round island and left the drowned crater, the caldera, in which your ship anchored. To arrive on Santorini is to sail into the wound.

Before that eruption, the island was home to a thriving town at Akrotiri on the southern coast, closely connected with the Minoan civilisation of Crete. Its people lived in multi-storey houses with drainage systems and walls painted with vivid frescoes: blue monkeys, swallows, boxing boys, a fleet of ships sailing between coastal towns. Then the town was buried under metres of volcanic ash. Strikingly, archaeologists have found almost no human remains and few valuables, which suggests the inhabitants had warning and fled, though where they went no one knows. The site was excavated from 1967 by the Greek archaeologist Spyridon Marinatos, and today you walk through its streets beneath a protective roof. Some of its frescoes are displayed in the Museum of Prehistoric Thera in Fira. Because a lost city buried by catastrophe sounds so much like Plato's tale of Atlantis, the two have often been linked, but that connection is speculation, a romantic theory rather than established fact.

Life returned. Centuries later, settlers from the Greek mainland founded a town high on the rocky ridge of Mesa Vouno, above the black beaches of Kamari and Perissa. Ancient Thera, as it is called, grew over a thousand years, and later served as a base for the Ptolemaic kings of Egypt. Walking its windswept ruins today, with the sea on both sides, gives you a sense of how islanders chose high ground for safety.

The name Santorini itself comes from the Middle Ages, from Santa Irini, Saint Irene, a name the Venetians and other Latin sailors used for the island. After the Fourth Crusade, Venetian lords of the Duchy of the Archipelago ruled the Cyclades, and Santorini's people built fortified villages known as kastelia against pirates. You can still see their shape in Pyrgos, Emporio and the castle ruins at Oia: houses packed together to form an outer wall, lanes twisting inward so raiders would lose their way. Later the island passed under Ottoman control, before joining the new Greek state in the nineteenth century.

Look also at Santorini's distinctive architecture. On an island short of timber, people carved homes into the soft volcanic rock of the cliffs. These cave houses, the skaftá, stay cool in summer and warm in winter, and many of today's caldera hotels are converted from them. In Oia, grander neoclassical mansions belonged to sea captains who made the island prosperous in the nineteenth century, a story told in the town's small Maritime Museum.

Then the earth moved again. In July 1956 a powerful earthquake struck the region, badly damaging villages across the island, especially Oia, and many residents left. For years parts of the island stood half-abandoned. Rebuilding, and in time the arrival of tourism, transformed Santorini into the place you see now.

Even the island's wine is part of this story. Vines grow low, twisted into basket shapes called kouloures to protect the grapes from wind, rooted in volcanic soil so poor that the phylloxera pest that destroyed Europe's vineyards never took hold. Some vines here are very old indeed. Taste a glass of Assyrtiko or the sweet, sun-dried Vinsanto, and you are tasting the volcano itself, the same force that buried Akrotiri and made the cliffs beneath your feet.

name: Venetian Stones, Ottoman Domes: The Many Masters of Chania
description: Chania's harbour looks like a postcard of Venice, but walk a few lanes inland and you will find mosques, a synagogue, Minoan foundations and the memory of a battle that changed the war.
details:
The first thing most people see in Chania is the curve of the Venetian harbour, the stone lighthouse at its tip, the pastel houses along the quay. It feels Italian, and in a way it is. But stand on the waterfront long enough and the eye catches something else: a low building topped with domes, an Ottoman mosque sitting right on the harbour, and behind it a skyline of minarets and bell towers. Chania is a palimpsest, a manuscript that has been written over again and again, with earlier text still showing through.

The oldest layer lies under your feet. The low hill of Kastelli, just above the harbour, was the site of the Minoan town of Kydonia, an important Bronze Age settlement. Excavations in the neighbourhood have exposed foundations and finds from that period, and you can glimpse some of them in fenced pits among the houses. Kydonia lived on through Classical and Roman times, a major city of western Crete.

The great visible layer, though, belongs to Venice. After the Fourth Crusade in the early thirteenth century, Crete passed to the Venetian Republic, which held it for more than four centuries. The Venetians fortified Chania with massive walls and bastions, built the harbour, the arsenals where galleys were repaired, the lighthouse and the elegant palazzi of the merchant class. You can still see the arched Neoria, the old shipyards, along the eastern harbour. The town they built, which they called La Canea, was a centre of Venetian Crete, with a mix of Venetian and Greek families, and Cretan culture flourished in the encounter.

In 1645 the Ottomans landed, and Chania fell to them after a siege. The rest of Crete took longer; Heraklion held out until 1669. Under Ottoman rule churches became mosques and new mosques were built. The Mosque of the Janissaries on the harbour is the most visible reminder, and in the quarter of Splantzia the church of Agios Nikolaos still has both a bell tower and a minaret. In the nineteenth century, during a period of Egyptian administration, the lighthouse was rebuilt in the form you see today.

Crete's long struggle for union with Greece is woven into Chania's identity. After repeated revolts, the island became autonomous at the end of the nineteenth century and was formally united with Greece in 1913. Chania was its capital for a time, and the town's most famous son, Eleftherios Venizelos, rose from Cretan politics to become one of modern Greece's most important prime ministers. He is buried on a hill on the Akrotiri peninsula with a sweeping view over the town and the bay.

The old town also has a quieter, more painful story. In the lanes near Kondylaki Street stands the Etz Hayyim Synagogue, the last surviving synagogue on Crete. The Jewish community of Chania was ancient. In 1944, under German occupation, its members were arrested and deported; the ship carrying them, the Tanais, was sunk at sea, and the community was lost. The synagogue has since been restored as a place of prayer, memory and reconciliation, and it is one of the most moving places you can visit in Greece.

That occupation followed one of the most dramatic episodes of the Second World War. In May 1941, German forces launched an airborne invasion of Crete, parachuting thousands of troops around Chania and the airfield at Maleme. Greek and Commonwealth forces and Cretan civilians fought back fiercely; the Battle of Crete was won by the Germans only at heavy cost. The peaceful Souda Bay War Cemetery, near the port where your ship docks, holds the graves of Commonwealth servicemen.

Walking Chania today, you move through all of this without trying: a Venetian doorway, an Ottoman fountain, a Minoan wall, a memorial. The harbour may look like Venice, but the town behind it belongs to everyone who has ever fought over it, and above all to the Cretans who outlasted them all.

name: Where the Games Began: The Sacred Valley of Olympia
description: The modern Olympics borrowed their flame and their name from a quiet, pine-shaded valley less than an hour from this little port. Here is what made it holy.
details:
Katakolon itself has a modest history. It grew up in the nineteenth century as a port for exporting the region's currants, small dried grapes that were then a major cash crop of the western Peloponnese, shipped from here to northern Europe. Nearby, close to the beach at Agios Andreas, lie submerged remains associated with the ancient harbour of Pheia, which served the region long before. But the real story waits inland, along the river Alfeios, in a green valley where Greeks gathered for more than a thousand years.

Olympia was not a city. It was a sanctuary, a sacred precinct called the Altis, dedicated above all to Zeus. People came here to worship, to make offerings, and every four years to compete. According to the traditional reckoning, the first recorded Olympic Games took place in 776 BC, and the Greeks later used the four-year Olympiad as a way of counting time. In the early centuries the main event was a simple footrace the length of the stadium. Over time came wrestling, boxing, chariot racing, the pentathlon, and the brutal pankration, a combat sport with very few rules.

During the games a sacred truce was proclaimed so that athletes and spectators could travel safely across a Greek world otherwise often at war. Winners received not gold but a crown of wild olive, cut from a sacred tree. Glory, statues, poems and lifelong privileges at home followed. The competitors were free Greek men, and they competed naked. Married women were barred from watching the men's games, though there were separate games for young women in honour of the goddess Hera.

As you walk the site, the ruins tell this story. Enter the stadium through its vaulted stone tunnel and you emerge onto the long earthen track itself, with the stone starting and finishing lines still in place, framed by grassy slopes where spectators once sat. Visitors often find themselves running a few steps of it. Near the entrance stand the bases of statues called the Zanes, bronze figures of Zeus paid for with fines imposed on athletes caught cheating, a warning lined up along the path to the stadium.

At the heart of the sanctuary lies the Temple of Zeus, whose massive column drums still lie where earthquakes toppled them. Inside it once stood a seated statue of Zeus by the sculptor Pheidias, made of gold and ivory, counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. The statue is long lost, but archaeologists have identified Pheidias's workshop nearby, and among the finds was a small clay cup inscribed with words meaning "I belong to Pheidias". It is one of the most intimate objects in the museum: a sculptor's drinking cup, left behind beside his greatest work.

The older Temple of Hera is where the Olympic flame for the modern games is lit, using a parabolic mirror to focus the sun's rays, before it is carried by relay toward the host city. The ceremony connects today's global spectacle with this quiet corner of the Peloponnese.

The ancient games ended in late antiquity, traditionally dated to the reign of the Christian emperor Theodosius I at the end of the fourth century AD, as pagan festivals were suppressed. Over the following centuries, earthquakes, floods and shifting rivers buried the sanctuary under layers of silt. Systematic excavations by German archaeologists began in 1875, and work continues today.

In the museum you will find the sculptures from the Temple of Zeus, and the graceful marble Hermes holding the infant Dionysus, traditionally attributed to Praxiteles, though scholars debate whether it is his original. Spend a little time there, then walk back out into the pines, and listen. Olympia is a place where you can still feel how sacred sport once was.

name: The Island That Never Fell: Corfu Between Venice, France and Britain
description: Corfu Town looks unlike anywhere else in Greece, and the reason is that the Ottomans never managed to take it. Walk its arcades and fortresses to find out why.
details:
Stroll through Corfu Town and you might wonder if you have left Greece. Tall shuttered houses rise over narrow lanes, an arcaded promenade could be in Paris, a cricket pitch lies in front of a Georgian palace, and two great fortresses guard the bay. Corfu's history is different from most of Greece's, and you can read it in the stones.

Long before any of that, Corfu was known to the ancient world as Kerkyra, an important Greek city whose quarrel with Corinth helped spark the Peloponnesian War. Local tradition has also long identified the island with Scheria, the land of the Phaeacians in Homer's Odyssey, where the shipwrecked Odysseus washed ashore and met the princess Nausicaa. That identification is tradition rather than proof, but islanders are fond of it, and several coves claim the honour of being the spot.

The defining chapter began in 1386, when Corfu came under the control of Venice. For the next four centuries it was a vital Venetian outpost guarding the entrance to the Adriatic. The Venetians reinforced the Old Fortress on its rocky promontory, cutting a sea channel to separate it from the town, and later built the New Fortress above the harbour. These defences, and the islanders who manned them, withstood major Ottoman sieges, notably in 1537 and 1716. Corfu thus became one of the few parts of the Greek world never ruled by the Ottomans, which is why its architecture and culture have such a strongly Italian flavour.

Corfiots credit their survival in 1716 not only to the fortifications and the German-born commander Count Schulenburg, whose statue stands at the Old Fortress, but to their patron, Saint Spyridon, whose relics rest in the church that bears his name, its red-domed bell tower rising over the old town. Tradition holds that the saint drove away the besieging forces, as well as saving the island from plague and famine. Several times a year his relics are carried in procession through the streets, and you will hear many Corfiot men named Spyros.

When the Venetian Republic fell in 1797, Corfu passed through French hands, a brief Russian-Ottoman protectorate, then the French again. It was the French who began the Liston, the arcaded row along the Spianada inspired by Paris's Rue de Rivoli. After Napoleon's defeat, the Ionian Islands became a British protectorate in 1815. The British built the neoclassical Palace of St Michael and St George as the residence of their Lord High Commissioner, and left behind ginger beer, a taste for cricket, and roads across the island. In 1864 Britain ceded the Ionian Islands to the Kingdom of Greece.

Corfu also gave Greece its first head of state after independence, Ioannis Kapodistrias, a Corfiot who had earlier served as a foreign minister of the Russian Empire. And it drew royalty. In the 1890s Empress Elisabeth of Austria, known as Sisi, built the Achilleion palace at Gastouri as a retreat, filled with statues of her hero Achilles; after her assassination it was acquired by Kaiser Wilhelm II. Just outside town, the villa of Mon Repos was the birthplace in 1921 of Prince Philip, later Duke of Edinburgh.

In 2007, the Old Town of Corfu was inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List as a rare example of a fortified Mediterranean port town that remained largely intact. It is still very much a lived-in place, with laundry overhead and children playing in the squares. Walk its lanes in the evening and you will feel the layers: Venetian stone, French arcades, British palaces, Greek voices, and a saint keeping watch over them all.

name: The Emperor's House That Became a City
description: A Roman emperor built himself a retirement palace by the sea, and seventeen centuries later people are still living in it. No ruin in Europe is quite so alive.
details:
Near the end of the third century AD, the Roman Empire was ruled by Diocletian, a soldier of humble origins from the province of Dalmatia who rose to become emperor. He reorganised the empire, divided its rule among several co-emperors, and launched the last and harshest persecution of Christians. Then, in 305, he did something almost no Roman emperor had done: he retired voluntarily. He returned to his home region and lived out his days in a huge fortified palace he had built on the shore, a few kilometres from the provincial capital of Salona.

That palace is the heart of Split. It was part villa, part military camp, roughly rectangular, with massive walls, towers and four gates. The southern side, facing the sea, held the emperor's private apartments, raised on vast vaulted substructures to level the sloping ground. Those substructures survive almost intact, and you walk through them today as the cellars beneath the palace, cool vaulted halls that give you a precise ghost of the floor plan of the rooms above.

At the centre lies the Peristyle, a ceremonial courtyard of granite columns and arches leading to the vestibule of the emperor's residence. Here Diocletian, who presented himself as a god-like ruler, would have appeared to his subjects. A black granite sphinx, one of several brought from Egypt, still sits here, quietly watching visitors pose for photos.

Beside the Peristyle stands Diocletian's octagonal mausoleum. And here history plays one of its great ironies. Centuries after his death, the tomb of the emperor who persecuted Christians became a Christian cathedral, dedicated to Saint Domnius, a bishop of Salona martyred during Diocletian's persecution. The emperor's sarcophagus disappeared long ago. The bell tower added beside it in the Middle Ages is now the symbol of the city, and the view from the top over the palace roofs and the harbour is worth the climb.

How did a palace become a town? In the seventh century, Salona was sacked during the invasions of Avars and Slavs, and refugees fled to the safety of Diocletian's walls. They moved into the palace, built houses inside its halls and corridors, and over time turned an emperor's residence into a medieval town. Walk the streets inside the walls today and you will see Roman columns embedded in house fronts, medieval windows cut into ancient masonry, Renaissance palaces built over imperial rooms. People still live, work and hang laundry here.

Split's later history adds more layers. Like much of the Dalmatian coast, it came under Venetian rule in 1420 and stayed so until the fall of the Republic in 1797, followed by Napoleonic France, Austria, and in the twentieth century Yugoslavia and finally an independent Croatia. Each left a mark: Venetian Gothic windows, Austrian promenades and public buildings, socialist-era housing on the outskirts.

Outside the northern Golden Gate stands a towering bronze figure by the Croatian sculptor Ivan Meštrović: Grgur Ninski, Gregory of Nin, a tenth-century bishop remembered for championing the use of the Slavic language in church liturgy. Locals and visitors rub his big toe for luck, and it shines gold from all the attention. In 1979 the palace and the historic centre were inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List.

So when you sit on the Peristyle steps in the evening, coffee in hand, with music echoing off ancient stones, remember that you are sitting in an emperor's front hall, in a city that grew up inside a single building. Few places on earth let you live so casually inside the past.

name: Libertas: The Little Republic Behind the Walls
description: For centuries this tiny city-state survived between great empires by wit, diplomacy and trade. Its walls tell only half the story.
details:
The walls are the first thing you see, and they are magnificent: nearly two kilometres of stone ramparts, towers and bastions wrapped around a city of terracotta roofs. But Dubrovnik's real genius was not in fighting. It was in not having to fight. For several centuries this small city was the Republic of Ragusa, an independent maritime state that survived between powerful empires by negotiation, trade and remarkable political skill.

Ragusa, the city's Latin and Italian name, grew from a settlement founded in the early Middle Ages by refugees, according to tradition from the Roman city of Epidaurum, today's Cavtat. Over time it became a prosperous trading port with a merchant fleet that sailed across the Mediterranean and beyond. After a period under Venetian control, it established its own self-governing republic in the fourteenth century and later paid tribute to the Ottoman Empire in exchange for protection and trading privileges, all while maintaining good relations with Christian powers. It was a delicate balancing act sustained by diplomacy.

The republic's government was designed to prevent any one man from gaining too much power. The head of state, the Rector, served for only a month at a time and was not allowed to leave the palace during his term except on official business. Real power lay with councils of the city's noble families. You can visit the Rector's Palace, a Gothic and Renaissance building just off the main street, where an inscription above the council chamber urged officials to forget private interests and attend to public affairs. The republic's motto was Libertas, liberty, and it remains the city's symbol.

Ragusa was also, in some respects, ahead of its time. In 1377 it introduced a quarantine system for travellers arriving from plague-affected areas, one of the earliest such measures in Europe. Later, quarantine buildings known as the Lazareti were built just outside the city's eastern gate, where they still stand. The Franciscan monastery inside the Pile Gate houses a pharmacy founded in the early fourteenth century, among the oldest still operating in Europe.

Stand on the Stradun, the gleaming main street, and you are standing in a city rebuilt after catastrophe. In 1667 a devastating earthquake struck, killing a large part of the population and destroying much of the city. The town was rebuilt in a more uniform Baroque style, which is why the houses along the Stradun look so harmonious, with shops at street level and arched doorways.

The republic's long independence came to an end in the Napoleonic era, when French forces occupied the city and abolished the republic in 1808. After Napoleon's fall, Dubrovnik became part of the Austrian Empire, and later of Yugoslavia.

Look closely at the rooftops from the walls and you will notice that some tiles are bright orange and new, while others are faded and mottled. That patchwork tells the most recent chapter. During the Croatian War of Independence, Dubrovnik was besieged by Yugoslav forces from late 1991 into 1992, and the old town was shelled. Many buildings were damaged and lives lost. After the war, a careful restoration effort repaired the city, using traditional methods and materials wherever possible. A map near the Pile Gate marks the places where shells struck. The Homeland War Museum on Mount Srđ, inside the Napoleonic fort that defenders held throughout the siege, tells this story from the city's own perspective.

Watch for the stone statue of Orlando, the knight Roland, on the square in front of St Blaise's Church. Flags were flown from it, public announcements read beside it, and his forearm was once used as a unit of length in trade. He stands there as he has for centuries, a symbol of the city's freedom, keeping watch over the little republic that refused to disappear.

name: Saints, Sailors and Stone: The Bay of Kotor Through the Centuries
description: Behind the fairy-tale walls of Kotor lies a long story of seafarers, saints and empires, and a tiny island built, so the legend goes, one stone at a time.
details:
As your ship glides into the Bay of Kotor, the mountains close in and the water narrows, and it becomes obvious why people have fought over this place. A deep, sheltered bay at the edge of the Adriatic, protected by mountains and easily defended, has always been valuable to anyone who wanted to control trade and the sea. Over the centuries Illyrians, Romans, Byzantines, Serbian rulers, Venetians, Austrians and Yugoslavs have all claimed it. Today it belongs to Montenegro, which regained its independence in 2006.

The heart of Kotor is the Cathedral of Saint Tryphon, a Romanesque church consecrated in 1166 and dedicated to the city's patron saint, whose relics, according to local tradition, were brought here in the ninth century. The cathedral has been damaged by earthquakes many times and rebuilt, which is why its two bell towers do not quite match. Kotor's identity has long been tied to Saint Tryphon, and the city's seafaring brotherhood, the Boka Navy, which traces its origins back many centuries, still performs a traditional dance in his honour.

Look up from the old town and you will see the walls climbing the mountain behind it in a jagged line to the fortress of San Giovanni. Much of what you see dates from the long period of Venetian rule, from 1420 to the fall of the Republic in 1797, when Kotor, which the Venetians called Cattaro, served as one of their important outposts against the Ottoman Empire. The winged lion of Saint Mark, symbol of Venice, still appears over gates and walls across the bay.

The people of the bay were famous sailors. In the little town of Perast, captains built baroque palaces along the waterfront, each with its own coat of arms, and the town became renowned for its maritime school. According to tradition, Tsar Peter the Great of Russia sent young noblemen to Perast at the end of the seventeenth century to learn navigation from a local master, Captain Marko Martinović. It is a story the town tells with understandable pride.

Just off Perast sit two small islands. One, Saint George, is natural and holds an old Benedictine abbey. The other, Our Lady of the Rocks, is man-made, and its story is part history and part legend. According to local legend, in the fifteenth century two sailors found an icon of the Virgin Mary on a reef in the bay, and in gratitude for their safe return, seafarers began dropping stones around the reef and sinking old ships to build an island, on which a church was eventually built. Every year in July, the people of Perast row out to the island in decorated boats and throw stones into the water around it, a ritual called the Fašinada that keeps the tradition alive. Inside the church hang hundreds of silver votive plates left by sailors in thanks for survival at sea, and a remarkable embroidery said to have been stitched over many years by a local woman, partly with her own hair, while she waited for her husband to return from the sea. That last detail belongs to local tradition rather than documented record.

Kotor's later history brought Austrian rule in the nineteenth century, when the bay became an important naval base for the Austro-Hungarian Empire, and many of its fortifications were rebuilt. In 1979 a powerful earthquake struck the region, damaging the old town badly; the same year, Kotor and its surroundings were inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List, and restoration followed.

High above, on the summit of Mount Lovćen, lies the mausoleum of Petar II Petrović-Njegoš, the nineteenth-century prince-bishop and poet who is Montenegro's great national figure. From there, the whole bay spreads out below like a map of everything that has happened here: saints and sailors, empires and earthquakes, and a small island built by faith, one stone at a time.

name: The City of the Siren: Layers of Naples, from Greeks to Kings
description: Naples is chaotic, loud and gloriously alive, and beneath its streets lie three thousand years of Greeks, Romans, saints and kings. Here is the key to reading it.
details:
Naples begins with a legend. The ancient Greeks told of the siren Parthenope, who, having failed to lure Odysseus with her song, cast herself into the sea and washed ashore here. A settlement grew up, according to tradition, around her tomb. Whatever the truth of that myth, Greek colonists did found a city here, and around the sixth century BC they founded a 'new city', Neapolis, from which the name Naples comes. Neapolitans still call themselves Partenopei after the siren, and you will see her name everywhere.

The Greek city's street plan survives remarkably clearly. The long straight street nicknamed Spaccanapoli, the 'splitter of Naples', follows one of the ancient main roads, and the narrow parallel lanes of the historic centre still trace the grid laid down more than two thousand years ago. Beneath them lies another city. Naples is built on soft volcanic tuff, and for millennia people quarried stone from beneath their own houses, leaving a labyrinth of tunnels, cisterns and aqueducts. Tours of Napoli Sotterranea take you down into this hidden world, which has served as water storage, quarry, and air-raid shelter in the Second World War.

Under Rome, the Bay of Naples became a playground for the wealthy. Villas lined the coast, and towns like Pompeii and Herculaneum prospered beneath the green slopes of Vesuvius until the eruption of AD 79 buried them. Those cities, rediscovered in the eighteenth century, give us an unparalleled snapshot of Roman life, and many of their finest treasures, from mosaics to frescoes, are in the National Archaeological Museum in Naples.

After Rome, Naples became the capital of a kingdom that endured, under various names and dynasties, for centuries. The French house of Anjou built the massive Castel Nuovo, known as the Maschio Angioino, near the port. The Aragonese followed, adding a triumphal Renaissance arch to its entrance. Then came the long period of Spanish viceroys, who reshaped the city; the great street of Via Toledo takes its name from the viceroy Pedro de Toledo. In the eighteenth century the Bourbon kings made Naples one of the largest and most brilliant cities in Europe, building the Royal Palace on Piazza del Plebiscito and the Teatro di San Carlo, which opened in 1737 and is among the oldest continuously active opera houses in the world. In 1861, the kingdom was absorbed into a newly unified Italy, and Naples lost its role as a capital, a loss still felt in the city's sense of itself.

Faith runs through all of this. The city's patron saint, San Gennaro, a bishop martyred in the early fourth century, is venerated in the cathedral, where a vial said to contain his dried blood is displayed several times a year. If it liquefies, it is taken as a good omen for the city; if it does not, many Neapolitans worry. The Church does not ask believers to accept it as a miracle, but for many in Naples it is a deeply felt part of life.

And then there is pizza. Naples is the birthplace of modern pizza, and the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo is recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage. A popular story says the margherita was created in 1889 by a pizzaiolo named Raffaele Esposito for Queen Margherita of Savoy, with tomato, mozzarella and basil echoing the colours of the Italian flag. Historians debate the details, and similar pizzas existed earlier, but it is a story Naples loves to tell.

Walk Spaccanapoli at dusk, past shrines to the Madonna, crèche-makers on Via San Gregorio Armeno, and grandmothers lowering baskets from balconies, and you will feel all these layers at once. Naples does not keep its history behind glass. It lives in it, noisily, every day.

name: From Trajan's Harbour to the Eternal City
description: Your ship docks where emperors once built a port, and the city an hour inland is a place where every era of Western history is stacked on top of the last.
details:
Most travellers rush through Civitavecchia on their way to Rome, but the port itself is part of the story. In the early second century AD, the emperor Trajan ordered a new harbour built here to serve Rome, and the town that grew up around it was called Centumcellae. After the Middle Ages it became the principal port of the Papal States, and the massive fortress that dominates the waterfront, Forte Michelangelo, was begun in the early sixteenth century under Pope Julius II. Its name reflects the tradition that Michelangelo contributed to its design, though how much of the finished work was his remains debated. The town suffered heavy bombing in the Second World War, which is why much of it looks modern, but the ancient harbour lines still shape the port where your ship ties up.

Inland, the hills around Civitavecchia hold even older stories. This was the land of the Etruscans, the sophisticated people who dominated central Italy before Rome rose to power. At nearby Tarquinia and Cerveteri, their great necropolises preserve painted tombs and burial mounds. The Etruscans influenced early Rome in everything from religion to engineering, and according to tradition, Rome's early kings included Etruscans.

Then comes Rome itself. The best way to understand it is not as a single ancient city, but as a city built in layers, each era building on top of, or with the stones of, the last. At the bottom lies the Rome of the Republic and the Empire. The Roman Forum, a valley of broken columns and temple foundations, was the political and religious centre of the ancient city. Above it rises the Palatine Hill, where, according to legend, Romulus founded Rome, and where emperors later built their palaces; the word 'palace' itself comes from the Palatine.

The Colosseum, properly the Flavian Amphitheatre, was begun under the emperor Vespasian and inaugurated in AD 80 under his son Titus. It held tens of thousands of spectators for gladiatorial games, animal hunts and public spectacles. Its broken outer ring and the honeycombed holes in its stones are reminders of later centuries, when it was damaged by earthquakes and quarried for building material, and its iron clamps were pried out. A short walk away, the Pantheon, rebuilt under the emperor Hadrian in the second century AD, still has its original concrete dome, with an open oculus at the top. It survives so well largely because it was converted into a church in the seventh century.

That conversion points to the next layer: Christian Rome. The emperor Constantine legalised Christianity in the fourth century, and the city became the seat of the popes. Basilicas rose over the tombs of martyrs, most famously St Peter's, built over the traditional burial place of the apostle Peter. The present basilica, constructed over more than a century in the Renaissance and Baroque periods, involved Bramante, Michelangelo, who designed the dome, and later Bernini, who shaped the great colonnaded square in front of it.

The Renaissance and Baroque popes transformed the city into a stage. Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling in the early sixteenth century. In the seventeenth century, Bernini and Borromini filled Rome with fountains, churches and sweeping piazzas. The Trevi Fountain, completed in the eighteenth century, is the end point of an ancient aqueduct, the Aqua Virgo, still carrying water into the city.

In 1870 Rome became the capital of a newly unified Italy, adding grand nineteenth-century boulevards and the gleaming white monument to King Victor Emmanuel II on Piazza Venezia. Mussolini later carved roads through ancient neighbourhoods. Each era left its mark. Walking through Rome, you move from one century to another in a few steps, and that is its magic. It is called the Eternal City not because it stood still, but because it never stopped building on itself.

name: The Parthenon: A Temple Built Without a Straight Line
description: Everyone photographs it. Few notice that the most famous building in the Western world was designed to fool your eye, and that it has been a church, a mosque and a powder magazine.
details:
You come up through the Propylaea, the monumental gateway of the Acropolis, jostled by the crowd and squinting in the white light, and then it is there in front of you: the Parthenon. Even half ruined and wrapped in scaffolding, it is one of the few buildings in the world that lives up to its reputation. It was built between 447 and 432 BC, in the age of Pericles, as a temple to Athena Parthenos, Athena the Virgin, the city's patron. Its architects were Iktinos and Kallikrates, and its sculpture was overseen by Phidias.

The first thing to understand is what it was for. The Parthenon housed a colossal statue of Athena, nearly twelve metres high, made of gold and ivory over a wooden core, by Phidias himself. The statue is long gone; only ancient descriptions and small Roman copies survive. The temple was also, in effect, a treasury, a statement of Athenian wealth and power after the victory over the Persians, paid for in part with funds from Athens' allies.

Now look closely, because this is what most visitors miss. The Parthenon contains almost no straight lines. The platform on which it stands curves gently upward in the middle, so that it would not appear to sag. The columns lean very slightly inward, and if you could extend them upward, they would meet far above the building. Each column swells subtly in the middle, a refinement called entasis, so that it does not look thin. The corner columns are a little thicker than the others, because columns seen against the bright sky appear slimmer. All of this was done to make the building look perfectly straight, balanced and alive to the human eye.

Then imagine it in colour. The marble you see is pale and golden, but in antiquity the sculptures and parts of the building were painted in strong colours. The frieze around the inner wall showed a procession, generally interpreted as the Panathenaic procession in honour of Athena, with horsemen, musicians and sacrificial animals. The pediments at either end showed the birth of Athena and her contest with Poseidon for the city. The metopes, square panels high on the outside, showed mythical battles.

The building's later history is almost as remarkable. In the early Christian period, it became a church, dedicated to the Virgin Mary. Under the Ottomans, it became a mosque, with a minaret. In 1687, during a siege by the Venetians, the Ottoman garrison stored gunpowder inside, and a Venetian shell struck it. The explosion blew out the centre of the building and destroyed much of the sculpture. In the early nineteenth century, Lord Elgin removed many of the surviving sculptures, which are now in the British Museum in London. Greece has long called for their return.

The scaffolding you see is part of a restoration project that began in 1975. Restorers are taking down earlier, poorly done repairs, replacing corroded iron clamps with titanium, and fitting original fragments back into place where they can, using new marble from the same Mount Pentelikon quarries only where necessary. It is a slow, careful process, and the building will never be complete again, but it is being saved.

Walk around the Parthenon if the paths allow, and look at the Erechtheion, the smaller temple to the north, with its porch of the Caryatids, six maidens who act as columns. The ones on the building are copies; five of the originals are in the Acropolis Museum below, and one is in the British Museum. Near the Erechtheion, an olive tree grows on the spot where, according to myth, Athena planted the first olive tree in her contest with Poseidon.

Finally, go to the edge of the rock and look out. On a clear day, you can see the sea at Piraeus, where your ship is docked, and the mountains that ring the city. The ancient Athenians looked out from here, too, at their harbour and their fleet, the source of the wealth that built the temple behind you.

The Parthenon is not just a beautiful ruin. It is a building designed with obsessive care to look perfect, a symbol of a city at the height of its power, and a survivor of two and a half thousand years of war, conversion and loss. Give it time, and look for the curves.

name: The Acropolis Museum: Standing Above Ancient Athens
description: Most people come for the statues. The glass floor beneath your feet and the empty spaces on the top floor tell stories that are just as powerful.
details:
The Acropolis Museum stands at the foot of the Acropolis rock, a modern building of glass, concrete and steel that opened in 2009. Many visitors treat it as an afterthought to the climb, but it is one of the great museums of the world, and it makes the ruins above it make sense. Designed by the architect Bernard Tschumi, with Greek architect Michael Photiadis, it was built to hold the finds from the Acropolis and, its builders hoped, one day the Parthenon sculptures in London.

The first thing to notice is the ground under your feet. As you approach the entrance, and inside on the ground floor, parts of the floor are made of glass. Beneath you, excavated and preserved, are the remains of an ancient Athenian neighbourhood, with houses, streets, workshops and drains dating from many periods. The museum was built above it on pillars, and the excavation is now open to visitors on a lower level. It is a reminder that the Acropolis was not just a sacred hill but rose above an ordinary city where people lived and worked.

The ground-floor gallery slopes gently upward, like the path to the Acropolis, and is lined with offerings and objects from the sanctuaries on the slopes of the hill. Then, on the first floor, you meet the Archaic period. Here stand the korai, statues of young women dedicated to Athena in the sixth century BC. Look closely at them. Many still show traces of their original paint: patterns on their clothes, colour in their hair and lips. They are reminders that ancient Greek sculpture was not white, as later centuries imagined, but brightly coloured.

On the same floor are the five original Caryatids from the Erechtheion, the graceful maidens who served as columns on its porch. The sixth is in the British Museum. You can walk around them and see the intricacy of their braided hair from behind, something impossible on the Acropolis, where the copies stand.

The top floor is the heart of the museum, and it is extraordinary. It is a glass gallery, rotated to align exactly with the Parthenon, which you can see through the windows. Arranged around its walls at the same dimensions as the temple itself is the Parthenon frieze, the long sculpted procession that ran around the building. Some of the panels are originals. Others are plaster casts, in a paler colour, standing in for the pieces that are in the British Museum in London. The contrast is deliberate. It makes visible what is missing, and it is the museum's quiet argument that the sculptures belong together, here, in sight of the temple they were made for.

Take your time on the top floor. Walk slowly around the frieze and follow the procession: horsemen, chariots, elders, musicians, girls carrying vessels, animals led to sacrifice, and finally the gods, seated and waiting. Then look up through the glass at the Parthenon itself, and the connection becomes physical.

There are things that visitors often miss. The museum has a café and terrace with a superb view of the Acropolis. Its display of the votive offerings and everyday objects gives a sense of the people who worshipped here. And there are the excavations on the lower level, which many people never find.

A practical note: if you visit in the heat of summer, many people find it best to climb the Acropolis early and come to the museum afterwards, when the sun is fierce. The museum is cool and calm, and it explains what you have just seen.

The Acropolis Museum is not just a container for treasures. It is a building that looks up at the Parthenon and asks what it would mean to make it whole again. Stand on the top floor, look from the casts to the temple and back, and you will feel the question too.

name: The Ancient Agora: Where Democracy Went Shopping
description: Below the Acropolis lies the place where Athenians voted, argued, traded and judged, where Socrates taught and where the best-preserved Greek temple still stands.
details:
If the Acropolis was the sacred heart of ancient Athens, the Agora was its everyday heart. This open area below the north-west slope of the rock was the city's marketplace and civic centre for centuries. Here Athenians bought and sold, gossiped and argued, met friends and enemies, held courts, ran their government and worshipped. Socrates spent much of his life here, questioning anyone who would talk to him. In many ways, this is where Athenian democracy was lived.

At first glance, the Agora can be confusing. It is a large, grassy, tree-shaded expanse scattered with foundations, column stumps and broken walls, and it takes some imagination to see what was here. But a few landmarks stand out, and they make it come alive.

The first is the Temple of Hephaestus, standing on a small hill on the western side. Built in the fifth century BC, around the same time as the Parthenon, it is the best-preserved ancient Greek temple in Greece, with its roof, columns and much of its structure intact. It was dedicated to Hephaestus, god of metalworking and craftsmen, which suits its location above an area once filled with workshops; archaeologists have found evidence of metalworking nearby. Its survival owes much to its later use as a church, which protected it from being quarried for stone. Walk around it slowly, and you can see what a Greek temple looked like as a complete building.

The second is the Stoa of Attalos, the long, two-storey colonnaded building on the eastern side. A stoa was a covered walkway, used for shops, meetings and shelter from the sun. This one was originally built in the second century BC by King Attalos II of Pergamon, a gift to the city where he had studied. What you see today is a careful reconstruction built in the 1950s by the American School of Classical Studies, which excavated the Agora. It houses the Agora Museum, full of objects that bring the place to life.

And that museum is where most visitors rush and should not. It holds ordinary things that tell extraordinary stories: ostraka, pottery fragments on which Athenians scratched the names of politicians they wanted to exile, which is where the word 'ostracism' comes from; a kleroterion, a stone allotment machine used to select citizens for jury duty at random; a water clock used to time speeches in court; children's toys; weights and measures used to keep merchants honest. These are the objects of a working democracy.

There is more to find. The remains of the Bouleuterion, where the city council met; the Tholos, a round building where council members ate and slept; the site of the Royal Stoa, where laws were displayed. Near the southern edge stands the small Byzantine church of the Holy Apostles, built around the end of the tenth century, with fine frescoes inside. Along the edge runs the Panathenaic Way, the route of the great procession to the Acropolis, which you can still walk.

The Agora is also one of the best places in Athens for a quieter visit. Its trees give shade, its paths are less crowded than the Acropolis, and turtles and cats wander among the ruins. In the morning, it is peaceful, and the view up to the Acropolis is superb.

So when you walk through the Agora, picture it as it was: crowded, noisy, full of traders, politicians, philosophers and citizens arguing about how their city should be run. It is a place that gave the world ideas we still live by, and it still feels like a public square.

name: The Panathenaic Stadium: Marble Built for Running
description: Built for ancient games, rebuilt in marble for the first modern Olympics, it is the only major stadium in the world made entirely of marble. Few visitors stop long enough to run its track.
details:
The Panathenaic Stadium sits in a natural hollow between two pine-covered hills, a short walk east of the National Garden, and it is one of the most striking sights in Athens. A long horseshoe of gleaming white marble seats rises around a track, and on a sunny day it is almost too bright to look at. Many visitors simply photograph it from the gate and walk on. That is a mistake.

The stadium has two lives. The first began in the fourth century BC, when the statesman Lycurgus built a stadium here for the athletic contests of the Panathenaic Games, the great festival held in honour of Athena. In the second century AD, the wealthy Roman-era benefactor Herodes Atticus rebuilt it in marble, with seating for many thousands of spectators. Over the following centuries, as the ancient city declined, the stadium was abandoned, and its marble was carried away and burned for lime. By the nineteenth century, it was a grassy hollow with little more than its shape remaining.

Its second life began with the modern Olympic movement. When the first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens in 1896, the stadium was excavated and restored in marble for the occasion, funded largely by the wealthy Greek benefactor Georgios Averoff, whose statue stands outside. It hosted the opening and closing ceremonies of those Games, and in 2004, when the Olympics returned to Athens, it was used for the archery competition and as the finish of the marathon.
