Today, it is the place where the Olympic flame is handed over to the host country after it is lit at Olympia. It is often described as the only major stadium in the world built entirely of marble.

Notice its shape. Unlike a modern oval stadium, it is long and narrow, with tight hairpin turns at the curved end. Ancient runners raced up and down the straight, and the bends were difficult; you can see how hard it would have been for later athletes, too.

Look at the seats. The front rows, the most prestigious, are carved with backs and arms, like thrones. Near the curved end, at the top, a tunnel leads out of the stadium, which in Roman times may have been used for animals and participants in spectacles. Inside is a small exhibition of Olympic torches and posters from the modern Games, which many visitors miss.

The best thing to do here is the thing many visitors forget: walk down onto the track, and run. Visitors are allowed onto the track, and it is a strange and wonderful feeling to run a few metres on the same ground as the first modern Olympians. If you are feeling brave, you can stand on the winners' podium for a photograph.

Climb to the top of the seating, too. From there, the view looks over the stadium to the Acropolis in the distance, and you can sit quietly in the marble, away from the crowds of the old town. Early morning and late afternoon are best; at midday in summer, the marble reflects the heat and the light intensely.

The stadium is close to the Temple of Olympian Zeus, Hadrian's Arch and the National Garden, so it fits easily into a walk around central Athens.

The Panathenaic Stadium links the ancient and modern Olympic Games in a single, shining space. Do not just photograph it. Go in, walk the track, sit in the marble and imagine the roar of the crowd in 1896, when the world's athletes came back to Athens.

name: Akrotiri: A Bronze Age Town Waiting Under Its Roof
description: Beneath a vast modern roof lies a town abandoned before one of history's greatest eruptions. Its streets, staircases and storage jars are still exactly where their owners left them.
details:
Akrotiri lies near the southern tip of Santorini, about twenty-five minutes by road from Fira, and it is one of the most remarkable archaeological sites in the Mediterranean. Here, under metres of volcanic ash, lies a town of the Late Bronze Age, buried in the great eruption of around 1600 BC that tore the island apart. Because the ash covered it so completely, Akrotiri has been preserved in extraordinary detail: two- and three-storey houses, paved streets, staircases, drains, and the everyday objects of people who lived here more than three and a half thousand years ago.

The first thing you notice is the roof. The whole excavation is covered by an enormous modern bioclimatic roof that protects the ruins from sun and rain. Walkways run above and through the town, so you look down into rooms and along streets as if from a balcony. It can feel more like an indoor museum than an open-air site, and in the heat of summer, the shade is very welcome.

Akrotiri was excavated from 1967 under the Greek archaeologist Spyridon Marinatos, who had long believed that a great Bronze Age eruption of Santorini might help explain the decline of Minoan Crete. He died at the site in 1974, and he is buried there. Excavation and research continue, and only part of the town has been uncovered.

What were the people of Akrotiri like? They were prosperous traders, closely connected to Minoan Crete and the wider Aegean. Their houses had upper floors, large windows and indoor drainage, and many rooms were decorated with vivid wall paintings. Those frescoes, showing a fleet of ships, boys carrying fish, swallows among red lilies, monkeys and young boxers, are among the finest art of the ancient world. Most of the originals are now in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, with some in the Museum of Prehistoric Thera in Fira, but you can see where they once hung.

Here is the great mystery that most visitors pass without noticing: almost no human remains and very few valuable objects have been found. The people of Akrotiri seem to have left before the eruption, perhaps warned by earthquakes that damaged the town beforehand. Archaeologists have found evidence of repairs and of building materials piled in the streets, as if the inhabitants had begun to clear up and rebuild, and then left. Where they went is unknown.

Look for the details that make this a real town. There are large clay storage jars, pithoi, still standing in the rooms where they were placed, some containing remains of food. There are millstones for grinding grain, and in one place, a staircase that cracked in two during an earthquake before the eruption, the steps still broken where they fell. There are plaster casts made by pouring material into the holes left by decayed wooden furniture, such as a bed, much as was done at Pompeii.

Akrotiri has inevitably been linked to the legend of Atlantis, Plato's story of a great island civilisation swallowed by the sea. It is a tempting connection, and you will hear it often, but it is a theory rather than a fact.

A practical note: Akrotiri is a timed, ticketed site, and it is best visited with a guide or an audio guide, because without explanation, the ruins can feel like an enclosed jumble of walls. Combine it with the Museum of Prehistoric Thera in Fira, which holds frescoes and objects from the town, and the story becomes much richer. The nearby Red Beach is often visited at the same time, though the path to it has been affected by rockfall risk, and warning signs should be respected.

Standing on the walkway above Akrotiri, it is easy to forget that this town was alive with families, traders and painters before the island exploded. Look down at the broken staircase and the storage jars, and imagine the day they walked away and never came back.

name: Nea Kameni: Walking on the Youngest Land in Greece
description: In the centre of the caldera, a black island of lava is still being built. Walk to its crater, and you are standing on ground younger than your grandparents.
details:
From the cliffs of Fira, look down into the caldera, and you will see a dark, barren island in the middle of the blue water. It looks like a pile of coal. This is Nea Kameni, the 'new burnt island', and it is the active heart of the Santorini volcano. Boats run from the Old Port beneath Fira and take only around twenty minutes to reach it.

Nea Kameni is young. While the great Bronze Age eruption created the caldera around 1600 BC, the islands in its centre were built by later eruptions, rising from the seabed. Palea Kameni, the 'old burnt island', appeared in antiquity. Nea Kameni began to form in the early eighteenth century, and eruptions in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries added to it. The most recent eruption took place in 1950. Some of the ground you walk on is less than a century old, which makes it among the youngest land in the Eastern Mediterranean.

The island is a protected geological site, and visitors pay an entry fee on landing. A marked path climbs from the small jetty across black, jagged lava fields and grey cinder slopes towards the summit craters. It is not a difficult climb, but it is steep in places, and the ground is loose and very hot in summer; proper shoes, a hat and water are essential. It takes about thirty to forty-five minutes to reach the top.

As you walk, look at the colours and textures. The lava flows from different eruptions have different shades and surfaces: some smooth, some rough and blocky. Near the top, you reach the craters, and in places you can see steam rising and smell sulphur. Here and there, yellow deposits stain the rocks. Put your hand near the ground in some places, and you may feel its warmth. The volcano is dormant, not dead, and scientists monitor it closely.

From the summit, the view is one of the best on Santorini. You see the whole ring of the caldera around you, with the white villages of Fira, Imerovigli and Oia strung along the cliff tops, Thirasia to the west, and the open sea beyond the gaps. It is the clearest way to understand that you are standing in the middle of a volcano.

Most boat tours also stop near Palea Kameni, where there are hot springs. The water in a small cove is warmed by volcanic activity and coloured orange-brown by iron. You swim from the boat into the cove. Be warned that the 'hot' springs are often only a few degrees warmer than the sea, and the iron-rich water can stain light-coloured swimwear.

What do most visitors miss? The quiet. If you go early in the day, before the large tour boats arrive, the island can be almost silent, and the strange, lunar landscape becomes far more powerful. They also miss the small details: the lichen that has slowly started to colonise the older lava flows, and the way the colour of the rock changes from black to rust to grey.

Nea Kameni is not a beautiful island in the usual sense. It is stark, hot and barren. But it is the reason Santorini exists in the shape it does, and it is one of the few places where you can walk across land being made. Stand at the crater, smell the sulphur, look at the cliffs around you, and you will understand the island in a way no view from the top ever can.

name: Ancient Thera: The City on the Ridge
description: High on a windswept mountain between two black beaches lie the ruins of the island's ancient capital, with temples, a theatre and graffiti carved by its citizens.
details:
Ancient Thera stands on the ridge of Mesa Vouno, a limestone mountain rising more than three hundred metres above the east coast of Santorini, between the beaches of Kamari and Perissa. It is the island's ancient capital, and it is one of the most dramatic archaeological sites in the Aegean. Yet most cruise passengers never see it.

After the Bronze Age eruption, the island was left uninhabited for a long time. When people returned, among them Dorian Greeks traditionally said to have come from Sparta under a leader named Theras, after whom the island was named, they chose this ridge for their city. It was high, defensible and away from the sea, with views of the coast in both directions. The city was occupied from around the ninth century BC through the Hellenistic, Roman and early Byzantine periods.

The site stretches for several hundred metres along the narrow ridge, and you walk the length of the ancient main street. Along the way are the remains of temples, houses, an agora or market square, a theatre, baths and a gymnasium. In the Hellenistic period, Thera served as a naval base for the Ptolemies of Egypt, and many of the buildings date from that time.

There are details that reward attention. At the terrace of the Gymnopaedia, near the southern end, visitors can see inscriptions carved into the rock, some of them ancient graffiti naming young men, in some cases with messages that scholars have long discussed. It is one of the oldest collections of Greek inscriptions anywhere. There is a sanctuary of the Egyptian gods, a reminder of the Ptolemaic presence, and a shrine carved into the rock. The theatre looks out over the sea, and you can imagine performances with the Aegean as a backdrop.

Everywhere, there is the view. To the north lies Kamari, with its long beach and the airport behind it. To the south lies Perissa, with its black sand stretching away. On clear days, you can see the island of Anafi to the east. The wind is often strong up here, and the light is brilliant.

Getting there is part of the adventure. From Kamari, a steep road climbs in a series of switchbacks to a small parking area near the site, and from there it is a further walk up. From Perissa, a stony footpath climbs the mountain, a strenuous hike of around forty-five minutes to an hour. Either way, wear sturdy shoes, take water, and go early in the day, as there is little shade at the top. The site has limited opening hours and is closed one day a week, so check before you go.

What do most visitors walk past? The inscriptions, which are easy to miss on the rock, and the sheer scale of the city along the ridge. Many people reach the first ruins, look around, and turn back. Keep walking to the southern end, where the ground drops away and you can see both sides of the island at once.

Ancient Thera is not as famous as Akrotiri, and it has no frescoes or roof. But it has something else: a sense of how people lived in a windswept mountain city, high above the sea, looking out over the Aegean. Stand at the end of the ridge, with the wind in your face, and you will feel very far from the crowds of Fira.

name: The Castle of Oia: Ruins Built for the Sunset
description: Every evening, thousands gather on a crumbling Venetian wall to watch the sun go down. Most of them never wonder what the wall was for.
details:
At the western tip of Oia, at the end of the marble lanes, stands a small ruined fortification on a rocky point above the sea. It is known as the castle of Oia, or the Kasteli of Agios Nikolaos, and it is the most famous sunset spot in Greece. Every evening in summer, crowds gather on its walls and on the terraces around it, sometimes an hour or more before sunset, and when the sun finally drops into the sea, they often applaud.

Few of those spectators stop to think about what the castle was. It is one of the old fortifications built on the island during the Venetian period, when Santorini was ruled by Venetian lords as part of the Duchy of Naxos. Pirates were a constant threat in the Aegean, and islanders built fortified settlements and watchtowers. Oia's castle protected the northern tip of the island and its harbour. Much of it was destroyed in the earthquake of 1956, and what remains is a ruin: low walls, the base of a tower and a viewpoint.

The position explains everything. From the castle, you can see the whole length of the caldera to the south, with the white villages of Imerovigli and Fira on the cliffs, and the islands of Thirasia and the Kamenis in the water. To the west and north lies the open sea. A watchman here could see ships approaching from any direction. Today, the same view makes it the perfect place to watch the sun go down.

Look down from the castle, and you will see Ammoudi Bay, Oia's tiny harbour at the foot of the cliff. Before the age of tourism, Oia was a prosperous town of sea captains and sailors, and Ammoudi was its port. A long stairway still links the village to the harbour, and walking down it gives you a sense of how the people of Oia once lived between the sea and the cliff top.

Turn around and look back at the village, too. From the castle, you get one of the finest views of Oia itself: the cascade of white cave houses, blue domes and windmills tumbling down the cliff. The windmills, on the ridge to the north, are reminders of the island's agricultural past.

What do most people miss? The castle in the morning. At sunrise, the light comes from behind you, and Oia glows gold and white against a deep blue caldera. The walls are almost empty. You can sit on the ruined stones and watch the village wake up, and it is far more peaceful than the sunset crowd.

A word about the sunset. If your ship stays late and you want to see it, arrive very early to find a spot, be patient with the crowds, and be prepared for a slow exit afterwards. Many people prefer to watch from a restaurant terrace or a quieter point along the caldera path.

The castle of Oia is a small ruin with an enormous view. It was built to watch for danger. Today, it watches the sun. Go once at dawn and once, if you can, at dusk, and you will see two different Santorinis from the same broken wall.

name: The Venetian Lighthouse: Chania's Slender Sentinel
description: It is on every postcard of Crete. Walk out along the breakwater to its foot, and you will find it has been built, rebuilt and claimed by three different empires.
details:
At the end of the long stone breakwater that shelters Chania's harbour stands the lighthouse, slender and pale against the sea. It is the symbol of the city, and almost every visitor photographs it from the waterfront. Fewer walk out to it, and fewer still know its story.

The first lighthouse here was built by the Venetians, who ruled Chania from the thirteenth century until 1645. They built the breakwater to protect the harbour, which was an important base for their ships, and placed a lighthouse at its end. After the Ottomans took Chania in 1645, the harbour continued in use, and the lighthouse with it.

The lighthouse you see today, however, is largely the work of a different power. From 1830 to 1840, Crete was governed by Egypt, under Mehmet Ali, as part of the Ottoman system. During this period, the lighthouse was rebuilt, and its tall, slender stone tower, rising from a broad base, gives it something of the look of a minaret. Look at it with that history in mind, and the resemblance becomes obvious. Locals sometimes call it the Egyptian lighthouse. It was restored again in the late twentieth century after being damaged during the Second World War.

Walking out to it is one of the great pleasures of Chania. The breakwater is long, and the path along it is uneven and exposed to the wind and the sea; on stormy days, waves can wash over it. But on a calm morning or evening, the walk is beautiful. On one side is the open sea; on the other, the harbour, with its fishing boats and the curved line of Venetian houses behind.

Turn around when you reach the lighthouse, and you will see the whole of Chania laid out before you: the domed Mosque of the Janissaries, the line of tall houses around the harbour, the Venetian arsenals, the Firkas fortress at the harbour mouth, and, rising behind the town, the White Mountains, often capped with snow well into spring. This is the best view in Chania, and many visitors never see it.

Look at the breakwater itself, too. Part of it is built on ancient foundations, and along it you can see traces of old fortifications. At its base, near the harbour, the Venetians built a fort to defend the entrance. The water here is the harbour mouth, through which galleys, Ottoman ships, steamers and fishing boats have all passed.

The best times to visit are early in the morning, when the light is soft and the breakwater is quiet, and at sunset, when the whole harbour glows. In the middle of the day in summer, the walk is hot and exposed.

The lighthouse of Chania has been built by Venetians, rebuilt by Egyptians under the Ottoman flag, damaged in war and restored by Greeks. In that, it is a small version of the city's own story. Walk out to it, and look back. You will see Chania as sailors have seen it for centuries.

name: The Mosque of the Janissaries: A Dome on the Water
description: The oldest Ottoman building on Crete stands where everyone walks past it. Its domes, its missing minaret and its new life as a gallery tell a story of the island's turbulent past.
details:
On the eastern side of Chania's harbour, right on the waterfront, stands a low, square building topped by a large central dome and smaller domes around it. It is the Mosque of the Janissaries, also known as the Küçük Hasan Mosque, and it is one of the most recognisable buildings in Chania. Many visitors photograph it as part of the harbour view without asking what it is.

It was built shortly after the Ottoman conquest of Chania in 1645 and is considered the oldest Ottoman building on Crete. The Janissaries were the elite infantry of the Ottoman Empire, and the mosque became associated with them; it was used by the garrison of the town. For more than two centuries, it served the Muslim community of Chania.

Look at its structure. The main dome is broad and low, and it is surrounded by smaller domes covering a portico. The building has an elegant simplicity typical of early Ottoman architecture. The minaret that once stood beside it was demolished in the twentieth century, and the space where it stood is part of the reason the mosque now looks so compact.

After Crete gained autonomy in 1898 and joined Greece in 1913, the Muslim population of the island gradually declined, and in 1923, under the population exchange between Greece and Turkey, the remaining Muslims of Crete left for Turkey. The mosque was no longer used for worship. Over the following decades, it served various purposes, including as a museum and a tourist information office.

Today, it is used as an exhibition hall, hosting art exhibitions and cultural events, and when it is open, you can step inside and look up into the great dome. The interior is spare and white, but the space is beautiful, and the light from its windows is soft.

What do most visitors miss? First, the small courtyard around the mosque, with its palm trees and old stones, which was once part of the mosque's grounds. Second, the way the building relates to the harbour: it was built facing the water, at the heart of the Ottoman town, as a statement that the city now belonged to a new power. And third, the fact that, standing in front of it, you can see the Venetian buildings and the Egyptian-rebuilt lighthouse, a single view that spans three empires.

It helps to remember how central this building once was. For more than two centuries, the call to prayer rang out from its minaret across the harbour, the Ottoman garrison and the town's Muslim families came here to pray, and the harbour front around it was the busiest part of the Ottoman town. When you stand in front of it today, among the café tables and the strolling crowds, you are standing in what was once the religious heart of a community that has since vanished from Crete entirely.

The mosque is at its most beautiful in the evening, when its domes are lit and the harbour is full of people strolling and dining. In the early morning, it is quiet, and you can see it in clear, soft light.

The Mosque of the Janissaries is a reminder that Chania was an Ottoman town for more than two hundred years, a chapter that is sometimes overlooked. Pause in front of it, and remember the people who prayed here, and the history that made the harbour what it is today.

name: Etz Hayyim: The Synagogue That Came Back
description: Hidden in a lane of the old Jewish quarter is a small synagogue that was left in ruins after its community was lost, then lovingly brought back to life.
details:
Etz Hayyim, the 'Tree of Life', stands in a narrow lane in the old Jewish quarter of Chania, a few minutes' walk from the harbour. From the outside, it is easy to miss: a gate, a small courtyard, a modest stone building. Inside, it is one of the most moving places in Crete.

The building has a long history. It was originally a Venetian church, and in the Ottoman period it was converted into a synagogue for the city's Jewish community, which had lived in Chania for many centuries; Jews lived on Crete from antiquity. The synagogue served the community through the Ottoman period and into the twentieth century.

In May 1944, during the German occupation of Crete, the Jewish community of Chania was arrested. The prisoners were put aboard a ship, the Tanais, along with other prisoners, and in June 1944 the ship was sunk in the Aegean. Almost the entire Jewish community of Chania died. After the war, the synagogue was left abandoned, and it fell into ruin.

In the 1990s, the building was restored, largely thanks to the efforts of Nikos Stavroulakis, a scholar and artist of Cretan Jewish heritage, supported by international donors. It reopened as a synagogue, and today it is a place of prayer, study and remembrance, welcoming visitors of all faiths and none.

When you enter, notice the courtyard and its trees, a peaceful space in the middle of the busy old town. Inside the synagogue, look at the simple wooden fittings, the bimah, the platform from which the Torah is read, and the ark in which the scrolls are kept. The atmosphere is quiet and contemplative. In the courtyard and garden, there are graves of rabbis and a memorial bearing the names of those who were lost in 1944.

Etz Hayyim has also been through difficult times since its restoration. In 2010, it was damaged by arson attacks, and it was restored again with support from the local community and from people around the world. Its survival is itself a statement about memory and tolerance.

What do most visitors miss? Simply the synagogue itself. Many people walk through the old Jewish quarter, the Evraiki, admiring its pretty lanes, without realising that this was once a living community, or that its synagogue is still open. Others pass the gate without knowing what lies behind it.

Etz Hayyim is more than a memorial. It has a small library, it hosts study, lectures and cultural events, and it describes itself as a place of prayer, recollection and reconciliation, open to all. Many of the people who keep it going are not Jewish, but feel strongly that the memory of Chania's Jewish neighbours belongs to the whole city. That spirit of openness is part of what makes a visit here so affecting.

When you visit, dress modestly and speak quietly. Check the opening times before you go, as they can be limited. Visitors are welcome, and the staff and volunteers are generous with information.

Etz Hayyim is a small building with a large story: of a community that lived in Chania for many centuries, of its sudden and terrible end, and of a determined effort to remember. Spend a few minutes in its courtyard, and you will carry the memory of Chania's lost neighbours with you.

name: The Firkas Fortress: Where Crete Became Greek
description: At the mouth of the harbour, a squat Venetian fort holds a maritime museum and the flagpole where Crete's long struggle for union with Greece finally ended.
details:
At the western end of Chania's harbour, where the sea wall meets the town, stands a low, solid fortress with thick stone walls. This is the Firkas, built by the Venetians to defend the harbour entrance, and it is one of the most historically important places in Crete. Many visitors walk past it on the way to the lighthouse viewpoint without going in.

The fortress dates from the Venetian period, when Chania's harbour was a key naval base, and it guarded the entrance alongside the lighthouse opposite. Under the Ottomans, it was used as a barracks and a prison. Its name is thought to derive from the Turkish word for barracks.

Its most important moment came in 1913. After decades of uprisings against Ottoman rule, Crete had become an autonomous state in 1898 and had long been pressing for union with Greece. On 1 December 1913, at a ceremony attended by King Constantine I of Greece and the Cretan statesman Eleftherios Venizelos, the Greek flag was raised over the Firkas, marking Crete's formal union with Greece. A flagpole still stands on the bastion, and for Cretans, this is a deeply symbolic place.

Inside the fortress is the Maritime Museum of Crete, one of the best small museums on the island. It traces the island's long relationship with the sea, from the Bronze Age to the present: models of Minoan ships, Venetian galleys and modern vessels; maps, nautical instruments and paintings; and exhibits on the naval battles fought around Crete, including the Battle of Crete in 1941. For anyone interested in seafaring, it is fascinating, and it helps explain why so many powers wanted this harbour.

From the walls of the Firkas, you get a fine view across the harbour mouth to the lighthouse and out to sea, and back along the curve of the waterfront. In the evening, the light on the water is beautiful.

What do most visitors miss? The significance of the flagpole, which looks like any other until you know its story. The museum, which is often quiet. And the remains of the Venetian walls and bastions running along the western side of the old town from here, which you can follow on foot into the quieter Topanas quarter.

It is worth pausing on what that moment in 1913 meant to the people standing here. For generations, Cretans had risen against Ottoman rule, often at terrible cost, with villages burned and families scattered. The autonomous Cretan State of 1898 had been a step, but union with Greece, enosis, was the goal that many had fought and died for. When the flag went up over the Firkas, it was the end of a struggle that had shaped the lives of grandparents and grandchildren alike. Cretans still mark the anniversary, and the flagpole still matters.

In the summer, the courtyard of the Firkas has been used for open-air performances and events, and on a warm evening, sitting within these old walls by the sea, it is easy to feel the weight of the place and the lightness of the present at the same time.

The Firkas is not the most beautiful building in Chania, but it is one of the most meaningful. Stand by the flagpole, look out at the sea that brought Venetians, Ottomans and Egyptians to this harbour, and remember that it was here that Crete finally became part of Greece.

name: The Temple of Zeus: A Wonder Lying Where It Fell
description: Its giant columns lie toppled on the ground exactly as an earthquake left them. Inside, there once sat one of the Seven Wonders of the World.
details:
At the heart of the sanctuary at Olympia lies the Temple of Zeus, or what remains of it: a vast stone platform, scattered with enormous column drums lying on their sides in long rows, as if a giant had knocked them down like dominoes. Most visitors pause, take a photo, and move on to the stadium. It is worth staying longer.

The temple was built in the fifth century BC, completed around 456 BC, and designed by the architect Libon of Elis. It was the largest temple in the Peloponnese, built in the Doric style of local limestone, covered with fine stucco to look like marble. It stood at the centre of the sanctuary, dedicated to Zeus, the king of the gods, in whose honour the Olympic Games were held.

Inside stood one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world: a colossal statue of Zeus seated on a throne, made by the sculptor Phidias around 430 BC. It was about twelve metres tall, with skin of ivory and robes of gold, and the god's head almost touched the roof. Ancient writers said that if Zeus stood up, he would raise the roof off the temple. Visitors came from all over the Greek world to see it. The statue was later removed, and it was eventually lost; according to one account, it was taken to Constantinople and destroyed in a fire there. Nothing of it survives.

Look at the column drums. They are huge, each one taller than a person when standing upright. Their positions, lying in rows, show that the temple was brought down by earthquakes, probably in the sixth century AD. One column was re-erected in 2004, for the Athens Olympics, and it gives an idea of the temple's original height. Stand beside it and look up.

Notice the platform itself, the stylobate, on which the columns stood, and the ramp leading up to it on the east side. The entrance faced east, towards the rising sun. Around the temple, there were once hundreds of statues dedicated by victorious athletes and by cities, and you can still see some of their stone bases.

The temple's sculptures, carved for its pediments and metopes, survived much better than the building. The east pediment showed the preparations for the chariot race between Pelops and Oinomaos, a founding myth of Olympia. The west pediment showed the battle between the Lapiths and the Centaurs, with the god Apollo standing calmly at its centre. The metopes showed the twelve labours of Heracles, who in one tradition founded the Games. All of these are displayed in the Archaeological Museum nearby, and they are among the finest sculptures of the classical period. Seeing them after the temple makes the ruins come alive.

What do most visitors miss? The workshop of Phidias, just to the west of the temple, where the great statue was made. It was later turned into a Byzantine church, but archaeologists found tools, moulds for the gold drapery and a small cup inscribed 'I belong to Phidias', which confirmed its identity. Standing there, you are in the room where one of the wonders of the world was made.

The Temple of Zeus is now a field of broken stone under the pines, but for nearly a thousand years it was the focus of one of the greatest gatherings of the ancient world. Stand on the platform, look east along the ramp where pilgrims entered, and imagine coming face to face with the gold and ivory god.

name: The Stadium at Olympia: Through the Tunnel
description: A stone tunnel, a strip of earth, two grassy banks. Few places on earth are so simple, or so moving, as the stadium where the Olympic Games began.
details:
Of all the places at Olympia, the stadium is the one that most visitors remember, and for good reason. After the crowded ruins of the sanctuary, you walk through a long, vaulted stone tunnel, and emerge into a vast, open, grassy space: a long, flat track of earth, enclosed by gently sloping embankments. That is all. And yet it is one of the most evocative places in Greece.

The tunnel is the first thing to notice. Known as the krypte, it was built in the Hellenistic period, around the third century BC, as a ceremonial entrance for the athletes and judges. Its stone arch is one of the earliest examples of a vaulted passage in Greece. Walking through it, you follow in the footsteps of the competitors, moving from the sacred precinct into the arena.

The stadium itself has gone through several phases. The version you see is the one developed in the classical period, moved slightly east of earlier tracks. The track is about 192 metres long, the length of one stade, the original Olympic race and the origin of the word 'stadium'. At each end, stone slabs with grooves mark the starting and finishing lines, where the runners placed their feet. You can still see them.

There were no stone seats for ordinary spectators. They sat or stood on the grassy embankments, which held tens of thousands of people. On the south side, there was a stand for the judges, the Hellanodikai, who wore purple robes. Opposite them, on the north side, was an altar of Demeter Chamyne, whose priestess was the only married woman permitted to watch the Games.

Ancient writers describe the scene during the Games: the heat of midsummer, the crowd packed onto the banks, vendors selling food and drink, and the intense competition. The athletes competed naked, and the shortest race, the stade, was the most prestigious event; the winner's name was used to identify the Olympiad.

Now, the thing to do. Walk onto the track and run. Almost everyone does, and it is perfectly allowed. Many visitors race their friends or family from one starting line to the other, and it is a joyful, slightly ridiculous experience. Whatever your pace, you are running where athletes ran for over a thousand years.

What do most visitors miss? The row of stone bases just before the tunnel, where the Zanes stood. These were bronze statues of Zeus, paid for with fines from athletes caught cheating or bribing, and inscribed with the names of the offenders. Every competitor walked past them on the way to the stadium, a public reminder of the shame of cheating. Also missed: the quiet. In the early morning or late afternoon, when the groups have left, the stadium can be almost empty, and the silence is profound.

The stadium at Olympia is a simple strip of earth between two grassy banks, but it gave the world the Olympic Games. Walk through the tunnel slowly, step onto the track, and feel the history under your feet.

name: The Temple of Hera: Where the Flame Is Born
description: An older, humbler temple than Zeus's, it is where every modern Olympic flame is kindled from the sun. Look closely at its columns: no two are quite alike.
details:
Near the foot of the pine-covered hill of Kronos, in the northern part of the sanctuary at Olympia, stand the remains of the Temple of Hera, the Heraion. A few columns are still standing, and the long stone platform is clear. It is smaller and less grand than the Temple of Zeus, but it is older, and in some ways more important today.

The Heraion was built around 600 BC, making it one of the oldest monumental temples in Greece. It was dedicated to Hera, queen of the gods and wife of Zeus, and possibly at first to both of them. It is a Doric temple, long and narrow, and it is a key monument in the history of Greek architecture.

Look closely at the columns, and you will see something unusual. They are not all the same. Some are thicker, some thinner, some have different numbers of flutes, and their capitals vary in shape. The reason, according to the ancient traveller Pausanias, is that the temple's columns were originally made of wood and were replaced over time, one by one, with stone, in the style of whatever period they were replaced. When Pausanias visited in the second century AD, he reported that one wooden column still remained. The variety you see is a record of centuries of slow change.

In front of the temple stood an altar of Hera. It is here, by tradition, that the Olympic flame for the modern Games is lit. Several months before each Games, at a ceremony at the temple, an actress dressed as a high priestess uses a parabolic mirror to focus the rays of the sun and ignite a torch. The flame is then carried in relay to the host city. This ceremony began with the 1936 Games in Berlin, and it has taken place for every Summer and Winter Olympics since. The ceremonial area is marked off, and visitors should respect the barrier.

In antiquity, the Heraion also housed precious objects and statues. One of the most famous finds from Olympia, the statue of Hermes holding the infant Dionysus, often attributed to Praxiteles, was found in the Heraion in 1877. It is now in the Archaeological Museum, along with a large stone head, thought to be from a statue of Hera.

The Heraion was also linked to the Heraia, a festival in honour of Hera that included foot races for young unmarried women, held separately from the men's Games. It is a reminder that women, though barred from competing in the Olympics, had their own athletic tradition here.

What do most visitors miss? The variety of the columns, which is easy to overlook unless you know to look. And the setting: the Heraion stands at the foot of the hill of Kronos, among pines, with a sense of age and quiet that the grander monuments lack.

Stand by the Heraion's broken columns, and imagine the sunlight focused into a mirror and the flame catching. Every time the Olympic torch is lit, it begins here, at one of the oldest temples in Greece.

name: The Archaeological Museum of Olympia: The Gods Come Indoors
description: Outside, Olympia is broken columns. Inside the museum, the sanctuary's gods, heroes and athletes are still standing, including one of the most famous statues in the world.
details:
Many visitors to Olympia spend so long in the sanctuary that they arrive at the museum tired, hot and short of time. That is a pity, because the Archaeological Museum of Olympia is one of the finest museums in Greece, and it holds the sculptures and objects that bring the ruins to life.

The museum stands just across the road from the site, and it is arranged roughly chronologically, from prehistoric times to the Roman period. In the early rooms are bronze figurines and offerings brought to the sanctuary from the eighth century BC onward: small horses, warriors and animals, as well as bronze tripods and cauldrons dedicated to Zeus. There are also helmets and armour, dedicated as spoils of war, including, by tradition, a helmet dedicated by Miltiades, the Athenian general at Marathon.

The great central hall is the heart of the museum. Here, the sculptures from the pediments of the Temple of Zeus are displayed at their original width, facing each other. On the east pediment, Zeus stands at the centre between the figures of Pelops and Oinomaos, preparing for their chariot race. On the west pediment, Apollo stands calmly at the centre of a violent battle between the Lapiths and the Centaurs, who are trying to carry off the Lapith women. Look at the faces and the movement of the bodies. These sculptures are among the masterpieces of the early classical style. Around the hall are the metopes, showing the labours of Heracles.

In a room of its own stands the statue that most visitors come to see: Hermes holding the infant Dionysus, found in the Temple of Hera. It is often attributed to the great fourth-century sculptor Praxiteles, though some scholars believe it may be a later work. Either way, it is exquisitely carved, with an extraordinary softness to the marble, and it is one of the most famous statues of the ancient world.

Another highlight is the Nike of Paionios, a marble statue of the winged goddess of victory, made in the late fifth century BC. She once stood on a tall pillar in front of the Temple of Zeus, so she appeared to be descending from the sky, her robes blown back against her body by the wind. Even damaged, she is breathtaking.

What do most visitors miss? The finds from Phidias' workshop, including the small cup with his name, which proved where the statue of Zeus was made. The room devoted to the Games, with athletic equipment such as jumping weights. And the many smaller bronze offerings, each one left by an individual who came to Olympia hoping for the god's favour.

A practical tip: in hot weather, many visitors find it best to see the outdoor sanctuary first, early in the day, and then come to the museum, which is air-conditioned, when the sun is strongest.

The museum turns Olympia from a field of ruins into a place full of people, gods and stories. Give it at least an hour, and stand for a while in front of Hermes and the Nike. They are the reason Olympia is remembered not only for its athletes but for its art.

name: The Old Fortress: Corfu's Rock of Defiance
description: Cut off from the town by a sea moat, Corfu's Old Fortress held back Ottoman armies and gives the best view on the island. Most visitors only see its walls from the café terrace.
details:
At the eastern edge of Corfu Town, across a broad green square from the Liston, a rocky promontory juts into the sea, crowned by two peaks and ringed with massive walls. This is the Old Fortress, the Palaio Frourio, and it has dominated the town for centuries. Many visitors admire it from the cafés of the Spianada without crossing the bridge. It is worth going in.

The promontory was fortified long before the Venetians arrived, and in the Byzantine period it was the heart of the town, with its two peaks providing natural defences. When the Venetians took control of Corfu in 1386, they made the fortress the key to their defence of the island. In the sixteenth century, they cut a channel across the base of the promontory, the Contrafossa, turning it into an artificial island separated from the town by a sea moat. You cross it today by a bridge.

The fortress was put to the test in the great Ottoman sieges of 1537 and 1716. Both times, Corfu held out, and it was never conquered by the Ottomans, unlike almost all of Greece. The successful defence in 1716 was credited by Corfiots to their patron, Saint Spyridon, and celebrated with a procession every year on 11 August.

After the Venetians, the French and then the British occupied the fortress. The British left their mark most visibly in the Church of Saint George, built in the 1840s inside the fortress in the form of a Greek temple, with Doric columns. It looks oddly classical among the Venetian walls, and it is used today for exhibitions and occasional events.

Walk up through the fortress to the top of the higher peak, where a lighthouse and signal station stand. The climb is steep in places, but the view is the best in Corfu: the whole of the old town, the harbour, the New Fortress across the bay, the green hills of the island and, across the strait, the mountains of Albania and the Greek mainland. On a clear day, it is spectacular.

What do most visitors miss? The Venetian lion of Saint Mark carved on the walls, a reminder of who built them. The tunnels and passages inside the fortifications. The sea moat itself, the Contrafossa, where small boats are moored under the walls. And the quieter corners of the fortress, where you can sit in the shade with the sea below and the noise of the town far away.

It is worth imagining the fortress under siege. In 1716, a large Ottoman army landed on the island and attacked the town's defences for weeks. The defenders, under the command of the German-born Count Johann Matthias von der Schulenburg, who was serving Venice, held out until the Ottomans withdrew. A statue of Schulenburg stands at the entrance to the Old Fortress, honouring the commander who helped save Corfu. Many visitors walk past it without a glance.

The fortress also houses a library and some cultural spaces, and it hosts concerts and events in summer.

Many visitors to Corfu spend their time in the old town and never cross the bridge. But the Old Fortress is the reason Corfu Town exists in the form it does. Walk up to the top, look out across the strait, and you will understand why empires fought for this island, and why it never fell.

name: The Church of Saint Spyridon: The Saint Who Saved an Island
description: A red-domed bell tower, a silver casket and a queue of locals waiting to kiss it. In this church, a fourth-century bishop is still very much a member of the community.
details:
Rising above the rooftops of Corfu's old town is a tall bell tower with a red dome, visible from almost anywhere. Below it is the Church of Saint Spyridon, the most important church on the island, and the home of its most beloved figure. Many visitors step inside briefly to admire the decoration. To understand Corfu, you need to know why the locals are there.

Saint Spyridon was a fourth-century bishop of Trimythous in Cyprus. He was known for his simplicity, his care for the poor and the many miracles attributed to him. After his death, his body was taken to Constantinople, and before the city fell to the Ottomans in 1453, it was brought out, and eventually came to Corfu in the fifteenth century. The church you see was built in the late sixteenth century to house his relics.

For Corfiots, Spyridon is not a distant historical figure. He is their protector, and he is credited with saving the island from plague, famine and invasion, including the Ottoman siege of 1716. Many Corfiot boys are named Spyridon, and families say a prayer to him in times of trouble. Four times a year, his relics are carried in procession through the streets of the old town, accompanied by clergy, brass bands and huge crowds: on Palm Sunday, Holy Saturday, 11 August and the first Sunday of November.

Inside, the church is richly decorated, in a style that mixes Orthodox and Venetian influences. Look up at the ceiling, covered with painted panels showing scenes from the saint's life; the originals were painted in the eighteenth century, and the panels you see today are later copies. There are silver lamps, icons and chandeliers, gifts from the faithful over centuries, hanging from the ceiling. The iconostasis, the screen of icons at the front, is made of marble.

To the right of the altar, in a small side chapel, is the saint's silver casket. Here, you will see what makes this church special: a constant stream of locals coming to pray, light a candle and venerate the relics. On some days, the casket is opened, and the saint's preserved body can be seen. People queue quietly, kiss the casket and leave. Visitors are welcome, but it is important to be respectful: dress modestly, keep your voice low, and follow the lead of those around you. Photography is often not permitted; check the signs.

A local tradition holds that the saint walks the island at night, helping those in need, and that his slippers wear out as a result; they are replaced periodically. It is a story Corfiots tell with affection, and it says much about how close they feel to him.

What do most visitors miss? The quiet moments of devotion, which are easy to overlook among the decoration. The silver offerings, often small plaques shaped like eyes, hearts or limbs, left by people asking for healing. And the sense that this is not just a historic church, but a living centre of faith.

Step inside the Church of Saint Spyridon, stand quietly to one side, and watch. You will see Corfu's heart.

name: The Achilleion: An Empress's Palace for a Greek Hero
description: Built by a grieving Empress of Austria and later owned by the German Kaiser, this hilltop palace is a monument to one woman's obsession with ancient Greece.
details:
About ten kilometres south of Corfu Town, on a hillside near the village of Gastouri, stands the Achilleion, a white neoclassical palace surrounded by terraced gardens with sweeping views over the sea. It is one of the most visited sights on Corfu, and its story is one of royalty, grief and romance.

The palace was built in the early 1890s for Empress Elisabeth of Austria, known to the world as Sissi. Famous for her beauty and her restlessness, Elisabeth spent much of her life travelling, escaping the stiff formality of the Habsburg court in Vienna. She loved Corfu and its landscape, and she was fascinated by ancient Greece and especially by Achilles, the hero of Homer's Iliad. After the death of her only son, Crown Prince Rudolf, in 1889, she built this palace as a retreat and named it after her hero.

Look at the decoration, and you will see her passion for Greek myth everywhere: statues of gods and muses in the gardens, paintings of mythological scenes inside. In the gardens stands a statue of the dying Achilles, trying to pull the arrow from his heel, a moving image that Elisabeth commissioned. Inside, there is a painting of the triumph of Achilles. The architecture is a romantic nineteenth-century vision of ancient Greece rather than a faithful copy of it.

Elisabeth did not enjoy her palace for long. In 1898, she was assassinated in Geneva by an anarchist. The palace was later bought by the German Kaiser, Wilhelm II, who used it as a summer residence and added his own touches, including a colossal bronze statue of Achilles in full armour, standing at the end of the gardens and looking out to sea. The two statues of Achilles, Elisabeth's dying hero and Wilhelm's triumphant warrior, tell you a great deal about the two very different people who lived here.

During the First World War, the Achilleion was used as a military hospital. Later, it passed to the Greek state, and for a time it housed a casino. In recent years, it has been restored, and it is now a museum.

What do most visitors miss? The view. From the terraces at the back of the gardens, you look out over a green landscape of olive groves and cypresses down to the sea and along the coast, and it is easy to see why Elisabeth chose this spot. The personal objects of the empress inside the palace, which give a sense of the lonely, complicated woman behind the legend. And the quieter corners of the gardens, away from the tour groups.

The Achilleion is a short drive from Corfu Town, and it can get busy when several cruise ships are in port. Early or late in the day is quieter.

The Achilleion is not an ancient monument, and it does not pretend to be. It is a palace built by a grieving empress who found consolation in the myths of ancient Greece. Stand in the garden by the dying Achilles, look out over the sea, and you will feel something of her longing.

name: Vlacherna and Mouse Island: Corfu's Picture-Perfect View
description: A white monastery on a causeway, a wooded islet beyond and planes landing just overhead. This is Corfu's most famous view, and it comes with a legend about Odysseus.
details:
At the tip of the Kanoni peninsula, a few kilometres south of Corfu Town, is a viewpoint that appears on more postcards of Corfu than any other. Below you, in a calm lagoon, a small white monastery sits on a tiny islet, linked to the shore by a narrow causeway. Beyond it, a little wooded island rises from the sea, with a chapel half hidden among its trees. The monastery is Vlacherna, and the island is Pontikonisi, Mouse Island.

The name Kanoni comes from a cannon that the French placed here during their occupation of the island in the early nineteenth century. From the viewpoint, a path and steps lead down to the causeway and the monastery.

The Monastery of Vlacherna is a small, whitewashed convent dedicated to the Virgin, dating from the seventeenth century. It is simple and peaceful, with a small church and a bell tower, and it is reached by walking along the causeway, with the water lapping on either side. Visitors can enter the church; dress modestly and be respectful.

Pontikonisi lies just beyond, reached in season by small boats from the causeway. It is covered with trees, and at its summit stands the small Byzantine chapel of Pantokrator. Its name, Mouse Island, is said by some to come from its shape, or from the white path of steps up to the chapel, which looks like a mouse's tail.

Then there is the legend. According to a local tradition, Pontikonisi is the ship of Odysseus, turned to stone by Poseidon after the Phaeacians helped the hero return home to Ithaca. In Homer's Odyssey, Poseidon does turn the Phaeacian ship to stone as it returns to port, but whether that happened here is a matter of local legend rather than fact. Several places in Corfu claim the story. It is a wonderful one to remember as you look at the island.

Behind you, as you stand on the causeway, the runway of Corfu's airport stretches across the lagoon. Planes come in to land low over the water, close enough to make visitors duck, and plane spotters gather at the viewpoint to watch. It is an unexpected and slightly surreal addition to the scene, and many visitors find it exhilarating.

What do most visitors miss? The walk itself. Many people stop at the viewpoint, take a photograph and leave, without walking down to the causeway or visiting the monastery. Early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light is soft and the tour groups have gone, the walk along the causeway is peaceful, and the reflections in the lagoon are beautiful. They also miss Mon Repos, the wooded estate near Kanoni where Prince Philip was born, with the ruins of the ancient city of Corcyra in its park.

Kanoni is about four kilometres from Corfu Town, and it is easily reached by bus or taxi.

Vlacherna and Pontikonisi make the most famous view in Corfu, and with good reason. Walk down to the water, stand on the causeway between the monastery and the shore, and look out at the island that might, or might not, be Odysseus's ship. You will understand why this view has been loved for so long.

name: The Peristyle: Coffee in an Emperor's Courtyard
description: Granite columns, a headless sphinx and a dome open to the sky. The ceremonial heart of Diocletian's palace is now Split's favourite place to sit down.
details:
In the middle of Diocletian's Palace, where its two main streets once crossed, lies a long, open courtyard lined with tall columns of red-flecked granite, carrying graceful arches. This is the Peristyle, and it is the heart of Split. Cafés set cushions on its stone steps, tour groups gather in its centre, and on summer nights it becomes an open-air stage. It is easy to treat it simply as a pretty square. It was designed to be much more.

When Diocletian built his palace around the turn of the fourth century, the Peristyle was its ceremonial core. At its southern end, a raised porch, the Protyron, led towards the emperor's private apartments. Here, it is believed, the emperor appeared before his subjects, who were expected to prostrate themselves before him; Diocletian presented himself as a semi-divine ruler. To the east stood his mausoleum, an octagonal building now the cathedral. To the west were temples, one of which survives as the baptistery. Everything about the space was designed to impress.

Look at the columns. Some are of granite brought from Egypt, and the effort and cost of transporting them across the Mediterranean says much about the emperor's power. Then look for the sphinx. Diocletian brought several Egyptian sphinxes to his palace, and one, of black granite, still sits beside the cathedral steps, headless and patient. It is more than three thousand years old, older than the palace by many centuries.

Now look at how the city has moved in. Medieval and Renaissance houses are built into the arches, with windows and balconies tucked between the columns. Shops and a hotel occupy rooms that were once part of the palace. This mixing of Roman and later buildings is exactly what makes Split unique.

From the Protyron, go through the doorway into the Vestibule, a round, domed hall that once formed the entrance to the emperor's apartments. Its dome has an open hole at the top, through which you see the sky. Originally it was probably covered and decorated with mosaics. The acoustics in this space are remarkable, and it is here that klapa singers, groups performing traditional Dalmatian a cappella harmonies, often sing. Klapa is recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage. If you hear it here, stop and listen. The voices fill the dome in a way that is unforgettable.

What do most visitors miss? The view of the Peristyle from above, from the cathedral's bell tower. The red granite and the white limestone of the columns, which reveal different origins. And the Peristyle in the early morning, when the cafés are just setting out their cushions, the stone is cool and the courtyard is almost empty.

In summer, during the Split Summer Festival, the Peristyle becomes an open-air stage for opera, the steps turned into seating and the columns into scenery. Around noon in season, actors dressed as Roman soldiers and as Diocletian himself appear on the Protyron, a bit of theatre that delights some visitors and amuses others.

Sit on the steps with a coffee, look up at the columns, and remember that you are sitting in the ceremonial hall of a Roman emperor, where people once fell to the ground before him. Today, they just order another espresso.

name: The Cathedral of Saint Domnius: A Persecutor's Tomb Made Holy
area: Cathedral of Saint Domnius & Bell Tower
description: It may be the oldest building in the world still used as a cathedral, and it began life as the mausoleum of the emperor who martyred its saint.
tags: Cathedral of Saint Domnius & Bell Tower
details:
On the eastern side of the Peristyle stands an octagonal building, surrounded by a colonnade, with a tall, slender bell tower rising beside it. This is the Cathedral of Saint Domnius, and it holds one of history's great ironies.

The building was constructed as the mausoleum of Emperor Diocletian. He intended to be buried here, at the heart of his palace, and when he died, around 311 or 312, he was laid to rest within it. Diocletian was the emperor who launched the last and most severe persecution of Christians in the Roman Empire. Among those martyred was Domnius, bishop of the nearby city of Salona, executed in 304.

Several centuries later, after the people of Salona had taken refuge within the palace, the mausoleum was converted into a Christian church and dedicated to Saint Domnius. Diocletian's tomb disappeared, and his remains were never found. The relics of the saint he had martyred were placed within his mausoleum. Many in Split enjoy that turn of history. The building is often described as the oldest Catholic cathedral in the world still in use in its original structure.

Look at the exterior. The octagon is surrounded by columns, and inside, the circular space is ringed by two levels of columns, Roman in origin, beneath a dome. Look up at the frieze around the base of the dome. Among the carved figures, there are medallions believed to show Diocletian and his wife, Prisca, a strange survival of the emperor in the church built over his tomb.

The cathedral's great wooden doors were carved in the thirteenth century by a local master, Andrija Buvina, with twenty-eight scenes from the life of Christ. Inside, look for the carved Romanesque pulpit and the altars of Saint Domnius and Saint Anastasius, the latter with a fine relief of the flagellation of Christ by the fifteenth-century sculptor Juraj Dalmatinac. The choir stalls are among the oldest surviving in Dalmatia.

Then climb the bell tower. Construction began in the thirteenth century and continued for centuries, and the tower was substantially rebuilt in the early twentieth century. The climb is steep, with narrow stone steps and, near the top, open metal stairs through which you can see down; it is not for those who are nervous of heights. But from the top, you see the entire palace spread out below, the Riva, the harbour, Marjan Hill and the islands. Be aware that the bells ring on the hour, and they are very loud.

What do most visitors miss? The treasury, which holds medieval manuscripts, reliquaries and church vestments. The crypt, beneath the cathedral, a dark, round chamber once used for worship. And the black granite sphinx outside, older than the building by more than a thousand years.

The cathedral is a working church, and Mass is celebrated regularly. Dress modestly, and be aware that sightseeing is restricted during services. Tickets cover the cathedral and other parts of the complex in various combinations.

Stand inside the octagon and look up at the medallions in the frieze. Somewhere above you, an emperor who tried to destroy Christianity is still looking down, from inside a cathedral dedicated to one of his victims.

name: Diocletian's Cellars: The Palace Beneath the Palace
description: Under Split's streets lie vast vaulted halls that mirror the lost rooms of the emperor's apartments. For centuries they were a rubbish dump; now they reveal the palace's original plan.
details:
Step through the Bronze Gate from the Riva, the seaside entrance to Diocletian's Palace, and you find yourself in a long, vaulted passage lined with stalls selling jewellery, lavender, souvenirs and local crafts. It is busy and cool, a welcome refuge on a hot day. Most visitors walk straight through it on their way to the Peristyle. But this passage is part of one of the most remarkable survivals of Roman architecture anywhere: the substructures, or cellars, of the palace.

When Diocletian built his palace, the ground sloped down towards the sea. To create a level platform for his private apartments on the southern side, his builders constructed a series of massive vaulted halls underneath them. These substructures supported the floors of the imperial rooms above, and they replicated their layout, wall for wall. Because the upper rooms have long since disappeared under later buildings, the cellars are now the best evidence of how the emperor's apartments were arranged.

After the palace became a town, these halls were gradually filled with rubbish and waste from the houses above. For centuries, they were inaccessible, and the rubbish preserved them. In the twentieth century, they were excavated and cleaned out, and today large parts of them are open to visitors.

Beyond the central passage, a ticketed section takes you into the eastern and western halls. They are vast, dim and atmospheric, with stone vaults, massive piers and long corridors. You can trace the shapes of rooms: a great hall that would have stood beneath the emperor's dining or audience room, smaller chambers, passages. In some places, you can see ancient features such as a well and remains of an oil press, from the period when people of the town used these spaces.

Game of Thrones fans may recognise some of the halls, which were used as a filming location for scenes set in Meereen, including the dungeon where Daenerys Targaryen kept her dragons. That has brought many new visitors to the cellars.

What do most visitors miss? Look for the places where the walls and vaults were left unexcavated, still packed with debris, which show how deep the rubbish once lay. Notice the stone itself, the white limestone from the island of Brač, which was used throughout the palace. And step out of the central passage into the quieter side halls, where the scale of the Roman engineering becomes much clearer.

Think, too, about how the palace was built. The stone came largely from the quarries of Brač, across the water, and it was cut, shipped and assembled by thousands of workers, many of them probably slaves or conscripted labourers. The cellars, being purely structural, show that work without decoration: plain, massive and precise. They are the engineering beneath the elegance of the Peristyle above, and they tell you as much about Roman power as any column or statue.

The cellars also host exhibitions, events and the occasional concert, and in the heat of summer they are a cool place to spend an hour.

Above you, the city goes about its business, unaware of the vast halls beneath it. Down here, in the dim, cool light, you can see the bones of an emperor's palace, the plan of rooms that disappeared centuries ago, preserved by the rubbish of the people who came to live inside it.

name: The Golden Gate and Gregory of Nin: A Bishop Who Stands for a Nation
area: Golden Gate & Gregory of Nin statue
description: Outside the palace's grandest gate towers a bronze bishop whose big toe shines from millions of hopeful touches. Few know why he matters so much to Croatia.
tags: Golden Gate & Gregory of Nin statue
details:
The northern gate of Diocletian's Palace, the Golden Gate, was its main entrance in Roman times, facing the road that led inland to Salona. It is the most ornate of the four gates, decorated with niches that once held statues, and above it, within the wall, is a small early medieval chapel, the Church of Saint Martin, built into the guards' corridor. Just outside the gate, in a small park, stands a colossal bronze statue of a bearded man in bishop's robes, with one arm raised and a book in his hand. This is Gregory of Nin, and he is one of the most important figures in Croatian history.

Gregory was a tenth-century bishop of Nin, a small town on the Dalmatian coast. At church councils held in Split around that time, he argued for the use of the Slavic language in the liturgy, rather than only Latin. The Croatian liturgy was written in Glagolitic, an early Slavic script, and Gregory's defence of it has made him a symbol of Croatian national and religious identity.

The statue was made by Ivan Meštrović, Croatia's greatest modern sculptor, and was completed in 1929. It originally stood on the Peristyle, in the heart of the palace, where it dwarfed the Roman columns. During the Second World War, it was moved, and in the 1950s it was re-erected outside the Golden Gate, where it stands today. Its sheer size and its stylised, powerful form make it one of the most striking works of twentieth-century sculpture in Croatia.

Look at the statue's left big toe. It shines bright gold, polished by the touch of countless hands. According to local tradition, rubbing it brings good luck and ensures that you will return to Split. Locals and visitors line up to touch it, and it is one of the city's best-loved rituals.

Then turn to the Golden Gate itself. Look at the niches, the columns and the arches, and imagine the gate as it was in Diocletian's time, the formal entrance to the palace for visitors arriving from the Roman city. Climb the stairs inside the gate to the Church of Saint Martin, a tiny, narrow chapel tended by Dominican nuns, with an eleventh-century stone altar screen. It is one of the most atmospheric small spaces in Split, and few visitors find it.

What do most visitors miss? The chapel above the gate. The park around the statue, which offers shade and benches on a hot day. And the meaning of the statue. Many people rub the toe without knowing that Gregory represents the right of Croatians to worship in their own language, a cause that mattered deeply through centuries of foreign rule.

If you are interested in Meštrović, his former summer villa on the Marjan peninsula, now the Meštrović Gallery, holds a large collection of his work, and it is one of the most beautiful museums in Split.

Rub the toe, by all means. Everyone does. But stand back for a moment, too, and look up at the bishop with his book and raised arm. He stands for a nation that kept its language and faith through centuries of other people's empires.

name: The City Walls: Walking the Republic's Armour
description: Two kilometres of stone, towers and bastions encircle the old city. Walk them early, and you will see the roofs, the sea and the scars of 1991 in a single, unforgettable circuit.
details:
Dubrovnik's walls are among the most complete and impressive city fortifications in Europe. They run unbroken around the old town for roughly two kilometres, reaching heights of up to around twenty-five metres on the landward side, and they are punctuated by towers, bastions and forts. Walking the full circuit is the single most popular thing to do in Dubrovnik, and it is genuinely one of the great walks of the Mediterranean.

The walls were built and strengthened over several centuries, from the medieval period onward. Their great expansion came in the fifteenth century, especially after the fall of Constantinople to the Ottomans in 1453, when the Republic of Ragusa feared attack. Architects and engineers, including Michelozzo di Bartolomeo from Florence and the Dalmatian master Juraj Dalmatinac, worked on the defences. On the landward side, the walls are thick and tall; on the seaward side, they are lower but built on cliffs.

The most important tower is the Minčeta, on the highest point of the walls on the northern side. It is a massive round tower, the symbol of the city's strength, and from its top you look over the whole of the old town. On the western side, outside the walls, stands Fort Lovrijenac on its own rock. To the south is the Bokar fortress, and to the east, the Revelin fortress guards the eastern gate and the old port.

As you walk, look down. The walls give you a view straight into the life of the city: the terracotta roofs, the church domes, small courtyards with lemon trees, washing lines, rooftop terraces and children playing in narrow lanes. Look closely at the roof tiles. Many of them are brighter orange than others. Those are new tiles, put on during the restoration after the siege of 1991 and 1992, when the city was shelled. The older, faded tiles are those that survived. From the walls, you can read the damage of the war across the rooftops.

Then look out. On the seaward side, the walls rise above the cliffs, and the view across the Adriatic to the island of Lokrum is spectacular. You may see swimmers diving from the rocks below, and small bars perched on the cliffs outside the walls.

Practical matters are important here. The walk is about two kilometres, with many steps, and almost no shade. In summer, it is very hot, and the walls are crowded from mid-morning to mid-afternoon, especially when several cruise ships are in port. The best times are early in the morning, when the walls open, and late in the afternoon. Walking is one-way, so you cannot turn back. Take water and a hat, and allow between one and two hours. The ticket is relatively expensive, but the Dubrovnik Pass includes it, along with several museums.

What do most visitors miss? The details of the towers, such as the carved stone figures of Saint Blaise, the city's patron, holding a model of the city. The small exhibitions in some of the towers. And the moment of quiet, early in the morning, when the swifts scream over the rooftops and you have a stretch of wall almost to yourself.

Dubrovnik's walls were built to keep enemies out. Today, they let you see the city as a whole: its roofs, its sea, its scars and its life. Walk them early, and take your time.

name: The Rector's Palace: Where the Ruler Was a Prisoner of the Republic
description: The Republic of Ragusa's head of state lived here for just one month, and could not leave without permission. The palace is a lesson in how a small city kept its freedom.
details:
On the south side of the Luža Square, near the church of Saint Blaise and the Sponza Palace, stands an elegant building with a graceful arcaded loggia of carved columns. This is the Rector's Palace, the seat of government of the Republic of Ragusa, and it is one of the most important buildings in Dubrovnik. Today, it is home to the city's Cultural History Museum.

The Republic was governed by an aristocratic system designed to prevent any one person from gaining too much power. The rector, its nominal head of state, was elected from among the noble families, but served for just one month. During that month, he lived in the palace and was not allowed to leave it except on official business, and then only with permission. He could not see his family except under strict conditions. It was a system that made the rector a kind of honoured prisoner, and it helped preserve the Republic's independence for centuries.

The building itself has been damaged and rebuilt several times. A medieval fortress stood on this site. In the fifteenth century, the palace was rebuilt after gunpowder explosions, and architects including Onofrio della Cava and Michelozzo di Bartolomeo worked on it. It was damaged again in the great earthquake of 1667. As a result, the palace combines Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque styles.

Look at the loggia, its columns topped by richly carved capitals. One of them is often said to show Asclepius, the Greek god of medicine, in his workshop, a tribute to the tradition that he was born in nearby Epidaurum, today's Cavtat. Above the entrance to the council chamber, a Latin inscription reminds officials to forget private affairs and attend to public ones.

Inside, the palace is arranged around a beautiful atrium, with a double staircase leading up to the first floor. The acoustics are excellent, and the atrium is used for concerts during the Dubrovnik Summer Festival. In the atrium stands a bust of Miho Pracat, a wealthy merchant and shipowner from the island of Lopud who left his fortune to the Republic; he is said to be the only commoner honoured with a monument by the Republic.

Upstairs, the museum recreates the rector's rooms, with period furniture, portraits, the Republic's documents and coins. There are also exhibitions about the city's history, its laws and its diplomacy. Look for the keys to the city gates, which were given to the rector each evening.

What do most visitors miss? The inscription over the council chamber door. The carvings on the capitals of the loggia. And the meaning of the building: this was not a royal palace but the official residence of a republic, built to remind its rulers that they served the city, not the other way round.

The palace was also the place where the Republic did its business. Its councils met here, its courts sat here, its prisons held offenders in the basement, and its arms and gunpowder were stored here, which is why it suffered so badly from explosions. Walking through it, you pass from council chamber to courtroom to cell, and you get a sense of a whole state run from a single building.

Stand in the atrium, look up at the staircase and imagine the rector, elected for a month, living in these rooms, unable to leave. It was a strange way to run a state, but it worked for centuries.

name: Fort Lovrijenac: Freedom Is Not Sold for Gold
description: On a sheer rock outside the walls stands Dubrovnik's most dramatic fortress, with a Latin motto above its gate that sums up the soul of the Republic.
details:
Just west of Dubrovnik's walls, beyond the Pile Gate, a fortress stands on a rocky headland rising thirty-seven metres above the sea. This is Fort Lovrijenac, also known as Saint Lawrence's Fortress, and it is often called Dubrovnik's Gibraltar. Many visitors see it from the city walls or from the water. Fewer climb up to it, and they miss one of the best views in the city.

The fortress is very old, and it was built to guard the western approaches to the city, by land and sea. A local tradition tells that the Venetians planned to build a fortress on this rock, from which they could control the city, and that the people of Ragusa raced to build their own fortress here first, completing it in just three months. Whether that is exactly true or not, it reflects the city's constant fear of Venetian domination. The fortress was rebuilt and strengthened in later centuries.

Its shape is remarkable. It is triangular, following the shape of the rock, and its walls are very thick on the side facing the sea and the open land, but thinner on the side facing the city. The story goes that this was deliberate: if the fortress were ever taken by an enemy or by a rebellious commander, the city could bombard it easily. It is a fine example of the Republic's caution, in which even its own defenders were not entirely trusted.

Above the entrance gate is a Latin inscription, perhaps the most famous words in Dubrovnik: 'Non bene pro toto libertas venditur auro', Freedom is not sold for all the gold in the world. It sums up the spirit of the Republic of Ragusa, which kept its independence for centuries through diplomacy, wealth and caution.

Inside, the fortress is spare, with a large courtyard and terraces. Its acoustics and setting make it a magical stage, and for decades it has been used for performances of Shakespeare's Hamlet during the Dubrovnik Summer Festival. In recent years, it was also used as a filming location for Game of Thrones, representing parts of the Red Keep in King's Landing.

Climb to the top terraces, and the view is extraordinary. You look across the small cove below to the walls of the old city, with the Bokar fortress opposite, and along the coast in both directions. At sunset, it is one of the most beautiful places in Dubrovnik.

What do most visitors miss? The inscription, which many people walk under without reading. The view back at the old city, which is better from here than from almost anywhere. And the small cove below, where locals swim.

It is also worth looking at the fortress from the outside, from the city walls near the Pile Gate or from the water. From there, you can see how it sits on its rock like a ship's prow, with the sea breaking at its foot, and how perfectly it complements the Bokar fortress across the cove. Together, the two guarded the western entrance to the city, by land and by sea.

Lovrijenac requires a climb up a long flight of steps from the Pile area. Entry is often included with the ticket for the city walls, so it is worth keeping your ticket.

Stand under the inscription, read the words, and then look out over the walls of the city that lived by them. Few mottos have been so faithfully kept.

name: The Franciscan Monastery: A Pharmacy Seven Centuries Old
description: Just inside the Pile Gate, a quiet cloister of carved capitals hides one of the oldest working pharmacies in Europe. Most visitors walk straight past the door.
details:
Enter Dubrovnik through the Pile Gate, and almost immediately on your left is the Franciscan Monastery, its simple façade and bell tower easy to overlook in the rush along the Stradun. Behind them lies one of the most peaceful and fascinating places in the city.

The Franciscans came to Dubrovnik in the thirteenth century. Their first monastery stood outside the city walls, but for safety, they moved within the walls in the fourteenth century, and the present monastery was built at that time.
