It was badly damaged in the earthquake of 1667, and much of the church was rebuilt in the Baroque style, but the cloister survived.

The cloister is the monastery's treasure. It is a Romanesque-Gothic courtyard, built in the fourteenth century, surrounded by double columns topped with carved capitals. Look closely at the capitals, and you will find an astonishing variety of carvings: human heads, animals, flowers and fantastic creatures, each one different. One capital is said to show a man with a swollen face, often described as suffering from a toothache. In the centre of the cloister is a garden with palms, orange trees and a small fountain. It is a calm oasis just a few steps from the crowded street.

Off the cloister is the monastery's pharmacy. It was founded in 1317, and it has been in operation ever since, which makes it one of the oldest working pharmacies in Europe. Today, it sells modern medicines, as well as creams and lotions made to traditional recipes, which make popular souvenirs. Beside it, a small museum displays the old pharmacy's equipment: jars, mortars, scales and books of recipes, as well as paintings, gold and silverwork, and other treasures of the monastery.

The monastery also has a library of great importance, with manuscripts and early printed books. Parts of its collection can be seen in the museum.

Look at the walls of the cloister, too. During the siege of 1991 and 1992, the monastery was hit by shells, and the damage was later repaired. In the museum, you can see evidence of the damage, a reminder of how recently the city's treasures were in danger.

Outside the monastery's entrance on the Stradun, many visitors try a local custom: balancing on a stone head that juts from the monastery wall near the ground, while facing the wall, and trying to take off their shirt. It is said to bring luck in love. Whatever its origin, it is a lighthearted ritual, and it is fun to watch.

Look, too, at the church itself. Its main portal, on the Stradun side, has a carved Pietà above the door, a late Gothic work that survived the earthquake. Inside, the church is largely Baroque, rebuilt after 1667, and it remains in use by the friars, who still live in the monastery. Not far away, near the Pile Gate, stands Onofrio's Great Fountain, built in the fifteenth century as the end point of the city's aqueduct, which brought fresh water from the hills. Water, medicine and faith were all part of the Republic's care for its citizens, and you can see all three within a few steps of each other.

Inside the cloister, take a moment to sit on a bench under the columns and listen. The noise of the Stradun fades, and you can hear birds and the fountain. Seven centuries ago, Franciscan friars were mixing remedies in the room next door, and in a sense, they still are.

name: The Cathedral of Saint Tryphon: Twin Towers and a Martyr's Relics
description: Kotor's Romanesque cathedral has survived earthquakes, rebuilding and centuries of devotion. Its mismatched towers and its relics chapel tell the town's story.
details:
In the heart of Kotor's old town, on a square that bears its name, stands the Cathedral of Saint Tryphon, its two bell towers rising above the rooftops. It is the most important building in Kotor and one of the finest Romanesque churches on the Adriatic. Many visitors photograph its façade from the square and move on. It rewards a closer look.

Saint Tryphon was an early Christian martyr from Asia Minor, executed in the third century. According to tradition, his relics were brought to Kotor in the ninth century, and a church was built to house them. The local maritime brotherhood, the Bokelj Navy, traces its origins to the reception of those relics. The present cathedral was consecrated in 1166, and it has been rebuilt and restored several times since, especially after earthquakes.

Look at the two towers. They are not identical. After a severe earthquake in 1667 damaged the cathedral, the towers were rebuilt in a Baroque style. Look carefully, and you may notice that one appears slightly different from the other; the story most often told is that funds ran out before the second tower could be finished in the same way. Between them, above the entrance, is a large rose window. The facade, with its arch connecting the towers, is one of the most recognisable sights in Montenegro.

Inside, the cathedral is simple and harmonious, built of pale stone, with columns of red and white stone dividing the nave from the aisles. Look up at the arches, and look for the fragments of fourteenth-century frescoes that survive on the walls and vaults, showing saints and scenes painted by artists influenced by Byzantine traditions. Above the main altar is a magnificent fourteenth-century ciborium, a canopy supported by columns of red stone, with a silver-gilt altarpiece below it.

The cathedral's great treasure is its relics chapel and treasury, upstairs, which holds the relics of Saint Tryphon, along with reliquaries, crosses, silverwork and church vestments, many of them gifts from the seafarers and wealthy families of the Boka. A large carved wooden crucifix is particularly striking.

In 1979, a powerful earthquake caused severe damage to the cathedral, along with much of Kotor. It was carefully restored, and that restoration also revealed some of the frescoes you can see today.

Saint Tryphon's feast is celebrated in February, and the Bokelj Navy plays a key part in the festivities, performing its traditional circle dance, the kolo, in the square in front of the cathedral. If your visit happens to coincide, you will see one of the oldest living traditions on the Adriatic.

What do most visitors miss? The frescoes, which are faint and easy to overlook. The ciborium above the altar. And the treasury upstairs, which many people never find. The cathedral is a working Catholic church, so dress modestly, and avoid visiting during services if you are sightseeing.

Kotor is a town where Catholic and Orthodox churches stand a few steps apart, and Saint Tryphon is the heart of its Catholic tradition. Stand in the square in front of it, look up at the mismatched towers, and you are looking at more than eight hundred years of the town's faith, disasters and recoveries.

name: The Walls of Kotor: Climbing to the Fortress of Saint John
area: Kotor Walls & Fortress of Saint John
description: The walls of Kotor climb the mountain behind the town in an improbable zigzag. The climb is hard and hot, and the view from the top is one of the best in the Mediterranean.
tags: Kotor Walls & Fortress of Saint John
details:
Look up from almost anywhere in Kotor, and you will see them: a line of stone walls climbing the sheer mountain behind the town in a dramatic zigzag, with a small church halfway up and a fortress at the top. These are the walls of Kotor, and climbing them is the most memorable thing to do in the town.

The fortifications of Kotor run for several kilometres, enclosing the old town on its flat triangle of land and then climbing the mountainside behind it to the Fortress of Saint John, Sveti Ivan, about 260 metres above the sea. They were built and strengthened over many centuries, but their present form largely dates from the Venetian period, from 1420 to 1797, when Kotor was a frontier town facing the Ottoman Empire, whose territory lay just beyond the mountains.

The climb begins at entrances near the old town. A path of stone steps and ramps, with around 1,350 steps by common count, zigzags up the mountainside inside the walls. There is very little shade. It takes most people between one and two hours to go up and come back down, and the effort is considerable, especially in summer heat. Wear shoes with good grip, carry water and a hat, and go early in the morning or late in the afternoon. There is an entrance fee.

About halfway up stands the small Church of Our Lady of Remedy, Gospa od Zdravlja. It was built, according to tradition, in the sixteenth century, by survivors of a plague epidemic, in thanks for their deliverance. It is a welcome place to rest and catch your breath, with a lovely view down to the old town and the bay.

From the top, at the Fortress of Saint John, the view is breathtaking. Below you, the old town of Kotor lies like a triangle of red roofs, with the walls marking its edges. Beyond it, the Bay of Kotor winds away between the mountains, and you can see ships, villages and the islands near Perast. The fortress itself is a ruin, with remains of walls, gun emplacements and barracks, but its position explains why it was built: from here, defenders could watch the whole bay and the road from the mountains.

What do most visitors miss? The details along the way: the layers of masonry from different periods, the gun loops and embrasures, the ruined buildings within the walls. The view from the church halfway up, which many people rush past. And the small plants and flowers growing between the stones in spring.

There is also a famous route around the back of the mountain called the Ladder of Kotor, an old mule path that leads up towards the village of Njeguši. It offers spectacular views, but it is a separate hiking trail and does not provide a way into the fortress itself.

At night, the walls are lit, and from the old town or the bay, they appear as a line of lights climbing the dark mountain. It is a beautiful sight.

The walls of Kotor are one of the great climbs of the Mediterranean. Go early, take your time, stop at the church, and when you reach the top, look down at the town and the bay and remember that for centuries, soldiers stood here, watching for the enemy beyond the mountains.

name: Our Lady of the Rocks: An Island Built by Faith
area: Our Lady of the Rocks, Perast
description: Off the village of Perast, a church stands on an island that sailors made by hand, one stone at a time, and they are still adding to it every summer.
tags: Our Lady of the Rocks, Perast
details:
In the waters of the Bay of Kotor, just off the village of Perast, two small islands sit side by side. One is natural, covered with cypress trees, and holds the Benedictine monastery of Saint George. The other is artificial, crowned by a church with a blue dome. This is Gospa od Škrpjela, Our Lady of the Rocks, and its story is one of the most moving in the Adriatic.

According to local tradition, in the fifteenth century, two fishermen from Perast found an icon of the Virgin Mary on a rock in the bay. They took it as a sign and vowed to build a church there. From then on, every sailor returning safely from a voyage dropped a stone on the reef. Over time, with stones and even old sunken ships filled with rocks added to the pile, the reef grew into an island. The church was built on it, and it was rebuilt in its present form in the seventeenth century.

The tradition continues today. Every year, on the evening of 22 July, the people of Perast row out to the island in decorated boats and throw stones into the sea around it, in a ceremony called the Fašinada. It is a living link to the sailors who built the island centuries ago.

Small boats run from the Perast waterfront to the island, a short trip of a few minutes. Inside the church, the walls and ceiling are covered with paintings, many by the seventeenth-century Perast artist Tripo Kokolja. Look at the walls, too, which are lined with silver votive plaques, offerings left by sailors and their families in thanks for safe return or in hope of protection. Each one represents a story, a storm survived or a prayer answered.

The church has a small museum with a remarkable object at its heart: an embroidered icon, said to have been made over many years by a local woman, Jacinta Kunić, while she waited for her husband to return from the sea. According to the story, as her hair turned grey, she wove strands of it into the embroidery, and you can see the colour of the threads change. It is a legend told with great affection, and the embroidery is beautiful.

Turn and look back at Perast from the island. The village stretches along the shore below the mountains, with its baroque palaces and the tall bell tower of the church of Saint Nicholas. Perast was a wealthy seafaring town under Venetian rule, famous for its sailors, and its families built many of the churches and palaces you see.

What do most visitors miss? The details of the votive plaques, which reward close looking. The view of Saint George island next door, with its cypress trees and its quiet monastery, which is generally not open to visitors. And the Fašinada, if they happen to be in the area in late July.

In the middle of the day, especially when cruise ships and tour groups are in the area, the island can be crowded. Early morning and late afternoon are calmer.

Our Lady of the Rocks is a small island with an enormous story of faith, hope and the dangers of the sea. Stand on its shore, look at the stones beneath the water, and imagine generations of sailors adding one more, in thanks for coming home.

name: The Sea Gate and the Square of Arms: Entering Kotor
area: Sea Gate, Square of Arms & Clock Tower
description: Almost everyone enters Kotor through the same gate and stops in the same square. Look up, and the gate, the clock tower and the stone pillar beside it tell you who ruled here and how they kept order.
tags: Sea Gate, Square of Arms & Clock Tower
details:
The Sea Gate, on the western side of the old town facing the harbour, is the main entrance to Kotor, and almost every visitor passes through it. It is easy to walk straight through, eager to see the town. Stop for a moment, and look.

The gate dates largely from the sixteenth century, during the Venetian period. Above it, look for the carved lion of Saint Mark, the symbol of Venice, a reminder of the centuries when Kotor was a Venetian town. You may also notice a date and an inscription commemorating the liberation of the town at the end of the Second World War, on 21 November 1944, a reminder of a much more recent chapter. Inside the gate, look for a relief of the Virgin with Saints Tryphon and Bernard.

Pass through the gate, and you enter the Square of Arms, the largest square in the old town. It takes its name from the weapons once stored and repaired here in the Venetian period. Around it stand buildings that tell the town's history: the Rector's Palace, the old Venetian administrative building; a former arsenal; and, at one end, the Napoleon Theatre, built during the brief period of French rule in the early nineteenth century. Today, the square is lined with cafés, and it is a lively meeting place.

At one corner of the square stands the clock tower, built in the early seventeenth century. Look closely, and you may notice that it leans slightly, possibly as a result of earthquakes. In front of it stands a stone pyramid-shaped pillar, known as the pillar of shame. In the past, people who had committed crimes or offences were tied to it and exposed to public ridicule. It is a small, easily overlooked object with a grim story.

From the Square of Arms, the maze of the old town begins. Narrow lanes lead off in all directions to other squares, churches and palaces. Locals navigate by these squares rather than by street names, and visitors usually get lost. That is part of the pleasure.

What do most visitors miss? The details on the gate. The pillar of shame. And the outer gates and walls along the other sides of the town: the North Gate, near the river Škurda, and the South Gate, whose oldest parts are among the oldest fortifications in the town. Walking around the outside of the walls, along the moat and the river, gives a sense of how carefully the town was defended.

The Square of Arms is busiest in the middle of the day, when cruise passengers arrive. Early in the morning, it is quiet, and the stone is washed and cool. In the evening, the cafés fill with locals and visitors, and the gate and walls are lit.

The Sea Gate is where you arrive in Kotor, and it is easy to see it simply as a doorway. But stop, look up at the lion of Venice, glance at the leaning clock tower and the pillar of shame, and you will begin to read the town's long history before you have taken ten steps.

name: Pompeii: A City Stopped in a Single Day
description: In AD 79, a thriving Roman town was buried by Vesuvius. Walk its streets today, and you can still see the ruts of its carts, its bakeries, its graffiti and its people.
details:
Pompeii lies at the foot of Vesuvius, about twenty-five kilometres south-east of Naples, and it is one of the most famous archaeological sites in the world. In the year 79, the volcano erupted, burying the town under metres of pumice and ash. It lay hidden for centuries until excavations began in the eighteenth century. What has been uncovered since is an entire Roman town, frozen at the moment of its destruction.

Pompeii was a prosperous town of perhaps eleven thousand people, according to many estimates, with a forum, temples, theatres, baths, an amphitheatre, shops, bars, bakeries and houses ranging from small rooms to grand villas. It had already been damaged by an earthquake in AD 62, and some buildings were still being repaired when the eruption came.

The scale of the site surprises many visitors. It covers a large area, and it is impossible to see everything in a single visit. It is best to choose a route, ideally with a guide or a good map, and focus on a few key areas: the Forum, the heart of public life; the Stabian Baths; the House of the Faun, one of the largest and grandest houses; the theatres; and the Amphitheatre, the oldest surviving Roman amphitheatre.

Look at the streets. They are paved with large blocks of volcanic stone, and you can still see deep ruts worn by the wheels of carts. At intervals, there are raised stepping stones, which allowed pedestrians to cross without stepping into the street, which was often wet and dirty, while carts passed between them. Look at the walls, too, where you will find graffiti and painted signs: election slogans, advertisements, notices and personal messages, scrawled by the people who lived here.

Then look at the everyday places. There are bakeries with large stone millstones and ovens. There are thermopolia, street-food counters with large jars set into stone counters, where Pompeians bought hot food and drink. There are fountains at street corners and the remains of shops. These are the details that bring the town to life.

And then there are the casts. When archaeologists in the nineteenth century, led by Giuseppe Fiorelli, found hollow spaces in the ash left by the bodies of victims, they poured plaster into them, creating casts that preserve the positions of people at the moment of death. Some of these are displayed at the site, and they are deeply moving.

Excavation and research continue at Pompeii, and new discoveries are still being made. The site has introduced measures to manage visitor numbers, including limits on daily visitors and named tickets, so it is important to book in advance and check the current rules.

Practical matters are important. Pompeii is very exposed to the sun, with very little shade, and in summer it can be extremely hot. Wear comfortable shoes for uneven stone, take water and a hat, and arrive early. Many of the finest frescoes and mosaics found at Pompeii, including the great Alexander Mosaic from the House of the Faun, are in the National Archaeological Museum in Naples.

What do most visitors miss? The quieter streets away from the main routes, where you can walk alone and imagine the town as it was. The graffiti. And the view of Vesuvius from the Forum, looming over the town that it destroyed. Stand there, look at the volcano, and remember that the people of Pompeii did not know it was a volcano at all.

name: The National Archaeological Museum: Pompeii's Treasures Come to Naples
description: Many of the finest mosaics, frescoes and sculptures from Pompeii and Herculaneum are not at the sites but here, in one of the great museums of the world.
details:
The National Archaeological Museum of Naples, known as MANN, stands at the northern edge of the historic centre, in a large building that was once a cavalry barracks and later the seat of the university. It is one of the most important archaeological museums in the world, and yet many visitors to Naples, rushing to Pompeii, never set foot in it. That is a great loss, because this is where many of Pompeii's greatest treasures are.

The museum's collection grew from the Farnese collection, a vast assembly of ancient sculpture inherited by the Bourbon king Charles of Bourbon from his mother, Elisabetta Farnese, and from the finds made at Pompeii, Herculaneum and other sites around Vesuvius from the eighteenth century onward. The Bourbon kings brought them here, and the museum has grown ever since.

On the ground floor are the Farnese sculptures, among the most famous classical statues in existence. The Farnese Hercules shows the hero resting, exhausted, on his club after his labours, his muscles enormous. The Farnese Bull, a colossal group carved from a single block of marble, shows the punishment of Dirce, tied to a raging bull. It is one of the largest sculptural groups to survive from antiquity.

On the mezzanine are the mosaics from Pompeii, and the greatest of them is the Alexander Mosaic, from the House of the Faun. It shows Alexander the Great in battle against the Persian king Darius, made of over a million tiny tiles, and it is one of the most important works of ancient art to survive. Look at the faces, the horses and the sense of movement. Nearby, smaller mosaics show fish, animals and scenes from daily life with astonishing realism.

Upstairs are the frescoes, removed from the walls of Pompeii and Herculaneum, showing gods, heroes, landscapes, still lifes and portraits. There are also displays of everyday objects: cooking pots, tools, glass, jewellery and even food carbonised by the eruption. The model of Pompeii, made in the nineteenth century, gives a sense of the whole town.

The museum also has the Secret Cabinet, a collection of erotic art and objects from Pompeii and Herculaneum, once kept locked away and shown only to a select few. It is open to visitors today, and it gives a frank picture of Roman attitudes to sexuality.

What do most visitors miss? The Villa of the Papyri finds, from Herculaneum, including bronze statues and the carbonised papyrus scrolls found there. The Egyptian collection, one of the most important in Italy. And the building's great hall upstairs, the Salone della Meridiana, with its sundial line on the floor.

Practical matters: the museum is large, and it is best to choose a few sections rather than try to see everything. It is a good place to visit in the heat of the day, after or instead of a hot morning at Pompeii, and it is particularly worthwhile if you have visited the sites and want to see what they contained.

Stand in front of the Alexander Mosaic, and remember that it once lay on the floor of a house in Pompeii, where a wealthy Roman walked across it every day. Then you will understand why this museum is the other half of Pompeii.

name: The Sansevero Chapel: The Veil Made of Stone
description: In a small chapel off a narrow street lies a marble Christ beneath a veil so fine you will swear you can see through it. Its story is wrapped in legend.
details:
The Cappella Sansevero is a small chapel tucked away in a narrow street in the historic centre of Naples, just off Piazza San Domenico Maggiore. From the outside, it is unremarkable, and there is often a queue. Inside, it holds one of the most astonishing sculptures in the world.

The chapel was the funerary chapel of the princes of Sansevero, the di Sangro family. In the eighteenth century, it was transformed by Raimondo di Sangro, the seventh prince of Sansevero, a soldier, inventor, alchemist and Freemason, who filled it with sculpture and symbolism. He was a mysterious and controversial figure in his own time, and legends gathered around him.

At the centre of the chapel lies the Veiled Christ, the Cristo Velato, carved by the Neapolitan sculptor Giuseppe Sanmartino in 1753. It shows the dead Christ lying on a bed, covered entirely by a thin shroud. The shroud is carved from the same block of marble as the body, and it is so fine that you can see the face, the wounds and the body through it. The illusion is extraordinary. Stand at different angles, and the veil seems to cling and drape, as if it were cloth.

A legend grew up that Raimondo di Sangro had used an alchemical process to turn a real cloth veil into marble. It is a story that has been told for centuries, but studies of the sculpture have confirmed that it is carved from a single block of marble. The legend is part of the chapel's mystery, but the truth, that a sculptor achieved this with a chisel, is even more remarkable.

Around the Veiled Christ are other masterpieces. Modesty, by Antonio Corradini, shows a woman wrapped in a transparent veil, a memorial to the prince's mother. Disillusion, by Francesco Queirolo, shows a man struggling to free himself from a net, carved in marble with astonishing intricacy, a memorial to the prince's father. Look at the net, carved in stone and almost detached from the figure.

Downstairs, in the chapel's crypt, are the 'anatomical machines', two human skeletons with their circulatory systems reconstructed in fine detail. How they were made has been debated for centuries; they were long associated with legends of the prince's experiments, but research suggests that the blood vessels were reconstructed using materials such as wire and wax. They are strange and unsettling.

Practical matters: the chapel is small and very popular, and it is essential to book tickets in advance. Photography is not allowed inside. Visits are timed, and you will not have long, so look carefully.

What do most visitors miss? The ceiling fresco. The floor, once a labyrinth pattern. And the details of the other sculptures, which many visitors overlook in their rush to see the Veiled Christ.

Stand by the Veiled Christ, look at the face under the shroud and try to remind yourself that it is solid stone. Few works of art play such a convincing trick on the eye, or touch the heart so deeply.

name: The Duomo and San Gennaro: Waiting for the Miracle
area: Naples Cathedral & Chapel of San Gennaro
description: Three times a year, Naples crowds into its cathedral to see whether the dried blood of its patron saint will turn to liquid. The chapel that holds it is one of the most opulent in Italy.
tags: Naples Cathedral & Chapel of San Gennaro
details:
Naples Cathedral, the Duomo, stands on Via del Duomo, at the edge of the historic centre. Its neo-Gothic façade, added in the late nineteenth century, hides a much older building, begun in the late thirteenth century under the Angevin kings. Inside, it holds the heart of Neapolitan faith: the relics of San Gennaro, Saint Januarius, the city's patron.

Gennaro was a bishop of Benevento, martyred in the early fourth century, during the persecution of Diocletian. According to tradition, a woman collected some of his blood after his death. That blood, kept in two glass phials, is now one of the most famous relics in the Catholic world.

Three times a year, on the Saturday before the first Sunday in May, on 19 September, his feast day, and on 16 December, the phials are displayed, and the faithful pray for the dried blood to liquefy. When it does, a white handkerchief is waved and the crowd erupts. A quick liquefaction is taken as a good omen for the city. When it fails to liquefy, Neapolitans take it seriously, as a warning; failures have been linked in popular memory to disasters. The Church has not declared it a miracle officially, and scientists have offered various explanations, but for many Neapolitans, the event is deeply meaningful.

The relics are kept in the Royal Chapel of the Treasure of San Gennaro, on the right side of the nave. It was built in the seventeenth century, paid for by the people of Naples after the city was spared from a plague, and it is one of the most opulent baroque chapels in Italy, with marble, bronze, frescoes by Domenichino and Giovanni Lanfranco, and altarpieces. The treasure itself, displayed in a museum beside the cathedral, includes jewels, a mitre covered with thousands of precious stones and a necklace donated by kings and queens over the centuries. It is often described as one of the richest treasures in the world.

There is more in the cathedral. On the left side, the Basilica of Santa Restituta, an earlier church incorporated into the cathedral, dates back to the early Christian period, and beside it is the baptistery of San Giovanni in Fonte, often described as the oldest baptistery in the West, with fifth-century mosaics in its dome. Beneath the cathedral are excavations revealing Greek and Roman remains.

What do most visitors miss? The baptistery and its mosaics. The excavations. And the meaning of the relic. San Gennaro's image is everywhere in Naples, on street shrines, in shops and homes, and he is invoked against Vesuvius as well as against plague. In the eruption of 1631, according to tradition, his relics were carried towards the lava flow, which halted.

Practical matters: the cathedral is a working church, so dress modestly, keep your voice down and avoid sightseeing during services. On the days of the liquefaction, it is extremely crowded.

Stand in the Chapel of the Treasure, look at the silver bust of the saint, and remember that for centuries, a whole city has looked here for reassurance. In Naples, faith is not a quiet thing. It is a matter of life and death, and of a little phial of blood.

name: The Colosseum: An Arena Built to Entertain an Empire
description: For four centuries, Rome came here to watch men and animals fight and die. Look past the crowds, and the building itself reveals how the spectacle worked.
details:
There is no building more closely associated with Rome than the Colosseum. Its broken oval of travertine arches rises above the traffic at the eastern end of the Forum, and even after nearly two thousand years of earthquakes, fires and stone-robbing, it is overwhelming in scale. Most visitors know it as the place where gladiators fought. Fewer understand how it worked, or what it meant.

Its proper name is the Flavian Amphitheatre. It was begun under the emperor Vespasian, around AD 70, on the site of an artificial lake in the gardens of Nero's vast palace, the Golden House. Building a public arena on land that Nero had taken for himself was a political statement: the new dynasty was giving the city back to its people. The amphitheatre was inaugurated in AD 80 under Vespasian's son Titus, with games said to have lasted one hundred days. The name Colosseum probably came later, from a colossal statue of Nero that stood nearby.

The Colosseum could hold tens of thousands of spectators, with estimates often given as around fifty thousand, and they were seated strictly by rank: the emperor and senators closest to the arena, then other citizens, and women and the poor at the very top. Look at the arches on the outside. They are numbered, and spectators entered by the number on their tokens, so the vast crowd could enter and leave quickly. The building's design is still studied for its efficiency.

Look, too, at the outer wall, with its three levels of arches framed by columns in different styles, Tuscan, Ionic and Corinthian, and a fourth level above. Along the top, there were brackets for poles that supported the velarium, a huge awning that could be stretched over the seating to shade spectators from the sun, operated by sailors.

What happened here? Gladiator fights, wild animal hunts, executions and other spectacles. Exotic animals from across the empire, lions, elephants, bears and many others, were brought to fight and be killed. It was entertainment, propaganda and a display of imperial power, all at once.

The part most visitors miss is underground. Beneath the arena floor lies the hypogeum, a two-level warren of tunnels, cages and chambers where animals, gladiators and equipment were held before the games. Lifts and trapdoors raised them dramatically into the arena. Today, the arena floor is partly missing, so you can look down into the hypogeum, and special tours sometimes allow access to it.

After the end of the games, the Colosseum was damaged by earthquakes, used as a quarry for building stone for other monuments, and occupied by houses, workshops and a fortress. The holes you see all over its walls are where iron clamps holding the stones together were removed for their metal. In the eighteenth century, it was consecrated to the memory of Christian martyrs, though historians debate whether Christians were actually martyred here. On Good Friday, the Pope leads the Way of the Cross at the Colosseum.

Practical matters: entry is by timed ticket, which often sells out in busy periods, so book ahead. The ticket typically also includes the Roman Forum and the Palatine Hill. Expect crowds and security checks.

Stand on the upper level, look down into the arena and the tunnels below, and listen to the noise of the modern city around you. Then imagine fifty thousand Romans roaring as a lion was released from a trapdoor. The Colosseum is a marvel of engineering, and a reminder of how brutal ancient entertainment could be.

name: The Pantheon: Two Thousand Years Under the Same Sky
description: A perfect sphere of space, a hole in the roof open to the sky and the largest unreinforced concrete dome on earth. No ancient building has survived so completely.
details:
Walk into Piazza della Rotonda, in the heart of the historic centre, and you will see a massive portico of granite columns attached to a great round building. Step inside, and you enter what many consider the most perfect interior in the world. The Pantheon is the best-preserved major building of ancient Rome, and it has been in continuous use for nearly nineteen centuries.

The inscription on the portico reads M·AGRIPPA·L·F·COS·TERTIVM·FECIT, meaning 'Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, consul for the third time, built this.' Agrippa, the friend and general of the emperor Augustus, built the first temple on this site in the late first century BC. But that building burned, and the Pantheon you see today was rebuilt by the emperor Hadrian, around AD 125. Hadrian kept Agrippa's inscription, perhaps out of respect, and for centuries this led people to believe the whole building was Augustan.

Its name means 'all the gods', and it was probably a temple dedicated to the gods of Rome, though its exact use is still debated. In 609, it was given by the Byzantine emperor to Pope Boniface IV and consecrated as a church, Santa Maria ad Martyres. That conversion is the main reason it survived so well, while so many other ancient buildings were stripped for their materials.

The interior is astonishing. The dome is a perfect hemisphere, and its height from the floor to the top equals its diameter, about forty-three metres, so the space within would fit a perfect sphere. At the top is the oculus, a round opening about nine metres across, open to the sky. It is the only source of natural light, and as the sun moves, a circle of light travels across the walls and the floor. When it rains, the rain falls through the oculus, and small drainage holes in the floor carry it away.

The dome is made of unreinforced concrete, and it remains the largest of its kind in the world. Its builders made it lighter towards the top, using lighter aggregate in the concrete and coffering, the sunken square panels you see in the ceiling. Look up at them, and notice how they get smaller as they rise, creating a sense of greater height.

The Pantheon is also a place of burials. The painter Raphael is buried here, and his tomb bears an epitaph often translated as saying that while he lived, Nature feared to be outdone, and when he died, she feared to die too. The first two kings of united Italy, Vittorio Emanuele II and Umberto I, are also buried in the Pantheon.

What do most visitors miss? The bronze doors, which are ancient, though much restored. The columns of the portico, each a single block of Egyptian granite. And the floor, which is largely original, with its pattern of circles and squares in coloured marble.

The Pantheon now charges an entry fee, and it is busy for much of the day. Early in the morning is calmer. It is still a church, and Mass is celebrated there on Sundays and religious holidays.

Stand in the centre of the Pantheon, under the oculus, and look up. Above you is the same circle of sky that Romans saw in Hadrian's day. Few experiences connect you so directly with the ancient world.

name: St Peter's Basilica: The Church Built on a Grave
description: It is the largest church in Christendom, crowned by Michelangelo's dome, but its real centre lies deep underground, beneath the high altar.
details:
St Peter's Basilica stands at the western end of the great colonnaded square designed by Gian Lorenzo Bernini in the seventeenth century, whose two curving arms reach out as if to embrace the world. It is one of the largest churches in the world, and the spiritual heart of the Catholic Church. Most visitors are overwhelmed by its size and splendour. Fewer understand why it stands exactly where it does.

According to Christian tradition, Saint Peter, the leader of the apostles, was martyred in Rome in the first century, during the persecution under Nero, and buried in a cemetery on the Vatican Hill. In the fourth century, the emperor Constantine built a great basilica over the site of the tomb. That church stood for more than a thousand years. By the fifteenth century, it was in poor condition, and the popes decided to replace it.

The new basilica took more than a century to build, from 1506 to 1626, and many of the greatest architects of the Renaissance and Baroque worked on it, including Donato Bramante, Raphael, Michelangelo, Carlo Maderno and Bernini. Michelangelo designed the great dome, one of the largest in the world, which was completed after his death. Maderno designed the long nave and the façade.

Inside, the scale is hard to grasp. Look at the cherubs holding the holy water stoups near the entrance; they look small from a distance, but they are huge. On the floor of the nave, markers show the lengths of other great churches around the world, to show how much larger St Peter's is.

Just to the right of the entrance, behind protective glass, is Michelangelo's Pietà, carved when he was in his early twenties. It shows the Virgin Mary holding the dead Christ across her lap, and it is one of the most beautiful sculptures in the world. It is the only work Michelangelo ever signed, on the sash across the Virgin's chest.

At the centre of the basilica, beneath the dome, stands Bernini's great bronze canopy, the baldacchino, supported by four twisting columns, above the papal altar. Below the altar, according to tradition and the results of twentieth-century excavations, lies the tomb of Saint Peter. Beneath the basilica, the Vatican Grottoes hold the tombs of many popes, and deeper still is the necropolis, the ancient cemetery, which can be visited only on special small-group tours booked well in advance.

Look for the bronze statue of Saint Peter, seated, in the nave. Its right foot has been worn smooth by the touch and kisses of pilgrims over centuries.

What do most visitors miss? The climb to the dome. You can take a lift part of the way, then climb a narrow staircase between the inner and outer shells of the dome, to a walkway around the lantern at the top. The view over St Peter's Square, the Vatican Gardens and the whole of Rome is spectacular. It is not suitable for people with claustrophobia or limited mobility.

Practical matters: entry to the basilica itself is free, but security queues can be long. A strict dress code applies: shoulders and knees must be covered. It is a working church, and areas reserved for prayer should be respected.

Stand under the dome, look down at the altar, and remember that this vast building was raised over a grave. Everything here, the dome, the canopy, the colonnade, exists because of a man who, according to tradition, was buried on a hillside here nearly two thousand years ago.

name: The Sistine Chapel: Michelangelo's Ceiling and the Last Judgment
description: At the end of a long walk through the Vatican Museums lies a single room where popes are elected and where Michelangelo painted the creation and the end of the world.
details:
The Sistine Chapel lies at the end of the Vatican Museums, and most visitors reach it after a long walk through galleries of sculpture, tapestries, maps and the rooms painted by Raphael. By the time they arrive, they are tired and crowded, and the room is packed. Guards call for silence, and photography is forbidden. And then they look up.

The chapel was built in the late fifteenth century for Pope Sixtus IV, from whom it takes its name. It is a large, rectangular room, and it is still used for the most important ceremonies of the Catholic Church, including the conclave, the election of a new pope. During a conclave, the cardinals vote here, and the smoke from the burning of their ballots rises from a chimney on the roof: black for no decision, white for a new pope.

The walls were painted first, in the early 1480s, by some of the leading painters of the day, including Botticelli, Perugino, Ghirlandaio and others, with scenes from the lives of Moses and Christ. These are masterpieces in their own right, and most visitors barely notice them.

In 1508, Pope Julius II commissioned Michelangelo to paint the ceiling. Michelangelo considered himself a sculptor, not a painter, and he was reluctant, but he accepted. Working on scaffolding for about four years, until 1512, he painted scenes from the Book of Genesis along the centre of the ceiling, from the separation of light and darkness to the drunkenness of Noah, surrounded by prophets, sibyls and the ancestors of Christ. He did not paint lying on his back, as is often said; he worked standing, craning his neck upward, as he described in a humorous poem.

The most famous scene is the Creation of Adam, in which God reaches out to give life to Adam, their fingers almost touching. Look for it near the middle of the ceiling. Then look at the other scenes, and at the powerful figures of the prophets and sibyls along the sides, which are among the most extraordinary figures in Western art.

More than twenty years later, Michelangelo returned to the chapel to paint the Last Judgment on the wall behind the altar, completed in 1541. It shows Christ at the centre, raising the saved to heaven and casting the damned down to hell, with hundreds of figures twisting and falling. The nudity of the figures caused controversy, and after Michelangelo's death, another artist was commissioned to paint draperies over some of them. Look closely at the flayed skin held by Saint Bartholomew; the face on it is often interpreted as a self-portrait of Michelangelo.

In the 1980s and 1990s, a major restoration removed centuries of candle smoke and grime, revealing the brilliant colours you see today. The brightness surprised many people at the time.

Practical matters: the Vatican Museums are usually closed on Sundays, except for the last Sunday of the month, and tickets should be booked in advance. The museums are long, and it is easy to spend hours reaching the chapel. Dress modestly. Photography is not allowed inside the chapel, and guards enforce silence.

What do most visitors miss? The wall paintings, the floor of inlaid marble, and the sheer pleasure of standing still for a few minutes and looking. Find a spot at the side, lean against the wall, look up and take your time. You are standing in the room where popes are chosen, beneath the work of an artist who did not want to be a painter.

name: Museum of Ancient Greek Technology "Kostas Kotsanas"
description: A small, hands-on museum of working reconstructions of ancient Greek inventions, from Archimedes' devices and an ancient automatic servant to siege engines and the Antikythera mechanism, all handmade in Greece by researcher Kostas Kotsanas. Staff demonstrate how many of the machines work, which makes it a favorite with families and engineers alike. A genuinely surprising find a few minutes from the pier.
mapQuery: Museum of Ancient Greek Technology Kotsanas Katakolon
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in; free entry, donations welcome
Getting there: On the Pyrgos–Katakolon road at the edge of the village, ~5 min walk from the cruise pier.
Hours: Mon–Sat 9:30–15:30; closed Sunday

name: Golden Taste Katakolo
description: A family-run café on the shopping street known for hot loukoumades, Greek honey doughnuts, topped with ice cream, plus coffee and gelato. Friendly owners hand out samples and a few words of Greek.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: On Anthéon street, the main pedestrian lane, ~5 min walk from the pier.

name: TASTES OF ELIS
description: A waterfront taverna serving regional Elis dishes with exceptionally warm hospitality, sometimes ending in dancing.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in — +30 697 048 2707

name: MaMer
description: A harborside café-restaurant with feta dip, gyros and free Wi-Fi.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in — +30 698 319 1403

name: Kavos, Katakolo

details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in — +30 2621 041012

Reservations / tickets: Walk-in

name: Mercouri Estate

details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in; call ahead — +30 2621 041601
Getting there: Korakochori, ~4 km north of the pier; 10 min taxi.
Hours: Mon–Fri 9:00–15:00; Sat 9:00–14:00; closed Sunday

name: Archimedes Museum

details:
Reservations / tickets: Free; donations welcome

name: Museum of the History of the Olympic Games of antiquity

details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in; groups book ahead — +30 697 771 4530
Getting there: Outskirts of Ancient Olympia, walkable from the village.

Reservations / tickets: Book ahead — +30 2624 022739

Reservations / tickets: Book ahead — +30 2624 023021

details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in — +30 2621 069183
Getting there: Latzio, ~20 min from Pyrgos.
Hours: Mon–Fri 9:00–17:00; closed weekends

name: Mother of Lord Skafidia Holy Convent

details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in; modest dress
Getting there: Skafidia, ~8 km north of Katakolon.
Hours: Mon–Sat 8:00–13:00 & 17:00–20:00; Sun 7:00–13:00 & 17:00–20:00

name: Paralia Kourouta

details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: ~15 km north of Katakolon; ~20 min taxi.

description: A beachfront gastro-bar where sunbeds come free with food and drinks.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in — +30 698 006 1612
Getting there: On Kourouta beach.

name: JOJO beach bar kourouta.
description: A relaxed beach bar with day beds and a good playlist.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: Kourouta beach.

name: Acropolis Museum Archaeological Excavation
description: Beneath and beside the Acropolis Museum lies an excavated Athenian neighbourhood of houses, streets and workshops dating from classical through Byzantine times. Most visitors walk over it on the glass floor and never go down; the lower level lets you stroll the ancient lanes themselves and see how ordinary Athenians lived at the foot of the Parthenon.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Included in the Acropolis Museum entry ticket
Getting there: Exit the Acropolis Museum and turn left, following the path down the slope. Metro: Akropoli (Line 2).
Hours: Mon 9:00–17:00; Tue–Sun 9:00–20:00

name: Museum of Popular Art and Tradition Angeliki Hatzimichali
description: The Plaka mansion of Angeliki Hatzimichali, Greece's first folklorist, preserved with her collections of embroidery, costumes, carved furniture and household tools. Few tour groups find it, and the house itself, with its period rooms, is as much the attraction as the exhibits.
mapQuery: Museum of Popular Art and Tradition Angeliki Hatzimichali Athens
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: Angelikis Chatzimichali 6, in the quiet upper lanes of Plaka; 10-minute walk from Syntagma.
Hours: Tue–Fri 11:00–16:00; Sat–Sun 10:00–15:00; closed Mon

name: Maria Callas Museum
description: A beautifully staged museum devoted to La Divina, born to Greek parents and rooted in Athens, where she studied and first sang. Rooms themed on Norma, Tosca and La Traviata, her stage gowns and recordings playing throughout make it a moving hour even for non-opera fans.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in; tickets at the door
Getting there: Mitropoleos 44, between Syntagma and Monastiraki, near the Metropolitan Cathedral.
Hours: Tue–Thu, Sat–Sun 10:00–19:00; Fri 10:00–21:00; closed Mon

name: Philopappos Hill
description: A pine-covered hill directly facing the Acropolis, laid with marble paths designed by architect Dimitris Pikionis and dotted with ruins, including the cave traditionally called the Prison of Socrates. It gives the classic Parthenon view without the crowds of the main sites, and sunset here is superb.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: Main paved entrance opposite the Acropolis on Dionysiou Areopagitou, by the church of Agios Dimitrios Loumbardiaris. Metro: Akropoli or Thiseio.
Hours: Listed as open 24 hours; paths are poorly lit after dark

name: Philopappos Monument
description: The marble funerary monument of Philopappos, a Roman-era prince of Commagene who died in Athens in the early second century AD, crowning the Hill of the Muses. The summit gives one of the widest panoramas in the city, from the Acropolis down to Piraeus and the Saronic Gulf.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: At the top of Philopappos Hill, about 15–20 minutes' uphill walk from the Dionysiou Areopagitou entrance.
Hours: Open access; area is not well lit at night

name: Pnyx Hill
description: The meeting place of the ancient Athenian citizens' assembly, where speakers such as Pericles and Demosthenes addressed the city from the rock-cut speaker's platform, the bema. It is quiet, shaded by olives and pines, and faces the Acropolis head-on, a far calmer alternative to Areopagus.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: Between Philopappos Hill and the Hill of the Nymphs; reached on footpaths from the Philopappos entrance or from Thiseio.

name: Hill of the Nymphs
description: The quietest of the three western hills, crowned by the 19th-century National Observatory of Athens. Views stretch to the Acropolis on one side and to Piraeus and the sea on the other, so you can catch both the sunset and the lit Parthenon from the same spot.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: Walk up from Thiseio, past the Observatory grounds, or along paths from Pnyx Hill.

name: Areopagus Hill
description: The bare marble outcrop below the Acropolis entrance, seat of an ancient council and court and traditionally where the apostle Paul preached to the Athenians. A short climb gives a close-up view of the Acropolis and a sweep over the Agora and the city.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: Just below the Acropolis entrance; climb the metal staircase to the right of the main path. The polished rock is very slippery.
Hours: Open access

name: Sanctuary of Artemis Brauronia (Acropolis)
description: Rock-cut foundations of the Acropolis precinct dedicated to Artemis of Brauron, a sanctuary most visitors walk straight through without noticing. Pause here for its connection to the far older sanctuary at Brauron on the east coast, and for the views over the city.
mapQuery: Sanctuary of Artemis Brauronia Acropolis Athens
details:
Reservations / tickets: Acropolis ticket required; book timed entry on the official Hellenic Heritage site
Getting there: On the Acropolis, just inside and to the right after the Propylaia.
Hours: Follows Acropolis hours

name: Roman Agora
description: The marketplace built under Julius Caesar and Augustus, home to the octagonal Tower of the Winds, a marble horologion with sundials and reliefs of the eight winds. Much quieter than the Ancient Agora and right beside Monastiraki and Plaka.
mapQuery: Roman Forum of Athens Roman Agora Athens
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ticket at entrance or online; included in the combined archaeological ticket
Getting there: Polignotou 3, between Monastiraki and Plaka.
Hours: Daily 8:00–18:30

name: Holy Church of the Holy Apostles of Solakis
description: A small 10th-century Byzantine church standing in the southeast corner of the Ancient Agora, one of the oldest surviving churches in Athens, with fragments of later wall paintings inside. Most visitors rush past it on the way to the Temple of Hephaestus.
mapQuery: Church of the Holy Apostles of Solakis Athens
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ancient Agora ticket required
Getting there: Inside the Ancient Agora archaeological site; enter from the north entrance near Monastiraki.
Hours: Site daily 8:00–17:00; interior opening varies

name: Little Metropolis (Panagia Gorgoepikoos & Agios Eleftherios)
description: A tiny Byzantine church dwarfed by the cathedral beside it, its walls built almost entirely of reused ancient and early medieval marble reliefs, with zodiac signs, crosses and carved animals set into the facade. A fascinating architectural jigsaw that takes ten minutes and costs nothing.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: Plateia Mitropoleos, next to the Metropolitan Cathedral.
Hours: Daily 10:00–17:00

name: Holy Church of Saint Nicholas Rangavas
description: An 11th-century Byzantine church tucked high in Plaka near Anafiotika, associated with the Rangavas family. Its bell is said to have been the first to ring in Athens after liberation from Ottoman rule; it is a peaceful stop on the way up to the whitewashed lanes of Anafiotika.
mapQuery: Church of Saint Nicholas Rangavas Athens
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: Prytaneiou 1 at Epicharmou, upper Plaka.
Hours: Mon, Tue, Thu–Sat 9:00–13:00; Sun 7:30–14:00; closed Wed

name: Holy Church of the Holy Unmercenaries of Kolokynthis
description: A 17th-century church in upper Plaka belonging to the Patriarchate of Jerusalem, with a shaded courtyard and benches that make an easy pause from the heat. At Orthodox Easter it receives the Holy Light flown in from Jerusalem before it is distributed across Athens.
mapQuery: Church of the Holy Unmercenaries Kolokynthis Athens
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: Erechtheos 18, upper Plaka near Anafiotika.
Hours: Daily 6:00–20:00

name: Choragic Monument of Lysicrates
description: An elegant circular monument from the 4th century BC, built by the sponsor Lysicrates to display the bronze tripod won by his chorus in a theatrical contest. It stands on Tripodon Street, an ancient road lined with such monuments, in a small square ringed by cafés.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: Epimenidou 3, in Plaka between Hadrian's Arch and the Acropolis slopes.
Hours: Open access

name: Arch of Hadrian
description: A marble gateway raised in honour of Emperor Hadrian, inscribed on one side as the city of Theseus and on the other as the city of Hadrian. Free to see, it frames the Acropolis through its arch and stands beside the Temple of Olympian Zeus.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: Leof. Vasilissis Amalias 50, a short walk from Syntagma and Akropoli metro.
Hours: Open access

name: Museum of Ancient Greek Technology Kotsanas
description: Working reconstructions of ancient Greek inventions, from the Antikythera Mechanism to automata, water clocks and steam devices, demonstrated by enthusiastic staff. A hands-on counterpoint to marble-heavy museums and excellent with children.
mapQuery: Museum of Ancient Greek Technology Kotsanas Athens
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in; some rooms (musical instruments, armour) charge a supplement
Getting there: Pindarou 6, Kolonaki; about 10 minutes' walk from Syntagma.
Hours: Daily 10:00–18:00

name: Church of the Holy Trinity (Soteira Lykodimou)
description: An 11th-century Byzantine church on Filellinon Street that now serves the Russian Orthodox community of Athens. Visitors can tour the church and the excavated levels beneath it with a guide, a rarely visited glimpse of Athens' layered past right off Syntagma.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Paid entry on site for the underground tour
Getting there: Filellinon Street, 3 minutes' walk from Syntagma Square.
Hours: Mon–Sat 11:00–19:00; closed Sun

name: Stathatos Mansion (Museum of Cycladic Art)
description: An Ernst Ziller–designed neoclassical mansion linked to the Museum of Cycladic Art, used for temporary exhibitions. The building alone, with its period interiors, is reason enough to visit, and it is far quieter than the main galleries.
mapQuery: Stathatos Mansion Museum of Cycladic Art Athens
details:
Reservations / tickets: Museum of Cycladic Art ticket
Getting there: Irodotou 1 at Vasilissis Sofias, Kolonaki; connected to the main museum.
Hours: Mon, Wed, Fri, Sat 10:00–17:00; Thu 10:00–20:00; Sun 11:00–17:00; closed Tue

name: B. & M. Theocharakis Foundation
description: A private art foundation opposite the National Garden showing changing exhibitions of Greek and international art, with occasional evening concerts. Overlooked by most visitors, it has a pleasant café and a well-chosen shop.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in; concerts ticketed
Getting there: Vasilissis Sofias 9 at Merlin 1, beside the National Garden.
Hours: Mon–Wed, Fri–Sun 10:00–18:00; Thu 10:00–20:00

name: Benaki Museum
description: A family mansion holding a sweeping collection of Greek culture from prehistory to the 20th century, with folk costumes, jewellery and reconstructed Macedonian mansion rooms. Far less crowded than the big archaeological museums; the rooftop café looks out to the National Garden.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: Koumpari 1 at Vasilissis Sofias, Kolonaki.
Hours: Mon, Wed, Fri, Sat 10:00–18:00; Thu 10:00–00:00; Sun 10:00–16:00; closed Tue

name: Byzantine & Christian Museum
description: A spacious, cool museum in the 19th-century villa of the Duchess of Plaisance, tracing art from the late Roman world through Byzantium. Icons, mosaics, frescoes and textiles fill underground galleries, and the garden café is a hidden oasis.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: Vasilissis Sofias 22; Metro Evangelismos (Line 3).
Hours: Mon, Wed–Sun 8:30–15:30; closed Tue

name: Numismatic Museum of Athens
description: Housed in Iliou Melathron, the opulent 1881 mansion Ernst Ziller designed for Heinrich Schliemann, the excavator of Troy and Mycenae. Painted ceilings and mosaic floors are as compelling as the coin collection, and the garden café is a quiet retreat.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: Panepistimiou 12, 5 minutes from Syntagma.
Hours: Mon, Wed–Sun 8:30–15:30; closed Tue

name: Zappeion Garden
description: Formal gardens around the neoclassical Zappeion Hall, built for the first modern Olympic movement and still used for national events. Shady paths link the National Garden to the Panathenaic Stadium, with a café under the trees.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: Leof. Vasilissis Olgas 1, south of the National Garden.
Hours: Mon–Fri 7:00–19:00; Sat–Sun 7:00–21:00

name: National Garden
description: Queen Amalia's 19th-century royal garden behind Parliament, a shady maze of paths, ponds with turtles, ancient fragments and exotic trees. Locals use it to escape the heat; it adjoins the Presidential Mansion, where the Evzones guard can sometimes be seen.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: Entrances on Amalias Avenue beside Parliament and on Vasilissis Sofias.
Hours: Generally open sunrise to sunset; gates are locked at night

name: Lycabettus Hill
description: The highest hill in central Athens, crowned by the chapel of Agios Georgios, with a 360-degree view from the Acropolis to the sea. The summit is crowded at sunset; locals' secret is to stop partway up at the terrace café for the view without the crush.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free; funicular ticket required if riding
Getting there: Walk up from Kolonaki (about 20–30 minutes, steep), or take the funicular from Aristippou Street.
Hours: Hill open access; funicular runs daily from morning to late night

name: First Cemetery of Athens
description: The city's grand 19th-century cemetery, an open-air gallery of neoclassical sculpture including the celebrated Sleeping Maiden by Giannoulis Chalepas. Heinrich Schliemann rests here in a temple-like mausoleum; please visit quietly, as it remains a working cemetery.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: Logginou 3, Mets, a 10-minute walk beyond the Panathenaic Stadium.
Hours: Daily 7:30–20:00

name: Archaeological Museum of Piraeus
description: A compact museum holding some of the finest original Greek bronzes anywhere, including the Piraeus Apollo, Athena and Artemis, found by chance during roadworks in 1959. Ideal for cruise passengers: close to the port and rarely busy.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in; reviewers report cash only
Getting there: Char. Trikoupi 31, Piraeus; 15–20 minutes' walk or short taxi from the cruise terminals.
Hours: Mon, Wed–Sun 9:00–17:00; closed Tue

name: Mikrolimano
description: A small horseshoe harbour of fishing boats and yachts below Kastella, ringed with seafood tavernas that come alive at sunset. It feels like an island waterfront minutes from the cruise port.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in; book dinner tables at weekends
Getting there: Akti Dilaveri, Piraeus; 10-minute taxi from the cruise terminals, or Metro Line 1 to Neo Faliro and a 10-minute walk.
Hours: Waterfront open access; restaurants mostly lunch to late

name: Palio Limani
description: A small, owner-run restaurant a few minutes from the main Mikrolimano strip, praised for seafood and slow-cooked dishes prepared in-house. A more personal alternative to the bigger harbourside tavernas.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Recommended for dinner; call +30 21 0412 7762
Getting there: Akti Dilaveri 1, Mikrolimano, Piraeus.

name: NEST Rooftop – Monte Kastella
description: A hotel rooftop on the slope of Kastella with a sweeping view over Mikrolimano and the Saronic Gulf. Good for a coffee in the morning or a drink at sunset, and far less known than the waterfront bars below.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in; reserve for sunset
Getting there: Leof. Al. Papanastasiou 109, Kastella, Piraeus.
Hours: Daily 7:30–23:00

name: Holy Church of the Prophet Elias, Kastella
description: A whitewashed church on the summit of Kastella hill, the highest point in Piraeus, reached by stepped lanes through an old neighbourhood. The view over the harbours and out to Salamis and Aegina rewards the climb.
mapQuery: Holy Church of the Prophet Elias Kastella Piraeus
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: Idis Street, Kastella; steep stepped walk up from Mikrolimano.

name: Votsalakia Beach
description: A small pebble city beach on the Kastella shore with sunbeds, showers and table service at modest prices. A real Piraeus locals' swim, near the cruise port.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in; sunbeds charged
Getting there: On the coastal road below Kastella, between Mikrolimano and Zea marina.

name: Battleship Georgios Averof
description: An armoured cruiser built in Italy and acquired by Greece in 1911, flagship in the Balkan Wars and now a floating museum. Walk its decks, engine spaces and officers' quarters; the reconstructed trireme Olympias is moored nearby.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in; tickets at the gangway
Getting there: Trocadero Marina, Flisvos, Palaio Faliro; 15-minute taxi from Piraeus.
Hours: Tue–Fri 9:00–14:00; Sat–Sun 10:00–17:00; closed Mon

name: Stavros Niarchos Park
description: A Renzo Piano–designed park and cultural centre with the National Opera and National Library, a long canal and dancing fountains. Climb to the glass Lighthouse terrace for views over Athens and the sea.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free; performances ticketed
Getting there: Leof. Andrea Siggrou 364, Kallithea; free shuttles run from Syntagma; 15 minutes by taxi from Piraeus.
Hours: Daily 6:00–24:00

name: Vouliagmeni Lake
description: A brackish thermal lake beneath a limestone cliff, fed by underground springs and holding a mild temperature year-round. Tiny fish nibble at your feet, and the deck, sunbeds and restaurant make it a gentle half-day.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Paid entry at the gate; weekends busier
Getting there: Leof. Poseidonos, Vouliagmeni; about 45 minutes from central Athens or Piraeus by taxi.
Hours: Daily 8:30–18:00

name: Limanakia Coves
description: A string of rocky coves below the coast road past Vouliagmeni, with deep clear water and low cliffs for jumping. There is no sand, no shade and a steep scramble down; the coves are adults-oriented and partly nudist.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: Stops 'A' and 'B' Limanakia on the coast road south of Vouliagmeni; bus from Elliniko metro.

name: Olive Bar Restaurant
description: A hotel rooftop restaurant in Glyfada serving modern takes on Greek dishes, with sea views over the rooftops and warm, attentive service. A refined evening away from the busy centre.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Recommended; call +30 21 4410 3462
Getting there: Pandoras 3, Glyfada.
Hours: Sun–Thu 7:00–24:00; Fri–Sat 7:00–1:00

name: Temple of Poseidon, Sounion
description: The 5th-century BC marble temple on a cliff at the southern tip of Attica, where Lord Byron carved his name into a column. Sunset here, framed by the columns over the Aegean, is unforgettable.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Ticket at the site entrance
Getting there: About 70 km from Athens, 1.5–2 hours via the coastal road; plan as a half-day by tour or taxi.
Hours: Varies by season; usually stays open until sunset

name: Temple of Athena Sounias
description: The scant remains of a temple to Athena on a low rise below the Poseidon temple, skipped by nearly every tour. It is free, peaceful and gives you the context of the whole sanctuary of Sounion.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: A short walk from the Temple of Poseidon car park.
Hours: Daily 9:00–18:45

name: Ancient Theatre of Thorikos
description: One of the oldest surviving theatres in Greece, with an unusual oval seating plan, built for a mining community near ancient Laurion. It is free, usually empty, and atmospheric at sunset.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: Just north of Lavrio; park at the small gate and walk the short path up.
Hours: Open access

name: Mineralogical Museum of Lavrion
description: A small volunteer-run museum of minerals from the Lavrion silver mines, which funded Athens' classical fleet. Limited hours, but the collection is stunning.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: Andrea Kordela 6, Lavrio.
Hours: Wed, Sat, Sun 10:00–12:00

name: Legrena Beach
description: A long, unorganised sandy beach near Sounion, protected from development and rarely crowded. Bring your own shade and water, and combine with a sunset at the Temple of Poseidon.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: Off the coastal road a few km before Sounion; parking along the road.

name: Holy Monastery of Daphni
description: A UNESCO-listed 11th-century monastery renowned for its mosaics, above all the stern Christ Pantocrator in the dome. Few visitors find it, though it lies just outside the city.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: Iera Odos, Chaidari; about 25 minutes by taxi from central Athens.
Hours: Mon, Wed–Sun 8:30–17:00; closed Tue

name: Kaisariani Monastery
description: A Byzantine monastery set in pine and cypress woods on the slopes of Mount Hymettus, with frescoed church and old monastic buildings. Quiet trails lead further up the mountain.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: On Hymettus above Kaisariani; 20 minutes by taxi from the centre.
Hours: Mon, Wed–Sun 8:30–15:00; closed Tue

name: Archaeological Site of Brauron
description: The sanctuary of Artemis in a marshy valley near the east coast, where young Athenian girls once served the goddess. Its stoa and small museum are rarely visited and close to the airport, ideal before a flight.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Separate tickets for site and museum
Getting there: Vravrona; about 45 minutes from Athens, 10 minutes from the airport.
Hours: Mon, Wed–Sun 8:30–15:30; closed Tue

name: Archaeological Museum of Marathon
description: A small museum near the battlefield of Marathon, beside the burial mound of the Plataeans who fought alongside Athens in 490 BC. It also holds unexpected Egyptian-style statues from a Roman-era sanctuary.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in
Getting there: Vranas, Marathon; about an hour from Athens.
Hours: Mon, Wed–Sun 8:30–15:30; closed Tue

name: Eleusis Archaeological Site
description: The sanctuary of Demeter and Persephone, site of the secret Eleusinian Mysteries for more than a thousand years. Little shade but very few people.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Single ticket covers site and museum
Getting there: Elefsina; about 30–40 minutes from Athens.
Hours: Mon, Wed–Sun 8:00–19:00; closed Tue

name: Archaeological Museum of Eleusis
description: The museum within the Eleusis site, explaining the Mysteries through sculpture and votive offerings. Visit it first to make sense of the ruins outside.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Included in Eleusis site ticket
Getting there: Inside the Eleusis archaeological site.
Hours: Mon, Wed–Sun 8:30–15:15; closed Tue

name: Amphiareion of Oropos
description: A healing sanctuary in a wooded ravine where pilgrims slept to receive cures in dreams. Theatre, stoa and baths sit amid pines, and the site is rarely visited.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Small entry fee; cash only per reviews
Getting there: Near Kalamos, northern Attica; about 1 hour from Athens.
Hours: Daily 8:30–15:30

name: Etz Hayyim Synagogue
description: Crete's only surviving synagogue, tucked into a quiet courtyard in the old Jewish quarter of Evraiki. Restored and reopened in 1999 after the island's Jewish community was destroyed in 1944, it is now a place of memory, study and welcome. The small courtyard garden and caring staff make it one of the old town's most moving stops.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Walk-in; donation welcome
Getting there: Parodos Kondylaki, a 2-minute walk from the Venetian harbour. From the cruise port at Souda: about 15 minutes by taxi or bus to Chania town.
Hours: Mon–Thu 10:00–16:00, Fri 10:00–15:00; closed Sat–Sun

name: Souda Bay Commonwealth War Cemetery
description: A beautifully kept cemetery on the shore of Souda Bay holding about 1,500 Commonwealth servicemen, many killed in the 1941 Battle of Crete, with hundreds of headstones for soldiers whose names are unknown. It is a deeply peaceful, moving place right beside the cruise port.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: Souda, about 5 minutes by taxi from the cruise terminal; large free parking area and beach access.
Hours: Open access

name: Seitan Limania
description: A tiny, dramatic cove at the end of a narrow cliff-walled inlet on the Akrotiri peninsula, with brilliant turquoise water and rocks for jumping. Getting there is an adventure: a steep hairpin road, then a rocky scramble down. There are no facilities on the beach.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: About 20–25 minutes by car from Souda port. Small car park at the top fills early (on-road parking further up). The rocky path down takes 10–15 minutes and is steep; wear proper shoes, and the left-hand path is reported to be easier on the way down.
Hours: Open access; arrive by 9:00 in summer

name: Katholiko Monastery & Bay
description: The haunting ruins of one of Crete's oldest monasteries, built into a wild gorge on the Akrotiri cape. A stone stairway leads down past the cave of St John the Hermit to a stone bridge and a tiny fjord-like bay. It feels far from everything, though it is only half an hour from the port.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free; modest dress; this is monastery land, so swimming is discouraged by posted rules
Getting there: Park free at Gouverneto Monastery (about 30 minutes from Souda), then hike about 40 minutes downhill on a stepped path to the ruins and bay. The return is steep and uphill (about 260 m of climb) with little shade, so go early or late and carry water.
Hours: Access roughly 9:00–21:00

name: Gouverneto Monastery
description: A fortified 16th-century Venetian-era monastery still home to a small community of monks, set in a lonely landscape on the tip of Akrotiri. It is quiet and spiritual, the monks make skin-care products sold in a little shop, and it marks the start of the Katholiko trail.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Small donation (about €2.50); modest dress (shoulders and knees covered)
Getting there: About 30 minutes by car from Souda; large free car park.
Hours: Mon, Tue, Thu 9:00–12:00 & 17:00–19:00; Sat–Sun 5:00–12:00 & 17:00–20:00; closed Wednesday and Friday

name: Holy Trinity Tzagarolon Monastery (Agia Triada)
description: A golden-stone 17th-century monastery built by Venetian-Cretan brothers, approached along an avenue of cypresses and surrounded by olive groves and vineyards. The monks produce wine, olive oil and honey you can taste and buy, and there is a small museum.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Entry about €3; separate wine cellar tour can be arranged in advance
Getting there: Akrotiri, about 25 minutes by car from Souda; free parking.
Hours: Daily ~7:00–20:00 (Mon from 8:00; weekends from 6:30)

name: Archaeological Site of Aptera
description: The hilltop ruins of a major ancient city-state overlooking Souda Bay, with a restored Roman theatre, vast vaulted Roman cisterns and the remains of a monastery. It sees few crowds and has superb views.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Tickets at the gate (about €10)
Getting there: Near Megala Chorafia, about 15 minutes by car from Souda port; free parking. Allow 1–1.5 hours.
Hours: 8:00–18:30; closed Tuesday

name: Lake Kournas
description: Crete's only natural freshwater lake, cradled by hills, with clear water, terrapins, pedal boats for rent and a few tavernas. It is a gentle, green contrast to the coast and great for families.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Pedal boats about €10 per hour
Getting there: About 40 minutes by car from Souda (near Georgioupoli); free and paid parking.
Hours: Open access

name: Gonia Monastery (Odigitria)
description: A 17th-century seaside monastery at Kolymvari with peaceful courtyards and a fine museum of Byzantine icons and relics. It sits at the start of the wild Rodopou peninsula.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Entry about €4; modest dress
Getting there: Kolymvari, about 40 minutes by car west of Souda port.
Hours: Daily 9:00–19:00

name: Cave of Agia Sofia
area: The Far West: Kissamos, Balos & Falasarna
description: A huge, atmospheric cave high in the Topolia gorge with stalactites and a small chapel inside, used for worship for centuries. Griffon vultures often soar over the gorge outside.
tags: The Far West: Kissamos, Balos & Falasarna
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: Near Topolia, about 1 hour 15 minutes from Souda on the road toward Elafonisi. Park on the roadside (the last stretch is single-lane) and climb about 150 steps. Half-day.
Hours: Daily 8:00–20:00

name: Milia Mountain Retreat
area: The Far West: Kissamos, Balos & Falasarna
description: A restored abandoned stone hamlet deep in the chestnut forests, now an eco-retreat whose restaurant serves outstanding traditional Cretan food from its own produce. Come for lunch, a walk and total silence.
tags: The Far West: Kissamos, Balos & Falasarna
details:
Reservations / tickets: Call ahead for lunch or dinner — +30 694 575 3743
Getting there: Above Vlatos village, about 1 hour 30 minutes from Souda. The final 3–5 km are a steep dirt road; drive slowly (fine for a normal car with care). Half-day.
Hours: Daily from early April to November (weekends only in winter)

name: Botanical Park & Gardens of Crete
description: A sprawling garden of fruit trees, herbs, tropical plants and flowers, planted on hillside land burned by a 2003 forest fire, at the foot of the White Mountains. Peacocks and donkeys roam, and the restaurant cooks with garden produce.
mapQuery: Botanical Park and Gardens of Crete Chania
details:
Reservations / tickets: Tickets at the entrance
Getting there: Fournes road, about 35 minutes by car from Souda; buses also run from Chania. The loop trail descends then climbs gently; a shorter route skips the steepest parts. Allow 1.5–2 hours.
Hours: Daily 9:00–20:30 (closes earlier off-season)

name: Therisos Gorge
description: A dramatic, little-visited gorge with towering walls on a winding road up to Theriso, the historic mountain village where Venizelos launched the 1905 revolt. Goats wander the road, and the village tavernas are known for grilled meats.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
Getting there: About 30 minutes by car from Souda via Perivolia. This is mainly a scenic drive, with few places to pull over; mind goats and sharp bends.
Hours: Open access

name: Imbros Gorge
description: A quieter, shorter alternative to Samaria: about 8 km downhill through a narrow, tree-shaded canyon with a famous pinch point where the walls nearly touch. It ends near the Libyan Sea at Komitades.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Entry about €5 at the kiosk
Getting there: Trailhead at Imbros village, about 1 hour 15 minutes from Souda. The real entrance is at the end of the village (earlier signs are taverna parking). About 8 km and 2.5–3.5 hours downhill over loose stones; taxis shuttle hikers back up from Komitades (about €28 shared). Half-day.
Hours: Open daily in season; start early in summer

name: Aradena Bridge
description: A rickety-looking metal-and-wood bridge spanning the plunging Aradena gorge, about 138 m above the gorge floor, beside an abandoned stone village. It is a bungee-jump site and a spectacular viewpoint reached by an equally spectacular mountain drive.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free; bungee jumping booked separately
Getting there: Above Chora Sfakion via Anopoli, about 2 hours from Souda on very winding roads; cars can drive across. A full-day trip.
Hours: Open access

name: Church of Agios Pavlos & Beach
description: A tiny Byzantine-era stone chapel standing alone on a remote south-coast beach where, tradition says, St Paul landed. It has faded frescoes, cool spring-fed water and one quirky fish taverna, and is reached only on foot or by boat.
mapQuery: Church of Saint Paul Sfakia Chania
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free; arrange boats locally
Getting there: Hike about 1.5–2 hours from Agia Roumeli on the E4 coastal path, or take a small boat from Agia Roumeli or Loutro. A full-day trip from the cruise port and only realistic on an extended stay.
Hours: Open access

name: Glyka Nera (Sweetwater Beach)
description: A long pebble beach beneath cliffs where fresh springs bubble up through the stones, giving it its name, Sweet Water. It has crystal-clear water and no road, and part of the beach is clothing-optional.
details:
Reservations / tickets: Free
